# HERE BEGINS THE PREFACE OF DIOSCORIDES IN THE BOOK ON THE VIRTUES OF HERBS

Many ancient authors wanted <gloss>to write</gloss> about the powers of herbs and the compositions of vegetables, and because very many younger scholars [seek this] with a loving reputation, I too will attempt to prove myself to you in this present work, and [show] how those [others] were able to complete neither the beginning nor the end. But from history—that is, from diverse instruction—I spread out for you and <gloss>also</gloss> diligently show the things [to be sought], both the preparations of individual things and the virtues of pigments <note>original: "pimentorum"; here referring to medicinal substances or spices</note>. For I will diligently show you which things written by the ancients <unclear>ancients</unclear> are to be presented or rejected, or which rejected things [should be reconsidered]. For Iolaus of Bithynia and Heraclides of Tarentum touched upon this kind of teaching lightly, passing over the virtues of herbs; they also left out metallic and aromatic species. Andreas the physician <note>original: "andres medicus"; likely referring to Andreas of Carystus</note> was most prudent regarding herbs, a cutter of the roots of diverse herbs; they were able to collect the powers and virtues of pigments, ordering them better than the ancient authors. Although even they passed over many roots and names of herbs and powers, other writers of this kind seem to have passed over almost everything. I hand over their names into the knowledge of all: that is, Vasilius, Tellius, and Meleratus, and Nigros, and Petronius, and Diodotus. All these were followers of Asclepiades <note>original: "hasclepiadii"; referring to the school of Asclepiades of Bithynia</note> who wanted [to show] the virtues of species by proof, who were able to demonstrate lightly, but rather than handing them down from the outcome of proof, they are held [only] by heat <note>likely a reference to the "Methodist" school of medicine which focused on the state of the body's pores and internal heat</note>. In these matters, they followed necessity for the sake of a word rather than full instruction; of whom one certain [author] wanted Euphorbium <note>a medicinal resin from a succulent</note> to be the juice of the herb *chamaelea* <note>original: "cameleque"; likely Daphne oleoides</note> which grows mostly in Italy. Similarly, he wanted *Androsemen* <note>Tutsan or St. John's Wort</note> to be *hypericum* <unclear>text lost due to hole</unclear>

<summary>This preface introduces Dioscorides' herbal, criticizing previous medical authors for their incompleteness and lack of practical proof while establishing the author's intent to provide a comprehensive guide to medicinal plants and substances.</summary>
<keywords>Dioscorides, herbal medicine, pharmacology, Iolaus of Bithynia, Heraclides of Tarentum, Andreas the Physician, Asclepiades, Euphorbium, botanical virtues</keywords>

<meta>This page serves as the preface to a Latin translation of Dioscorides' De Materia Medica, establishing the author's credentials and the scope of the work.</meta>

Elsewhere he also spoke of the cause, saying it was born in Judea. Other things he wrote were falsehoods; he even erred in the arrangement <note>original: "constituendi"</note>, as is demonstrated by the properties <note>original: "uirtutib;" - referring to the medicinal powers or virtues of plants</note> and in all the varieties of pigments <term>pigments: here referring to raw medicinal ingredients or spices</term>.

We, however, having been free from the desire for wealth from our earliest age, have visited the lands of many regions, especially while leading a military life in Asia. For the sake of this military service, I learned by traveling through all the provinces, and after the terms of my service were completed, being granted leisure by God, I studiously and diligently set this labor upon myself: to show in five books the powers and properties of herbs, and the preparations of oils, so that I might demonstrate in writing those things which were passed over by others, my dearest brother.

For which reason I ask you, when you deign to read these five books, do not attend to my words alone, but to the properties of the pigments or herbs. For these things which I have written down thus far <gloss>which</gloss> I have learned, I did not come to know from opinion or rumor, but I learned them from reading and from experience. For, being not ignorant of the situation of many provinces and observing them, I instruct most clearly according to the climate and genus, and we have written down all things. Their properties are necessary for medicine and for composition, and their powers are invincible when you wish to prepare any medicament. You shall inspect the properties of the pigments, and from some of them you shall make a single preparation; then you will be able to assist the case.

Besides this, it is also fitting to know from which places herbs are to be gathered and in what they should be stored. The opportunity of the proper time must also be sought, so that you do not delay in gathering what is seasonal, lest you pluck them either too dry or immature. For in gathering them, unless you arrive at the right time, they lose the possibility of their powers and virtues. Great...

<summary>In this preface, the author (Dioscorides) defends his empirical methods, citing his extensive travels during military service as the basis for his five-book treatise on the medicinal properties of herbs and oils. He emphasizes the importance of gathering plants at the correct time and climate to ensure their medicinal potency.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on botanical knowledge, following the previous page's introduction to medicinal plants. The catchword "tet." likely refers to the beginning of the next section or a specific plant name.</meta>

For it is a matter of great importance to know the proper time for gathering herbs: whether they should be collected in dry, damp, cold, or warm weather; whether from high and mountainous places, or from valleys and plains; and whether from moist or drier locations. Indeed, herbs that grow in damp plains are stronger, especially if they feel some shade from the sun. For those herbs are to be chosen which do not spring from an old root.

Furthermore, this should not escape your wisdom: that certain regions of the earth bring forth herbs according to the soil, which either cultivation commands to grow, or the nature of the places brings forth at the mature time. For we know many herbs that have both flowers and sweet-smelling leaves in the winter <gloss>1</gloss> <note>The gloss likely refers to a specific seasonal observation or a local climate variation.</note> season. Many also bloom in their second year <gloss>1</gloss> of fertility. Therefore, whoever wishes to have knowledge of this kind must diligently know at what time they are sown and when they bloom, so that he may gather their roots or the herbs themselves, and so he may know their natures—which are potent, or what qualities they possess in their composition—so that he may easily test and recognize them.

I shall also demonstrate the signs of the herbs: which ones have many leaves and which have few. For error has deceived many who are ignorant. Indeed, many writers of these matters, who could not know these things because the truth was hidden from them, have erred, saying that some have neither flowers, nor branches, nor seed—such as *agrostis* <note>original: "agrostis i d e gramen"; likely couch grass or common field grass</note>, that is, grass, or *berbeu* <note>possibly vervain or a similar wild herb</note>, or *pentafillā* <note>original: "pentafillā"; Cinquefoil or Five-Finger Grass</note>. These do not rejoice in flowers at any time.

It is also necessary for the physician to know how long each herb lasts <gloss>1</gloss>. Both hellebores, the white and the black <gloss>1</gloss>, can last for one year. Others, however, last for three years, the names of which I have cast below—especially those which grow in hard or chalky soil. That is: *facados* <note>likely a variant of phakos/lentil or a specific wild legume</note>, *camedrion* <note>Wall Germander</note>, *pilion* <note>possibly Pennyroyal or a related mint</note>, *broton* <note>Southernwood</note>, *senison* <note>Groundsel</note>, *absenciom* <note>Wormwood</note>, *yssopus* <note>Hyssop</note>, and those similar to the ones written above. These herbs ought to be gathered when they are full of seed, and their flowers should be picked before they fall.

Their seeds, however, should not be dried in the same way <gloss>thus</gloss> as the herbs themselves. Furthermore, they should be dried along with their flowers. The "tears" <note>original: "lacrimae"; refers to the resins or saps that exude from the plant</note> of the herbs are to be gathered from the greener plants. The roots and the fleshy parts of the roots, as we have said above, should be taken when the plants are mature. At the time when you wish to dry the skins of those roots, it is necessary for this to be done when they have already begun to shed their leaves at the end of the season <note>original: "tempore ad acto"; literally 'the time having been driven to its end'</note>, especially for one who wishes to collect the roots of herbs. And one ought to place them, clean, in dry places; and if they are not clean—that is, full of earth—they must be washed and then stored. The flowers of the herbs and their seeds should be gathered into small chests or wooden boxes, or kept in papers or in their own leaves, for in this way seeds are accustomed to be preserved. But if you wish to preserve the juices for liquid medicines, they must be stored in glass, silver, or horn vessels. However, if you wish to preserve juices for eye medicines <note>original: "oculorum medicamina"; likely referring to collyria or salves</note> which receive in their preparation liquid pitch, vinegar, or cedar oil <note>original: "cedriam"; resin or oil from the cedar tree used for its preservative and medicinal qualities</note>, make them in vessels of bronze or tin. # HERE BEGIN THE VIRTUES
## OF THE PIGMENTS <note>In this context, "pigments" refers to medicinal ingredients or drugs used by an apothecary.</note>
### PERTAINING TO THIS SYSTEM OF REASONING
### CONCERNING THE ILLYRIAN IRIS

The Illyrian Iris has leaves similar to the *silphium* plant <note>a medicinal plant, possibly extinct, highly prized in antiquity</note> but larger, broader, and thicker. It also has flowers on the upper part of various colors; that is, white or honey-colored or purple or a fine red. It has roots underneath that are knotty and curved, full of a good scent. These roots should be gathered and threaded onto a linen cord, and thus hung up to dry. However, the best Irises are those from Macedonia or Illyria, which are especially knotty, shorter, and reddish in color.

<meta>This page continues a discussion of botanical pharmacology, likely concluding a section on a specific root or resin (possibly Iris or Aristolochia) before beginning a new chapter on Acorus (Sweet Flag).</meta>

Book I.

...and should be chosen for their good scent. It is quite hot to the taste, and when it is pounded, it produces sneezing <note>original: "Sternutamenta"</note>. This variety is also somewhat whiter and more bitter to the taste. These are considered effective even when they have been kept in an old leather skin; they have hollow cavities, and at that time they smell better, though they are inferior in potency. These are of a warm nature and act as a thinning agent <note>original: "leptinacer," a term for substances that thin the humors</note>. They heal wounds and easily draw out splinters <note>original: "sanecer," likely a corruption of "sanies" or "spinis"</note> and purge bile when taken with honey-water <note>original: "mulsā"</note>. **VII.** When administered, they purge: they induce sleep: and when drunk with vinegar, they soothe griping pains of the bowels <note>original: "tormina"</note>. It acts against the poisons of beasts: it heals those suffering from spleen disorders and those afflicted by a cold in the head when given with wine. They provoke menstruation, and a decoction of them is useful as a warm compress for hardness of the womb, which they soften. They treat sciatica when used as an enema <note>original: "clistere"</note>. Also, when pounded and made into medicinal pastes <note>original: "collyria"</note> with honey, they clean out fistulas and abscesses <note>original: "pendigines"</note>, fill them with new flesh, and lead to scarring. These pastes, when made and inserted in the manner of a pessary, draw out the afterbirth in women. They should also be acquired for old hard tumors, applied as a plaster <note>original: "cataplasma"</note> after being cooked. Their powder, too, when placed on wounds with honey—even where bones have been laid bare—fills them up. For a headache, a plaster applied to the head with rose oil and vinegar gives relief. It removes freckles and pimples that <margin>white hellebore</margin> grow on the face when mixed with double the amount of white hellebore <note>original: "ellebore albo"</note>: a plaster made with honey gathers, applies, and purges. They are mixed into saw-like preparations <note>original: "serrarū"</note>, emollient salves, and non-irritating ointments <note>original: "acopis"</note>: and it is powerful in all things that require warming.

### II. CONCERNING ACORUS.

**A**corus <note>Sweet Flag (Acorus calamus)</note> has leaves similar to an iris, but narrow, and the roots are different; they are twisted and not straight, but jointed and knotty. They are whitish underneath, with a pungent bite and a sweet odor. However, the better kind is white and hard, not scorched, but sturdy on the outside.

<summary>This page details the diverse medicinal applications of a warming botanical agent, including its use for wound healing, gynecological issues, and skin conditions, followed by the botanical description of Acorus (Sweet Flag).</summary>
<keywords>pharmacology, herbal medicine, Acorus, wound care, gynecology, sneezing, plasters, ancient remedies</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions from Book I, concluding the entry for Acorus (Sweet Flag) or a related root, and moving into the medicinal properties and physical descriptions of Meum (Spignel) and Cyperus (Galingale).</meta>

...especially the Galatian and Chalcedonian varieties. Here among the Galatians, it is called *aspeion* <note>original: "aspeion," a regional name for Acorus</note>. Its root has a warm potency. <margin>purgative <note>original: "cat.", likely an abbreviation for catharticum (purgative) or cataplasma (poultice)</note></margin> Indeed, the water in which it is boiled is diuretic <note>original: "deuriaca," a substance that promotes urination</note>. It is also effective for pleurisy <note>inflammation of the lungs</note>, chest ailments, and for those suffering from liver conditions, griping of the bowels, or a diseased spleen. It is even more powerful for strangury <note>original: "stranguiriar," a condition where passing urine is painful or difficult</note>.

It is effective against snake bites and is useful as a treatment to promote the menstrual flow in women. Likewise, its roots clear away the dimness of the eyes. It is also mixed into antidotes <note>original: "anadoris," likely a corruption of "antidotis"</note> and softening ointments <note>original: "amacas," likely a corruption of "malagmas"</note>.

### III. ON MEUM ATHAMANTICUM.

Meum, which is called *atamanticu* <note>named after Mount Athamas where it was said to grow</note>, is born in Macedonia and Spain. It is similar to dill in its leaves and branches, rising from the earth to a height of two cubits. Its roots are scattered and tender, some short and others long, with a pleasant smell and a warm taste that bites the tongue. When ground and boiled in water, it is given as a drink; it is effective for kidney pain and for conditions of the bladder, as it provokes urine. It also eases flatulence of the stomach and mitigates the griping of the intestines. It cures "saticas" <note>original: "saticas," likely a scribe's corruption of "hystericis"</note>—that is, it treats pain of the womb. If ground up, it eases rheum <note>a discharge of fluids</note> of the chest. Given as an electuary <note>original: "electarii," a medicinal paste made with honey</note> when pounded with honey, it is beneficial. It also provokes the menstrual flow. A plaster <note>cataplasma</note> placed over the pubic region <note>original: "pectine"</note> relieves strangury in infants; however, if too much of it is used, it stirs up a headache.

### IIII. ON CYPERUS.

Many call Cyperus "cyperon." Others call it "iet palatus" <note>original: "iet palatus," likely a corruption of a Greek synonym such as "erythropetalos"</note>, but this is incorrect. This plant has leaves similar to a leek, but they are longer, tender, and firm, rising from the ground to a height of one and a half cubits. The stalk is angular, similar to a rush, and it produces seed at its head. Beneath the earth, it has roots that are round like black olives; many grow joined together, black in color, with a pleasant smell and taste...

### V. ON CARDAMOM
Cardamom is better when coming from Armenia, Commagene, and the Bosphorus; it also grows in India and Arabia. However, one should choose that which is brittle, full of seeds, and closed, with a sweet smell but a taste that is unpleasant and bitter, because <margin>Warm potency:</margin> this type has the strongest potency of all. Its nature is warm; if it is drunk with water, <margin>For epileptics.</margin> it is beneficial for those suffering from epilepsy; it helps a cough. <margin>For cough and [suffering].</margin> It treats those with sciatica and heals paralytics. It counters snake bites and restores health in cases of griping <term>tormina: severe, twisting abdominal pain or colic</term>; when drunk, it expels "belly animals" <note>intestinal worms</note>. Taken with wine, it helps those with kidney disease <note>original: "nefreaticor."</note> and acts as a diuretic; it healthfully cures the stings of scorpions or any snakes. It is given with the root, or with the bark of the roots; it is given with one laurel bulb, <unclear>namely</unclear> one unit <note>original: ". I .", likely a specific weight measure like a drachma</note>. Ground down when dry and brittle, it breaks up stones; it brings down the menstrual flow through fumigation; ground with vinegar, it heals people with the itch <note>original: "scabiosos", those suffering from scabies or contagious skin irritations</note>. It is also mixed into the preparation of medicinal oils.

### VI. ON NARD
There are two kinds of nard <note>also known as spikenard, a highly valued aromatic herb and perfume</note>: one is Indian and the other is Syrian. It did not receive this name because it is found in Assyria, but because the mountain where it grows has part of its range extending into India, while another part is known in Syria. However, the nard found in that part of the mountain facing Syria is seen <unclear>whence</unclear> it is of an [inferior] sort. ### LIB. I.

[Cardamom] possesses a short and brittle spike in flavor, but in the mouth, it has a sweetness mixed with bitterness if it is held there for a long time. The variety that comes from the region of India is called *gangiar* <note>original: "gangiar", referring to Ganges Spikenard (Nardus Indica)</note>, named either after the river or after the mountain where it grows, or perhaps for its potency. For the weaker plants that grow near water produce a spike that is oblong and very thick; they produce many branches from a single root in a circuit, but they have no strength in their scent. However, on the peak of that same mountain, because it is not troubled by water, a more useful kind grows, spreading its scent widely, similar to *cyperus* <note>original: "qui pero", a corruption of *cyperus* (galingale)</note> and very similar to *propheria* <note>original: "properia", likely a corrupted plant name</note>. Another variety is called *samfiriga* <note>original: "samfiriga", likely a corruption of *sympheriga*</note> among the Syrians, taking its name from the nearby [Mount] Homloa; these have an oblong, whitish spike and the shrub has a greater scent, though not a very sweet one. Merchants soak these in water to break them apart so they might lose an excessively white color and deceive the minds [of buyers]. This may be recognized in this way: because it is either white, or it changes color if soaked. It is found to be more brittle and longer [when faked]. This type is adulterated. For instance, sand is ground up and then it is irrigated and weight is added. Then one recognizes the <margin>Potency of heat.</margin> adulterated plant because it appears heavier and darker. For they even place the mud of the earth upon its roots to confirm the deception, so that it is not believed to have been soaked. But when you see the signs written above, you may know whether it is spoiled or pure. All these have a warm, dry, and diuretic <term>diuretic: a substance that encourages the flow of urine</term> potency. Wherefore they bind a loose <note>original: "diuitum", likely a scribe's error for "fluentem" (flowing/loose)</note> belly, and stay the flow of the womb and <gloss>vomiting</gloss> vomiting. Taken as a drink with cold water, they inhibit nausea. They also resolve gas in the stomach when given as a drink; they [help] those with liver complaints <term>epatias: from the Greek *hepatikos*, referring to liver ailments</term>, those with jaundice <term>hictericos: those suffering from *icterus* or yellowing of the skin</term>, and those with kidney disease <note>original: "neu freatis", a corruption of *nephreticos*</note>. Decoctions in which they have been boiled dissolve hardnesses of the womb through fomentation; the same water takes away itches of the eyes, and even though it is slightly biting, it is used in eye-salves <term>anthidotis: here referring to *antidotos*, medicinal compounds or salves</term>.

### Celtic Spikenard
Now concerning Celtic Nard <note>original: "Celticacuero," a contraction of "Celtica vero" (But concerning the Celtic [variety])</note>. That is, **Celtic Spike** <note>Valeriana celtica, a fragrant alpine plant</note> grows in the Ligurian mountains. While it is not found among the eastern varieties, this variety also grows in Syria. It has short and thick shrubs above the ground; it is gathered in handfuls <note>original: "acitibus," likely a corruption for "handfuls" or "bunches"</note> along with its roots, making **bundles** <note>original: "fasces"</note> that a full hand can hold. For this reason, it is called "Celtic Bundles" by some.

This plant has oblong, broad, and reddish leaves; it possesses a honey-colored flower with a scent concentrated around its root. But because other herbs with a similar scent grow among them and are collected together, when you wish to prepare medicines from them, do not crush them immediately. Instead, you should clean them and spread them out to dry in a damp place. You shall place them upon the aforementioned bundles and sprinkle them, bedewing them from above with water so they may all **"sweat"** <note>A process of light fermentation or softening to help separate the plants</note>. After one day has passed, when you clean them the next day, you will find within those same bundles other leaves and exceedingly long roots resembling the Celtic variety. You must separate these, and from the good leaves themselves, you should crush them. Grind them in wine, shape them into <term>trochisks</term> <note>small medicinal lozenges or discs</note>, and store them in an earthenware vessel that is carefully closed.

The plant should be used when it is fresh. It ought to be sweeter in scent, fuller in its roots, or thicker and brittle. If it possesses these qualities, it will be potent in its virtue. If it is lean, it is a <term>diuretic</term> <note>a substance that promotes the production of urine</note> and is beneficial for those with liver ailments <note>original: "iecorosis"</note>, tumors, and jaundice <note>original: "hictericis," from the Greek "icterus"</note> or the **"royal disease"** <note>original: "morbo regio," an old name for jaundice, so called because it was thought the patient required the costly comforts of a king to recover</note>. For bloating of the stomach, it is taken with water in which **wormwood** <note>original: "auxentio," a corruption of "absinthio"</note> has been boiled. It disperses ailments of the spleen, heals the bladder, and is effective for the kidneys. When given with wine, it is useful for venomous bites. It is utilized in <term>malagmas</term> <note>emollient poultices or plasters used to soften the skin or reduce inflammation</note> and should be mixed into hot applications and ointments.

There is also another variety called **Mountain Celtic**, which is called "sickle-shaped" <note>original: "falcata"</note> or "stony green" <note>original: "petraia uiritis"</note> by many. This grows in the Alps, having a similarity to...

# CONCERNING ASARABACCA
**Asarabacca** <note>original: "Asarum"; *Asarum europaeum*, also known as Wild Ginger</note>, which many call the **wild spike**, has thin leaves similar to ivy. It bears flowers between the leaves near the base of the stalks; these are purple in color and resemble the henbane plant <note>original: "iosquiami," from the Greek *hyoskyamos*</note>. They have seeds similar to <unclear>bubarum</unclear> <note>This may be a corruption of the Greek word for "grapes" or "ox-eye"; historical texts often compare these seeds to grape-stones</note>. It has numerous roots that are knotted and tender, similar to **couch grass** <note>original: "agrostis .i.d.ē. gramen"</note>. It possesses a sweet scent, a warming quality, and a biting taste. It is also a <term>diuretic</term> <note>A substance that promotes the production of urine</note> and is beneficial for those suffering from dropsy <note>edema or swelling caused by excess fluid</note> and sciatica. It also induces menstruation. If five <term>drachmas</term> <note>a unit of weight; the symbol used is $\div$ u.</note> of it are administered with honey-water, it purges the belly just like white hellebore. It is also mixed into various fragrant oils. It grows in shady and mountainous places in Phrygia, Pontus, and Italy.

<margin>Valerian</margin>
# CONCERNING PHU
Many call **Phu** <note>Valeriana officinalis or Garden Valerian</note> the "wild nard." It grows in the region of Pontus; its leaves are similar to hellebore or horse-parsley <note>original: "ipposelino"</note>. They grow from the earth to a height of one cubit or more, having a smooth and soft stem. Beneath the purple, knotted part is a flower similar to the narcissus in its structure, with a color like purple. The roots are the thickness of a little finger, similar to those of black hellebore but reddish in color, with a pleasing scent like nard. Its property is warming. It is also a diuretic, and a <term>decoction</term> <note>original: "helixatura"; a concentrated liquor resulting from heating or boiling the plant</note> of it helps with pain in the side. It stimulates menstruation. The dose is five <term>drachmas</term> <note>original: "d̄ .̄v̄."</note>. It is sometimes adulterated with the roots of **butcher's broom** <note>original: "oxi m̄rsinis" (oxymyrsine)</note>. But you should know how to distinguish between the two: for Phu is more fragile and has a strong scent, whereas the false variety has moisture but no scent.

# VIII. CONCERNING MALABATHRUM, THAT IS, THE LEAF
Many have thought **Malabathrum** <note>Cinnamomum tamala, or Indian Bay Leaf</note> to be Indian nard, but it is actually a leaf, though it is similar in scent. There are many false species that have a similar scent and the appearance of nard.

### CONCERNING CASSIA

**Cassia** <note>A spice similar to cinnamon, derived from the bark of *Cinnamomum cassia*</note> grows in Arabia, where many and various aromatic plants grow. It has thick shavings <note>original: "astu," likely *astulas*</note> along with its bark, and leaves similar to those of pepper. Those to be chosen are the ones that are reddish in color, somewhat ruddy like coral, or oblong and dense and full of tubes <note>original: "fistulis," referring to the "quills" or curled bark typical of the spice</note>. It has a biting taste, with a certain warming quality, full of aromatic scent. One variety, which has a flavor like wine when rubbed <note>original: "uini subtritat saporē"</note>, is called *talliracibus* <note>this may be a corruption of a local trade name</note>; others call it *absalu*. Among the Alexandrian merchants, it is named *Daphnitis* <note>original: "Da flinarabala xandrinis," a corruption of *Daphnitis* (laurel-like) and *Alexandrinis*</note>. There is also another variety, blackish with a full purple color. Though its scent is not at all sweet, it is extremely necessary for medicine. There is a second variety from the middle region <note>original: "medianae"</note>, and a third Cassia which is called *blator* <note>perhaps a corruption of a regional name or *xylo-cassia*</note> with a sweet scent. Although there are many other types of cassia, they are considered branching and of poor quality <note>original: "inrazonabiles," literally unreasonable or substandard</note>. This specific variety is more fragile and shorter, which is why it is named *Cedal* <note>possibly referring to a province or specific port of origin</note> after the name of its province.

BOOK 1.

For **False Cassia** <note>original: "pseudo cassia"</note> is similar to dock <note>likely *Rumex*, a common herb</note> and is easy to identify. These are found to be sweet in taste and flat in shape. It is wide and soft, with divided parts of a whitish and rough color. It is warm, a <term>diuretic</term> <note>a substance that encourages urination</note>, and has drying properties with a slightly biting taste. It is effective against dimness of the eyes and is a necessary ingredient in <term>emollients</term> <note>original: "malagmatibus," soothing or softening medicinal pastes</note>; when ground with honey, it clears spots on the face. It provokes menstruation and, when drunk with water, it counters poisonous stings. Taken as a drink, it calms swelling of the intestines and provides a <term>fomentation</term> <note>a warm, medicated compress</note> for kidney pain. Through fumigation, it is used to treat a prolapsed womb <note>original: "descensum matricis"</note>. In medicinal compounds, it is added at double the weight required for cinnamon. It is truly powerful in all these things.

### XI. CONCERNING CINNAMON

There are many kinds of cinnamon which are named there by their shavings <note>original: "astu," likely referring to the chips or bark strips</note>; many are wild, but the best of all is that which is similar to the Mosyllitic cassia <note>original: "cassiae morsillitae," referring to Mosylon, an ancient port in modern-day Somalia famous for the spice trade</note>. It should be fresh, dark in color, and it dissolves when put in wine; it consists of tender "claws" <note>likely the small, curved ends of the bark</note> and bare, divided pieces, full of fragrance like that of rue <note>a bitter, aromatic herb</note>. 

Indeed, this is the test for cinnamon: if it is similar to cardamom and, when placed in the mouth, its strength is sharp and biting, leaving a taste that is slightly salty with a certain heat. When its shavings are broken, it releases a powder. This quality is also found when the shavings are pulled from the earth and the roots of the same plant follow. This too is a test for cinnamon.

There is another kind of mountain cinnamon, which is rougher to the touch and has less juice. It is thicker and reddish in color. A third kind of cinnamon is similar to the Mosyllitic cassia, tending toward a blackish color, smooth to the touch, and possessing a great scent. There is a fourth kind of cinnamon, white in color and soft to the touch, thicker in its wood, fragile, and with a larger root. There is a fifth kind with a scent similar to cassia, reddish in color, and with a bark similar to cassia.

# Book I. 1.

...and green, soft to the touch, and having a flavor and scent like oregano. The Pontic variety <note>original: "ponticum," referring to the region of Pontus on the Black Sea</note> is reddish to the sight, not long, and fragile. The clusters are full of seeds and have a sharp, oily scent <note>original: "sapaco," likely a corruption of "stactico," referring to a pungent, oil-like fragrance</note>; this kind is to be chosen. It is sharp/oily and provides sleep; it also settles swellings when mixed into <term>cataplasms</term> <note>a medicated paste or poultice spread on cloth and applied to the body</note>. When applied as a poultice, it aids swollen eyes; it is also used to bathe the body to relieve tumors of the internal organs when mixed with raisin wine. As a poultice, it settles the conditions of women <note>likely uterine inflammation or cramps</note> and acts as a medicinal steam. 

This, when drunk hot, is beneficial for those with kidney ailments and liver disease, as well as for those suffering from gout. It is mixed into various perfumes and combined with many wonderful and varied scents. It is adulterated in this way: by the gathering of a herb called *amomis* <note>a wild or lesser variety often used as a filler</note>, which is similar to the flowers of amomum but without the seed. If it has a scent similar to oregano, it should be chosen; however, such a plant has many branches coming from a single root.

**XIII. CONCERNING COSTUS**

Arabic Costus is useful; one should choose that which is white, light, and very fragrant. Second is the Indian variety, which is thicker, somewhat black, and light like a stalk of giant fennel. Third is the "Simatic" <note>original: "simaticum," likely referring to Samyrian or Syrian costus</note>, which is heavier in weight, boxwood-colored, and has a sharp, oily scent. It is effective when it is fresh, white, and full; it should be entirely hard and dry without any holes, and it is found to have a sharp and biting taste. Its virtue is warming and <term>diuretic</term> <note>promoting the production of urine</note>. It provokes menstruation when added to <term>pessaries</term> <note>medications inserted into the vagina</note>; that is, it mitigates pain of the womb. For venomous bites, two drachms are taken; it gives relief when taken with wine and wormwood <note>original: "absintio"</note>.

## XIIII. ABOUT SQUINUS
<margin>Palladius <note>Likely a reference to the Roman writer Palladius, or a specific remedy named after him.</note></margin>
Squinus <term>Squinus</term> <note>also known as Camel Grass or Schuenanth (*Cymbopogon schoenanthus*), a fragrant grass related to lemongrass</note> grows in the regions of Libya, as well as in Arabia, Nabataea, and Babylonia. But the Libyan variety is worthless; the Arabian and Babylonian should be chosen. It is best when reddish and fresh, with its flower-spike separated into parts. These have a rose-like scent; when rubbed in the hands, it releases a pleasant fragrance. 
<margin>yurt <note>This marginal mark, appearing twice on this page, may be a scribal pen trial or a shorthand for "virtus" (property/power).</note></margin>
When chewed in the mouth, it feels biting and warm. Its property is warming and diuretic, and it is astringent <note>original: "sapica," likely a corruption of "stactica"</note>, cleansing, and aids digestion. It provokes menstruation and moves internal gas <note>original: "uentositatē," flatulence</note>, though it may make the head feel heavy. The powder of its flower is beneficial for those who spit blood. It helps with pains of the stomach, lungs, <unclear>actotis</unclear> <note>possibly a corruption of "hepatis" (the liver)</note>, and kidneys. It is mixed into remedies. Its root is astringent, which is why it is given for an upset stomach. A decoction of this helps as a warm compress for pains of the womb. 

## XV. ABOUT CALAMUS AROMATICUS
Calamus aromaticus <term>Calamus aromaticus</term> <note>Sweet Flag (*Acorus calamus*), a wetland plant valued for its scented rhizome</note> grows in India. It is of this kind: reddish in color, with thick joints, and fragile. 
<margin>yurt</margin>
It is full of <gloss>sand</gloss> <note>or "gritty texture"</note> fibers <note>original: "aranea," literally "spiderweb," referring to the internal fibrous structure of the rhizome</note>. Growing a cubit or more in height, it is whitish underneath and is perceived to have an astringent taste. Its property is <gloss>i.e., sticky</gloss> and diuretic. If you mix this with grass seed and celery seed and boil them together, it is given as a drink with warm water. It is a help for those with dropsy <note>edema or swelling</note> and kidney disease, and it acts as a diuretic.

## ABOUT BALSAM
Balsam is a tree similar to Boxthorn <note>original: "Lyciū," a thorny medicinal shrub</note> and is of the same height as Firethorn <note>original: "piracantæ," referring to the Pyracantha shrub</note>. It has leaves similar to rue, which are somewhat white, and its flower does not fall off. It grows only in Judea and Arabia. It is called *humidisse* <note>this term is obscure; it may be a corruption referring to the plant's moisture or a local name</note> in its early, tender age, and it is oblong. This [plant] is useful in all its parts and is very easily dried. XVII

## ABOUT BALSAM JUICE
<gloss>that is, the juice</gloss> That which is called Opobalsam <term>Opobalsamum</term> <note>the highly prized resin or "juice" of the balsam tree</note> is the sap <note>original: "lacrimus," literally "tears"</note>. These "tears" are collected during the Dog Days <note>original: "dieb; canicularib;," the hottest part of summer in July and August</note> by using iron hooks to make incisions in the trees described above. Because it grows in very few places, barely six or seven [measures] are collected per year. Because it is so rare, its price in that place is two pounds of silver for one pound of balsam. One should choose "tears" that are fresh rather than old, possessing a very strong scent that is not sour, and a taste that is sweet yet biting. If it is adulterated, it is usually mixed with turpentine oil, lentisk oil <note>original: "lenascinū," likely *lentiscinum* or mastic oil</note>, or with privet oil <note>original: "orinū"</note>, ben-nut oil <note>original: "balaninū"</note>, galbanum oil <note>original: "metopiū"</note>, honey, myrtle ointment, or liquid henna oil.

<margin>The test for opobalsam.</margin>The test is as follows: let a drop fall onto a wool cloth. When you wash that cloth, it should dry easily without leaving any stain. If it has been adulterated, this result will not occur. 

Item, another test: it curdles goat's milk if a drop is let fall into it. 

Item, another test: if a drop falls into water, it should mix so thoroughly that it cannot be seen; but if it is altered, it spreads over the surface of the water like drops of oil. And if it is kept for an indefinite amount of time, it loses its strength <note>original: "exminatur," possibly meaning the essence vanishes or is weakened</note>. Many people are also mistaken when they say that a drop put in water should vanish or rise to the top and spread out. XVIII

### XX ABOUT BRION

Many have called *Brion* <note>Tree moss or lichen, often specifically *Usnea* or *Parmelia* species.</note> <unclear>aplacion</unclear>. It is found in valleys on the cedar tree, the poplar, or the [strawberry tree]. The best was shown to be from Cnidus; the second is from Lebanon. One should choose that which is white, full of scent, and good; the black kind is found to be useless. The power of the white kind is astringent; its decoction, used as a compress, closes the obstructions of the womb. It is mixed into medicinal preparations and strengthens soothing ointments <term>acopis</term> <note>From the Greek *akopa*, meaning "without fatigue," these were topical salves for muscle pain.</note> and perfumes <note>original: "amiamatib," a corruption of the Greek *thymiamata*, meaning incense or aromatic substances.</note>.

### XXI ABOUT AGALACON

It has a sweet odor and is full of astringency; bitter in the taste, it has a bark similar to leather with varied colors. Its decoction settles the liver <gloss>liver</gloss> <note>original gloss: "fecores," a medieval variant of *iecur*.</note>. Having a scent like frankincense when burned, its shavings <note>original: "zipota," likely referring to chips or wood fragments.</note> restore the stomach from laxity. It eases pain in the side and liver complaints; drunk, it benefits those with dysentery and griping pains <term>torminosis</term>.

## XXII ABOUT CANCAMMUM

<margin>Strength?</margin> <note>original: "yiro?", possibly a scribal abbreviation for *vires* (powers/properties).</note>
Cancamum <note>original: "Cancamū"; a gum resin from an Arabian tree, often identified with *Commiphora kataf* or a similar species.</note> is also a tear [gum] from an Arabian tree similar to myrrh, with a pungent taste. This is mixed especially into swellings; when mixed with myrrh and water-germander <note>original: "scordiam," referring to *Teucrium scordium*.</note>, it makes a heavy-scented incense. Its power is thinning <term>leptuntica</term> <note>From the Greek *leptyntikos*, meaning it has the property of thinning or breaking down humors in the body.</note>; its smoke makes overweight people leaner. It is also drunk in the weight of three obols <note>An ancient unit of weight; three obols is roughly 1.5 to 2 grams.</note> with water or oxymel <note>A medicinal mixture of vinegar and honey.</note>. Similarly, it is beneficial for those with spleen issues and asthma. It is likewise effective for shortness of breath and epilepsy; it provokes the menses. It clears mists from the eyes and heals scars; when boiled in wine, nothing is more effective for the decay of the gums <note>original: "putridine zingibarum," likely referring to the gingiva or gums rather than ginger.</note> and for toothache.

## XXIII ABOUT KYPHI

Kyphi is an aromatic mixture for a gift to the god; the Egyptian priests use it for this purpose. It is also mixed into antidotes and given to asthmatics in a potion. There are various recipes for its preparation, but you should know that the best is the one that takes one ounce of galingale <note>original: "cyperum," likely *Cyperus longus*.</note>, and one of juniper berries <note>original: "arce uadis," a corruption of the Greek *arkeuthos*.</note>, and three pounds of raisins, nine pounds of resin, two pounds of sweet flag <term>calamo aromatico</term>, two pounds of camel grass <note>original: "squinocentur," a corruption of *schoenanthus*.</note>, two pounds of bitumen <note>original: "aspalto".</note>, twelve pounds of "troglodyte" myrrh <note>A high-quality myrrh supposedly from the "Troglodyte" coast of the Red Sea.</note>, eight half-pints of good wine, and three pounds of good honey. You must pound what needs to be pounded, and grind what needs to be ground with the wine, and leave the mass itself to soak for one day; then boil the honey until it is thick and mix it in. Store it in an earthenware vessel.

## XXIV ABOUT SAFFRON

Saffron <note>original: "Crocus".</note> is also powerful for medicinal use. The Corycian kind <note>Saffron from the Corycian cave in Cilicia (modern Turkey) was considered the highest quality in antiquity.</note> is best: it is fresh, strong in color, slightly whitish [at the base of the filament], long, not brittle, and full. Its touch should stain the hands, and it should not have a musty smell. If it does not have these signs, it is old or has been soaked [to extract the dye]. The second best saffron is from Mount Olympus in Lycia...

Corycian saffron is adulterated in this way: it is mixed with saffron dregs <term>magma</term> <note>The residue or dregs left after the primary oil or juice has been pressed out.</note>, litharge <note>original: "spuma argenti"; lead monoxide, often used in ointments.</note>, or lead ore <note>original: "mollibdena".</note>; these are cooked and mixed in to increase the weight. Saffron is digestive, softening <term>malactica</term>, [warming], diuretic, and cooling <note>The text says "refrigeriosa," though saffron was more commonly classified as warming in ancient pharmacology.</note>; when drunk with a sweetener, it aids digestion. It is applied as an ointment for rheum of the eyes, and when applied over them, it restrains the flow.

Mixed with breast milk, it is also applied to conditions of the intestines and the anus as a poultice. It is necessarily applied to the womb and the anus; it stimulates sexual desire. It is applied over the swellings of "sacred fire" <note>original: "ignis sacri"; a term for erysipelas, a painful skin infection, or sometimes shingles.</note> and soothes them. It mitigates ear pain and is even said to be drunk to counteract poisonous humor <note>original: "lim uenenosum"; likely referring to toxic fluids or secretions.</note>, so that it may be more easily expelled. It should be placed in the sun, and when it has dried, it should be removed to the shade and ground with wine added. Or, if there is no sun at the time, you may heat it on a tile. Its root, when drunk, acts as a curative diuretic.

## XXV ABOUT SAFFRON DREGS

Saffron dregs <note>original: "Croco magma".</note> are made from the remains of saffron after the juice has been pressed out, prepared with aromatics, dried in vessels, and formed into lozenges <term>trocisca</term>. Its scent is somewhat like myrrh, heavy and dark; its color is clear of woody bits. When it is dissolved, it is smooth, slightly bitter, and saffron-colored. When applied to the mouth, it stains the teeth and coats the tongue. 

<margin>Strength?</margin>
But that which comes from Syria is stronger in potency and more pungent. These clear the mists of the eyes; it is also a warm diuretic and a digestive <note>original: "pepaca"; from the Greek *peptikos*.</note>, and they possess nearly the same properties [as raw saffron].

## 26. ON ELECAMPANE <note>original: "HELENIO"; the plant Inula helenium, traditionally used for respiratory and digestive issues.</note>

There was [a plant]. Some call Elecampane <term>mulassin</term> <note>Likely a local or corrupted name for the plant; names for herbs often varied wildly between regions.</note>; others call it "Persian" or "Median" <note>Referencing its supposed origins in Persia or Media (modern-day Iran).</note>. In Sicily, they call it <term>nectaria</term>. Others call it <term>uatu</term> or <term>flemum</term>. It has leaves similar to mullein <note>original: "flo mo," likely from the Greek "phlomos" (mullein).</note>, narrow, soft, and oblong. They do not grow high, but the plant spreads out wide over the ground. The root is huge and fragrant, reddish and sticky, with a taste that is not sweet. Its stalk is similar to a lily; it grows in mountainous, shady, and damp places. 

Its root, when dug up and dried, or the water from its decoction <term>elixaturae</term>, provokes urine and brings on menstruation. Its crushed root, when added to honey as an electuary <note>original: "elatarnu"; a medicinal paste or syrup.</note>, soothes a cough and cures orthopnea <note>original: "ortopnicus"; a condition where a person can only breathe comfortably when sitting or standing upright.</note>; it also heals venomous bites. Its nature is warm. Its leaves, when crushed and added to poultices <term>cataplasmatibus</term>, heal sciatica. Many people use these same leaves dried, with salt and sweetener added, for the health of the stomach; they are dried with salt just as capers <note>original: "cappare".</note> usually are. 

Crateuas <note>A famous Greek herbalist and physician to Mithridates VI of Pontus.</note> also asserts that Egypt has another kind of Elecampane. These have stems one cubit <note>An ancient unit of measurement, approximately 18 inches (45 cm).</note> in length, but near the ground it is similar to wild thyme <note>original: "herpili".</note>. The leaves are like <term>dionacula</term> but more numerous and longer around those same stems. The roots are smaller and greener, about the thickness of the little finger; the upper part is thicker, tapering down to a thin point. They grow in dark places near the sea <note>original: "mariamu".</note> and in drier places. In the mountains, the root is drunk to heal [the bites of] venomous creatures. **27.**

# BOOK I

Oil is the base for preparations and is an especially necessary medicine in general. Both fresh and fragrant oil is mixed into these [remedies]. It is also good for the stomach because it tastes best with honey <note>original: "cum mē."; likely an abbreviation for "cum melle" (with honey).</note>. When held in the mouth, it settles the rheum <note>A discharge of fluid or mucus from the mucous membranes.</note> of the gums <note>original: "zingibarum"; likely a phonetic misspelling of "gingivarum" (of the gums).</note> and teeth. It restrains sweat in the sick when used as a thick ointment, and old oil is mixed into heated preparations. 

Furthermore, every oil is warm and <term>emollient</term> <note>original: "malacticū"; a substance that softens or soothes the skin.</note>; it protects the body from the person performing a massage and it softens the bowels. When mixed into preparations, it assists their power and increases their effectiveness. It is also given as a drink against heavy poison to induce vomiting, frequently mixed with the juice of <term>asarum</term> <note>Also known as wild ginger or hazelwort, often used as an emetic or to clear the bowels.</note>. One <term>cotula</term> <note>An ancient Roman unit of volume, approximately equivalent to half a pint or 0.27 liters.</note> [of oil] softens the belly; given as a drink, it is beneficial for griping pains <note>original: "torminib;"; referring to abdominal cramps or colic.</note>. Boiled with rue, it kills intestinal worms. <term>Pergamum oil</term> <note>Oil likely originating from or prepared in the style of Pergamon, a major center for medicine in the ancient world.</note>, when added to an enema, cures <term>ileus</term> <note>original: "hileos"; a painful intestinal obstruction or blockage.</note>. 

Old oil, however, has a warm and <term>diaphoretic</term> <note>Sweat-inducing; used in ancient medicine to expel toxins or balance humors.</note> power. Oil applied as an ointment clears dimness of the eyes. If old oil is not at hand, take whatever [oil] you have and cook it until it is reduced to the thickness of honey. The power of this cooked oil is as follows: 

### Wild Olive Oil <note>original: "oleuo le astrion" / "oleastrino"; oil made from the wild olive tree, Olea europaea sylvestris.</note>

This is made from the wild olive; its power is effective for headache. If rose oil is not available, you may use wild olive oil instead. It stops sweat in the sick and, when applied to falling hair, it helps it grow back. It heals slimy and ulcerous conditions. If someone uses this constantly, they will turn gray slowly. 

Oil is also whitened to a pale color; this is better done with oil that is more than a year old. It should be put in an earthenware vessel with a wide mouth and exposed to the sun at dawn, and it must be frequently stirred. Let it be moved and poured back every day, and let it be whitened so that the frequency of stirring raises a foam. On the eighth day, soak fenugreek in hot water, and when it has softened, add it to the above-mentioned oil and mix it in.

...it reduces the richer fatness <note>original: "petuine pinguiorē"; "petuine" is unclear, but the context describes refining the oil's texture.</note> for eight days, and so it must be moved again. If it is to be whitened: It is placed in an earthenware vessel washed with old wine; under this vessel, a layer of honey-wash is to be spread. 62 [units]. Similarly, <term>echirrhillinica</term> <note>original: "echirrhillinica"; likely a botanical or mineral ingredient used for coloring or stabilizing the mixture.</note> is to be spread in an equal weight, and it should also be brought back into the sun. Let it form eight "edges" <note>original: "acies"; likely referring to layers or surfaces formed during the settling process.</note> until it has been whitened. 

And another composition is made similarly to the one written above: put into a wide-mouthed bronze vessel coated with tin <term>gremial oil</term> <note>original: "oleum gremialem"; likely oil from the first pressing or the highest quality available.</note> similar to that described above, 100 pounds, and 50 pounds of water. Cook it gently, and it must be stirred <note>original: "uagitandū"; likely a transcription error for "agitandum" (to be stirred).</note>; and when it has boiled, it must be removed from the wine <note>original: "uini deponendū"; possibly "removed from the fire" if "uini" is a corruption of "igni".</note>, cooled, and stirred with a ladle. When water is mixed in again and it boils again, the oil should be finished according to that transparency. 28.

### ON THE PREPARATION OF SICYONIAN OIL.

Sicyonian oil <note>Highly prized oil from Sicyon in Greece, often infused with aromatic or medicinal herbs.</note> is prepared thus in the strength of a <term>ceroma</term> <note>original: "streroma"; likely a corruption of "ceroma," an ointment made of oil and wax used by athletes.</note>. Its power is warm; it is effective for fevers and also relaxes contracted nerves. If used for a long time by women on the face, it makes the complexion clear.

### XXVIIII ON THE FILTH COLLECTED IN THE BATHS.

The filth collected in the baths—that is, <term>gloios</term> <note>original: "glio"; the mixture of oil, sweat, and skin cells scraped from the body with a strigil in ancient baths.</note>—possesses a warming power and is <term>emollient</term> <note>original: "malactica"; softening.</note> and <term>diaphoretic</term> <note>original: "diaforetica"; inducing sweat.</note>. It is effective for fevers and for <term>rhagades</term> <note>original: "ragadū"; cracks or fissures in the skin.</note> by anointing. Such power is also found in the dregs of the <term>ceroma</term>; when ash is added, it dissolves <term>condylomata</term> <note>original: "condilomata"; small warty growths or swellings.</note> of the fingers. It is effective for <term>sciatica</term> <note>original: "sciadiarū"; pain originating in the hip or sciatic nerve.</note> if it is applied warm or as a softening plaster. The filth from the walls of the baths or from statues, when heated, resolves hardnesses. It is also beneficial for the wounds of the elderly.

### XXX ON HONEY-OIL

<term>Oleomeli</term> <note>Literally "oil-honey"; a sweet, medicinal sap or balsam found in the East.</note> from Palmyra in Syria comes from a tree that produces an oil with a taste similar to honey. When two to four [measures] are taken, they purge <term>bile</term> <note>original: "colora"; likely a corruption of "cholera," referring to yellow or black bile.</note> from the bowels. They also dissolve [ailments] with warmth, as is the nature of honey-oil.

...and concerning the richness and the preparation of oils. The better kind is the richer and thicker, the virtue <note>The "virtue" or *virtus* refers to the inherent medicinal power or "active ingredient" of the substance.</note> of which is warm; it is beneficial for dimness of the eyes and for pains of the nerves.

## 31. CONCERNING CASTOR OIL <note>original: "Oleo Cycyno"; derived from the Greek *kikinon*, referring to oil from the castor bean plant.</note>.

You shall prepare castor oil by taking the plant called <term>croton</term> <note>The castor oil plant (*Ricinus communis*), so named because its seeds resemble ticks, which are called *croton* in Greek.</note>; take as much of the ripe plant as you wish and dry it in the sun until it sheds its husk. Take what remains clean and crush it in a <term>girba</term> <note>Likely a transcription error for a specific type of mortar or vessel.</note> and put it into a vessel coated with tin with a sufficient amount of water. Cook it until it has released all its potency through the liquid; then, having removed it from the fire, collect the oil that floats on top and set it aside. The Egyptians indeed, who use it the most, prepare it in another way: they take the castor seeds and clean them, and having put them in a mill, they grind them; then, putting them into baskets, they press them by adding weight. But it is better prepared at that time when the castor seeds are ripe, which you will recognize when the clusters themselves fall from the branches. For the aforementioned oil is effective for <term>achores</term> <note>Crusty skin eruptions or ulcers, typically on the head.</note> and for scabs, and for swellings of the <term>hedra</term> <note>From the Greek word for "seat," referring here to the anus or rectum.</note> which the common people call a prolapse <note>original: "recle diacur"; likely a corruption of *procidentia*, referring to a rectal prolapse or hemorrhoids.</note>. It clears dark scars, soothes earaches, or is usefully mixed with various medicines. When drunk, it softens the belly and destroys worms.

## 32. CONCERNING ALMOND OIL

Almond oil, which many call <term>metopium</term> <note>original: "metopium"; while sometimes a distinct galbanum-based unguent, it was often used as a synonym for bitter almond oil in ancient pharmacy.</note>, you shall prepare thus: take one <term>modius</term> <note>A Roman unit of dry measure, roughly 2 gallons or 8.7 liters.</note> of bitter almonds—that is, eighteen Alexandrian <term>sextaria</term> <note>A *sextarius* is roughly equivalent to a pint.</note>—and dry them in the sun. Pound them for a long time until the mass is finely crushed, then pour in one hundred *sextaria* of water and let it sit until it thickens again. And pound it once more and squeeze it through a palm-fiber basket, and collect the oil that comes out. And for a third time, pour the mass into water and stir it, and collect what floats on the surface using feathers <note>Skimming oil with feathers was a common technique for collecting fine layers of oil without disturbing the water below.</note>. This is almond oil. Furthermore, it is effective for pain of the womb <note>original: "matrias"; from the Greek *metra* (womb).</note> when added to a <term>pessary</term> <note>A medicinal plug or suppository inserted into the vagina.</note>, and it is beneficial for hysterical suffocations <note>A historical medical term used to describe a variety of symptoms (anxiety, breathing difficulties) believed to be caused by "wandering" or distressed wombs.</note>. And besides...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of medicinal oils. The previous page concluded the description of Castor oil (Cycyno) and its uses for skin conditions. This page begins with the properties of Iris oil and moves through several other specialized plant-based oils, focusing on their preparation and various healing "virtues."</meta>

Iris oil <note>original: "Iriae"; likely referring to oil made from the iris root (*Iris florentina*).</note> is mixed into all kinds of <term>pessaries</term> <note>Medicated plugs or suppositories inserted into the body, typically used in ancient medicine for gynecological or localized internal treatments.</note>; it suppresses headaches and soothes ear pain, and quiets ringing in the ears. Taken as a drink, it benefits those suffering from kidney conditions <note>original: "neufreticis"; refers to nephritic or renal distress.</note> and acts as a diuretic. It also cures coughs <note>original: "cuculosis"; likely referring to whooping cough or chronic coughing fits.</note> and asthma. Mixed with honey, it removes spots from the face and cleanses the scars of wounds. If you mix lily roots with it and make a mixture with rose oil, it smooths out wrinkles, firms up sagging breasts <note>original: "didas pendentes"; *didas* is a vulgar or corrupt form of the Greek *titthos*, meaning breasts.</note>, and wipes away dimness from the eyes. Mixed with wine, it softens the skin and corrects dandruff.

### XXXIII CONCERNING BEN OIL <note>original: "Balanino"; oil from the *Balanos* or Ben-nut (Moringa), highly prized in antiquity for perfumes and medicine.</note>

Ben oil is prepared in the same way as almond oil. Its virtue <note>The "virtue" or *virtus* refers to the inherent medicinal power or "active ingredient" of the substance.</note> soothes cataracts and removes spots from the skin. Taken by mouth, it clears the stomach and suppresses ringing and pain in the ears—this is especially effective if it is taken mixed with goose fat.

### XXXIIII CONCERNING SESAME OIL

Sesame oil <note>original: "Sesaminum oleum"</note> and walnut oil <note>original: "carinu"; likely *caryinum*, oil made from walnuts.</note> are prepared in the same way as described above. Its virtue is the same as that of Ben oil <note>original: "ualacchino"; a scribe's variation of *balanino*.</note>.

### XXXV CONCERNING HENBANE OIL <note>original: "Hosquiamo"; referring to *Hyoscyamus*, a plant in the nightshade family used as a sedative and analgesic.</note>

Henbane oil is prepared if you collect the white seeds of the henbane plant and dry them; you then crush them and form them into masses. It is made with hot water and fermentation just as the preparation of almond oil is done. Henbane oil is also prepared by drying the seeds in the sun until they have turned a black and rotted color, then pressing the liquid through a strainer and storing it. It settles ear pain and is mixed into "softening" <term>pessaries</term> <note>original: "malupaciis"; likely a corruption of *malacticis*, meaning emollient or softening.</note>.

### XXXVI CONCERNING CNIDIUM OIL <note>original: "Cindino"; oil derived from the berries of the Spurge Flax (*Daphne gnidium*).</note>

The preparation of Cnidium oil is similar. You must take the seeds of the Cnidium berry. Its virtue is for cataracts and it softens the belly. It has a preparation similar to the oil mentioned above <note>original: "anino"; likely a corruption of *balanino*.</note>, and its virtue is similar to the one above but a little stronger.

### XXXVII CONCERNING RADISH OIL

Radish oil <note>original: "Rafaninu"</note> is prepared from radish seeds; one takes clear radish seeds and prepares them likewise.

BOOK 1

The aforementioned preparation <note>original: "fectio superiorib;"; likely "confectio," the end of the entry from the previous page.</note>, the <term>virtue</term> <note>The "virtue" (*virtus*) refers to the inherent medicinal property or active power of the substance.</note> of which is warming, is effective for those who suffer from lice <note>original: "peduclos"; lice infestations were often associated with chronic illness in ancient pathology.</note> due to illness, and it removes roughness from the face. The Egyptians use this most frequently, and they also mix it into other things to be eaten, for as I said above, it is beneficial for those with lice.

### XXXVIII CONCERNING BLACK CUMIN <note>original: "Melantino"; oil made from *Nigella sativa*, often called black cumin or fennel flower.</note>
The preparation of **Black Cumin** is similar. It has the same virtue and is similar to radish oil.

### XXXVIIII CONCERNING MUSTARD
Take **Mustard**, pour it into hot water, and rub it thoroughly. Mix in oil, press it out, and store it; it is effective for various ailments during the winter season.

### XL CONCERNING MYRTLE OIL
**Myrtle oil** is prepared in this way: take the leaves of wild myrtle—that is, the black myrtle—crush them, and press them. Mix these with an equal weight of oil and cook it gently over coals until it is fully blended. Whatever floats on the surface, you shall collect with a feather <note>original: "me pinna colliges"; a common ancient technique for skimming pure oil or essence from a mixture.</note>.

### ALSO AN EASIER PREPARATION
Many take many myrtle leaves and put them in oil and set them in the sun. Some also, who wish to make it with <term>sapa</term> <note>A syrup made by boiling down grape juice or "must" until it reaches a thick consistency.</note>, prepare it thus: they take pomegranate rinds <note>original: "sidia"; from the Greek *sidion*.</note>, cypress seeds, galingale <note>original: "quiperu"; likely *Cyperus*, an aromatic root.</note>, and "rush-flower" <note>original: "quinuenter"; a corruption of the Greek *schoinanthos*, a fragrant marsh grass.</note>, and they mix in myrtle leaves and cook it in a double boiler. One should choose a myrtle oil that is green in color, full of scent, bitter to the taste, and clear. Its virtue is <term>astringent</term> <note>original: "sapaca"; likely a corruption of *styptica*.</note> and drying. It is useful in medicines for scabs, <term>condylomas</term> <note>Wart-like growths or swellings, usually in the genital or anal area.</note>, and it checks immoderate sweats in the sick. It is indeed a thickening and condensing agent.

### XLI CONCERNING LAUREL OIL
**Laurel oil** <note>Oil of the bay laurel (*Laurus nobilis*).</note> is prepared thus: collect ripe laurel berries and follow the same method as for castor oil <note>original: "crotonu"; referring back to the "Cycyno" or castor oil mentioned on the previous page.</note>. Put them in water and collect the oil with a feather. Others, however, prepare it this way: they infuse common oil <note>original: "oleo gremiali"; a term for basic or "crude" olive oil used as a base.</note> with galingale, camel grass <note>original: "squinantus"; an aromatic flowering grass.</note>, and aromatic reeds <note>original: "calamu aromatica"; sweet flag.</note>, and then the leaves. It is necessary for treating rashes <note>original: "exantematibus"; skin eruptions or breakouts.</note> and is beneficial for massages.

## XLII CONCERNING LENTISK OIL <note>original: "Scinino"; oil derived from the *Schinus* or Mastic tree (*Pistacia lentiscus*).</note>

## XLIII CONCERNING TEREBINTH OIL

## XLIIII CONCERNING MASTIC OIL
**Mastic oil** is prepared thus: that is, from **mastic**, the power of which is similar to the resin itself. It is used for cases of <term>sciatica</term> <note>original: "scieri cas"; pain affecting the back, hip, and outer leg.</note>, warming gently. It dissolves "biting" hardness of the stomach and is mixed into <term>cerates</term> <note>original: "cerotis"; wax-based ointments.</note>. It is effective for internal issues and looseness of the bowels. It clears spots from the face and beautifies it. This oil is more useful for marvelous or scented preparations and is mixed in when appropriate. It was necessary to write down this preparation, but because it is similar to <term>marjoram oil</term> <note>original: "amarticiano"; likely a corruption of *amaracinum*.</note> and saffron and <term>parsley oil</term> <note>original: "celino"; likely *selinum*.</note> and many such preparations, [the instructions are brief].

## XLV CONCERNING ROSE OIL
**Rose oil** is prepared thus: you take 5 pounds and 8 ounces <note>original: "lib v . cc viii"; the 'cc' likely refers to a fractional weight measure like ounces or cyathi.</note> of <term>camel's hay</term> <note>original: "squinanti"; *Schoenanthus*, a fragrant grass used as an aromatic base.</note> and 3 pounds and 8 ounces of oil. Also, in another way: take 2 pounds of roses and the [aromatic] seasonings; cook them in water and strain it. Mix the water itself with oil, to which rose honey is added, and rub it thoroughly. With hands anointed in rose honey, let him dip into the oil and stir it by hand.

### XLVI CONCERNING ELATINUM <note>Oil derived from the shoots of the palm tree or fir.</note>

Elatinum is prepared thus: take one palm shoot from a palm tree and, after bruising it, stir it into oil. The oil used should be especially <term>virgin oil</term> <note>original: "gremialerit"; oil from the first pressing of unripe olives.</note>. It must be stirred for three days; on the fourth day, you press it and strain it through a basket. It is also mentioned that the palm wood should be steeped equally with the oil and stored carefully. Its power and use are similar to rose oil, but it softens the belly [more].

### XLVII CONCERNING MELINUM <note>Quince oil.</note>

Melinum is prepared thus: add six and a half <term>sextarii</term> <note>A Roman unit of volume, roughly a pint.</note> of virgin oil and ten <term>hemina</term> <note>original: "ss"; a unit equal to half a sextarius.</note> of water. Once mixed, add four half-measures of bruised palm stalk and <term>lentisk</term> <note>original: "ſiquinu"; likely *schino*, the mastic tree.</note>; after letting it sit for one day, cook it. When it has been thoroughly cooked, pour it back into a wide-mouthed vessel, in which vessel you have made a small grate of reed stalks.

Its power: it is cold and <term>styptic</term> <note>original: "staptica"; an astringent that shrinks tissues and stops bleeding.</note>. It cures mange and all wounds, and heals spider bites. When added for dysentery, it takes away the pain of the stomach <note>original: "stericus"; likely a corruption of *stomachicus* or *hystericus*.</note>. It checks the <term>rheum</term> <note>original: "reuma"; a watery discharge or inflammation.</note> of recent sores on the gums. In sick people, it wipes away sweat. If one drinks it, I believe it helps against <term>blister beetles</term> <note>original: "cantariis"; poisonous beetles sometimes used or accidentally ingested.</note> or <term>buprestis beetles</term> <note>original: "busis"; toxic beetles known to poison cattle.</note>, and it assists with ailments of the head if one drinks it. Moreover, the proof of its quality is that it should have the scent of quinces.

### XLVIII ON WILD VINE OIL
<note>original: "DE OLEO ENANTINO"; oil made from the flowers or clusters of the wild vine.</note>

Wild vine oil is prepared thus: you take the clusters of wild vines and dry them in the shade for two days. After they have rested, put them in <term>unripe olive oil</term> <note>original: "oleo gremiali"; oil pressed from green olives, prized for its astringent qualities.</note>. Let the mixture be shaken, and let the part that rises to the top settle for two days.
<margin>Power</margin>
After they are pressed, store it. Its power is styptic, similar to rose oil, but it should be chosen for use without loosening the belly. It should be of such quality that it possesses the scent of the wild vine flower.

### XLVIIII ON FENUGREEK OIL
<note>original: "DE TILINO . ID EST FINIGRECINO."</note>
<margin>Oil of...</margin>

Fenugreek oil is prepared thus: take 8 pounds of fenugreek, 5 pounds of <term>unripe olive oil</term>, 1 pound of <term>sweet flag</term> <note>original: "calamu aromatico"; an aromatic marsh plant.</note>, and 2 pounds of <term>cyperus</term> <note>original: "quiperu"; likely Cyperus longus, a sweet-smelling root.</note>. All these are crushed and mixed into the oil for seven days. One shall shake it three times a day, and after pressing everything, store it in a vessel.

Indeed, many put in <term>cardamom</term> instead of sweet flag, and they put in <term>xylobalsamum</term> <note>original: "silo balsamu"; the wood of the balsam tree.</note> instead of cyperus. They infuse these and create the scent in the oil first, and then they add the fenugreek to it, throw away the pressed remains, and thus store it.
<margin>Power</margin>
Its power: it is <term>emollient</term> <note>original: "malactica"; softening and soothing.</note> and digestible. It is useful for <term>abscesses</term> <note>original: "apostematibus".</note> and uterine issues, and it dissolves hardness.

### L. ON MARJORAM OIL
<note>original: "DE SÄSUCINO"; from *samsuchum*, a common name for marjoram.</note>

Marjoram oil is prepared thus: you take wild thyme <note>original: "serpilli"</note>, cassia, southernwood <note>original: "abrotono"</note>, water-mint flowers <note>original: "floris sisinbri"</note>, myrtle, and marjoram in equal weights. Pound them all together and pour them into unripe olive oil <note>original: "oleo gremiale"; oil from green olives, used as a medicinal base</note> so that they are all covered, lest they lose their strength. Let them sit for some days, and after this, press it out and throw away the herbs that were inside. Then pour in new spices again—that is, the ones mentioned above—at the same weight, and they shall remain infused for four days. And just as before, throw away the pressed-out remains. One should choose the fresher oil, of a darker color, having the scent of the finest marjoram. Its power is hot and <term>attenuating</term> <note>original: "lepitica", likely a corruption of *leptuntica*; a medicine that thins or breaks down thick bodily fluids</note>. It helps with coughing and constriction of the womb or bladder. It provokes menstruation and expels the <term>afterbirth</term> <note>original: "secunda"</note>. It resolves <term>hysterical suffocations</term> <note>original: "offocationes stericas"; a historical term for a feeling of choking or anxiety once attributed to the womb</note> and suppresses pain in the groin or hips. It is better if mixed with honey. Its power also tempers and removes the fatigue of travel. As an ointment or a poultice <note>original: "catuplasma"</note>, it may be mixed more strongly against <term>opisthotonos</term> <note>original: "opis totonias"; a severe muscle spasm where the head and heels arch backward</note>. Those with cramps should be anointed with it vigorously.

### L. II. ON SOUTHERNWOOD OIL
You shall prepare southernwood oil <note>original: "abrotoninum"</note> thus: take twelve pounds and five measures <note>original: "lib. XII. cc. V."; "cc" likely refers to *cyathi*, a liquid measure roughly equivalent to a small cup</note> of the first-press oil. Infuse southernwood leaves for one day and night; then, throw away the mentioned leaves after they have been squeezed out. If you wish to make it better, add new leaves three or four times.
<margin>Its potency</margin> Its power is warming and aids digestion. It is effective against hysterical suffocation <note>original: "suffocationē stericas"; historically, a condition where the womb was thought to "rise" and cause choking</note> and hard tumors. It regulates the menstrual cycle and expels the afterbirth.

### L. III. ON DILL OIL
You shall prepare dill oil thus: take eleven pounds and eight measures of green olive oil, and eleven pounds and eight measures of dill flowers. Infuse them in the oil for a day and night, and afterward, squeeze them and throw away the herb itself. If you do this twice or three times, it makes a better oil.
<margin>Its potency</margin> Its power is <term>anastomotic</term> <note>opening up the pores or vessels</note>; it affects the womb and is <term>malactic</term> <note>softening or emollient</note>. It is effective for periodic chills, relieves the fatigue of labor, and without any doubt, it assists with joint pain.

### L. IIII. ON LILY OIL, ALSO CALLED SUSINUM
The preparation of lily oil <note>original: "oleũ susinu"</note> is such that many call it "myrrh-scented" <note>original: "murinū"; likely a corruption of *myrrhinum*</note>. Take eight pounds and five measures of oil, five pounds and eleven measures of sweet flag <note>original: "calamo aromatico"</note>, and five measures of myrrh. Mix the crushed ingredients with fragrant wine and put that squeezed mass into the oil and cook it. You should also add three pounds of crushed and infused cardamom, infusing it into the mentioned oil. Then strain it and mix in cleaned lilies. You should store the oil in a wide-mouthed vessel and stir it with a hand coated in honey; then let it rest for a day and night. On the next day, pass it through a strainer <note>original: "liquatorium"</note>, and put what you have strained into another vessel. If the lilies remain in the oil for too many days, they rot and ruin the scent of the oil with their decay. Therefore, if you wish to make a better-scented oil, you must constantly pour it from one vessel into another.

### LV. ON NARCISSUS OIL

Narcissus oil is prepared thus: take 70 pounds and... <note>original: "uncias n."; the number of ounces is unclear</note> of oil, and 70 pounds of asphalt <note>original: "aspaltū"; bitumen or mineral pitch, used in ancient pharmacy</note>. Crush the asphalt and infuse it in water, and boil it just like the other part of the oil mentioned above, until the mentioned water is consumed.

When you have completed all the discipline mentioned, you shall add 3 pounds of oil and 1 [measure] of saffron. You shall mix this thoroughly for five days.

# LVIIII. ON IRIS OIL, PREPARE IT THUS.
<note>original: "DE OLEO HYRINO"; oil made from the roots of the Iris plant</note>
It aids the decay of wounds <gloss>along with</gloss> issues of the womb; it checks the gasping of tumors and uterine suffocation <note>historically called "suffocation of the mother," a condition believed to be caused by a displaced womb</note>. # LVIII. ON GLAUCINE OIL, PREPARE IT THUS.

All these things, crushed and mixed with oil and wine, let him combine and put into a vessel which you cover with a vine leaf. Shake it twice a day for thirty days; afterward, strain it and store it. Many use this instead of an <term>acopum</term> <note>a soothing ointment to relieve weariness or pain</note>.
