# LXI. ON DICROON OIL, WHICH IS PREPARED THUS.

Dicroon oil <note>original: "Oleum dicroū"; a complex compound oil</note> is made as follows: it takes <term>omphacine oil</term> <note>oil made from unripe olives</note>, and cardamom, and camel grass, and aromatic reed, myrrh, balsam fruit, galbanum, and terebinth resin. All these things are mixed with the aforementioned oil, but this one is more fragrant; however, one must choose an oil that is rich and full of scent. It draws out <term>humors</term> <note>bodily fluids that were believed to cause illness if imbalanced</note>, heals wounds, and provides the greatest effect for incisions of the nerves and muscles. It treats <term>hydrocele</term> <note>a fluid-filled swelling in the scrotum</note> and is effectively mixed into mallow and other ointments used for cold ailments, and for <term>opisthotonos</term> <note>severe muscle spasms where the body arches backward</note> and those suffering from convulsions. It induces sweating. It also serves as an <term>anastomatic</term> <note>a medicine that opens up the "mouths" of blood vessels or pores</note> and wonderfully dissolves hard swellings of the womb.

# LXII. ON MENDESIAN OIL.

It takes <term>ben nut oil</term> <note>original: "oleo balanino"; oil from the Moringa tree, prized for not going rancid</note>, myrrh, cassia, and terebinth resin. You shall follow the aforementioned method, for it is similar in its powers to <term>metopion oil</term> <note>an Egyptian oil traditionally made from bitter almonds</note>, but lighter in scent.

### LXIIII. ON CINNAMON OIL

It takes <term>balanum oil</term> <note>original: "oleum balaninum"; oil derived from the seeds of the behen nut tree, prized for not going rancid</note>, <term>wood-balsam</term> <note>original: "xilobalsamu"; the wood or twigs of the balsam tree</note>, <term>aromatic reed</term> <note>original: "calamu aromaticum"</note>, <term>camel grass</term> <note>original: "squinantos"; an aromatic grass used in ancient pharmacy</note>, and for the scent, cinnamon and balsam and the <term>seed of myrrh</term> <note>original: "semen murrae"; likely the first-pressed, liquid resin often called stacte</note>, of which four times as much as the cinnamon must be added. It cures everything. Let it ferment with honey and place that mass into the oil; according to the established method <note>original: "disciplinarum"</note>, one must choose a cinnamon oil with a sweet scent that is not sticky, while being full of the fragrance of myrrh and of a thick consistency and bitter to the taste, yet it should have the thickness of myrrh. It disperses swelling and draws out <term>sanies</term> <note>original: "sanias"; a thin, foul-smelling discharge from a wound or infection</note>; it assists in conditions of the womb <note>original: "matricis"</note> when a double portion of oil is mixed in. When added to two measures of wax and <term>goat marrow</term> <note>original: "medullae hir"</note>, it loses its green color and becomes a honey-like mixture, for on its own its power is [too] sharp. It softens hardness, treats <term>hydroceles</term> <note>original: "hidrocellas"; a swelling caused by fluid accumulation around the testicle</note>, and shows singular effectiveness for foul wounds. When mixed with cardamom, it treats <term>cankers</term> <note>original: "cancris"; spreading sores or ulcers</note>, periodic chills, and tremors, and acts against venomous bites. It may be drunk or used as an ointment; when made into a sharp potion, it helps with <term>jaundice</term> <note>original: "icteris"</note> and the bites of scorpions or snakes.

### LXV. ON NARD OIL

It is prepared in various ways: with the leaf of <term>malabathrum</term> <note>original: "malabatrī"; an aromatic leaf from India, likely a species of cinnamon or bay</note> and without it. It is mixed with balanum oil; take <term>omphacine oil</term> <note>original: "onfaciu"; oil made from unripe olives</note> to which you mix the spices. To the camel grass, for the purpose of purifying <note>original: "aluminandum"; to clear or refine the quality of the oil</note> the oil and for fragrance, one should add <term>costus</term> <note>an aromatic root used in perfumes and medicine</note>, amomum, <term>spikenard</term> <note>original: "spicanardi"</note>, myrrh, and balsam, and let the method be followed. The mixture of these concoctions is also effective when simple—not with a sharp odor but a sweet one—and full of the scent of spikenard or amomum. But if it has not been mixed with resin, this concoction will be liquid rather than thick. It is also prepared simply with omphacine oil, camel grass, aromatic reed, costus, and <term>Indian spikenard</term> <note>original: "spica indica"</note>.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of medicinal aromatic oils and resins from the previous page, which concluded with a recipe for cinnamon oil. ## LXVII. ON MALABATHRUM OIL

<term>Malabathrum oil</term> <note>original: "Oleum malabatrinu"; oil made from the leaves of the Cinnamomum tamala tree, often called Indian Bay Leaf</note> takes the same ingredients which we said were mixed in spikenard [nardo], but it contains more myrrh. For this reason, it is more <term>warming</term> <note>original: "termantacu" / "thermanticum"; a term in ancient medicine for substances that increase bodily heat</note>. It is similar in its virtues to amaranth oil.

## LXVII. ON THE BARK OF FRANKINCENSE

The bark of the <term>frankincense tree</term> <note>original: "Corio libani"; literally the "skin" or bark of the Boswellia tree</note> should be chosen that is thick, fatty, full of scent, fresh, and smooth. It is sometimes adulterated with the bark of the cypress, but if these are placed in a hearth, they give off the smell of [burnt] brick and raise a larger flame, which the true bark cannot do; for the true bark is similar to how frankincense itself burns. It is stronger than <term>frankincense</term> <note>original: "libanoto"</note>. From this, it is uniquely helpful for healing and checking a flow of blood; when burnt and reduced to ash, it calms the itching of the eyes with its stinging sharpness.

## LXVIII. ON STORAX

<term>Storax</term> <note>original: "Storax"; a fragrant resin obtained from the bark of the Styrax officinalis tree</note> should be chosen that is reddish and fatty, similar to resin, containing whitish fragments and full of scent; when softened by moisture, it gives off a substance like honey. It has a natural power for many uses and is fragrant. It works for a cough, checks <term>catarrh</term> <note>original: "catarrhon"; excessive discharge or buildup of mucus</note>, and [soothes] hoarseness of the throat. It clears ringing in the ears and [assists with] ailments and <term>suffocations of the womb</term> <note>original: "pibe & istemat offacationib"; likely a corruption of "vitiis et hystericis suffocationibus," a historical diagnosis for various gynecological distresses</note> and hard tumors. It is either drunk or added to <term>pessaries</term> <note>small medicinal plugs for vaginal or rectal use</note>; it is effective for the menses and commands the belly to be softened and loosened. Mixed with turpentine resin, it is a necessary ingredient in <term>softening poultices</term> <note>original: "malagmatib;" / "malagmata"</note>, <term>sweat-inducing remedies</term> <note>original: "diaforatis" / "diaphoretica"</note>, and <term>pain-relieving salves</term> <note>original: "acopir" / "acopa"</note>. In fumigation, it has a scent similar to frankincense; it is beneficial everywhere just as the "male" [frankincense] is.

## LXVIIII. ON BDELLIUM

That <term>bdellium</term> <note>original: "Bidellū"; a semi-translucent oleo-gum-resin from the Commiphora tree, related to myrrh</note> is stronger which is more bitter to the taste, clear, and similar to the juice of "fat glue," easy to soften, and free of wood or dirt; in fumigation, it is similar to [costly] ointments. The black and "bran-like" kind has the odor of asphalt; it resolves tumors and disperses hard growths. It treats <term>hydroceles</term> <note>original: "hidrocelias"; an accumulation of fluid around the testicle</note> and acts as an <term>opening agent</term> <note>original: "anastomaticae"; medicines used to open up the "mouths" of blood vessels or pores</note>. Dissolved in [the proper liquid], it checks indigestion. It aids the womb by fumigation; when applied as a suppository, it draws out humors and expels stones from the bladder.

These substances were primarily used for their warming effects, their ability to treat respiratory and gynecological issues, and their role in dissolving tumors and stones.</summary>

## LXX. ON FRANKINCENSE

<term>Frankincense</term> <note>original: "Thus"</note> is potent, especially the "male" variety, which is white. When you break it, it is found to be fatty inside, and in fumigation it catches fire more quickly. Mixed with milk, pitch, and vinegar, it heals other wounds of the body, as well as <term>creeping sores</term> <note>original: "ternas"</note> and <term>spider-like ulcers</term> <note>original: "araneas"</note>. Burnt and drunk with <term>wormwood</term> <note>original: "absynzia"</note>, it heals chilblains. With honey, it brings <term>whitlows</term> <note>original: "panaritia"; painful infections of the fingertip</note> to health. It assists with crushing injuries when combined with pitch. Mixed with wine, it treats earaches. For pain in the breasts, it is a singular remedy when mixed with <term>fine flour</term> <note>original: "amolia"; a very fine starch</note> and rose oil. It is mixed into noble and aromatic preparations. Drunk, it is an excellent protection against swelling of the intestines and for those <term>spitting blood</term> <note>original: "emoptoicis"; suffering from haemoptysis</note>. However, if healthy people drink it, they suffer from <term>madness</term> <note>original: "mamā" / "maniam"</note>. For if it is drunk too heavily with wine, it easily kills a person.

## LXXI. ON FRANKINCENSE WOOD AND THE MANNA OF FRANKINCENSE.

The <term>Manna of Frankincense</term> <note>original: "Mannaturis"; the small crumbs or "tears" of resin that fall from the tree</note> should be chosen that is white and clean, containing small fragments. Its power is similar to the frankincense plant but slightly stronger. It soothes swellings of the eyes. This also cleanses and fills eye wounds. In the same way, it clears the face when combined with the smoke of myrrh and <term>storax</term> <note>original: "storias"</note>, because it is similar to them; for they share a single power.

## LXXII. ON THE CYPRESS TREE AND SEEDS.

Its leaves, drunk with a sweetener and a small amount of myrrh, restrain <term>discharges</term> <note>original: "reumatismū"</note> of the bladder and heal <term>difficulty in urinating</term> <note>original: "disurus"; dysuria</note>. Furthermore, its potency, or its <term>cones</term> <note>original: "pila"; the "balls" or fruit of the cypress</note> when drunk, treats those spitting blood and is especially beneficial for dysentery and <term>abdominal pains</term> <note>original: "quiliacas"; celiac or intestinal distress</note>. Its decoction helps with coughing and <term>shortness of breath</term> <note>original: "ortum mas" / "orthopnoea"; the inability to breathe easily except when standing or sitting upright</note>, and it benefits the stomach as much as...

# ON THE GALLIC PINE.

The bark of the pine tree has <term>astringent</term> <note>original: "sapacum"; likely a corruption of the Greek 'styptikon,' a substance that shrinks tissues to stop bleeding</note> properties and heals abrasions when used in poultices. When dried

### LXXIIII ON THE MASTIC TREE.

The seeds, leaves, bark, and twigs of this tree are used together with the root—that is, an <term>astringent decoction</term> <note>original: "sapaca"; likely a corruption of the Greek 'styptikon,' a thickened liquid that shrinks tissues</note> is brewed.
The juice is made from the bark; the leaves and root are cooked with the bark in water for a long time, and when it has cooled, it is strained; the water itself is then cooked for as long as it takes to thicken.
For this astringent substance is a singular protection for those <term>spitting blood</term> <note>original: "emoptoicis"</note>, for dysentery, and for looseness of the bowels.
It binds the flux of the womb, cures <term>uterine conditions</term> <note>original: "causas stericas"</note>, and helps with prolapses. The decoction of its leaves is diuretic, and their juice strengthens loose teeth and is beneficial for similar cases.
Teeth rubbed with its green wood become white. Its resin is called <term>mastic</term> <note>original: "masticem"</note>; it is strained for those with chronic blood-spitting, and it suppresses a cough and is good for the stomach and belching.
It is effectively used in tooth powders; it makes the face bright, binds the hair, keeps away foul odors for a long time, and strengthens the gums.

### LXXV ON THE TURPENTINE TREE.

The leaves, seed, and bark of the Turpentine tree are collected with similar care for their <term>astringent juice</term> <note>original: "sapuco"</note>, just as with the <term>sweet rush</term> <note>original: "squinum"</note>. Its seed is good for a bad stomach; for it is warm and diuretic, it stimulates sexual desire, and when mixed with wine, it treats the bite of a <term>venomous spider</term> <note>original: "spalenzoni"; a corruption of 'phalangium'</note>. Its resin should be chosen thus: white, clear, and having a green tint.

Turpentine resins retain a scent sweeter than all other resins. Secondly, it heals a cough and various ailments when taken as an <term>electuary</term> <note>original: "electuario"; a medicinal paste made with honey or syrup</note> with honey. With honey added, it settles the afflictions of the chest, for it is <term>diuretic</term> <note>original: "diuretica"; promoting the passage of urine</note> and <term>peptic</term> <note>original: "pepeptica"; aiding digestion</note>, and it softens the belly. It binds the hair of the eyes <note>likely referring to treatment for eyelashes or eyelids</note>. With <term>Campanian verdigris</term> <note>original: "erugine campano"; a green pigment/medicine made from weathered copper</note>, burnt copper, and <term>blue vitriol</term> <note>original: "calcanto"; copper sulfate</note> or <term>natron</term> <note>original: "nitro"</note> added, it cleanses the skin of <term>leprosies</term> <note>original: "lepras"; used broadly in this period for various scaly skin diseases</note>. It also wipes away the itching of the genitals when mixed with honey and oil. It is necessarily mixed into <term>emollient poultices</term> <note>original: "malagmatib."</note> and other medications.

Soft resin prevents pain in the side; this is the same as <term>pitch-resin</term> <note>original: "pituina"</note>, <term>peradine</term> <note>unclear technical variety of resin</note>, and <term>colophony</term> <note>original: "colofonia"</note>, which took its name from the place <note>Colophon, an ancient city in Ionia</note>. These are better for a cough when given as an electuary. Resins are not all of one color, for they are either white or have the color of honey. If the resin is liquid, it is from the cypress, while among the other resins, the <term>petrouilina</term> <note>possibly a rock-resin or petroleum-based substance</note>, peradine, pituina, and <term>elatiana</term> <note>fir resin</note> are to be chosen.

Those which are fragrant and clear, and not overly liquid but like <term>cerates</term> <note>original: "ceratis"; waxy ointments</note> and not very brittle, are better than all. Pituina and elatiana are the best, for these are the most fragrant and have a pure scent. Pitch, petrouilina, and cypress resins have the least potency in them, for <term>stisitana</term> <note>possibly a corruption of "schistine"</note> are similar to turpentine. When any resin is to be boiled, you should take one <term>cyathus</term> <note>original: "cyatos"; a Roman measure of about 0.045 liters</note> and two cyathi of rainwater and put them in a bronze vessel over coals. Stir it frequently as long as it regains its scent, and let it not be scorched lest it become too brittle; as it cools, it is found to be more fragile. When it has cooled, it should be stored in an earthen vessel. It also becomes a fine white. Indeed, all resins are liquid; they are boiled without water, placed over coals, lightly at first.

**77. ON LIQUID PITCH**
It is collected from fatty, resinous woods; but the kind from Mount Ida is better. When pure and taken twice, it counteracts poisons. It helps those with coughs and chronic <term>catarrh</term> <note>original: "corsiar," likely "coryzas"; an inflammation of the mucus membranes</note>, and it is of great benefit to those spitting blood and those with asthma. It brings aid to the chest; taken in the manner of a thick <term>electuary</term> <note>a medicinal paste made with honey</note> in the amount of one <term>cyathus</term> <note>approx. 45ml</note>, it dissolves the moisture of the throat. But for the <term>uvula</term> <note>the fleshy part hanging at the back of the throat</note> and for <term>sore throats</term> <note>original: "linanciar," likely "synanchis" or "lynanche"</note>, it is treated when applied with a feather. Mixed with rose oil, it cleanses the <term>scaling</term> <note>original: "samias"</note> of the ears. Applied with ground salt and other ingredients, it helps with venomous bites. It also cleanses <term>skin eruptions</term> <note>original: "zernice"; likely referring to scaly skin conditions like lichen</note> and wounded nails. It heals <term>obstructions of the womb</term> <note>original: "duriciasterica," likely "duritias utericas"</note> and wounds when mixed with barley flour. For a child, when composed as a <term>cataplasm</term> <note>a poultice or medicated plaster</note>, it will heal <term>scrofula</term> <note>original: "scrofas"; a swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck</note> of the throat when mixed with sulfur. Mixed with the skin of a fatty pine or with bran and ground, it leads one back to health. It cleanses dirty wounds; mixed with frankincense powder and wax, it fills the cavities of wounds. Anointed upon them, it heals <term>fissures</term> <note>original: "ragadia," from the Greek "rhagades"</note> of the feet. Mixed with honey and raisins, it aids in healing <term>carbuncles</term> <note>severe, painful clusters of boils</note>. It removes the rot of wounds through these medicines.

### LXXVIII. ON PITCH OIL
Those who prepare pitch oil separate it like water; it floats on the surface during the boiling of the pitch, and they collect it using oily wool. When softened, it cleanses <term>alopecia</term> <note>patchy hair loss</note>. It is necessarily mixed into <term>poultices</term> <note>original: "cataplasmatib;"</note> with barley meal. It removes mange and treats the wounds of animals. The smoke of liquid pitch should also be collected, but the middle of the lid must be pierced for the collection; it is not the same as that which possesses the primary strength. It is sticky and fibrous. This <term>soot</term> <note>original: "stapum"; refers to the medicinal carbon residue collected from the smoke</note> is very beneficial for the eyes; it causes the eyelashes to grow and treats wounds of the eyes.

### LXXVIIII. ON HARD PITCH
Hard pitch is better if it is clear, fattier, has a good odor, and is of a reddish color similar to resin. Such are the <term>Lycian and Bruttian</term> <note>original: "licia et bricia"; referring to famous regions of production in Lycia and Southern Italy</note> varieties, whose nature is similar to resin. It heals wounds, treats [sore] nipples, and fills deep wounds. It is effectively applied in medicines; for they also speak of another pitch which is mixed with resin, which physicians call <term>apozema</term> <note>original: "apoma"; a decoction or medicinal infusion</note>. It is [used] for... <note>text becomes fragmented</note>... For others call the Holm-oak resin by this name.

### LXXXII. ON JUNIPER

Regarding Juniper, which many call <term>arceuthos</term> <note>original: "arceuadem"; from the Greek arkeuthos</note>: its smoke drives away serpents. If the seed is held in the mouth, it makes the breath fragrant. It strengthens the stomach and settles [disturbances] more quickly; it removes bloating and, when drunk, helps with <term>griping pains</term> <note>original: "tortionib;" or colic</note>. It provides a suitable aid against poisons. It possesses diuretic powers so that it is uniquely beneficial for spasms and <term>rheums</term> <note>original: "reumatib;"; watery discharges or inflammation</note>. It also removes <term>hysterical suffocations</term> <note>original: "offocationes stericas"; a historical medical term for a condition believed to be caused by the movement of the womb</note>.

### LXXXIII. ON SAVIN

Many call Savin <term>brathy</term> <note>original: "Bratios" or "braton"</note>; its leaves are similar to those of the cypress. If they have thorns, the odor is heavier. They have a reddish, larger, and hard fruit that is spongy, which many use as <term>incense</term> <note>original: "amiama"; from the Greek thymiama</note>. There is another kind similar to the tamarisk tree. Its leaves, mixed into <term>poultices</term> <note>original: "catteplasmatib;"</note>, cure spreading wounds and remove swelling. When applied with honey, it leads <term>black wounds</term> <note>likely necrotic or gangrenous sores</note> toward healing. It expels blood through the urine. It also causes the abortion of a fetus not yet formed; it is applied to the womb and is necessarily mixed into warm medicines.

### LXXXIIII. ON CEDAR

Cedar is the tree from which <term>cedar-resin</term> <note>original: "pisscedria"</note> is made. That kind is strong which is thick, clear, and has a very powerful odor; when you dip a finger into it, the resin flows down by its own fatness. Its power is such that it kills living moths. It keeps other things from rotting, and protects the bodies of the dead from decay when they are preserved with it, which is why it is called the <term>life of the dead</term> <note>original: "uita mortuorum"</note>. Because it possesses an excessive and high heat, it burns and dries if applied to skins. It clears the dimness of the eyes and, when smeared on, treats <term>glaucoma</term> <note>original: "dicuco matiis"; likely a corruption of glaucomatis</note> and scars.

<summary>This page details the medicinal uses of Juniper, Savin (Brathy), and Cedar, highlighting their roles as fumigants, diuretics, and preservatives, including the famous use of cedar resin for embalming.</summary>
<keywords>Juniper, Savin, Cedar resin, catarrh, gout, uterine health, embalming, ancient pharmacology, eye treatments</keywords>

### LXXXV. ON THE SEED OF THE CEDAR

The seed of the cedar tree is called "cedar." It quiets a cough, prevents spasms, and constricts <term>rheum</term> <note>original: "reuma"; a watery discharge or flux</note>. It heals <term>strangury</term> <note>original: "stranguriae"; painful or difficult urination</note> and regulates the menses. ### LXXXVI. ON LAUREL

A hot decoction of laurel [used as] a <term>fumigation</term> <note>original: "sifcasio"; corruption of "suffumigatio"</note> is applied so that the one being treated may sit over it; it is suitable for pain of the bladder and the womb. Its leaves, tasted while green, are crushed and applied as a <term>poultice</term> <note>original: "cataplasma"</note>; it prevents the spread of <unclear>bee-stings</unclear> <note>original: "apium percursu"; possibly referring to stings (apum) or a spreading skin condition like erysipelas</note> and all tumors.

### LXXXVIII ON THE PLANE TREE
The soft leaves of the Plane tree, boiled with wine and applied as a <term>poultice</term> <note>original: "cataplasma"</note>, check <term>rheum</term> <note>original: "creuma"; a watery discharge or inflammation</note> of the eyes and suppress swelling. If the dust from the flowers of this tree settles on the face, it causes a blemish; or if it enters dry ears, it causes deafness.

### LXXX VIIII ON THE APPLE TREE
The juice of the leaves of this tree, when drunk with wine or applied as a poultice, counteracts poisonous bites. Indeed, the bark, when burned and mixed with water, cleanses <term>leprosy</term> <note>original: "lepras"; in medieval contexts, this often referred to various scaly skin diseases rather than just Hansen's disease</note>. However, the sawdust from its wood, if drunk, causes a man to die <note>The original text claims "moriatur hominem facit," a warning that apple wood sawdust is lethally toxic, which may be a historical misunderstanding or a reference to a specific variety</note>.

### ON THE WHITE POPLAR

### ABOUT MACIR
Macir is the bark of a wood coming from "barbarian" lands <note>original: "de barbarico"; likely referring to the coastal regions of India or East Africa</note>. It is reddish in color, with a solid strength and a curved shape. It is highly <term>astringent</term> <note>original: "sapuca", a corruption of "styptica"; a substance that causes the contraction of body tissues</note> to the taste. When ground and drunk, it provides a unique remedy for those coughing up blood <note>original: "emoptoicis"</note>, those with dysentery, and those suffering from stomach ailments <term>celiacs</term> <note>original: "quiliacis"</note>.

### XCI ABOUT THE BLACK POPLAR
The leaves of the black poplar <note>original: "Egiros"</note>, when mixed with vinegar and applied as a poultice, heal <term>gout</term> <note>original: "podagras"</note>. Its resin is also mixed into necessary <term>malagmas</term> <note>original: "malacmatib;"; a softening medicinal plaster or poultice</note>. Its seed, drunk with vinegar, cures those with epilepsy. Some claim that the "tears" <note>the resinous sap</note> of this tree, distilled in the Eridanus River <note>original: "rodano"; the Po River in Italy</note> and solidified, create amber <note>original: "suauem", likely a corruption of "succinum"</note>; when ground and drunk, it binds a loose belly and settles the stomach.

### XCII ABOUT THE ELM
The leaves of the elm are <term>astringent</term> <note>original: "sapaca"</note>. When ground and applied as a poultice, they cure skin diseases and wounds. Its bark, used as a bandage, brings help to wounds. Its thicker bark, ground and mixed with wine and drunk, clears away phlegm. A decoction of its wood, used as a warm compress, strengthens fractures. The moisture found in its flowers <note>referring to the liquid inside the leaf galls</note> removes spots and wounds when mixed with water. When this liquid dries, small gnats are born from it. Its soft leaves are eaten boiled. The powder from the knots <note>original: "anuolis"</note> of the elm cleanses wounds and leads them to scarring; when mixed with anise, it brings health to spreading sores.

### XCIII ABOUT THE REED
There are two species of reed. One is called <term>nastos</term> <note>the solid-stalked reed</note>, from which arrows are made. The other they call the "female" reed, from which come the nibs for writing pens...

### XCIIII. ABOUT PAPYRUS

**Papyrus**, from which Alexandrian paper is made, is useful. Its ash cleanses foul wounds of the mouth and the whole body; burnt paper is known to have this effect.

### XCV ABOUT MIRICE, THAT IS, THE TAMARISK

The bark of the **tamarisk** <note>original: "mirice id tamariciu"</note>, when boiled, and the decoction itself drunk with wine, reduces swelling of the spleen. The decoction also aids in toothaches. When used in <term>pessaries</term> <note>a small medicinal plug or suppository</note>, it restrains the "humors of the mother" <note>original: "humoris matris"; vaginal discharge or flows from the womb</note> because of its <term>astringent</term> <note>tissue-contracting</note> properties. It kills lice and nits. Its juice <note>original: "anus", likely a corruption of "sucus" or referring to a decoction</note> similarly restrains menstruation. Cups <note>original: "caliaf", likely a corruption of "scaphia" or "calathos"</note> are fashioned from its wood, and it greatly helps those suffering from spleen ailments if they drink from them.

### ABOUT SEA-PURSLANE
**Sea-purslane** <note>original: "ALIMU"; Atriplex halimus</note> is a shrub found around gardens, similar to buckthorn <note>original: "ramnos"</note> but without thorns. It has leaves like those of an olive tree, but broader and softer. It grows in maritime places and around gardens. Its leaves are eaten boiled. One ounce of its root, taken to combat **spasms of the womb** <note>original: "uul-spasmi"</note>, restores health; it also stops **diarrhea** <note>original: "reuma"</note> and **colic** <note>original: "tormina"</note>. It also stimulates the flow of milk in women. **C**

### ABOUT CHRIST’S THORN, THAT IS, ZURA
The seed of **Christ’s thorn** <note>original: "PALIURO ID ZURA"; Paliurus spina-christi</note>, when drunk, suppresses a cough, breaks stones in the bladder, and counters venomous bites. Its medicinal power resides in the leaves and roots. A <term>decoction</term> <note>original: "elixatura"; a liquid produced by boiling medicinal plants</note> of this, when drunk, binds the bowels, provokes urine, and acts as an antidote to ingested poisons. Its leaves, when applied as a poultice, counter recent **abscesses** <note>original: "apostemata"</note>. **CI**

### ABOUT THE BARBERRY
**Barberry** <note>original: "OXIA CANTA"; likely Oxyacantha, referring to Hawthorn or Barberry</note>, which is also called *damamen*, though others have called it *pientem* or *perina*. It has seeds like those of the myrtle, reddish in color, and it is jagged like sugar <note>original: "dentatus ut zuccar"; the reference to sugar may describe a crystalline or sharp texture, or may be a scribal error for a similar sounding Latin word</note>. Its roots are widely spread and go deep. The seed of this plant, when burnt and drunk, restrains a loose belly and stops **menstrual flow**. Its root is applied as a poultice to draw out an embedded arrow. When drunk, it is said to prevent **miscarriage** <note>original: "abortum excludere prohibetur"</note>. **CII**

### ABOUT THE DOG-ROSE
The **dog-rose** <note>original: "CINOSBATU"; Cynosbatos</note>, that is, *saccu pallea*; many call it *oxia canta*. When its seed has ripened, it turns red; it has very rough "teeth" <note>thorns</note>. The seed is dry, without a husk... <note>the sentence breaks off</note>

### CIII ABOUT HENNA, THAT IS, ISSIPPAN

The leaves of **Henna** <note>original: "Cypro"; Lawsonia inermis</note>, when chewed, suppress swelling of the mouth. It is also applied as warm **poultices** <note>original: "cataplasmis"; a soft, moist mass of plant material applied to the body</note> for other swellings. A decoction of it heals burns. If the head is frequently washed with it, it benefits the hair, just as if the juice of the crushed plant were mixed in. If its flower is applied as a poultice with vinegar, it is known to relieve headaches.

### CIIII ABOUT MOCK-PRIVET

The leaves of **Mock-privet** <note>original: "Fillira"; likely Phillyrea latifolia</note> are **styptic** <note>original: "stiptica"; having an astringent quality that shrinks tissues or stops bleeding</note> and are similar to those of the wild olive tree. They are necessary for treatments requiring astringency; they especially cleanse all wounds. Chewing the leaves is also known to produce this effect. A decoction of the leaves used as a gargle provides a similar benefit. Drinking half a measure <note>original: ".ss."; likely an abbreviation for "semis," meaning half a sextarius or pint</note> of the decoction provokes the flow of urine.

### CV ABOUT IVY

**Cissea**, that is, **Ivy** <note>original: "Hedera"</note>, as some call it: drinking its flower with wine heals internal ailments. If applied as a poultice, it is confirmed to heal fresh wounds. Mixed with a wax salve, it treats burns and is usefully applied to old wounds. Near its roots grows **hypocistis** <note>original: "hipoquistis"; Cytinus hypocistis, a parasitic plant that grows on the roots of rockroses, but here associated with ivy</note>, which some call *tobriton* or something similar. One part of it is reddish and the other is white. This is crushed and the juice expressed, <gloss>similarly</gloss> to acacia juice. They dry it, infuse it, and boil it, then press it and boil the liquid again until it reaches the thickness of honey. It is used for its medicinal power, which is like that of acacia, but it is a little more styptic. It is used as a necessary treatment for loosening of the bowels and dysentery. It helps those spitting blood and stops the menstrual flow. There is another kind of ivy which some call *Andon*; it is a similar shrub, but it has longer leaves which are black and possess a certain oiliness.

...its potency is found upon the leaves. On the leaves, it has a flavor similar to the plant mentioned above <note>original: "superiori"; referring to the Cistus plant</note>; from it, **Ladanum** <note>original: "ladanū"; a sticky resin used in perfumes and medicine</note> is collected. The **he-goats** <note>original: "hirci cabrarū"</note> lightly chew the leaves of this herb; when they begin to graze upon it, the stickiness <note>original: "pinguidō"</note> that remained on the small leaves adheres to the beards and shoulders of the goats. With great care, it is collected from these goats and, after being processed, they make Ladanum. Others, however, drag a taut rope over the branches themselves, and if any of that stickiness sticks to the rope, they collect and use it. They follow this method: they rub it with their hands to oil and **soften** <note>original: "malaxant"; to knead or make supple</note> it, and they make small tablets from the Ladanum itself. It is useful, full of scent, green in color, easy to soften, and fatty; if it is mixed with sand, the resin becomes very brittle. The power of Ladanum <note>original: "ledine"</note> is warming and **emollient** <note>original: "malactaca"; softening to the skin</note>, and it is **aperient** <note>original: "anastomatè"; opening to the pores or vessels</note>. It treats thinning hair when mixed with wine, myrrh, and myrtle oil. It restores dark scars to a healthy skin color. Mixed with rose oil, it takes away the pain of the ears. Its smoke expels the **afterbirth** <note>original: "secundas"</note>, dissolves hardness of the womb, and treats **soft tumors** <note>original: "malacuma"</note>. Mixed with wine, it binds the belly <note>treats diarrhea</note> and stays the flow; it also has **diuretic** <note>term: diuretic; a substance that encourages the production of urine</note> properties.

### CVI. ABOUT EBONY

**Ebony** <note>original: "Ebenu"</note> which comes from Ethiopia is best if it has a solid color and is dense, smooth to the touch, quite hard, and has a flavor that is both rich and **pungent** <note>original: "mordax"; biting or sharp</note>. When it is placed upon coals, the fire quickly creeps through it, and when you rub it against the skin, it reveals a reddish glow. There is another kind from India with a variegated color, but the first is better. Many people craftily sell wood from the **maniceta** or **cantina** <note>likely local names for inferior substitute woods used to deceive buyers</note> because they look like ebony, but it is recognized as a fake because it is soft and blackish. When broken, the splinters themselves appear with a reddish color, but they have neither the same scent nor taste. Its power is **purgative** <note>original: "purgatoria"; cleansing or clearing</note>. Because of this, it clears away dimness of the eyes and **fluxes** <note>original: "reumatismū"; a discharge of fluids</note>, and it heals wounds.

Others pour the scrapings of its mature skin into wine for a day and a night and grind it like **eye-salve** <note>original: "colliria"; a medicated paste or wash for the eyes</note>. Others, however, strain it after grinding and proceed in this way; others add water and wine. It is also burnt in a raw, well-broken pot and placed in the hearth until it turns to ash; then it is taken up for grinding, which produces a powder for dryness of the eyes.

## CVII CONCERNING THE ROSE

The juice of the **Rose** <note>original: "Rosae"</note> and its "claws" <note>original: "unguiculus"; referring to the white base of the petals where they attach to the stem</note> should be collected. It is necessary for the preparation of eye-salves. Its petals are dried in the sun or boiled in wine for **headaches** <note>original: "dolore capitis"</note>. It acts as a drying agent for the eyes and for all sorts of **chaps** <note>original: "ragadur"; likely *rhagades*, or cracks in the skin</note>. It is more valuable than all other things for conditions of the **womb** <note>original: "matricis" or "passario"</note>. It heals in the same way if mixed as a **poultice** <note>original: "cateplusma"</note> from crushed petals. It is known to be especially beneficial for tumors of the **hypochondrium** <note>original: "ipocondriorũ"; the upper abdomen below the ribs</note> or for the stomach. Sprinkled over a sharp fire, it is dried and necessarily mixed into all sorts of powders. It is also burnt to make a powder and is used for dry eyes. When a powder is made from its flower and mixed with **ginger** <note>original: "zigıbır"</note>, it heals and constricts the flow of the bowels; similarly, it checks the flow of blood.

## CVIII. LYCIUM

**Lycium** <note>original: "Licuē"; a medicinal extract usually derived from shrubs of the *Berberis* or *Rhamnus* genus</note> is a wood of a reddish color on the inside and black on the outside; when split, it is not brittle. Its juice appears reddish and saffron-colored, and the taste is bitter. The **Indian** variety <note>original: "indica"</note> is the better kind. It clears mistiness from the eyes, treats **scabies** <note>original: "scabiae"</note> and itching of the eyes, and checks **rheum** <note>original: "reuma"; a watery discharge from the eyes or nose</note>. It heals old sores, purges the ears, and soothes swelling of the throat. It helps wounded gums and wonderfully cures **chaps** <note>original: "ragadia"</note> and ulcers of the tender parts. It is given as a drink and an enema for **dysentery** <note>original: "dissentetiar"</note> and **colic** <note>original: "quiliae"</note>. Taken with water, it cures coughs and those **spitting blood** <note>original: "emoptoicar"; from the Greek *haemoptysis*</note>. It is a protection against hiccups and the bites of a **rabid dog** <note>original: "rabiosi canis"</note>. It is given in the manner of a poultice and will heal. It dyes the hair, and when applied as an ointment, it heals **whitlows** <note>original: "panartia"; an infection of the fingertip or nail bed</note> and spreading wounds.

**CVIII. CONCERNING ACACIA.**

Its juice is usefully mixed into **eye-salves** <note>original: "colliriis"</note>. **CX. CONCERNING OIL LEES**

**Oil lees** <note>original: "Amurca"; the bitter, watery dregs of pressed olives</note> cooked in a copper vessel until it reaches a thickness similar to honey takes away the pain of teeth. Mixed with wine or vinegar and honey, it treats wounds. It is correctly mixed with medicines and eye-salves that improve with age. It offers health to natural wounds and excludes the rot of the **womb** <note>original: "matrias"; likely *matrices*</note>. Mixed with **omphacine oil** <note>original: "oleo onfacino"; oil made from unripe olives</note> and applied, it removes the **scabies** <note>a contagious skin disease caused by mites</note> of animals when used with the water in which lupins were cooked, and it treats camel-sores <note>original: "camelenta"</note>. **CXI. CONCERNING THE CHASTE TREE.**

### CXIIII ON ETHIOPIAN DIAGRIDIUM <gloss>I</gloss> <gloss>H</gloss> <gloss>C</gloss>

The Ethiopian olive is comparable in potency to the oil.

### ON OAK-GALLS

The oak-gall <note>original: "Gallas"</note> is a seed-like growth. It comes from the oak tree [drio], of which one type is called *omphacitis* <term>omphacitis: a small, heavy, and knobby variety of gall nut</term>, which is smaller, round, heavy, and knotty, and without holes; the other is smooth and perforated. Of all these, the one that is harder and stronger should be chosen. 

Both are astringent and act as hemostatics <term>katastaltika: substances that check or suppress flows, such as blood or discharge</term>; they cleanse spreading wounds, stop the discharge [rheum] of the gums, and are used as medicine for the tonsils and throat. The center of the gall, when hollowed out and placed into the cavities of teeth, takes away the pain. When prepared with vinegar, or vinegar and salt, or wine, their decoction dries the flow of blood from wounds. It is well applied as a warm soak for the prolapse of the uterus <term>histere: the womb or uterus</term>; they check the flow of fluids and dye the hair when infused with vinegar or water.

## 118. CONCERNING THE PALM which grows in Egypt

Its seed is the myrobalan <term>mirobalanos: here referring to a palm-kernel or the fruit of the Ben-oil tree, often confused with palm species in early texts</term>, which is similar to what the Egyptians call *tomata*. Its color is green, and it is similar to a quince <note>original: "quidoma"; likely a corruption of *cydonia*, the quince</note> in odor—but when it has matured and fallen, it is called the date-kernel <term>finicobalanos: literally "phoenix-berry" or date-fruit</term>. If this is drunk with harsh wine <note>original: "uino astero"; referring to *austere* or dry, tart wine</note>, it restrains internal decay and the flow of blood in women. Applied as a poultice to a fresh wound, it acts as a glue <term>paracolles: a substance used to bind the edges of a wound together</term>.

Dried palm kernels have a great deal of astringency. If they are mixed into wine, they cause a headache for the drunkard. Dried dates <term>dactuli: from the Greek *daktylos*, meaning "finger," describing the shape of the fruit</term> are used as a medicine for those coughing up blood <term>emobtoicis: hemoptysis, or the spitting of blood from the lungs</term>, for dysentery, and for stomach ailments. 

When dried <note>original: "sicum adomo"</note> and used in poultices with other ingredients, they restrain the pain of the bladder. Carian dates <term>carioticomis: a specific variety of date from Caria in Asia Minor, known for being fleshy and sweet</term> soothe the roughness of the windpipe. A decoction of dates... <unclear>rēb ācur</unclear>... when taken with honey and wine, they have a similar power; even the wine made from the dates themselves possesses this virtue. 

A decoction of dates is used as a wash or a gargle for its astringent properties. Their stones <note>original: "osse"</note>, cooked in a pot and steeped in wine, act in the place of *spodium* <term>spodiacis: a medicinal powder made from burnt minerals or bone, used for its drying effects</term> and have a drying power for the eyes. This astringency and <unclear>paraplusmati</unclear> <note>likely a type of plaster or eye-salve</note> remove the cause of eye ailments and these swellings <term>splomata: likely *spilomata*, referring to spots or growths on the cornea</term>. With the branches... <unclear>staluceŕ</unclear>... it heals growing wounds by forming a scar. 

Two types of date-stones are particularly good: those that come from Egypt, from the tree they call *camezelu* <note>possibly from the Greek *chamaizelos*, meaning "low-growing" or dwarf palm</note>, and dates which they call *mula eluten* or *spacus tumenico* <note>these names appear to be phonetic transcriptions of local Egyptian or Greek varieties</note>. While the tree is still in flower and foaming <note>original: "spūm tum"; likely referring to the sap or pollen</note>, they are used in the preparation of ointments. However, the best is that which is fragrant, astringent <term>sapaticus</term>, firm, and fleshy.

## 119. CONCERNING THE POMEGRANATE
**119. DE MALA GRANATA**

All its juice is beneficial for the stomach and for the digestion of those who are weak <note>original: "stomacum habentier cilu et atroso"; the Latin is corrupted but refers to different states of gastric health</note>. Of these, there are two kinds: the sweet and the sour. The sweet kind is pleasing to the stomach and heats the stomach to some degree, but it causes bloating <term>inflationem: the production of gas or swelling in the gut</term>, which is why it is given to those with fevers. It eases the burning and also the hardness of the stomach. Those pomegranates that are astringent, wine-like, or "opening" <term>anostomaica: from the Greek *anastomotikos*, referring to substances that open the mouths of vessels</term> have a moderate power. 

The hard part, which is the seeds of the sour pomegranate, when dried in the sun and made into a powder and added to food, restrains the "rheums" <note>reumas: discharges or flows of fluid</note> of the stomach and belly. Infused in water and <insert>m</insert> taken, it treats those spitting blood <term>optoias: corruption of *hemoptoicos*</term> and those with dysentery. 

When applied as a warm fomentation <term>fumento: a warm, medicinal compress</term>, their juice, squeezed out and cooked with honey mixed in, thoroughly heals wounds of the mouth and of the genitals <term>naturae: literally "nature," a common medieval euphemism for the private parts</term>. It heals hangnails <term>terrigia: sores or growths around the nails</term> and spreading wounds, and it strengthens recently healed areas. It removes the stench of ear pain. Its flower is also called *quitina* <term>quitina: from the Greek *kytinos*, the flower of the pomegranate</term>, and it is itself astringent. Both its juice and the "Attic" preparation <term>atticistalatum: likely referring to a refined medicinal extract</term> <gloss>a preparation for wounds</gloss> can heal wounds. Also, a decoction of pomegranate...

### CXXII. CONCERNING THE GREEK SILIQUA.

The Greek siliqua <term>siliqua greca: the carob fruit</term>, also known as *ceratia* <note>original: "ceratia"; the carob tree is *Ceratonia siliqua*</note>, is bad for the stomach when green; they loosen the belly. When dry, they bring strength to the stomach and are diuretic, and they bind the belly. Especially those made from the leaves, or when the harvest from the tree is taken with wine, it removes a cough, prohibits the spitting of blood <note>original: "sa sa duim"; likely *sanguinem*</note>, and breaks stones in the bladder.

### CXXIII. CONCERNING THE MATIAN APPLE <gloss>ma</gloss>

The apple known as the Matian apple <note>original: "malamatiana"; a variety of apple named after Gaius Matius, a friend of Julius Caesar</note> is astringent while it is still unripe. When it has ripened, it loses this virtue. If eaten in the spring, it causes "rotten bile" <note>original: "colera putrit"; likely referring to an upset of the choleric humor</note>, causes gas <term>inflatione: bloating or flatulence</term>, and is harmful to the nerves.

### CXXIIII. CONCERNING QUINCES.

The virtue of the quince <note>original: "mala quidonia"</note> is better when it is roasted. They are especially beneficial for those with dysentery, those spitting blood <term>emoptoicis: from the Greek *haimoptuikos*</term>, and provide a remedy for the hiccups of the choleric, especially if eaten raw. A decoction of them applied as a warm fomentation cures nail infections <note>original: "an eucia"; likely a corruption of *paronychia*</note> and helps with a prolapse of the womb <note>original: "histeri procidentia"</note>. They restrain the bowels. When applied raw as poultices to the stomach, they restrain the belly, extinguish heat <term>ardore: inflammation or burning sensations</term>, and soften the hardness of tumors in the breasts <note>original: "didarum"; likely *didymorum*, referring to the breasts or testicles</note>.

Given as a drink, it heals the stomach and the belly by checking their discharges. If one takes them raw, a decoction of them helps those with orthopnea <term>ortopnoicis: people who can only breathe comfortably when sitting or standing upright</term>.

### CXXV. CONCERNING THE APRICOT

The apricot <note>original: "Apruma"; likely a variant of *armeniaca* or *prunus*</note>, that is, the honey-apple <note>original: "melimele"</note>, loosens the belly and causes a burning sensation in those with bad stomachs <term>cacostomachas: having a weak or upset stomach</term>. Those from Epirus <note>original: "epirotica"</note>, which in Latin are called *orbiculata* <note>original: "orbem cladiaz"; likely a corruption of *orbiculata*, or "disk-shaped" apples</note>, are good for the stomach <term>eustomacae: beneficial for digestion</term>. They bind the belly and are used for swellings of the gums. Similar to quinces, there are also wild varieties which grow in the spring; these are all very astringent, especially when unripe.

### CXXVI. CONCERNING THE PEACH

Peaches <note>original: "Prosica," a corruption of *Persica*</note> are good for the stomach and soften the belly, especially if they are naturally [ripe]. When unripe, they bind the belly, especially if they have been sliced [and dried]. A decoction <term>elixatura: a liquid produced by boiling</term> of them checks the rheum <term>reuma: a discharge of bodily fluids or inflammation</term> of the stomach and belly. The smaller ones <note>original: "microtera," from the Greek for "smaller"</note>, which in Latin are called early-ripening <note>original: "pcoria," likely *praecocia*, the root of the word 'apricot'</note>, are also good for the stomach. They remove nausea <note>original: "fastidiu"</note> better than pears.

### CXXVII. CONCERNING PEARS

There are many species of pears; all are astringent, which is why they check rheum when applied in poultices. A decoction of them is as effective as the pears themselves. Eaten raw, they bind the belly, particularly if eaten on an empty stomach. Concerning wild pears: the wild pear <note>original: "pira saluatica"</note> is a sour species known to ripen slowly; they are more astringent than cultivated pears.

### CXXVIII. CONCERNING THE MEDLAR

<margin>good for the stomach <note>original: "eustomacha"</note></margin>
Medlars have a round and small seed. The flavor is sharp, and for this reason, it binds the stomach and the bowels. ### CXXVIIII. CONCERNING THE GRAPE

Unripe grapes, when collected and dried in the sun, bind the bowels. They are given for intestinal fluxes <note>original: "itatu sa et crisellata propulenta quilias"; these are highly corrupted terms likely referring to diarrhea or gastric discharge</note>. Their decoction, when drunk, should be given for all such conditions.

### CXXX. CONCERNING THE CORNELIAN CHERRY

The *granea* <note>likely the Cornelian cherry, *Cornus mas*</note> has a seed similar to an olive, being oblong in shape. They have an astringent flavor and treat looseness of the bowels and dysentery. If prepared with sweetness, it can be eaten; otherwise, they are preserved in salt like other fruits. When its leaves are placed on a fire, the moisture that is released from them is excellent for chilblains <term>perni: painful, itchy swellings on the skin caused by poor circulation in the cold</term>.

The plum <note>original: "Quoquimela"</note> is known to everyone, along with its tree. Its fruit is bad for the stomach <term>cacostomachū: from Greek, meaning "bad for the stomach" or causing indigestion</term> but it softens the bowels; however, the Syrian and Damascene varieties <unclear>... [are of a different quality?]</unclear>.

### CXXXII. CONCERNING THE STRAWBERRY TREE <note>original: "Comaru"; the *Arbutus unedo*</note>

### CXXXIII. CONCERNING <gloss>THE</gloss> ALMOND

The bitter root of the bitter almond, boiled and ground, clears spots from the face; the almond itself, applied in a poultice <term>cataplasmatib: a soft, moist mass applied to the body</term>, achieves the same. Used as a suppository, it provokes menstruation. Smeared on the forehead <note>original: "frona"; likely *frontem*</note>, it takes away a headache. It is most effective when dried and used with rose oil or vinegar. Mixed with wine, it clears spots on the body. Mixed with honey, it checks rotted and spreading ulcers. If eaten with honey, it prevents pain from the bite of a dog. It softens the belly and provokes sleep. They heal difficulty in urinating and those with bladder stones when taken with a sweetener. For those with liver complaints <term>epaticis: from the Greek *hepatikos*</term>, for those coughing, and for gas in the colon, they help when taken as an electuary in the size of a nut with honey and milk. If five of them are taken while fasting, it is said to prevent a person from becoming drunk. When combined with its juice, it is beneficial for those spitting up blood <term>emoptoicis: from the Greek *haimoptoikos*</term> when drunk with vinegar.

### 139. CONCERNING THE ROYAL NUT, THAT IS THE ALEXANDRIAN NUT <note>This refers to the common Walnut (*Juglans regia*)</note>

The royal nut, which the common folk call the "Persian nut," if eaten, is bad for the stomach <term>cacostomaca: from the Greek *kakostomachos*, harmful to digestion</term>, hard to digest, and nourishes bile <note>original: "colera"; refers to an imbalance of the "choleric" humor</note>. It causes headaches and is harmful to those with a cough. Eaten on an empty stomach, it provokes nausea. It counteracts poisons if eaten with dried figs <term>caricas: a specific type of dried fig from Caria in Asia Minor</term>. It cleanses the side <note>likely referring to the liver or pleura</note>. Applied as a poultice <term>cataplasmis: a soft, moist mass of herbs applied to the skin</term>, it suppresses the swelling of breasts. It is well applied with honey and rue for dislocations. With a small onion, honey, and salt, it brings the bites of dogs and humans to health. 

Crushed with the shell <note>original: "corio"; literally skin or bark, here the walnut hull</note> and placed on the navel <term>uilico: a phonetic spelling of *umbilico*, the navel</term>, it cures colic <term>torminib;: sharp, wringing pains in the bowels</term>. It halts menstruation if the nut meat itself is burnt and drunk with water.

If chewed and applied to fistulas <term>fistulas: deep, tube-like sores</term>, [it heals them]. An oil is made from them by force and pressing. Green [fresh] walnuts are less harmful to the stomach because they are sweet, [especially] if mixed as if with garlic...

### 140. CONCERNING THE MULBERRY, ALSO CALLED CELSA

<margin>bad for the stomach</margin>
The mulberry <note>original: "celsa"</note>, which many call *sicaminum*, is a tree known to all. Its seed is bad for the stomach <term>cacostomaticos: harmful to digestion</term>, and the juice—whether taken alone or pressed out—does the same. However, the juice itself is cooked in a bronze vessel and placed in the sun; it becomes more pleasant when you mix it with honey. It heals spreading sores of the mouth and leads them to health; it removes swelling of the throat. It is even stronger if you mix in frankincense, fissile alum <note>original: "alum sissiū"; a type of sulfate mineral used as an astringent</note>, oak galls in equal parts, and myrrh or saffron and other seeds, all ground up. Also, unripe mulberries, dried and ground, are mixed with Syrian sumac <note>original: "proros siriaco"; likely *rhus syriacus*, used for its tartness and medicinal properties</note>; this binds the bowels. A decoction of the bark <note>original: "cornū"; literally "horn," but here used for the tough outer bark or root-covering</note> of its root, cooked with water and administered, loosens the bowels and expels broadworms <term>lumbricos latos: tapeworms</term>. Because drinking the bark helps, its leaves, ground with oil and applied, heal burns. Cooked in rainwater and mixed with vine shoots and black leaves, it dyes hair black. Also, the juice of the leaves, if drunk, cures the bite of a spider <note>original: "splanziū"; a corruption of *phalangium*, a venomous spider</note>. A decoction of its bark and leaves heals the pain of teeth. If the root is harvested <note>original: "tinaria"; an obscure term likely referring to the digging up or time of collection</note> and produced with care, it works for toothaches and pustules; when taken, it softens the belly.

It subdues swelling of the spleen, removes stomach pain, and relieves chills <note>original: "fricus"; likely *frigus*</note> in the body. If the juice is kept too long in the heat, it spoils. 

There is another tree which grows nearby that has only one thing different from the ones described above: it has leaves similar to the wild [mulberry], but its seed is like the mulberry <note>original: "sicamino"</note> and is as sweet as cooked honey.

### 143. CONCERNING THE SAP, THAT IS, OF THE WILD AND COMMON FIG.

The sap <note>original: "opus," from the Greek *opos* for plant juice or latex</note> of the wild and common fig curdles milk just as lamb's rennet <note>original: "quagulum"</note> is known to do. However, if more is added, it dissolves what was curdled, just like vinegar. It wounds the skin like a caustic agent <note>original: "causticum"</note> and has a cleansing effect on the body <note>original: "anosomaticu": likely referring to the opening of pores or vessels</note>. It softens the belly. When drunk with starch <note>original: "amilo"</note>, it revives those suffering from hysteria <note>original: "histericas"</note>, and it regulates and induces menstruation. When used as a vaginal suppository <term>pessario: a medical substance inserted into the vagina</term> with egg and wax, and mixed with vinegar, it helps those with gout <note>original: "podagricis"</note> in the form of a poultice. It cleanses leprosy <note>original: "lepras"</note>, removes shingles <note>original: "serpias"</note>, and clears away skin spots <term>alfur: likely *alphos*, a skin condition characterized by white spots</term> and the itch <note>original: "scabia"</note>. Placed on scorpion stings, it helps against poisonous bites and counters [the bite of a] dog. It soothes the pain of teeth if applied to the cavity with a little wool <note>original: "lanulū"</note>. It [treats] warts <note>original: "mirmiicas"</note> as a poultice...

applied by hand <note>original: "adhibitae manur"</note> and placed upon the body, it is healthy. The juice of the leaves of the wild fig <note>original: "fici agrestis"</note> is also able to do this, but the juice is better collected by pressing the flower itself when it is in bloom. This juice is dried in the shade and mixed with the strength of Arabic medicines <note>original: "uis arab; medicamenum," likely referring to gum arabic</note> which is prepared for opening the bowels. ### CXLIIII ABOUT SODA, THAT IS, Olitrum
<note>The text identifies "Nitrum" (soda/natron) with "Olitrum." This likely refers to a plant from which soda was derived, such as Glasswort or Sea Orache, which the text notes is called "scopi" (broom) by the Alexandrians.</note>

This, which is spoken of as having many seeds, is called "broom" <note>original: "scopi"</note> by the Alexandrians. When boiled and used in poultices <term>cataplasmis: a soft, moist mass of medicinal ingredients applied to the skin</term>, it softens every type of hardness and treats scrofula <term>scrofas: a swelling of the lymph nodes, often associated with tuberculosis</term>. When applied raw with soda and flour, it removes "ant-warts" <note>original: "mirmicias," referring to small, painful warts known as myrmecia</note>. Its leaves also do these things when applied in a poultice with vinegar and salt; it cures dandruff <note>original: "pitorias capitis"</note> and mange <note>original: "tineas"</note>. For the former, the leaves taken from the decoction <note>original: "aco mata," likely "acomata" or "apothemata"</note> remove white spots <note>original: "leumcas," likely "leucas"</note> from the flesh. The leaves themselves, when mixed and applied as a poultice, are effective, especially if their tips are dried. Mixed with honey <note>original: "mēle"</note>, it provides a healthy effect for dog bites. If the plant itself is mixed into a poultice with the seeds of the wild poppy <note>original: "miconi agrestis"</note>, which they call "the executioner of bones" <note>original: "ossa carnifixae"</note>, and mixed with wax-salve <term>cerotis: a plaster or ointment made with wax</term>, it dissolves boils <note>original: "frunculus"</note>. The herb mixed with wine and used in a poultice works for the bites of weasels <note>original: "mustalae"</note>, shrews <note>original: "soricū"</note>, and centipedes <note>original: "olopendria"</note>.

### CXLV ABOUT FIG ASH

Ash <note>original: "ciner"</note> is made from the fig tree by burning the twigs <note>original: "saripsis," likely "sarmentis"</note>. It produces the same effect, and its power is increased when it has become aged. It is mixed well into medicinal treatments for chronic conditions; it cures gangrene <note>original: "cangrenas"</note>, which is to say, cancers <note>original: "cancerus"</note>. When applied, it consumes rotting flesh <note>original: "putrias carnis"</note>. It is also applied using a soaked sponge. Many, indeed, apply it to dangerous wounds <note>original: "perclis tere uulnerib;"</note> of the core <note>original: "cordis," literally 'of the heart,' but often meaning the deep center of a wound</note> to cleanse and fill them.

### CXLVI · THE PERSEA TREE

The Persea tree <note>The Persea described here is likely *Mimusops laurifolia*, not the modern Avocado (*Persea americana*)</note> grows in Egypt. Its fruit <note>original: "semen," literally "seed," but referring to the edible part</note> is easy to eat and good for the stomach. Venomous spiders <note>original: "phalagia"</note> which are called "cranio cullae" are found there, especially in the region of Thebaid, and they are quite vigorous. The leaves of this tree are a dry drawing agent <term>epispastica: a substance that draws out fluids or causes blistering to relieve internal inflammation</term>. When reduced to powder and applied, it stops bleeding. People once said this tree was deadly when it grew in Persia, but those who later planted it in treacherous Alexandria found the fruit could be eaten.

## THE LESSON OF DIOSCORIDES ON THE URCHIN CONCLUDES

**T**he sea urchin <note>original: "Ecina maritimus"</note> is beneficial for the stomach <term>eustomachon: a term used for substances that aid digestion or soothe the stomach</term>, and it softens the belly and acts as a diuretic <term>deureticae: a substance that promotes the flow of urine</term>. Its raw shell is mixed effectively into medications; or when burned, it cleanses foul wounds and causes overgrown flesh in wounds to subside. 

<margin>II</margin>
### ON THE LAND URCHIN 

The burned shell of the land urchin <note>This refers to the hedgehog</note>, when mixed with liquid pitch, heals alopecia <term>alopicis: baldness or patchy hair loss</term>. Its raw meat, drunk with oxymel <term>oximelli: a medicinal mixture of vinegar and honey</term>, is a singular protection for those with pleurisy <note>original: "peufretiae," a corruption of pleuritis</note>, for those with gouty pains <note>original: "posardiis," likely a corruption of "podagricis"</note>, for those with dropsy <term>hidropias: an old term for swelling caused by excess fluid in the body</term>, for those with muscle contractions, for stomach ailments, and for those suffering from cachexia <term>cacecticis: a state of severe wasting and ill health</term>. It dries the rheum <note>excess fluid or discharge</note> of their intestines; its liver, dried on a shard or boiled in the sun and applied, drains all fluids... it works wonderfully. 

### III. ON THE SEAHORSE

The seahorse <note>original: "Ippocampo"</note> is a small sea animal. Its collected ashes, mixed with liquid pitch or lard <note>original: "absungiae"</note> or marjoram oil <note>original: "miro amariano"</note> and used as an ointment, heals alopecia. 

### IIII ON THE PURPLE SHELLFISH 

The burned sea-purple <note>The *Purpura* or Murex snail, famous in antiquity for producing purple dye</note> has a drying virtue. It cleanses the flesh when it has grown excessively in a wound and forms a scar. Burned *coraces* <note>likely another variety of sea snail or shellfish</note> do this as well, but because they are naturally caustic <term>caustica: a substance that can burn or corrode organic tissue</term>, if they are filled with salt and burned in a pot <note>original: "cacabo"</note>, they remove tartar <note>original: "eruginē," literally "rust"</note> from the teeth. It is used in treatments as it dries wounds when applied; and unless it creates a scar <note>the text is marked with a chrismon-like symbol here to denote importance</note>, a fistula <term>fistula: an abnormal, narrow passage or hole that forms in the body</term> falls away because of it. Lime <term>calce: calcium oxide, produced here by calcining shells</term> is made from them just as was described above in the description of lime.

The trumpet shells <note>original: "Cionidas," referring to *Ceryces* or whelks</note> are also called the five shells and purple...

Book Two.

### XVI. ON THE SNAKE'S SKIN
Snake skin <note>original: "tunica colubrina," the sloughed-off skin of a serpent</note>
cooked in wine heals the pain of the teeth; it is a great help.
When crushed and applied, it especially relieves [pain] of the eyes.

### XVII On the land hare.
The brain of a hare, when eaten,
strengthens the teeth of infants. Its head, burned [and mixed] with bear
fat and applied as a poultice, cures <term>alopecia: "alopicias," or patchy hair loss</term>.
Its rennet <note>original: "coagulum," the curdled milk from the stomach</note> when drunk after childbirth draws out the menses through a woman's reproductive organs and binds a flux of the belly (diarrhea). It treats <term>epileptics: "epilenticis"</term>.
When drunk with vinegar, it helps against poisons.
It dissolves [clots or tumors] in the breasts of women; and it is drunk for the bite
of a viper; it dries out [the wound/poison]. Its warm blood cures and
heals spots and blemishes where it is applied.

### XVIII On the sea-stingray.

### XVIIII On the cuttlefish cooked with its own ink
It softens the belly in cases of <term>bad stomach: "cacostomacae"</term>. Its bone, specifically
the soft part, is necessarily mixed into eye-salves for <term>trachoma: "tracomaticis," a contagious bacterial eye infection</term>.
These same bones, when crushed, remove the <term>tartar: "erugine," literally "rust" or scale</term> from teeth. They clear away
spots on the flesh and restore its color. They also clear away <term>cataracts: "glaucomata"</term> in the eyes of humans or
animals when sprinkled or rubbed on.
Rubbing them on, especially with salt, leads to health [of the skin].

### XX On the red mullet, that is, the trigla
Frequently eaten, they remove <term>dimness: "caliginis"</term> from the eyes. Raw,
split open and applied, it removes [the pain of] a <term>scorpion</term> [sting].

### XXI On castoreum.
Castoreum <note>original: "castoreo," a pungent secretion from the scent glands of beavers</note>
provokes sneezing. Drunk with <term>pennyroyal: "puleio," a medicinal herb in the mint family</term>, it commands the menses [to flow].
It causes abortion and expels the <term>afterbirth: "secundas"</term>. Drunk with vinegar, it
removes flatulence. It heals griping pains and <term>hiccups: "subglutionibus"</term>.
It does not allow poisonous potions to do harm. For those in <term>lethargy: "letargis," a state of comatose unconsciousness</term>,
it is a singular protection. When smeared on the head with vinegar and rose oil, it
aids those in a <term>deep stupor: "cataphoro"</term>; this is done by applying it to the nostrils or by fumigation.

The skin of its stomach, dried and drunk, is for the stomach, especially if it is drunk with wine.

### XXXVIIII On Capon Broth
The broth, especially of a smaller bird, soothes exhaustion of the stomach. Simply prepared, the broth of a larger bird softens the belly. But for the larger ones, it should be prepared this way: the <margin>seeds</margin> <note>original: "ss" abbreviation</note> are removed while it is being seasoned <note>original: "incondatur"</note>, or if it has been eaten by them.

...their intestines <note>original: "enterena eorum," likely *interanea*</note> are prepared and thus gathered, and placed into twenty measures of water; let them boil as long as they remain [until reduced] to six and a half <note>original: "sex semis"</note>. ### XL On the Soft Egg.

A soft-boiled egg <note>original: "ouo molli"</note> is better for the stomach than a raw, sippable one. Even the yolk of a raw egg, roasted and mixed with wax-salve <term>wax-salve: "ceroto," a pharmaceutical mixture of oil and wax</term> and rose oil, heals pains of the eyes. It is rightly mixed into medicines for pains or <term>growths: "condilomata," often referring to small tumors or swellings</term> so that it may lead them back to health. Fried with gallnut <note>original: "galla"</note> or with resin <note>original: "rossina"</note>, it may be applied frequently to bind the belly <note>original: "absanduen trem," likely *abstringendum ventrem*</note>. The white of the egg also calms pains and swellings of the eyes. It treats burns. When applied to a wound of the bladder by means of an injection, it ensures the patient does not feel the [heat of the] sun. A poultice <note>original: "ana conlema," likely a corruption of *anacolima*</note> placed on the forehead and mixed with frankincense <note>original: "turae"</note> clears <term>eye rheum: "reuma oculoru," a watery discharge from the eyes</term> and prevents swellings. Mixed with rose oil, honey, and wine, and taken raw, it counters poisonous bites. Taken warm, it cures the bladder <note>original: "sificae," likely *vesicae*</note> and kidneys wonderfully. It mitigates the roughness of the windpipe <note>original: "arteriarū"</note> and cuts off the flow of blood; it halts rheum of the chest and long-lasting ailments <note>original: "catacron langius argã," likely referring to chronic (catachron) illness (languor)</note>.

### XLI On the Cicada.

Eaten roasted or drunk, it prevents pain of the bladder <note>original: "uissicae"</note>. Even the fumes [of a burnt cicada] wonderfully assist women suffering from difficulty in passing urine <note>original: "disuictimulerum," likely *dysuriam mulierum*</note>.

### XLII On the Shrew.

Dried and drunk in wine, it ensures that the bites of a scorpion do not harm; it is also effective when eaten.

### XLIII On the Blackbird.

Their dried livers <note>original: "epateur siccut," likely *hepata siccata*</note> are given in a drink with a spoonful of hydromel <term>hydromel: a mixture of honey and water, often fermented or used as a medicinal base</term> for the neck of the bladder; it stops [pain or blockage].

### XLIIII.

If you open the chicks of the first brood <note>original: "pulli de fetu primariu," likely referring to swallows</note> during the first moon, you will find in them two stones: one well-formed and the other misshapen. Provided that they do not touch the ground, you should bind them in the skin of a calf or a deer and tie them to the neck or the left arm; this cures an epileptic <note>original: "epilenticus"</note> if he does this continuously. These chicks are also eaten like fig-peckers <note>original: "ficetulem," the *ficedula* or beccafico bird</term>. In short, the ashes of burnt swallows <note>original: "arundines," a corruption of *hirundines*</note>, when the powder is mixed with honey and used as an ointment, wipe away the mists of the eyes <note>original: "caligines oculoru"</note>. This also benefits those suffering from quinsy <note>original: "sinancicis," an old term for severe sore throat or tonsillitis</note> and calms the swelling of the uvula and throat. Especially if the burnt chicks themselves are drunk, they treat quinsy.

### XLV On the Hoopoe.

On the virtue of ivory <note>original: "de hebore," likely *ebore*</note>: Ivory has medicinal power... <note>The text here is fragmentary or corrupted: "sapaca"</note>.

### XLVI On the Ash

The burnt skull <note>original: "testu," likely *testa*</note> of a pig, burnt as long as it takes to turn from black to white, is ground and drunk; it treats swelling of the colon and torments <note>original: "torciones," likely griping pains or cramps</note> of the bladder.

### XLVII On Deer Horn.

Burnt, washed, and drunk in two spoonfuls, it is a very great remedy for those spitting blood <note>original: "emoptoicas"</note> and for dysentery <note>original: "desinterias" </note>. It is also a supreme remedy for those with colic <note>original: "celicer," likely *coeliacis*</note> and jaundice <note>original: "icterias"</note>. With tragacanth <term>tragacanth: a natural gum obtained from the dried sap of several species of Middle Eastern legumes</term>, it calms bladder pain and checks the [menstrual] flow of women. It is burnt in this way: you break it into small pieces and put them in a new cooking pot <note>original: "cacabo novo"</note>; covered and sealed with clay, you put it in the furnace as long as it takes to turn a white color. Thus it also heals <term>warts: "mirmiscen," likely *myrmecias*, small warts that feel like ant bites</term> of the hands and neck. It is beneficial for eye-salves <note>original: "collyria"</note> that wish to stop a discharge <note>original: "reuma"</note> and for wounds of the eyes. For teeth, it cleans them when applied as a tooth-powder <note>original: "denta fricaū," likely *dentifricium*</note>. By fumigation, the raw horn drives serpents far away. Boiled with vinegar and held [in the mouth], it mitigates the pains of the teeth.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of animal-based remedies from Book II. The previous page discussed avian parts (livers of blackbirds, swallow stones, and burnt swallows) and began a section on medicinal virtues of various creatures.</meta>

BOOK THE SECOND.

**XLVIII On worms: ground and anointed with oil, they do not allow the power of serpents** <note>original: "uim serpentū non admittunt," implying the mixture acts as a repellent or a protection against the venom/attacks of snakes.</note>. **XLVIIII On blister beetles.** <note>original: "cantaridib;" i.e., *cantharides* or Spanish flies.</note> Those collected from wheat are good for storage. These are put into a glass vessel <note>original: "ficale," likely a corruption of the Greek *phiale*</note>, and you tie a cloth over the top and place it over a cooking pot <term>cooking pot: *cacubum*, a deep vessel used for boiling</term> where vinegar is boiling. The vapor from the boiling vinegar kills those enclosed within, and afterwards they are better if threaded on a linen string; the variegated, thick, and long ones are best. **L On pine caterpillars.** <note>original: "psicocāpos," referring to *pityocampa*, the pine processionary caterpillar.</note> When placed on an earthenware lid and burnt, their power is caustic <term>caustic: "sapaca" in the text, a common corruption of *septicus* or *psotica*, meaning a substance that burns or corrodes the skin for medicinal purposes</term> and hot, [suited] for wounding; for this reason, they are mixed into medicines for cancers and those with leprosy or skin diseases <note>original: "fernosis," likely referring to scaly or inflammatory skin conditions</note>. They are a singular remedy for those with discharges and they regulate menstruation. **LI On the salamander.** The power of the salamander is caustic, wounding, and hot; it is rightly mixed with caustic medicines just like blister beetles. For the eyelashes, it removes hairs from the eyelids. It is preserved thus: you disembowel it and remove the head and the ends of the feet, then put it in honey and use it when you wish. **LII On house spiders.** Ground and applied in a compress <note>original: "pagellæ"</note> to the forehead or temples, or ground and tied on, they prevent fevers <note>original: "perfusionib;" likely referring to the "outpourings" or chills associated with fever fits</note>. Their web, when applied, stops the flow of blood and keeps wounds from swelling. **LIII On another kind of spider.** The kind that weaves a white web: if tied in leather and hung from the neck, it is a remedy for quartan fevers <term>quartan fever: a form of malaria where the fever recurs every four days</term>. Cooked with rose oil, it mitigates earaches. **LIIII On the lizard.** <note>original: "saura," from the Greek *saura* for lizard.</note> It is drunk with wine; it causes such a burning in the belly <note>original: "uentrē fistulat ignere"</note> that nothing can soothe the heat except lettuce seed drunk with water. ### LXIII. ON BUTTER

Its power is softening <term>malactica: a substance that softens tissues or relieves inflammation</term> and it relaxes the bowels. Furthermore, if drunk, it is an antidote to poisons. If oil is not available, butter mixed until soft assists with the teething of infants <note>original: "denatib. infantū," likely a corruption of "dentitionibus infantum," referring to the eruption of teeth</note>. It should be mixed into necessary poultices; it suppresses swollen wounds. It is given as a drink to remove itching of the head, and it cures itches and hysterical ulcerations <term>stericas: likely "hystericas," referring to conditions of the womb</term>. If, however, the butter is old or has a good aroma, it is effective against dysentery and "lientery" <term>lientery: a form of diarrhea where food passes through the body undigested</term> and for ulcerations of the colon, especially when applied with a cloth. It brings aid to healing wounds and takes away the pain of the nerves <term>neruorū: in ancient texts, this often refers to tendons and ligaments as well as nerves</term>. It is most useful for all sorts of things; it cleanses and fills in foul wounds, and it does not allow "proud flesh" <note>original: "superflue carnes," excess granulation tissue that hinders healing</note> to grow in wounds. It keeps the effects of snake bites at bay. In cooking, it may be mixed in place of oil, and it can be added to sweets instead of suet. 

A preparation is made from its smoke: one should put butter into a lamp instead of oil and collect the smoke <note>original: "fumu," referring here to the soot produced by the flame</note> in the same way we described for collecting the soot of frankincense. Its power is drying, like frankincense, for the eyes; it dries and fills wounds and leads scars of the eyes back to health.

### LXV. ON RAW WOOL

When burned, they also possess medicinal power.
