### LXXII ON HOG LARD

Hog lard and lamb fat are prepared in this way: you take fresh and very fatty lard, specifically the kind that is found around the meat, for this is better. Put it in cold rainwater and wash the lard <gloss>and again with the hands, again</gloss>. 
Knead it for a very long time with your hands and pour off the water. Knead it again. Afterwards, put it in a new pot <term>cacabo: a cooking pot or cauldron, usually made of bronze or earthenware</term>; put water in that pot and place it on the fire. Stir it frequently and melt it with the water. Strain the lard itself, and once strained, put it into cold water. Melt it again and put it in that same pot and cook it. When it has settled, pour it into a mortar. 

What remains of the fat... and sheep fat <term>uerbecina: fat specifically from a wether or castrated ram</term> is prepared thus <unclear>and sheep fat is prepared thus</unclear> sheep fat is prepared thus: take the aforementioned fat, cleaned and purified by the aforementioned method <note>The text uses "disciplina" to mean the rigorous step-by-step procedure</note>, and put it in a mortar bit by bit with water. Grind it and stir it with your hands for as long as it takes to achieve a snowy color. Strain it and take the aforementioned quantity and grind it without water. Cook it and store it. 

Beef fat <term>bubula: fat derived from cattle</term> is pounded in a circle <note>likely referring to a circular motion in the mortar</note> with a sprinkling of seawater. Put it in a new pot with the aforementioned water and cook it until its flavor <note>original: "sapore," referring here to the heavy, raw smell of the fat</note> changes. Afterward, for each pound of lard, add four pounds of resinous wax <note>original: "ceretar rēn. ice," likely a corruption of "ceratum resinice"</note> and let it be cooked and strained so that the residue remains. Put it in another pot and place it in the sun until its color is different. 

Bull fat <term>taurina: fat from a bull, considered stronger than other cattle fat</term> is prepared thus: take the aforementioned fat and wash it in a river. Once washed, put it in a pot and cook it until it boils. First, pour off the water, and afterward put the fat itself in a mortar with clear water. Lift it out while stirring with your hands. Pour off the water and do the same a second time. Grind it, and again in the pot with water...

## On Marrows
### On all kinds of marrows
**Deer marrow** is best; after this, **calf marrow**, third is **bull marrow**, then **goat marrow**, and fifth is **sheep marrow**. However, these should be collected in autumn when they are still bloody and the bones themselves are brittle at that time. You should only trust the marrow when you have extracted it yourself from a broken bone, for many deceptions <note>original: "inposturae", referring to fraudulent substitutions by suppliers</note> are practiced. The healing power of all marrows is warming, softening, and helpful for <note>original: "latoria", likely referring to "lavatoria" or cleansing properties</note> pleurisy and wounds. Anointed with **deer marrow**, it drives away all wild pests <note>original: "beraariū", likely "bestiaria", referring to venomous creatures or vermin</note>; you shall prepare and store it just as you do with fats. **LXXVI**

## On All Kinds of Bile
All <term>bile: also called gall, this bitter fluid from the liver was a staple of ancient pharmacy</term> should be stored in this way: once taken, you tie it at its neck and submerge it in boiling hot water; and if it seems <unclear>bad</unclear>, you lift it out and dry it in a humid place—it is essential for the eyes. You shall collect bile thus: take the bile fresh and, once tied, submerge it in a jar of honey. The power of all biles is cleansing and burning, but in some, this power is greater or lesser. Great power is found in the bile of sea-creatures for the body... for a man to fish. The bile of the Atlantic mackerel <note>original: "colia", likely the "colias" or Spanish mackerel</note> and its sea-kin should be extracted with wine. Also the bile of the **peacock**, the **capon**, the **fallow deer**, and the **roe deer** in...
<margin>or which are mixed at other times.</margin>

### LXXVI ON OX DUNG

The dung of grazing **oxen**, when applied fresh, takes away the swelling of wounds. ### LXXVIII ON HUMAN URINE.

Anyone drinking their own **urine** is healed from the venom of a **viper** bite; it is beneficial to be drunk against poisons. It cures **dropsy** <term>dropsy: an old term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid in the body</term> in its early stages.

<margin>for leprosy</margin> It cures the stings of the **sea-dragon** <note>original: "acant," likely referring to the *acanthias*</note> and sea scorpions. **Dog urine** with **nitrum** <term>nitrum: a naturally occurring mineral soda or saltpeter</term> added, once the medicine is made, removes **leprosy** <note>original: "lebras," often used broadly for scaly skin diseases</note> and **itches** <note>original: "plurigines"</note>.

Old **human urine** cures **dandruff** <term>furfures: literally "bran-like" scales on the head</term>, scalp sores, **scabies**, and spreading wounds when used as a treatment. It also removes rot, <unclear>ground</unclear> substances, and pustules of the ears, and expels worms from the ears. 

If the dried rind of a **pomegranate** is boiled in the urine of a prepubescent boy and drunk, it cures **orthopnea** <term>orthopnea: a condition where a person has difficulty breathing unless standing or sitting upright</term>. When cooked with honey in a bronze vessel and smeared on, it heals wounds and the **gums**. It removes dimness of the eyes. When placed and cooked in copper vessels, it is used to solder gold. That which <note>The text here describes urine's effect on fire or heated copper, likely as a cooling agent or for tempering</note> falls into the vessel, it checks the sharp fire. **Goat urine** cooked in a vessel soothes; when added to a **pessary** <term>pessary: a medicinal substance inserted into the vagina</term> and applied, it cures **hysterical pain** <note>original: "dolori stericos," referring to pains believed to originate in the womb</note>; it also removes itches from wounds of the eyes.

# ON HONEY.

Good honey is that which is called **Attic** <note>original: "adacū," referring to the famous honey of Athens</note>, and from the *Insiditia* <note>possibly a corruption of a place name or "isidiana"</note>, and Sicilian honey, and that which is called **Hyblaean** <note>honey from the Hyblaean Mountains in Sicily, renowned in antiquity</note>. It is good, sweet to the sight, smell, and use; it is very thick yet liquid and strong, so that when you stir it with a finger, it rises up high. Its power is **astringent** <note>original: "astica," likely "styptica"</note> and **opening** <note>original: "nastomatica," likely "anastomotica," meaning it opens the pores or vessels</note>. It draws out humors and is beneficial for foul wounds. When cooked and applied, it fills up hollow [sores]. For **parotid swellings** <note>original: "paracolesis," a corruption of "parotidas," swellings of the glands near the ear</note> and wounds, it is effective when cooked with liquid **alum** <term>alum: a mineral salt used as an astringent to stop bleeding or dry out wounds</term>. When smeared on, it removes **rashes** <note>original: "ernas," possibly referring to "herpetas" (spreading sores) or "lichenas" (skin eruptions)</note> and cures lice and nits. Cooked with salt, it takes away the ringing of **tinnitus** <note>original: "tritoni sonus"</note> and ear pains. It causes the flesh to grow back on circumcised parts. 81

Smeared on with herbs, it clears the dimness of the eyes. Used as a **gargle** <note>original: "gurgarrismo"</note>, it cures wounds of the throat and **quinsy** <term>quinsy: a severe, painful swelling or abscess in the throat</term>. It promotes urination, softens the bowels, and is beneficial for those coughing. It counteracts poisonous bites and assists those who have drunk **meconium** <term>meconium: the juice of the poppy, or opium</term>, especially if it is drunk with warm water and rose oil. It also helps those who have eaten [poisonous] **fungi** <note>original: "fungor"</note>. It is most healthful for the bites of **mad dogs** <note>referring to rabies</note>, whether it is drunk or eaten. It also relieves bloating <insert>and</insert> and softens the bowels. 

Therefore, honey should be used **skimmed** <note>original: "dispumatū," referring to the removal of the surface scum/froth</note>. Spring honey is immediately better; winter honey is thick and less effective. Soon, if the honey has been in the comb, it will become like stone, which many call *olicorum* <note>the meaning of this term is unclear; it may refer to granulated or crystallized honey</note>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of honey’s varieties and medicinal uses, specifically focusing on bitter Sardinian honey and the substance known as "saccarum" (sugar), before moving into Chapter 82 on the properties and preparation of beeswax.</meta>

Sardinian honey <note>original: "mel sardonico"</note> is bitter because the bees themselves feed on **wormwood** <note>original: "absenzio"; a bitter herb famously used in medicine and spirits like absinthe</note>. It is effective for treating wounds and bruises on the face. It is produced in Heraclea and Pontus <note>regions along the Black Sea in modern-day Turkey</note> because good flowers grow there. If a **frenetic** person <term>frenetic: someone suffering from "phrenitis," a state of acute delirium or feverish madness</term> eats it, they will be overcome by sweats. These aids can be syrupy and salty; when eaten, they activate its medicinal power. It provokes sneezing when applied to the nostrils. It cures small wounds on the body, especially if this juice is mixed with salt; this mixture also removes bruises.

Another kind is produced which is called **sugar** <term>saccarum: a term used by ancient writers for a medicinal, honey-like substance found on canes, likely an early form of cane sugar</term>. It is a species of thick honey found in India and Arabia. It is found in fragile canes and, when placed in the mouth, it is like salt. It is truly beneficial for the stomach and for relaxing the bowels. If drunk, it remedies pains of the bladder and **kidney disease** <note>original: "neusrecia," likely a corruption of "nephritica"</note>.

### LXXXII ON WAX 

Good wax is reddish and fatty, having the scent of honey. Clean wax comes from Pontus and Crete. To make white wax from the red variety, put it in a new **cooking pot** <note>original: "cacabo"</note> with seawater. When it has melted, sprinkle it with ground **nitre** <term>nitre: a naturally occurring mineral salt (natron) used here as a bleaching agent</term>. After it has boiled two or three times, remove it from the heat. When it has cooled, take it out of the pot and purge away any dross or filth. Do this a second time. While it is boiling, place the bottom of a broken pot or something similar in the water so the wax is fully drenched. Then, place the wax in the sun, kept moist with water; the exposure to the open air creates a white color. It makes the wax much whiter than any other method. If placed upon herbs, it retains its **virtue** <term>virtue: the inherent medicinal power or "strength" of a substance</term> for a long time. 

<margin>Fatty wax has a second virtue; this is how wax ought to be whitened.</margin>

All waxes are **warming** <term>thermantica: substances that produce a feeling of heat in the body</term> and **softening** <note>original: "sclerotica"; while this usually means "hardening," in this medical context it likely refers to the treatment of hard swellings or is a corruption of "malactica" (softening)</note>. It is mixed into many remedies. For those with **dysentery** <term>dysentery: severe diarrhea with the passage of mucus and blood</term>, it can be taken in the form of grains the size of pitch-drops. It also dissolves curdled milk in the breasts. 83

# ON PROPOLIS.
Bee-glue <note>original: "propoli"</note> is effective when it is reddish and fragrant like **storax** <note>a fragrant resin from the *Styrax* tree, used in perfumes and medicine</note>. <gloss>and</gloss> It should be of such quality that you can pull it with your hands as you would with storax. It has a **hot** and **epispastic** <term>epispastic: a substance that draws out fluids or foreign objects by causing a mild irritation or blister</term> quality—that is, it is "drawing." It extracts things fixed in the body. When its smoke is inhaled with the mouth positioned over it, it cures old coughs and remedies scabs. This substance is found in the vessels of bees, where the bees seal their hives <note>original: "corpora frigunt," likely a corruption for sealing or reinforcing the hive structure</note>.

# ON WHEAT.
Wheat <note>original: "triticu"</note> is effective when fresh for treating dryness. There is also the variety known as "gnawed" <note>original: "adrosus"</note> and that which is called **three-month wheat** <note>original: "trimino"; a type of spring wheat that matures in three months</note>. Starch <note>original: "amula"</note>, if it is cleaned in this way, chewed raw and applied to the site, cures dog bites. Bread made from **fine flour** <note>original: "simila"; the highest quality white flour</note> adds more nourishment <note>original: "sucum"; literally "juice" or "essence"</note> to the body than that made from other grains. Similarly, flour from **siligo** <note>a variety of soft white wheat</note>, when henbane <note>original: "iosquiami"</note> juice is added and it is applied as a **poultice** <term>cataplasma: a soft, moist mass of herbs or flour applied to the body to relieve soreness and inflammation</term>, calms pains in the nerves.

Mixed with **oxymel** <term>oxymel: a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</term>, it removes bloating and clears freckles. Its bran <note>original: "furfore"</note>, when boiled with vinegar, removes leprosy <note>in this period, "lepra" often referred to various scaly skin diseases rather than just Hansen’s disease</note>. When applied, it calms every kind of swelling. Boiled with **rue** <note>a bitter medicinal herb</note>, it disperses swellings of the breasts. It heals poisonous bites and, when warmed, provides relief for cramps.

Its leaven has a drawing and hot quality; it disperses swellings of the soles of the feet and clears small pustules on the body. When barley salt is added, it is helpful. **Wheat starch** <note>original: "farini stiticma"</note> boiled with vinegar or wine into a paste <note>original: "gluten"</note>, when eaten, helps those suffering from **hemoptysis** <term>hemoptysis: the coughing up of blood from the respiratory tract</term>. For those with a cough, it is the greatest protection; when boiled with **mint** and **butter**, it soothes the roughness of the windpipes <note>original: "arteriarum"</note>. Its fine dust <note>original: "poliner"</note>, when cooked with honey, disperses swellings. If infused raw in water and strained, and mixed with cold things, it cures heat-related conditions.

## ON BARLEY

Barley <note>original: "ordeo"</note> is good if it is snow-white and clean; however, it adds as much gas <note>original: "venti"</note> to the body as wheat can. But the **barley-groats** <term>pulenta: a traditional porridge or flour made from toasted barley</term> made from it, and the gruel <note>original: "sucum"; literally "juice"</note> made from it, are better for use. It cures roughness of the windpipe <note>original: "arteriarium"</note> and tempers viscous and harsh humors. Indeed, wheat gruel is useful to the body and is a **diuretic**; it promotes milk in women when cooked with fennel seed and certainly provides relief for the swelling of the juices, yet it remains digestible. When drunk, it calms bubbling **pustules** <note>original: "papellae"</note> on the body. Barley flour cooked with **chicory** <note>original: "ecaria"; likely a corruption of cichorea</note> and **mead** <note>original: "mulsa"; honey-water</note>, when applied, disperses all tumors and hardnesses. With resin and pitch added, the smoke <note>original: "sumum"</note> benefits the colon in all cases of hardness. **Melilot** <note>a sweet clover</note> and poppy applied in the same way remove pain in the side <note>likely pleurisy</note> and benefit swellings, especially if it has been cooked with walnut and **rue** <note>original: "noce-ruta"</note> and fenugreek. With liquid pitch and wax added, as well as oil, this mixture, once cooked and applied, brings **scrofula** <term>scrofuas: a swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck, often associated with tuberculosis</term> to health. By dispersing it with myrtle oil, wine, pomegranate rind <note>original: "sidia"</note>, and bramble, it may restrain a flux of the belly <note>original: "reumatismā ventris"</note>. When applied with quince and cooked with vinegar, it disperses the swelling of **gout** <note>original: "podagrae"</term>. Cooked with vinegar and <unclear>ui sado</unclear> and applied, it helps lepers. The flour itself, applied after being soaked in water and cooked with liquid pitch and oil, causes abscesses to ripen <note>original: "matureseere facit"</note>. And cooked with hard pitch, it restrains the discharge of the joints; the juice of the groats is also accepted raw...

## 85 ON BRAN

Bran <note>original: "Furfa"; usually *furfur*</note> is made from barley. It acts as a **diuretic** <term>diuretic: a substance that encourages the passing of urine</term>, but it is contrary to the chest. It inflates the stomach membranes <note>original: "meningis"</note> more than the grain itself, and it nourishes a viscous humor. From this, a decoction is made which is called "infused barley," which some call **beer** <note>original: "camum"; a type of grain-based ale known in central Europe</note>. They use this as a stimulant <note>original: "ustimula"; likely *oestimula*</note>, though it provokes headaches and is a **malignant condition** <note>original: "cacoetnu"; from the Greek *cacoethes*</note> that is contrary to the nerves. Indeed, regarding wheat, similar fermented drinks <note>original: "fucata les"; likely *curmi* or ale</note> are made, especially in Iberia <note>original: "iniberit"</note> and in Britain.

## 86 ON SPELT

Of Spelt <note>original: "Zia"; from the Greek *zea*, likely emmer or einkorn</note> there are two kinds: one is **einkorn** <note>original: "monococcum"</note>, which has a single grain, and the second indeed has two grains joined together. From this food, bread is made which has less strength than barley but more than wheat.

## 87 ON CRITHON

**Crithon** <note>original: "Critmo"; a grain preparation or groats</note> is prepared from spelt and wheat, from which porridges are usually made. By its virtue, it benefits the stomach and adds a digestible juice to the body; it is very good for the belly, especially if the grains are prepared roasted.

## 88 ON OLYRA

**Olyra** <note>original: "Olera"; a type of grain similar to spelt</note> is born from the same source as spelt, but it is more beneficial when eaten as leavened bread.

## 88 ON ATHERA

**Athera** <note>a type of thick grain pap or gruel</note> is made from the fine flour of spelt. It is cooked with water until it reaches the consistency of a paste <note>original: "fucus"</note>. It is very good for feeding infants and is also used in poultices. It is made from un-toasted barley flour <note>original: "indepulenta"</note>. To make it from ground spelt: take one pound of spelt and add enough burnt **gypsum** <note>mineral plaster used here to help strip the husks</note>. Put it in a mortar and pound it lightly; then pass it through a fine sieve so that all the grit and gypsum are removed. It must be pounded gently so that the gypsum settles to the bottom of the mortar.

## 90 ON TRAGUM

**Tragum** <note>original: "Tragu"; a type of coarse grain groat</note> is similar to **chondrus** <term>chondrus: a refined groat or gruel made from emmer wheat</term>, but it fills the stomach just as spelt does. It softens the belly and is a **diuretic**...

## XCI ON OATS

**Oats** <note>original: "Bromos"</note> are reed-like. It rises like wheat and has leaves similar to wheat. Above, two seeds are joined where it has the most seed; the seed is used for **poultices** <term>poultice: a soft, moist mass of material, typically of plant material or flour, applied to the body to relieve soreness and inflammation</term>. Just as barley porridges made from it bind the belly, the juice is also made and drunk for a cough; it heals.

## XCII ON RICE

**Rice** <note>original: "Oridia"; likely a corruption of *Oryza*</note> is a species that grows in damp and watery places. It is **good for the stomach** <term>eustomica: beneficial for digestion or the stomach</term> and dries out the humidity of the head; it binds the belly.

## XCIII ON GROATS

**Groats** <note>original: "Condros"</note> are made from double-grain spelt <note>original: "gemina zia"</note>. It is good for the stomach, fills out the flesh, and binds the belly. It is used as a poultice with vinegar or wine for **leprosy** <note>original: "leprae"; in this context, likely refers to scaly skin conditions</note>; it also removes leprous nails. Applied at the onset, it cures **eye abscesses** <term>egilopia: a fistula or ulcer in the inner corner of the eye</term>. The juice, when administered as a suppository, cures dysenteric pains.

## XCIIII ON MILLET

Bread made from **millet** <note>original: "milio"</note> during illness binds the belly and provokes urine. Millet, roasted and placed in a small bag <note>original: "sacello"</note> and applied, calms griping and pains of the belly.

## XCV ON PANIC GRASS

**Panic grass** <note>original: "Panicum"</note> is weak as a food for everyone. Bread made from it and eaten binds the belly and provokes urine. Roasted in a pot and placed in a small bag, it is beneficial just as millet is.

## XCVI ON ELYMUS

**Elymus** <note>original: "Elimo"</note>, which some call *meline*, is a species of grain similar to millet. Bread made from it and eaten can do all the things mentioned above, but it is less effective at binding the belly.

## XCVII ON SESAME

**Sesame** <note>original: "Sesamu"</note> is **bad for the stomach** <term>cacostomacu: causing stomach distress or poor digestion</term>. When eaten, it causes bad breath. Used as a poultice, it settles the hardness of nerves and ailments. Prepared with food and applied, it is beneficial; it heals burns and, when taken, soothes swelling. Mixed with rose oil and wheat, it protects against headaches caused by heat; that is, the herb itself can also be used in wine.

### XCVIII ON DARNEL
<margin>conception</margin>
**Darnel** <note>original: "Lolium"</note>, as I say below, has a power when used in **poultices** <term>poultice: a soft, moist mass of plant material applied to the body to relieve inflammation</term> such that it can cleanse the decay of wounds; it restrains spreading wounds by consuming them. It removes **cancers** <note>original: "cancros"; in ancient texts, this often refers to any spreading, malignant-looking ulcer</note> when mixed with radishes and salts. Applied with bitter whey <margin>for leprosy</margin> it corrects **leprosy** <note>original: "lepra"; likely referring to scaly skin conditions</note>. If mixed with native sulfur, linseed, and pigeon dung, and cooked in wine and applied, it disperses **scrofula** <term>scrofula: a swelling of the lymph nodes, typically in the neck</term>, softens hard tumors, and breaks open abscesses. Cooked with **honeyed water** <note>original: "mulsa"</note> and applied, it cures sciatic pains. Or, if burned and mixed with saffron and used as a **fumigant** <term>fumigant: a medicinal smoke or vapor</term> from below, it makes women conceive more quickly.

### XCVIII ON STARCH
**Starch** <note>original: "Amilum"</note> is so named from the fact that the Greeks call mills *mylos* <note>original: "milos"</note>. Indeed, it is made without a mill. It is a substance made from winter wheat, or from Cretan or Egyptian wheat. The wheat is taken, washed, and soaked in good water; this is done carefully, and by night the water is changed until it becomes soft. It makes a better liquid if rubbed by hand, and when it has liquified, it is placed in the sun to be warmed, but it should not have much water when the liquid settles. It is used to treat **rheum** <term>rheum: a watery discharge from the mucous membranes, especially the eyes</term> of the eyes; it nourishes wounds, fills eye cavities, and removes roughness of the eyes. It is drunk for those spitting blood and is a singular protection. It softens roughness of the **arteries** <note>original: "arariarum," likely a corruption of *arteriarum*, referring to the windpipe or throat</note>. Mixed with raisins and dates, it is made into a confection. From the flour of **spelt** <note>original: "ziem"</note>, poured out and made similarly for one or two days, it is pressed by hand like **lard** <note>original: "absungia"</note> and dried in the sun. This starch is effective for these medical matters and for all the rest.

# 7 G ON FENUGREEK FLOUR
**Fenugreek flour** <note>original: "Farina fenigreci"</note>, which some call *mula bucerona*, *litezoceras*, *corfas*, *doto*, or *ceratedion* <note>these names are Latinized versions of various Greek synonyms for fenugreek, such as "boukeras" or "keratidion"</note>, has a **softening** <term>softening: "emaleptica" in Latin, referring to substances that soothe or reduce inflammation</term> power. It is used in **poultices** <term>poultice: a soft, moist mass of plant material applied to the body</term> with **honeyed water** <note>original: "mulsa"; a mixture of honey and water</note> to suppress both internal and external tumors by dispersing them, especially when nitre and vinegar are added. Applied as a plaster, it thins a swollen spleen. Its juice is used as a **fomentation** <term>fomentation: the application of warm, medicinal liquids to the body</term> for tumors and contractions of the **womb** <note>original: "matrices"</note>. It cleanses the hair of the head and keeps it clear of impurities. Its juice, mixed with goose fat, is added to a **pessary** <term>pessary: a medicinal substance inserted into the vagina</term> to <gloss> relax </gloss> <gloss> the </gloss> <note>original glosses "la ma" likely standing for "laxat matricem"</note> hardness of the womb.

# 7 C I ON LINSEED
**Linseed** <note>flaxseed</note> has a similar nature to fenugreek; it softens hardnesses just as fenugreek does. Mixed with oil and honeyed water and applied raw with nitre and ash, it prevents **uvulas** <note>the fleshy hangings at the back of the throat</note> from swelling. It can disperse all kinds of hardnesses. When applied with wine, it removes "spider" sores <note>original: "araneus"; likely referring to web-like skin lesions or small ulcers</note>. Mixed with **cardamom** and honey, it cleanses leprous nails. With honey added, it is useful for the chest, as it cleanses phlegm and heals a cough. Taken with honey and pepper, it stimulates sexual desire. If the juice is taken just like fenugreek, it serves as a fomentation that drives away pains of the womb.

# 7 C II ON CHICKPEAS
<margin> ... </margin> **Chickpeas**, when eaten, provoke urine, soften the belly, and cause flatulence. They produce a good skin color, bring on menstruation, and, when eaten by a woman, help to expel the embryo. A poultice made with foreign vinegar treats tumors of the testes, boils, skin eruptions, sores, cancers, and malignant **scabies** <note>a contagious, itchy skin condition</note>; it heals most healthfully when mixed with honey.

Another kind, which they call *grius* <note>original: "grius", likely from the Greek "krios" (ram), referring to the ram-head shaped chickpea</note>, has a power similar to the one above. A decoction of these, taken with **frankincense** <note>original: "libano"</note> <margin> % </margin> and used as a suppository, cures internal pains and the bites of venomous creatures, and it softens the belly.

### ON THE BEAN
**The bean** <note>original: "faba"; the broad bean or fava bean</note>, when eaten, causes flatulence, is hard to digest, and produces disturbing dreams. Mixed with wine, it treats cataracts and redness of the eyes; it checks these conditions with the healing power of the wine. Crushed by the teeth and applied to the forehead, it stops the flow of fluid to the eyes. For swelling of the **testicles**, if you apply it with wine, it relieves the weight of the testicles. Its skin, when cooked and applied as a poultice, corrects white spots on the skin. Used as a rub in the baths, it makes the hair thin. Mixed with oil and applied to the belly as a poultice, it helps with **scrofula** <term>scrofula: a form of tuberculosis affecting the lymph nodes of the neck</term> and stops the flow of blood.

# CXIII ON THE EGYPTIAN BEAN
**The Egyptian bean** <note>original: "Faba aegiptiaca"; likely referring to the *Nelumbo nucifera* or Sacred Lotus, which was known to the ancients as a type of bean</note> is called *mula pole acon* <note>this name appears to be a corrupted transcription of a Greek or local synonym</note>; it grows abundantly in Egypt. In Asia, it grows mostly in stagnant canals and marshes. It has very wide leaves and bears rose-colored flowers. As soon as it has flowered, leaves emerge from its center where there is a certain roundness; there, its pods grow. The flowers themselves are called *cuanoi* <note>original: "cuanoi," from the Greek *kyanos*, meaning dark blue or lapis-colored</note>. According to the method of cultivation, they are said to be sown in a particular way: it is their custom to make molds out of clay. They enclose the seed itself in these and place them so that they may grow. The root is much thicker than a reed; when cooked, it is eaten and is called *cocolocarea* <term>cocolocarea: a corruption of *colocasia*, the edible rhizome of the lotus or taro</term>. Its seed is eaten both dry and green, and is black in color.

### 106. ON THE LUPINE

The lupine <term>lupine: a legume of the genus *Lupinus*, widely cultivated in antiquity for its protein-rich seeds, which required soaking to remove bitter toxins</term> is known to all our people. Its flour, when eaten with honey or drunk with vinegar, expels intestinal worms <term>lumbrias: parasitic worms such as roundworms</term>. Boiled and bitter lupine, when eaten, provides the same benefit, and its water can do the same when drunk. If rue and pepper are added and the water is drunk, it heals those with spleen ailments <note>original: "spleneticos"; referring to disorders of the spleen, often linked to "melancholy" in ancient medicine</note>. Used as a fomentation, it is a singular defense against cancerous growths, poisonous bites, and scabies <term>scabies: a contagious skin disease caused by mites, resulting in intense itching</term>. When applied, it allows bad spots, bruises, and pimples <term>papulas: small, inflammatory elevations of the skin</term> to clear from the body. Its flour, mixed with honey and used as a suppository with myrrh <note>original: "musra"; likely a corruption of *myrrha*</note>, induces menstruation and causes abortion. Mixed with pearl barley, vinegar, and water and applied, it disperses tumors, causes scrofula <term>scrofula: a swelling of the lymph nodes, usually in the neck</term> to mature <note>meaning: to "bring to a head" or ripen an abscess so it can drain</note>, and is beneficial for carbuncles <term>carbuncle: a severe, multi-headed boil or skin infection</term>. Boiled with rainwater, it makes the face bright <note>original: "lipidos"; likely a corruption of *lepidos*, meaning charming or clear</note>. Cooked in dregs of oil <note>original: "anigre"; a corruption of *amurca*, the watery, bitter sediment left over from olive oil production</note>, it heals scabies in everyone. The root of the lupine is a diuretic <term>diuretic: a substance that increases the production of urine</term>, as are sweetened lupines. It removes foulness from the stomach and heals indigestion. The wild variety <note>original: "d'agrestis"; the *Lupinus angustifolius* or similar wild species</note> acts similarly, though it is quite small; being very bitter, it is effective enough for what it needs to do.

### 107. HERE BEGINS THE SECTION ON GARDEN VEGETABLES

The turnip <term>turnip: *Brassica rapa*, a root vegetable valued for both its bulb and its greens</term> is good, but it causes wind and bloating. Its juice benefits the body and stimulates the bowels. A fomentation of its decoction is a defense against gout <term>gout: a form of inflammatory arthritis caused by uric acid crystals</term> and chilblains. The root itself, crushed and applied, is known to do all these things. Its tops <note>original: "cima"; the young, edible flowering shoots of the turnip</note>, boiled and eaten, <insert>X heal stubborn pustules with vinegar and, when applied as a poultice, are helpful for scrofula.</insert>

### 108. ON THE WILD TURNIP

Wild turnip <term>Rapa agrestis: likely a species of wild brassica or field mustard</term> grows in dry places. It has a [distinct] color and is used in whitening agents made for the face or the whole body, suited for clearing skin blemishes <note>original: "aptum ad frigum mentis uultus"; likely a corruption referring to facial treatments or pigments</note>; it is mixed with lupine flour, bean flour, and vinegar.

### 109. ON BUNIAS, ALSO KNOWN AS THE FRENCH TURNIP

The bunias <term>Bunia: a type of turnip, likely *Brassica napus*</term> and the French turnip have the same power. Its root is preserved. It fills out wasting flesh <note>referring to its nutritive properties for emaciated patients</note>. Its seed counteracts poisons that have been consumed and is mixed into antidotes. Its root is preserved just as we described preserving the turnip.

## 111. ON SKIRRET
Skirret <term>Sifarum: likely *Sium sisarum*, also known as water-parsnip or skirret</term> <note>The chapter heading "Desideria" in the original may be a scribal error or a corruption of a vernacular name</note> is known to everyone. When eaten, it is good for the stomach. Its root, when boiled and eaten, is diuretic and removes nausea <note>original: "fastidium"; a lack of appetite or aversion to food</note>.

## 112. ON DOCK
There are two kinds of dock <term>Lapatium: plants of the genus *Rumex*, including common dock and sorrel</term>: one that is eaten [as a vegetable], and another called *oxylapathi* <term>oxylapathi: "sharp dock," referring to its acidic taste or pointed leaves</term>. It grows in damp and harsh places. It is better when it grows in hard soil, with the tips of its leaves being sharp. The third type is wild and smaller than the good kinds, resembling plantain; it spreads across the ground and is softer. The fourth kind of dock is what they call *milo zendu* <note>a vernacular or corrupted Greek name</note>, or *anasireda*, or simply dock.

Its leaves are similar to wild dock or *oxylapathi*. When drunk with wine and water, it is a great remedy for dysentery, for clearing the stomach, and for the sting of a scorpion. When drunk [infused in] half-boiled wine, it provides protection against scorpion stings.

The root of these plants, whether cooked or raw, applied as a poultice <term>cataplasm: a soft, moist mass of herbal material applied to the skin</term>, treats leprosy and scabs <note>original: "fernis"; likely referring to impetigo or similar skin eruptions</note>. It is similarly beneficial for leprous nails; however, one should first vigorously rub the affected areas with nitre <term>nitre: a naturally occurring mineral salt used as a cleansing agent</term> and vinegar.

A decoction <note>the liquid resulting from boiling the plant</note> used as a warm compress <term>fomentation: the application of heat and moisture to the body to relieve pain</term> or in baths removes itching of the body. It mitigates earaches. Boiled in wine and used as a gargle, it checks the pain of teeth. When boiled in wine and applied as a poultice, it disperses scrofulous swellings <term>scrofa: a swelling of the lymph nodes, often in the neck</term>. Cooked with vinegar and applied, it reduces an enlarged spleen. In the same way, its roots tied and hung around the neck prevent scrofula from developing and restrain the flow of blood in women <note>likely referring to excessive menstrual flow or uterine bleeding</note>.

## 114. NIPPLEWORT

## 115. ON BLITE

## 116. ON MALLOW
Mallow <term>Malua: plants of the genus *Malva*, known for their soothing mucilage</term> is better than these [others], and the wild variety is specifically good for the stomach. It softens the belly and especially heals the vessels of the intestines and the internal organs. Its raw leaves, applied as poultices <term>cataplasma: a soft, moist mass of herbs applied to the body</term> with a little salt and hyssop, are curative. It works for bee stings if the body is anointed with its raw juice; one may also mix in oil with milk. Boiled and applied as poultices, it removes scales and dandruff from the head. Its leaves, cooked and applied with a little oil, help with burns and "sacred fire" <note>original: "igni agro"; likely *ignis sacer* or erysipelas, a painful skin infection</note>. A decoction of it is used as a fomentation for uterine softening <note>original: "malopaciae... matrias"; likely referring to *malakia*, a softening or disorder of the womb</note>; it is applied as a warm soak for "bites" <note>cramps or sharp pains</note> in the intestines and the womb. It is also inserted as a suppository for the womb when necessary. Mallow boiled with its roots in a broth <note>original: "muscello"; a meat or vegetable broth</note> aids those who have been poisoned; if drunk frequently, it relieves the bite of the venomous spider <term>spalangion: a term used for various venomous spiders or harvestmen</term>. It stimulates milk in [nursing] women. The seed of wild mallow, when drunk with wine, soothes pain in the internal organs.

# 118. DE COLICULA HORTINO
# ON GARDEN CABBAGE

Garden Cabbage <term>Colicula hortino: likely *Brassica oleracea*, known as colewort or cabbage</term>, when thoroughly boiled, greatly softens the belly; however, if it is boiled twice <note>original: "si foras elixa" is likely a corruption of "si bis elixa"; ancient authors like Pliny noted that cabbage boiled once is a laxative, but boiled twice it becomes astringent</note>, it binds the belly, especially if it is eaten in warm broth <note>original: "anere caldo," likely *iure caldo*</note>. It is hard on the stomach <term>cacostomachus: a substance that causes indigestion or an upset stomach</term>. Those varieties which grow in Egypt are sticky and bitter; if eaten, they clear away mists from the eyes. They benefit those with consumption <term>phthisis: a historical term for a wasting disease, usually pulmonary tuberculosis</term> when eaten raw, and they prevent drunkenness at banquets <note>Cabbage was famously used in the Roman world as a preventative or cure for the effects of wine</note>. Its foliage is good for the stomach <term>eustomachon: an agent that promotes healthy digestion and appetite</term> and is a diuretic. When drunk with wine, it treats venomous bites. 

Mixed with fenugreek meal and vinegar, it is beneficial for gout <term>podagra: a painful form of arthritis, often in the big toe</term> and joint pain. It is a help for foul wounds. Its juice is added to various medicines; it cleanses the head. When mixed with iris <note>original: "siris," likely referring to the Iris root</note> meal and applied, it brings down the menses. Its leaves, whether raw and pounded or cooked as a poultice, are applied to lepers <margin>for lepers</margin>. It checks "sacred fire" <term>ignis sacer: "sacred fire," a historical term for skin inflammations like erysipelas or shingles</term> and similarly aids those with leprosy. When mixed with salt, it treats carbuncles <term>carbunculus: a cluster of protein-rich boils or a severe skin infection</term>. It treats thinning hair <note>original: "fluentib. capillis"</note>. Eaten raw with vinegar, it helps those with spleen issues. Its juice, if chewed and swallowed, clears an impeded voice. The decoction, when drunk, softens the belly and brings down the menses. Its flowers, ground and applied after childbirth, are said to assist in further conception. Cabbage seed is given to the sick to expel intestinal worms. Mixed with fat <note>original: "apati doti," likely a corruption of *adipi*</note>, it clears the complexion and removes skin scales <note>original: "lepagines," likely referring to lichen or scaly skin conditions</note>. The stalks of the cabbage, burned to ash and applied with old pig lard, take away pains in the side <note>likely referring to pleurisy</note>.

### 120. ON THE SEA-HERB
<note>The original heading "OLICYTOMANIMO" is a corruption, likely referring to *Helichrysum* or a variety of *Polygonum* (knotgrass)</note>

### 121. ON THE BEET

**B**eet is of two kinds: white and black. Black beet, when boiled and given, stops the bowels <note>Acts as an astringent</note>, especially if it is cooked with lentils. White beet, however, softens the belly. But both, when cooked, nourish the humors of the stomach. Its juice is harmful if poured into the nostrils, but when mixed with honey, it cleanses the head. When poured into the ears, it soothes pain. 

With its roots slowly boiled, it makes a cleansing wash <term>fomento: a warm, medicinal soak or compress</term> that is beneficial for snake bites. The raw leaves, when applied as a poultice <term>cataplasma: a soft, moist mass of herbs applied to the body</term>, clear away spots when rubbed with soda <note>original: "sanctitro," a corruption of *spuma nitri* (nitre/soda) used for skin conditions</note>. For those suffering from hair loss <term>lopicur: a corruption of *alopecia*</term>, an application previously prepared with hair-restoring ingredients will restore the hair. It checks spreading wounds <note>original: "pascentia uulnera," likely referring to gangrenous or "eating" ulcers</note>. Its raw leaves in a poultice turn black scars back to their natural color. When applied, it also cools "sacred fire" <term>ignem sacrum: a historical term for Erysipelas, a painful skin infection caused by streptococcus</term>.

### 122. ON ORACH
<note>original: "ANDRAFAXIS," from the Greek *andraphaxis*, commonly known as Orach or Mountain Spinach</note>

Orach has a soothing quality. When applied as a poultice with meal, it takes away headaches. It is a necessary remedy for swellings of the eyes. Applied to the stomach, it removes inflammation. Its seed heals those with kidney disease <term>neofreaci: a corruption of *nephritici*</term>. The leaves, crushed and applied, check "wild fire" <note>another term for *ignis sacer* or skin inflammation</note>. If the leaves are eaten, they cleanse bladder pain; similarly, they cut through the "rheum" <term>reuma: a discharge of fluid or mucus</term> of the stomach and prevent a loose belly. It is also beneficial for acute fevers, stops the spitting of blood, and aids those with dysentery.

### 123. ON ASPARAGUS

**A**sparagus has a certain roughness <note>original: "asprati," likely *asperitate*</note>. When its root is boiled in two parts [water] and drunk, it treats urinary problems <term>diurisi: conditions affecting the flow of urine</term> and aids those with sciatica or jaundice. It is forbidden for the broth of boiled asparagus to be drunk by dogs, for they will die from it. Others indeed say that if a ground-up goat's horn is scattered, asparagus will be born from it.

### 124. ON PLANTAIN

There are two kinds of plantain. One is called *enebro* or *plantopleuron* <note>original: "planto pleuron," from the Greek for "rib-leaf"</note> or *polypleuron* <note>original: "polipleoron," Greek for "many-ribbed"</note>. There is also another, smaller kind; this smaller one has tiny, narrow, and dense leaves. Its stem has many angles and is inclined toward the earth. It has a green flower, with the seed sitting upon the stem itself. The other kind is said to have broad leaves; this genus is the garden plantain. The stems of this kind are angular and reddish, reaching a length of one cubit <term>cubiti: an ancient measure of length, roughly from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</term>. From the middle of the stem upward, it is full of seed. They have many tender roots. It grows in watery places and in gardens, yet the larger variety has better potency.

When dried in the sun and used as an astringent <note>original: "stupaca," likely *styptica*</note>, <gloss>bruised</gloss> and applied as a poultice, it cleanses dirty wounds and dries up fluxes. it checks flowing blood, cures black spots and bruises <note>original: "primendas," likely *premindas*</note>, and easily brings about the scarring of wounds. It easily heals fresh wounds. For fresh wounds:

The wise Crateuas <note>original: "creteber," likely referring to Crateuas, a famous Greek physician and herbalist of the 1st century BCE</note> bears witness to this plant, saying: It is a shrubby plant <note>original: "furtex" for "frutex"</note> having a few leaves that are round and black, or similar to rocket <note>original: "eruge," referring to Eruca sativa or arugula</note>.

### 126. ON WATERMINT
->THAT IS, CYLULES<-

Watermint <note>original: "Sisimbrio," likely Mentha aquatica</note>, which many call "cardamine" by hearsay, is a moist herb just like water parsnip <note>original: "sion"</note>. Indeed, it is named *cardaminon* because it has leaves similar to cress <note>original: "cardami"</note> or cardamom. It produces round leaves when it first sprouts, but as it grows, the leaves split like those of rocket. Its nature is warm and diuretic. Whether raw or cooked, it is effective; it removes freckles from the face and clears up spots if applied for one night and the area is washed with water the next day.

### 127. ON SAMPHIRE

Samphire <note>original: "Critimo," likely Crithmum maritimum, also known as sea fennel</note> is a shrubby plant. It is an herb having two branches about a cubit in length <term>cubiti: an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches or the length of a forearm</term>. It grows in rocky and maritime places, having white, fleshy leaves similar to purslane <note>original: "andragnis"</note> but wider and long, with a sharp or sour taste. They have a white flower and seeds similar to wild celery <note>original: "sua potidi," likely a corruption of the Greek name for celery or parsley</note>, which are round and fragrant. When the root has dried until it turns reddish, it is about three or four fingers thick. The leaves, seeds, and root are full of a very sweet scent; when cooked with wine and drunk, it provokes urine, treats jaundice <term>hictericas: from the Greek "ikteros," meaning yellowing of the skin</term>, and regulates menstruation. It can be eaten raw or boiled, and it is also preserved in salt for eating.

Buck’s-horn plantain <note>original: "Corono podo," from the Greek "koronopus" meaning crow's foot</note> is a smaller herb spread out upon the ground with its little branches. It has compound leaves. The odor of the plant itself when cooked with the root...

### 128. ON SOW-THISTLE

There are two species of sow-thistle <note>original: "Sonchi," likely *Sonchus oleraceus*</note>. One is wild <note>original: "agrestis"</note> and thorny. The other is suitable for eating, having angular branches, and is hollow inside with sparse, limp leaves. Its nature is styptic <term>stiptica: an astringent quality that contracts tissues and stops bleeding or secretions</term>; if much is taken, it restrains the stomach and its discharges <note>original: "sagationem," likely referring to an excessive flow or flux</note>. Applied as a poultice <term>catacplasma: a soft, moist mass of herbs applied to the body</term>, its juice is swallowed to treat bites and it removes dimness of vision <note>original: "scoboma," likely a corruption of *scotoma*, dark spots or blurring in the eyes</note>. It stimulates milk in women and disperses tumors <note>original: "tumores"</note> of the womb <note>original: "matri," referring to the matrix or uterus</note>. Furthermore, its leaves and root, when applied as poultices, are effective against the sting of a scorpion.

### 130. ON CHICORY

There are two species of chicory <note>original: "Seris," referring to *Cichorium* or endive</note>: one is wild and the other is the "good" or cultivated kind. The wild kind is called *pikris* <note>original: "pignis," from the Greek *pikris* meaning bitter</note> or *syris* <note>original: "comon," possibly a local name or corruption</note>. One has leaves like lettuce <note>original: "lactuce"</note> and broad leaves; the other is bitter and has narrow leaves. The virtue of all kinds is styptic; it strengthens the stomach and mitigates its discharges when applied with barley meal <note>original: "polenta," referring to ancient barley flour rather than modern cornmeal</note>, and it alone soothes heart ailments <note>original: "cardiaca"</note>. Applied as a poultice, the leaves aid tumors of the eyes. It mitigates the sting of a scorpion if barley meal is added and applied; it also restrains "sacred fire" <note>original: "igne agrū," likely *ignis sacer* or Erysipelas, a painful skin infection</note> when mixed especially with vinegar. Moreover, it is helpful for all "hot" conditions <note>original: "calidi," referring to the humoral theory where diseases were classified by heat or cold</note>.

### 131. ON GUM SUCCORY

Gum succory <note>original: "Condrilon," likely *Chondrilla juncea*</note> has leaves, branches, and flowers similar to chicory <note>original: "cichoriū"</note>, from which much juice flows. Some say it has thin leaves and a gum-like substance <note>original: "gūm"</note> found on the branches... which is round like a bean. When mixed with myrrh and placed in a linen cloth in the shape of an olive and applied to the womb, it regulates menstruation. Its leaves and root, crushed with honey <note>original: "melle"</note>... clears up spots on the skin. When applied to the eyelids, it causes hair to grow. <margin>%</margin> The root, when cooked with vinegar, binds the belly; the wild variety especially constricts the stomach.

Its juice has a drying quality <note>original: "pepage," likely from the Greek *pepagas*, meaning to fix or congeal</note> and similarly benefits the eyelids. It grows in damp and cultivated places.

# 132. ON THE BITTER GOURD

The gourd <note>original: "Coloquintidas," referring to the Bitter Gourd or Colocynth</note>, when crushed raw and applied as a poultice <term>cataplasma: a soft, moist mass of herbs applied to the body</term>, drives away and cuts off abscesses <term>apostomatias: inflammatory swellings or abscesses</term> from the body; it is a very great remedy. Shavings applied to the head soothe the "flow" <note>original: "sugatione," referring to a discharge or flux</note> in infants. It helps with fluids in the eyes and is a very great remedy for gout <term>podagria: a painful form of arthritis, often in the big toe</term>. The juice of the shavings also soothes earaches. Mixed with rose oil, boiled and pressed with honey and natron <term>nitrum: a mineral salt used as a cleanser or medicine</term> added, it softens the belly when drunk. Indeed, if the raw gourd is hollowed out and <insert>immediately</insert> filled with wine, left there for a day and a night, and then drunk, it similarly softens the belly.

# <insert>133.</insert> 133. ON THE GOOD CUCUMBER

Cucumbers <note>original: "Cucumero," likely *Cucumis sativus*</note>, when eaten cold, relieve a sluggish stomach <note>original: "reteus tomacus," likely a corruption of *retentus stomachus*</note> that is suffering from some kind of ailment. Its scent, when applied, and its seed are very diuretic <term>diuretica: a substance that promotes the production of urine</term>. Mixed with breast milk and drunk, it heals internal wounds. Its leaves applied with wine as a poultice treat dog bites. Added to honey, it removes night-rashes <term>epinicidas: likely *epinyctis*, painful skin eruptions or pustules that appear at night</term>.

# 134. ON THE MELON.

The flesh of the melon <note>original: "Peponi," referring to *Cucumis melo*</note>, when eaten, is diuretic. Applied as a poultice, it takes away swellings of the eyes. Indeed, when placed upon the crown of the head and the skull <note>original: "corū uero 7 cereuello"</note>, it effectively protects [the health]; applied to the forehead, it stops the flow <term>rheuma: a watery discharge from the eyes or nose</term> of the eyes. The seeds and the middle part, mixed with flour and dried in the sun, when applied, make a woman's face clear. The root, boiled with honey-water <term>mulsa: a mixture of water and honey</term> and drunk, induces nausea if taken while fasting; it can do this [both] before and after a meal in a dose of two obols <term>obolus: a small unit of weight used in ancient medicine</term>.

### 136. ON LETTUCE
Lettuce <note>original: "Lactuca"</note>, when eaten, has both a cooling and stomach-soothing quality. It provides sleep <note>original: "sonū," likely a scribe's error for "somnum" (sleep)</note>, softens the belly, and stimulates milk in nursing women. Whether boiled or eaten raw, it is very good for the stomach; even unwashed lettuce, when eaten, heals the stomach. Its seed, when drunk, prevents excessive dreams <note>original: "sup flua somnia," referring to nocturnal emissions or vivid dreams</note> and binds the bowels. However, if eaten too frequently, it brings a dimness to the eyes. The juice has a similar power; the juice of wild lettuce is similar to "meconium" <term>meconico: the juice of the poppy, similar to opium</term>. Drunk with an obol-weight of vinegar-water <term>posca: a drink made of water and vinegar, common in the Roman military and medicine</term>, it purges the belly and removes spots from the eyes. It is used for burns with milk, and it is very much like opium <note>original: "opium opido. e."</note> in how it induces sleep. Smeared on the forehead, it helps headaches. A mixture <note>original: "miazut," a corrupted term likely referring to a specific preparation</note> is drunk to regulate the menstrual flow. It is also found to be effective in treating scorpion stings; for the bite of venomous spiders <term>falangionū: referring to "phalangia," a type of venomous spider</term>, this same mixture and its seed are drunk. This is most beneficial to all, as is the juice of the *horana* <note>possibly *horminum* or Clary Sage</note>, which can be squeezed out and dried in the sun to be preserved like opium.

### 137. ON GINGIDIUM
Gingidium <note>original: "Gingiziu," likely *Gingidium loricatum* or Chervil</note> grows mostly in Cilicia <note>original: "calica," referring to the region in modern-day Turkey</note> and is a herb similar to others. It is smaller and resembles *sectanace* <note>possibly *stachys* or a similar hedge-nettle</note>; its root is thin, somewhat white, and bitter. It can be eaten raw or boiled, and it can also be prepared with salt. Its medicinal virtue is diuretic <term>diuretica: promoting the production of urine</term> and good for the stomach.

### 138. ON SHEPHERD'S NEEDLE
Scandix <note>original: "Scandis," known as Shepherd's Needle</note> is a wild vegetable that is easily eaten. Its quality is digestive <note>original: "saptica," likely for "peptica"</note> and viscous, and it is slightly bitter. It is eaten raw, and its decoction is drunk to treat conditions of the bladder, kidneys <term>pneufreticas: a corruption of "nephriticas," relating to the kidneys</term>, and the liver <note>original: "opatiat," likely "hepaticas"</note>.

### 139. ON CAUCALIS
Caucalis <note>original: "Cauculis," referring to Bur-parsley</note>, which some call *mula dauca* <note>original: "mula dauca," likely a corruption of "wild carrot" or *daucus*</note>. It is a wild herb; indeed, it is smaller and has a sharp taste <note>original: "acelu"</note>. Its leaves are similar to fennel. Like the lettuce mentioned before, its leaves are fixed <note>prepared/gathered</note> and eaten raw.

### 111. ON ROCKET <note>original: "uzumo id eruca"</note>

Rocket, when eaten in large amounts, stimulates sexual desire <note>original: "uenerē stimulat," literally "stimulates Venus"</note>. Its seed is capable of doing all these same things and also acts as a diuretic <term>diureticus: a substance that encourages the production of urine</term>. When prepared as a condiment, its seed makes food easier to digest; it can also preserve meat from rotting. If mixed with milk or vinegar and formed into lozenges <term>trociscis: small, medicinal tablets or disks</term>, it can be stored for long periods.

### 141. ON WILD ROCKET

The small seeds of wild rocket are used in place of mustard for their medicinal virtues. It is a diuretic and is also said to clarify the eyesight <note>original: "uisā dior," likely a corruption of "visus clarior"</note>.

### 142. ON BASIL

Basil <note>original: "Ocimū"</note>, when eaten in great quantities, brings a dimness to the eyes, but it softens the belly, relieves flatulence, and acts as a diuretic. It stimulates the flow of milk in nursing women. When applied as a poultice <term>cataplasma: a soft, moist mass of herbs applied to the body to relieve soreness</term> with barley meal and rose oil, or with a little vinegar, it helps to reduce swellings. If drunk with wine, it mitigates the pain from the stings of the sea scorpion and the sea dragon <note>original: "draconis," likely the weever fish</note>. Its juice, when smeared on the eyes, clears away dimness and prevents rheum <term>rheumae: a watery discharge or mucus from the eyes or nose</term>. The seed, when drunk, is particularly beneficial for those suffering from celiac distress <note>original: "malis coeliacis"</note>, and it treats difficulty in urination and bloating. When applied to the nostrils, it provokes sneezing—an effect the herb itself can also produce. [A note is added here regarding a belief that basil, when chewed and left in the sun, breeds worms]. The Africans say that on the day a person is stung by a scorpion, if they eat basil, they will die immediately.

The flower is white or honey-colored. The root is the thickness of a finger; this root is dried in smoke and then split open. This herb...

### 113. ON GOAT'S BEARD <note>original: "Tragopone"</note>

Goat's Beard, which common people call *comin*, is a herb that has a stalk in its center and leaves similar to those of saffron <note>original: "croco"</note>. Its root is long and sweet; from this root, small stalks emerge that produce black seeds. This plant is also eaten in starch-based porridges <term>amulas: a thick, creamy dish made from wheat starch</term>.

### 114. ON STAR OF BETHLEHEM <note>original: "Ornitus gallæ," a corruption of Ornithogalum</note>

Star of Bethlehem is a herb that has a white and soft stalk in the middle, about two palms long. At the very top, it divides into three sections. Its flower is white. Its leaves are divided <note>the text here "cacrimula" is unclear; it may refer to a "little tear" shape</note>. The seeds themselves are put into bread, much like black cumin <term>melantniu: also known as Nigella sativa or black caraway</term>. The flower heads are easily eaten raw, and its root is eaten in the same way.

### 116. ON TRUFFLES <note>original: "Tubera"</note>

The truffle is a root that grows underground without leaves. It is round in shape, and from it, another oblong root grows which holds it in place. It is best collected during the springtime.

### 117. ON SMILAX, ALSO CALLED SYRIAN BINDWEED <note>original: "Ismilas id est Siriaca"</note>

This is a herb that grows in gardens; its seeds are called *obbia*. Some say it has leaves like ivy <note>original: "cisso," from the Greek kissos</note> but of a softer nature. It acts as a diuretic <term>diuretica: a substance that promotes the production of urine</term>, softens the belly, and induces good sleep.

### 119. ON MEDICK, ALSO CALLED SULLA <note>original: "Medica id est Sulla"</note>

Medick is similar to clover <note>original: "trifolia," literally "three-leaf"</note>. It has narrow leaves and small stalks similar to clover, upon which the seeds grow. Its seed is like a lentil, but it is mixed into bread for its aroma. It is also used as a boiled preparation or applied as a warm fomentation <term>fomto (fomentum): a warm, medicated compress applied to the body</term>. This herb is also eaten by cattle <note>original: "feni," usually meaning hay or fodder</note>.

Vetch is a small shrub that grows in damp places. It is similar to the lentil plant, with tender and oblong leaves...

### ON THE LEEK

<margin>VIII?</margin>
When eaten, the leek causes flatulence <note>original: "inflationis"</note> and its potency burns away harmful humors <term>humores: the bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which were believed to determine health</term>. It is a diuretic, softens the belly, induces long dreams, and possesses thinning properties <note>original: "leptinica," from the Greek for 'thinning' or 'diluting'</note>. If eaten in excess, it brings a dimness over the eyes. It regulates the menstrual flow. When crushed [and applied], it heals stings and all manner of wounds caused by stinging things <note>original: "remibus uulneratis," possibly a corruption of "serpentibus" (snakes) or "herpibus" (creeping sores)</note>. Cooked, it brings up phlegm from putrid moisture in the chest. The roots themselves, cooked in sea water and applied as a warm compress <term>fomento: a hot, moist medicinal application</term>, resolve hysterical suffocations <note>a condition where the womb was thought to rise and cause a feeling of choking</note> and hard growths.

The boiled leek, however, causes almost countless gas. The leaves are sticky and have antiseptic properties <note>original: "sapticas," from the Greek for 'decay-preventing'</note>. Their juice, squeezed out and applied, stops blood. Mixed with vinegar, it stops bleeding from the nose, especially if added to other moisture. It drains the chest, heals chills, and clears the windpipes. It is bad for the stomach <term>cacostomachus: from the Greek for 'upsetting to the stomach'</term>. For poisonous bites, the juice mixed with honey is a powerful remedy. Taking the leaves internally can achieve the same result.

Its juice, mixed with vinegar and frankincense <note>original: "libanotu"</note>, or with milk or rose oil, mitigates earaches. Crushed leaves applied with rosemary <note>original: "rossimaco," possibly referring to Rosmarinus or Lysimachia</note> remove spots from the body. They cleanse "night-pustules" <term>epinoctidas: painful skin eruptions that appear at night</term> and foul wounds, especially if they are applied with salt. Two scruples <note>original: "℈ ii," an ancient weight measurement equal to about 2.6 grams</note> of the seed, drunk with mead, are wonderfully beneficial for those suffering from internal ruptures <note>original: "crecientibus," likely a corruption of "crepantiis" (ruptures) or "cruentis" (bloody fluxes)</note>.

### CL II ON THE WILD LEEK

<note>original: "Ampelo Prasson," literally 'vine-leek'</note>
When eaten, it is bad for the stomach, but it is warmer than the garden leek and is a diuretic. It regulates the menstrual flow and counteracts poisonous bites.

When used with ash, it cures an itch <note>original: "scauia," a corruption of "scabiem"</note> of the eyes. With chicken fat, it calms ear pain and excessive ringing, and it is similarly beneficial for ulcerations of the ears. Truly, when raw or fried, it corrects patches of hair loss <term>alopecia: a condition causing hair to fall out in small patches</term>. Fried with sea-foam <note>original: "alpionio," likely "alcyonio," a mineralized sea-growth used in ancient medicine</note>, it benefits defects <note>original: "crimia," likely "crimina"</note> of the hair. If eaten in excess, it causes a headache. Drunk, it helps those with jaundice <note>original: "aleurgicos," likely a corruption of "ictericos"</note>. Eaten cooked, it is a diuretic <term>diuretic: a substance that encourages the production of urine</term>.

### CLIII ON GARLIC, ALSO CALLED SCORDON

Of Garlic <note>original: "Scordon," from the Greek "skordon"</note>, there are truly two kinds: the garden variety and that which is born in Egypt, though they are dissimilar in their nature. These types are hot and cause flatulence <note>original: "inflatilis"</note>, and they disturb the belly. Garlic dries the stomach and causes thirst; it harms the body [if overused]. Eaten, it expels long worms <term>lumbricos latos: tapeworms or other broad intestinal parasites</term>. It promotes urine and is wonderfully beneficial for poisonous bites. It restrains the flux of blood. If the juice is drunk with wine, it prevents the bite of a mad dog from causing harm. It is better eaten if drunk with wine; it prevents unknown water <note>meaning water from a foreign or suspicious source</note> from harming a person.

### ON THE LEEK-GARLIC <note>original: "iscorda prasso," referring to Scordoprasum</note>

It grows larger, like a leek, having leaves with the odor of garlic, wherefore it shares properties in common with both the leek and the garlic; it is eaten like a garden vegetable.

### 155 ON MUSTARD

Mustard should be chosen—especially the Pontic variety—which, when rubbed, appears green <note>original: "uuiridir"</note>... its properties are heating, thinning <term>leptanytica: a substance used to dilute or thin thick or viscous humors</term>, and drawing <term>epispastic: a substance that draws fluid to the surface of the skin to relieve internal inflammation</term>. It is effective for clearing phlegm <term>apophlegmatism: a medicine used to draw away mucus or "phlegm"</term>. Mixed with honeyed water <note>original: "mulsus"</note>, it disperses tumors of the throat and scrofula <term>scrofula: a swelling of the lymph nodes, often in the neck</term>. It soothes the roughness of the windpipes and is usefully applied as a gargle <term>gargarismus: a liquid used for rinsing the mouth and throat</term>. Ground, it is applied to the chest. It provokes sneezing, and its smoke is a great protection for those with epilepsy <note>original: "epilemaciis"</note> and suffocations. It aids with lethargy <term>lethargia: a state of deep or prolonged unconsciousness or drowsiness</term> if the head is shaved and the ground mustard is mixed with figs <note>original: "cariaz," from 'carica'</note> and applied.

### ON CARDAMOM <note>In this context, the text likely refers to Garden Cress (Lepidium sativum) rather than the modern spice cardamom.</note>

**Cardamom** is said to be quite useful. The **Babylonian** variety is the warmest seed of all. It is used for **bad breath** <term>cacostoma: a medical term for foul-smelling breath</term>. When it disturbs the belly, it expels slippery [waste] <note>original: "lubricū expellit"</note>, thins the spleen, and [relieves] those who find it difficult to breathe <note>original: "abhorat," likely from 'abhorret' or related to respiratory distress</note>. It stimulates sexual desire <note>original: "venerē fumulat," referring to its use as an aphrodisiac</note> through the thickening [of humors]. 

Its properties are similar to **mustard** and **rocket** <note>original: "eruce," referring to Eruca sativa or arugula</note>. When applied, it removes roundworms and other intestinal worms. With honey added, it softens hard swellings. It cures dirty wounds; if applied to **venomous bites**, it counteracts the poison. When drunk or used as a fumigation <term>fumigation: the historical practice of using medicinal smoke or vapors for healing</term>, it makes snakes flee. 

It helps with thinning hair. A small poultice <note>original: "carpusculus," likely a corruption of 'corpusculus' or referring to the fruit of the plant</note> cooked with **barley meal** <note>original: "pulema," for 'polenta'</note> and **vinegar** aids **sciatica** <term>sciatica: pain affecting the back, hip, and outer side of the leg</term>. It is known to disperse tumors and hardnesses. If mature **barley** is applied with cold water, the herb itself is known to do all these things, but it has a little less efficacy. 157.

## 158. ON BRIO, ALSO KNOWN AS ALCA

**Brio** <note>likely referring to a species of mallow (*Alcea*) or potentially a sea-heath</note> is a herb. Its branches are two cubits long, having many thin stalks upon which leaves grow. These are soft and white, similar to **cress**. At the top of the stalks, it produces seed and a white flower. The seed is thoroughly cooked with pork and eaten by the people of **Cappadocia** <note>a historical region in modern-day Turkey</note>. They use it like **pepper**, mixing it into stews and other foods.

## 159. ON ERYSIMUM, ALSO KNOWN AS SYRIAN ROCKET

**Erysimum** <note>likely *Sisymbrium officinale*, commonly known as Hedge Mustard</note> grows in cities, on walls, and along boundaries. It has leaves similar to **wild rocket**, and its stalk is likewise similar to rocket. It has honey-colored flowers and bears seeds at the top similar to **cress**. Its medicinal power is "warm." It checks **rheums** <term>rheum: a watery discharge from the mucous membranes, like phlegm</term> and cures the spitting of blood and coughs. It is beneficial for **jaundice** <note>original: "hicterias"</note> and **sciatica**. When drunk, it acts as an antidote to poisons. Applied as a **poultice** <term>poultice: a soft, moist mass of plant material applied to the body to relieve inflammation</term>, it excellently treats **cancers** <note>In historical medical texts, "cancer" refers to any spreading, malignant-looking ulcer or hard tumor</note>, hard swellings, and **parotid tumors** <term>parotid: relating to the glands located in front of the ears</term>. Its power also optimally cures tumors of the breasts and testicles.

### 109. ON PEPPER

The **pepper** tree is a native of **India**. Its seed is oblong, which is why it is called **long pepper** <note>original: "piper longum"</note>. If it has been processed, you will find a certain kind of opening at its tip. And after the long pepper itself has fallen, the pepper tree itself produces another fruit, which is the one we commonly use; and after that too has fallen, another is born in the manner of a cluster of grapes, which is called **white pepper**. This is collected while raw and not yet ripe. This white pepper is mixed especially into **eye-salves** <term>eye-salves: (original: "colloriacas") medicinal ointments for the eyes</term> in pharmacy and into antidotes, because it is harvested while still immature.

**Black pepper** is more potent <note>original: "uiscidiore", literally stickier or more robust</note> than the white. One should choose pepper that is hard, with whole grains, full, and not wrinkled or withered. All pepper has a **warming** property, and is **thinning**, **diuretic** <term>diuretic: promoting the production of urine</term>, **drawing** <term>drawing: (original: "epispastica") pulling fluids to the surface</term>, and **diaphoretic** <term>diaphoretic: inducing perspiration</term>. If applied, it clears away the **darkness of the eyes** <note>referring to blurred vision or cataracts</note> by soothing it. It heals **chills** and recurring fevers when drunk or eaten.

It counteracts **venomous bites**. It is eaten regularly to protect the genitals... especially if applied after sexual intercourse. It most skillfully cures **coughs** and all ailments of the **chest**. It is usefully mixed <insert>in</insert> **electuaries** and drinks. It is beneficial for **chronic fevers** <note>original: "sinccheas", from the Greek *synecheis*</note>, especially when mixed with honey. When drunk, it calms **griping pains** <note>original: "tortionibus", abdominal cramps</note>.

It is better if it is drunk with the juice of **laurel berries** <note>original: "bacalauri"</note> or their leaves. It is well applied as a **mouthwash** <term>mouthwash: (original: "apofleumatismocum") a treatment to draw out phlegm</term> with **stavesacre** <term>stavesacre: *Delphinium staphisagria*, a plant used to purge phlegm</term>. Prepared this way, it removes [phlegm] and aids **digestion**. It is mixed into **digestive salts** <term>digestive salts: (original: "oxiporiis") medicines to aid quick passage</term> and **vinegar-based sauces** <note>original: "oxicariis"</note>. Mixed with **pitch** <note>original: "picidurae"</note>, it disperses **scrofulous swellings** <term>scrofulous swellings: (original: "scrofus") swollen lymph nodes in the neck, often associated with tuberculosis</term> of the throat.

When added to **natron** <term>natron: a naturally occurring salt used for cleaning and medicine</term>, it clears away spots on the skin. It is roasted in this way: place it [in a vessel] over new coals and keep the pepper moving constantly so it is ready for medicinal preparations. For they say that... [unclear phrase]; they will perish together. [Some say] that the root of the pepper tree is **ginger** <note>original: "zingiber"; a common misconception in ancient and medieval herbals</note>.

### ON GINGER
**Ginger** <note>original: "Zingiber"</note> grows on a tree in **Arabia** in great abundance. The inhabitants frequently use its foliage, much like **rue** <note>a bitter herb commonly used in ancient cooking and medicine</note>, and it is especially used for eating. Indeed, the roots are small like **cyperus** <note>original: "quipiru", referring to the aromatic tubers of the Cyperus or sedge plant</note>, having a whitish color, a taste like pepper, and its own unique scent. One should choose ginger that is not worm-eaten and is heavy. Because many things decay, they place it here in vessels with cooked honey and store it; and they preserve the root, which they are accustomed to using frequently as a substitute for wheat <note>original: "tritici falso", the meaning is slightly obscure here; it may suggest a processed form or a ground preparation used like flour</note>. It has a **warming** <term>warming: (original: "termantica")</term> and **softening** <term>softening: (original: "maleptaca", likely *malactica*) a substance that softens hardness or inflammation</term> quality for the belly and stomach, and it clears the **darkness of the eyes** <note>referring to blurred vision or cataracts</note>. It is mixed into necessary **antidotes** <term>antidotes: (original: "antadota") complex medicinal compounds used to counteract toxins or diseases</term>, for its potency is very much like that of pepper. 162.

### ON WATER-PEPPER
**Water-pepper** <note>original: "Hidropiper"; the heading "NITRO PIPERIS" may be a scribal error for "HYDROPIPER"</note> grows in damp places. Its stalk is knotty, and from these knots the leaves grow; the knots are arranged like steps. These leaves are similar to **wild cumin** <note>original: "cimino estro", likely *cuminum agreste*</note>, but they are larger, better, and whiter. The taste is pungent like pepper, but it does not have the same smell. Its seed comes out of the stalks in tiny clusters, like the seeds of a grape cluster. When the leaves are <unclear>crushed</unclear> and applied, they disperse hardnesses and swelling of the temples; they clear up bruises. Dried and ground, it can be mixed in place of pepper; it is mixed into **stews** <note>original: "tuscellis", likely *iuscellis*</note> and can be mixed with salts. Its root is useless. 163. **ON SNEEZEWORT** <note>original: "DIPTARMIA", likely *ptarmica* or sneezewort</note>
