**Dittany** <note>original: "Diptamni"; likely referring to *Dictamnus albus* (False Dittany) rather than the Origanum variety</note> is an herb: it has a smaller shrub with many rod-like branches; it has thin and round stems similar to **southernwood** <note>original: "abrotonos"; a pungent-smelling plant related to wormwood</note> on which little twigs hold leaves that are oblong and similar to the olive, and many like **split-stalks** <note>original: "scuntam idos", likely a corruption of the Greek *schiston*</note> at the summit. It is recognized by its scent, from which—if the scent is drawn in—it provokes **sneezing** <term>sneezing: (original: "sternutamenta")</term>; hence it received its name <note>original: "agreatus accepit", likely a corruption of *ptarmicon*, the Greek word for sneezing</note> because it bites with a sneeze. Its seed and leaves, when applied <unclear>as a poultice</unclear> <note>original: "caticept"</note>, remove <unclear>growths</unclear> <note>original: "clibozer"</note> from the body; it is said to grow in mountainous and dry places.

## 164. ON SOAPWORT

**Soapwort** <note>original: "Strutio", likely *Struthium* or *Saponaria*</note> has two kinds. One has a smooth side and is used for **fumigation** <term>fumigation: (original: "fōmigio") the process of using medicinal smoke for healing</term>, because this fumigation cleanses **wool** <note>original: "limpidat lunara", likely *lanaria*; Soapwort was famously used to wash wool in antiquity</note>. The roots are round and long, and if they are drunk, they act as a **diuretic** <term>diuretic: (original: "diuretice") a substance that promotes the production of urine</term> and heal those with **liver disease** <note>original: "epaticis"</note>. They benefit those with a cough and those with **shortness of breath** <note>original: "optornicis", likely a corruption of *orthopnoicis*</note>; it is usefully applied for the **royal disease** <term>royal disease: (original: "morbo regio") an old name for jaundice</term> when cooked with honey—that is, it softens the belly when taken with **burnet saxifrage** <note>original: "ptenace", likely *pimpinella*</note> and the root of the **caper** plant. When drunk, it breaks and expels **bladder stones** <note>original: "cauculos uesice"</note>, and it disperses the "fury of the spleen" <note>referring to a swollen or painful spleen</note>. Placed in a **pessary** <term>pessary: (original: "matrice adpositus") a medicinal plug inserted into the vagina</term>, it commands the menses and causes an **abortion**. If drunk with **polenta** <note>original: "palentic"</note> and vinegar, it removes **leprosy** <note>original: "lepras"; used broadly here for various scaly skin conditions</note> and **pustules**; when applied with barley flour, it cleanses the skin. It is mixed into **eye-salves** <term>eye-salves: (original: "collirius")</term> and wipes away **dimness of the eyes** <note>original: "caligines oculorū"</note>. It is a necessary ingredient mixed into medicines. When crushed, it provokes **sneezing**; when crushed with honey and placed in the nostrils, it purges the head.

## 165. ON CYCLAMEN

**Cyclamen** <note>original: "Ciclamino"</note> has leaves similar to **ivy** <note>original: "cisso"</note> but painted with variegated colors, and between these it turns white; on the face of the leaf it is shaped like a palm. It has solid parts, or rather, it has flowers at the top like a rose and just like purple. Its root is black and thick like a **turnip** <note>original: "rapus"</note> and broad; this root, when drunk with water, brings down **phlegm** <term>phlegm: (original: "fleuma") one of the four bodily humors, associated with cold and dampness</term> and swellings through the bowels, and it aids the menses.

It commands [healing] when applied or drunk. It is said that <gloss>if</gloss> a pregnant woman should walk over its root, it causes an abortion. For those who have been in labor for a long time, the root placed under the thigh causes them to give birth more quickly. When drunk with wine, it is an antidote to poisons; it is especially beneficial to those who have drunk "sea hare" <note>original: "lepore marinū"; referring to *Aplysia depilans*, a sea slug considered a deadly poison in antiquity</note>. Those who have drunk it remain unharmed by wild beasts; applied as a poultice, it heals poisonous bites most healthfully.

Mixed with wine and drunk with a pessary <note>a medicinal plug for the vagina or rectum</note> or with honey-water, it cures those with **jaundice** <term>jaundice: (original: "ictericis") a yellowing of the skin and eyes often associated with liver disease</term>. This is effective if they remain in a warm place and are covered up, so much so that they are able to sweat; in which sweat you will find **red bile** <note>original: "colerā rufā"; in the theory of the four humors, an excess of bile was thought to cause various illnesses</note>. Its juice, mixed with honey and put into the nostrils, clears the head. For <unclear>ailments</unclear> of the anus, it draws down the humors when placed underneath. Ground up and placed upon the navel and over the **pubic bone** <note>original: "pectinē"</note>, it softens the belly and causes abortion.

As an ointment, it clears away **cataracts** <term>cataracts: (original: "suffusiones") a clouding of the lens of the eye</term> and **dimness of vision** <term>dimness of vision: (original: "caligines")</term>, especially if honey is added to the juice. It is correctly added to medicines to prepare for an abortion. Its powder, when sprinkled, brings back a protruding anus <note>likely referring to a prolapse or hemorrhoids</note>; its juice injected with vinegar can also do this. The squeezed juice is kept as a necessary supply.

Applied as an ointment, skin discolorations are cleansed. It cures pustules and is used as a medicine with vinegar for wounds. The dissolved root with honey can perform all these things. Applied as a poultice, it thins out a swelling of the **spleen**. It cures **hair loss** <term>hair loss: (original: "alopecias")</term> and clears away dirty spots. It assists with **gout** <term>gout: (original: "podagrias") a painful form of arthritis</term>; it should be used out of necessity for foul wounds, and it heals wounds of the head. When boiled <unclear>but</unclear> applied as a warm compress, it is a healthy remedy for **chilblains** <note>original: "pernionib;"; painful inflammation of small blood vessels in the skin caused by exposure to cold</note>, especially if it is smeared with oil. The root itself, once gathered and dried, is kept as a necessary supply. It is said that if drunk [in excess], it brings death. It is ground with water so that the <unclear>extract</unclear> may be collected. It grows in shady places, especially under trees.

# ON ANOTHER TYPE OF CYCLAMEN

There is another kind of cyclamen which is called <gloss>mountain cyclamen</gloss> <note>original: "mula ciclantamu"; likely a corruption of a Greek or local name for a specific *Cyclamen* species</note> having leaves similar to **arum** <term>arum: (original: "arso") the cuckoo-pint or lords-and-ladies plant, known for its arrow-shaped leaves</term> but smaller, with thick and knotty stalks; if these stalks are near a tree, they will entwine with it. It has a white and fragrant flower and seeds like clusters, resembling **cassia** <note>an aromatic bark or pod</note>, which are soft and viscid. It also contains a sticky substance <note>original: "uiscellagine"; a resinous or glue-like sap</note>. Its root grows along paths in dry and rough places. Its seed is drunk with white wine for eleven days; it acts through the urine and reduces a swollen belly and treats the spleen in a manner similar to <unclear>garden nut</unclear> <note>original: "e horto nucossi simili"</note>.

# 107. ON DRAGON-ROOT

**Dragon-root** <term>dragon-root: (original: "dracontea") likely *Dracunculus vulgaris*, a plant famous for its mottled, snake-like stem</term> has leaves similar to arum but larger and variegated, with stalks two cubits long, which are themselves mottled like the markings of a snake. Likewise, they have purple spots and are as thick as a finger; the seeds are in a cluster, green at first and saffron-colored when mature. It has a biting taste. The roots are round like bulbs and are thin like <unclear>sarcocolla</unclear> <note>original: "sacrocorum"; likely *sarcocolla*, a Persian tree resin used in medicine</note>, growing in shady places and in gardens.

<margin>Virtue</margin>
The juice of the pressed seed has a medicinal power; when oil is added, it cures earaches. For **lichens** <term>lichens: (original: "liche-") a general term for skin eruptions, scaling, or rashes</term>...

<margin>Polyp. Cancer.</margin>
...it is applied as an ointment and added to treatments for acne. It can be of the greatest benefit for a **polyp** <term>polyp: (original: "polipo") a growth on a mucous membrane, often in the nose</term>. It treats cancerous sores most effectively. Thirty grains of the seed drunk with **posca** <term>posca: a common ancient drink made of vinegar and water</term> corrects dimness of the eyes. When the flowers begin to wither, if their scent is smelled by a pregnant woman, it causes an abortion.

<margin>Virtue</margin>
The nature of its root is hot; for which reason it treats **orthopnea** <term>orthopnea: (original: "obtornoias") a condition where one can only breathe comfortably when standing or sitting upright</term>. It provides the greatest effect for those who are coughing and have <unclear>difficulty breathing</unclear> <note>original: "taticon"</note>. It reduces tumors of the chest if they are prone to return, especially if the root is taken dry or cooked. Dried and ground into a powder and added to honey, it can perform all these [healings]; it also serves as a diuretic for the belly when drunk with wine.

## 158. ON ARUM

**Arum** <term>arum: (original: "Aron") likely *Arum maculatum*, known as Lords-and-Ladies or Cuckoo-pint</term> has leaves like the *sunicantacae* <note>a corrupted plant name, likely referring to a specific variety of dragon-root or lily</note>, similar to dragon-root but smaller and variegated. They have a stalk two palms long of a purple color, with saffron-colored seeds. It has a white root similar to dragon-root; it can be eaten both raw and cooked because it is not very sticky. Its leaves, prepared in salt, are also eaten. 

The medicinal power in its seeds, root, and leaves is similar to dragon-root. Mixed with ox dung <note>original: "fumo bubulco", a common error for "fimo bubulo"</note> and applied as a poultice, it heals <margin>cyclamen</margin> gout <note>the margin note "ciclam." likely refers to a cross-reference with the previous section on Cyclamen</note>. The root is collected and stored just like dragon-root and cyclamen.

## 159. ON ASARUM

**Asarum** <term>asarum: (original: "Asaru") likely *Asarum europaeum* or Wild Ginger, used as an emetic or for skin conditions</term> has a smaller root and is greener than an olive. Applied as a poultice with arum, it leads spreading wounds to health by checking the pain. When mixed into a wash for fistulas <note>original: "siringia"</note>, the applied root dries out their nature in all living creatures.

# Book of Stalks

The herb **Asphodel** <term>asphodel: (*Asphodelus*) a hardy perennial plant traditionally associated with the afterlife in Greek mythology, but here valued for its medicinal properties</term> is known to everyone. It has leaves like a leek and a smooth stalk which many call *albucum* <note>original: "albucum"; the flowering stalk of the asphodel</note>. Atop this stalk it has seed, which they call *antericon*. It has roots that are oblong and round, similar to an acorn. The root is hot and drying in nature; it provokes urine and commands the menses <note>stimulates menstrual flow</note>. When one drachma <term>drachma: a Greek unit of weight, roughly 3.4 grams</term> is drunk with myrrh, it removes pain in the side and heals those suffering from bruises or coughs. 

It is said that whoever eats it may lead a happy day. It is an effective remedy against poisonous bites. Its leaves and root can achieve this when applied as a poultice <term>poultice: (original: "catept/cataplasma") a soft, moist mass of material, typically of plant material or flour, applied to the body to relieve soreness and inflammation</term>; its flower heals similarly when taken with wine. It most healthily cures spreading, dirty wounds, and tumors of the testicles and breasts. 

Applied to the skin, it disperses pustules and sties. It is especially effective for the eyes if it is cooked with wine dregs <note>the sediment at the bottom of a wine cask</note>, and applied with wine, honey, myrrh, and saffron all cooked together. It cleanses pains of the ears and fistulas <note>infected tunnels under the skin</note> when wine is added along with frankincense, honey, and myrrh. The juice should be poured warm into the ears. If a tooth aches on the right side, it is healed when the juice is poured into the left ear. The roots <unclear>applied below</unclear> are used for alopecia <note>patchy hair loss</note> and the seed is given for the same. The root, hollowed out and heated with oil, is a singular defense against chilblains <note>painful inflammation of small blood vessels in response to cold</note> and earaches. The root emends white spots on the skin if rubbed on while in the sun. The seed and flower are a defense against serpents if drunk with wine. The root, when drunk with water, softens the belly <note>acts as a laxative</note>. 171.

Bulbs <note>likely referring to the edible and medicinal bulbs of the tassel hyacinth (*Leopoldia comosa*)</note> are hot and drying; when eaten, they stimulate sexual desire, though they also roughen the tongue and throat. # ON THE SEA ONION

The power of the **Sea Onion** <term>Sea Onion: (original: "squilla") *Drimia maritima*, a plant used since antiquity as a heart stimulant, diuretic, and expectorant</term> is hot and burning. Roasted, it is a remedy for many things. It is roasted in this way: take clay and enclose the onion, or [wrap it] in coverings <note>original: "ab fungia"; possibly referring to sponges or a dough-like wrapping</note>, and put it in the oven or in hot ashes for as long <gloss>as long</gloss> as it takes for the clay itself to be baked. Or, if the covering is finished and it is not cooked enough, do this twice; for if it is not well cooked, it harms the internal organs. 

It is also cooked by putting it in a new cooking pot <term>cooking pot: (original: "cacabo") a deep vessel used for boiling or stewing</term> and covering it, and so it is put in the oven; and when it is cooked, you shall throw away all the outer leaves and collect the soft part that is inside. It is likewise cooked by putting it in a pot... in the open air with water added, and cook it by changing the water as long as the water tastes of the onion’s sweetness... [then spread it] on linen... and dry it in the shade; they should be dried so they may be joined together.

## CLXXVI ON THE RANUNCULUS <note>original: "Botraciu"; also known as Buttercup or Crowfoot</note>

**R**anunculus, which many call wild celery <note>original: "apiorum"</note>. There are many species of them with various medicinal powers. It has a sharp quality and its leaves cause blistering <note>original: "exuulnerenda"; referring to the caustic sap of the buttercup family</note>; they are similar to coriander but broader, white, and more fleshy. They have honey-colored flowers. Sometimes they are purple; they have long stalks but short, white roots which are bitter and split like those of hellebore; it grows in watery places. There is another genus, a wild one, which has long stalks and leaves cut in many places; this grows in many parts of Sardinia and is called wild celery. Its medicinal quality is very sharp indeed. And there is a third kind that has smaller leaves and an unpleasant odor, with a whitish flower. There is also a fourth kind with a milky flower; the leaves and roots of all of these are caustic <term>caustic: (original: "vulneratica") a substance that can burn or blister the skin; in ancient medicine, these were used to "eat away" growths</term>. Therefore, although it causes pain and sores when applied, it removes leprous nails <note>likely referring to fungal infections or psoriasis of the nails</note>. Likewise, the bark... treats hair loss <term>alopecia: (original: "alopecis") patchy hair loss</term>. When boiled, it helps as a warm fomentation. Its root... provokes the menses. When used dry, it takes away the pain of teeth; if the aching tooth is touched by the root itself, the pain is diminished by its power.

## CLXXVII ON THE ANEMONE

The Anemone is also called *emnion* or *ennino*. There are two types: the wild and the garden variety. One has a scarlet flower, the other has white, milky, or purple flowers. The leaves are small, like those of coriander, and divided; they have green stalks like those of the poppy <note>original: "meconis"; referring to the *Papaver* genus</note>. In the center, they have a heavy little head. The root is knotty, like an olive, and has a bark. The wild type is larger in all its parts, with broader leaves and a larger, oblong head.

### CLXXVIII ON THE ARGEMONE <note>likely the Prickly Poppy, *Argemone mexicana*, or a similar wild poppy</note>

**A**rgemone is similar in all respects to the wild poppy <note>original: "meconeo"</note>; it has leaves like an anemone and they are divided. It has thin stalks of a honey color. It has a small head like a poppy, but it is oblong and indented from above. Its root is round and the flower is saffron-colored. Its medicinal powers are astringent, wherefore it clears white spots on the eye <term>argema: (original: "argemas") a small white ulcer on the cornea, from which the plant takes its name</term> and cleanses dimness of the vision. ### CLXXVIIII ON THE ANAGALLIS <note>The Pimpernel</note>

**A**nagallis, which many call [corchorum?], consists of two species which are recognized by their flowers. One kind produces a blue flower <note>original: "laquinano", likely a corruption of "cyaneo"</note>, which is considered the female. The other kind produces a flower the color of a date <note>original: "dactili"; a reddish-orange or vermillion</note>, which is the male. Both of them trail along the ground; they have somewhat square leaves on small stalks, similar to chickweed <note>original: "celsine", likely "alsine"</note> but more rounded, with round seeds on top. Both are effective for wounds. They draw out inflammation if they are applied to the body, and they cleanse festering wounds. The juice also stops the pain of teeth; it is effective if it is used on the left side when the pain is on the right <note>This refers to the ancient practice of pouring juice into the ear opposite the aching tooth</note>.

...it plucks out hairs so that they will not grow back. With its roots, it relieves the pain of gout <term>podagris: (original: "podagris") gout or foot-pain</term>. CLXXXI.

### ON CELANDINE

Greater Celandine <note>original: "Celedonia maiore"; *Chelidonium majus*</note>, which common people call *ocimon* <note>original: "ocimon"; usually refers to basil, but here used as a vernacular name for celandine</note>, has a stem one cubit <term>cupidi: (original: "cupidi") a cubit, approximately the length of a forearm</term> long or more; the stems are tender and have many leaves arranged in a circle around the stem. These leaves are similar to butterbur <note>original: "butteratio"; likely a corruption of *batrachion*, or "frog-plant," which includes buttercups</note> but are better and whiter. It brings forth a golden flower and has a saffron-colored juice <note>original: "sucum croceū"; Greater Celandine is famous for its bright orange-yellow latex</note>. Its quality is slightly acidic, biting, and bitter, though it has a good scent. The root is single at the top; the seed of the flower is like that of the horned poppy <note>original: "meconi ceratitidis"</note>, being both small and slightly larger in some parts. 

The juice, with honey added and cooked in a bronze vessel over a charcoal fire, clears away dimness <note>original: "caliginis"</note> from the eyes. The leaves, the root, and the stem itself are dried in the shade during the summer and are prepared into lozenges <term>trocisci: (original: "trocisci") medicinal tablets or discs</term>. The root, mixed with vinegar and white wine and drunk, helps those with jaundice <term>hicteris: (original: "hicteris") yellowing of the skin</term>. Its leaves, applied with wine or as a poultice <note>original: "catapt"; likely a contraction of *cataplasma*</note>, clear away spots on the skin. <note>original: "masogara"</note> It prevents toothache. 

Indeed, it received its name <note>The name *Celandine* comes from the Greek *chelidon*, meaning swallow</note> because it is born with the arrival of the swallow and its life cycle is defined by their departure. It is even said that when swallow chicks have been blinded, their parents use the milk <note>original: "lactem"; the milky sap</note> of this herb for the chicks to eat, as I have said, and their sight is restored. CLXXXII.

### ON LESSER CELANDINE

Lesser Celandine <note>original: "Celedonia minore"; *Ficaria verna*</note>, which common people call *chiuirion* or "wild pear," is a small herb having tiny stems and leaves like ivy, but they are rounded, smaller, and thick. It has better roots, which are small and numerous, like small wheels <note>original: "trocos"</note>, with three or four in one cluster. It grows in watery places and in meadows. Its quality is caustic <note>original: "uisadat"; likely *vis acris*, meaning sharp or burning power</note>, similar to an anemone; if applied, it wounds the skin...

## CLXXXIII ON OTONNA

Otonna <note>a plant of the Asteraceae family, likely *Othonna cheirifolia* or a related species</note>, which many call the juice of Greater Celandine <note>original: "coledoni maiorem"</note>, or *liannocan* <note>likely a corruption of a Greek name</note>, or horned poppy <note>original: "metonis ceruatis," a corruption of *meconis ceratitidis*</note>, or the juice of pimpernel <note>original: "anagallidis"</note>. It grows in Egypt and Arabia. It has leaves similar to rocket <note>original: "eruce"; arugula</note> but they are perforated and fragile; however, it has many leaves. They have a saffron-colored flower <note>original: "croceu"</note>, which is why many have called it a species of anemone. Its juice is effective for the eyes and clears away dimness. Many say that when the juice is extracted from the herb itself, it flows out and is collected and stored in the form of a lozenge <term>trocisci: (original: "trocisci") medicinal tablets or discs</term>; it possesses a power similar to the herb itself.

## CLXXXIIII ON MOUSE-EAR

Mouse-ear <note>original: "Meosota"; *Myosotis*</note>, which many call *meotada*, grows with many stalks from a single branch. They are reddish in color and have narrow, long, and black leaves which grow in pairs; rarely are the leaves narrow at the end. Many stalks come from one branch, hyacinth-colored <note>original: "iacintino"; likely referring to a deep blue or purple hue</note>, but with a root that is quite solid, like fingers, and they have many roots gathered together. This herb is very similar to Hart’s-tongue fern <term>scolopendrio: (original: "scolopendrio") a fern named for its centipede-like appearance</term> but it is smooth. Its leaves, when taken and applied, clear out fistulas <note>abnormal passages or sores</note> of the eyes. Many also use it without its root.

## CLXXXV ON ISATIS, THAT IS, THE GLASS-HERB

Isatis <note>original: "Isatis"; Woad (*Isatis tinctoria*), famous for producing blue dye</note>, which dyers use for their things. It has leaves similar to plantain <note>original: "plantaginis"</note> but they are fatter and darker. The stalks are more than a cubit <term>cubito: (original: "cubito") about 18 inches, the length of a forearm</term> long. Its leaves, when taken and applied, soothe all tumors. Placed upon fresh wounds, they draw them together; they bind the flow of blood and heal malignant and foul ulcers most healthfully. It removes spots and extinguishes the "sacred fire" <note>original: "igne agrum," likely *ignis sacer*, a term for inflammatory skin conditions like erysipelas or shingles</note>.

## CLXXXVI ON TELEPHION

**Telephion** <note>likely *Sedum telephium*, commonly known as Orpine or Livelong</note>, which others call wild *aizoon* <note>original: "aizoon agreste"; from the Greek for "ever-living," usually referring to succulents like stonecrop</note>, wild purslane <note>original: "andragine agreste"</note>, or *brion*. Its leaves and stalks are similar to purslane, and between the leaves and stalks they have a sort of depression <note>original: "forsa"; likely *fossa*, a hollow or groove</note> where other stalks emerge. Above the stalks, it has a reddish, soft pod and white flowers. It is found in many places and grows easily in vineyards. The leaves, when applied, treat white spots <note>likely referring to vitiligo or leprosy</note>. If applied for six hours, crushed with vinegar, and used as an ointment, it removes the spots. If the area remains in the sun for a long time after being rubbed with this, the skin becomes clear and bright.

BOOK SECOND.

In the [first] two books, most beloved friend, we have delivered to you the preparation of spices and oils, of myrrh and trees, of seeds and legumes, of resins <note>original: "lacrimū"; literally "tears," referring to the gummy sap or resin exuded by plants</note>, of animals, of grain, and of vegetables, the juices of herbs, and all seeds with their leaves; we have made an arrangement of all medicines.

# ON AGARIC
<note>Agaric here refers to *Laricifomes officinalis*, the larch polypore, a wood-decay fungus highly prized in antiquity as a "universal remedy."</note>

Agaric is a root similar to *sufinon* <note>original: "sufinon"; likely a reference to a plant like silphium or a specific resinous root</note>, thus hard but softer; there are two types of agaric: male and female. The male is selected by its inner veins; it is round and compact, and both [types] are of one color. The taste is unique: at first they are sweet, but afterwards they seem bitter. It grows in Arabia and Samaria on many trees as roots. Others indeed say that it is a rot of the tree growing in itself, just as mushrooms <note>original: "micete"; from the Greek *mykes*</note> are born. In Asia, Cilicia, and Galatia, it comes from <term>oak</term> <note>original: "drı"; likely an abbreviation for the Greek *dryos*, oak</note> trees; it is fragile and soft in quality, and hot and styptic. For fistulas <unclear>sertopem</unclear>, reaching within, it drives out raw humors <note>In ancient medicine, the "four humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) had to remain balanced for health; "raw" humors were those not yet properly "cooked" or processed by the body’s heat.</note> <margin>vııc"</margin>. It is effectively administered in a decoction. Two <term>obols</term> <note>An obol was a small unit of weight, roughly 0.7 grams.</note> should be drunk by those without a fever; however, for those with many fevers, it provides the greatest effect for liver ailments, asthma, diarrhea, kidney <unclear>pains</unclear>, and jaundice <note>original: "hicterias"</note>. For suffocations <note>This often refers to "suffocation of the womb," a historical diagnosis for various internal distresses in women.</note>, it is necessarily applied; if taken, it improves a bad complexion and heals sores. For the spleen, <term>oxymel</term> <note>A common medicinal syrup made from honey and vinegar.</note> helps similarly, and it is beneficial for stomach ailments. When eaten, it <unclear>wipes away</unclear> blood, promotes digestion, and one obol taken with water relieves thoracic <note>original: "aderiacos"; likely a corruption of *thoracicos*, meaning pains in the chest or sides</note> and sciatic pains, and [treats] epilepsy.

<summary>This page introduces Book II of the treatise and provides an extensive entry on Agaric, a medicinal fungus described here as a "root" that grows on trees. The text outlines its physical varieties, origins in the Near East and Asia Minor, and its use in treating everything from jaundice and asthma to sciatica and epilepsy.</summary>

<keywords>Agaric, medical botany, humors, liver ailments, jaundice, oxymel, Arabia, Cilicia, Galatia, pharmacology</keywords>

--- Page 148 ---
<meta>This page continues the medical properties of birthwort (Aristolochia), likely following a missing or preceding section, before moving into detailed entries for rhapontic rhubarb and gentian. The "catchword" at the bottom of the previous page's original manuscript would have been "cis," which we see here completing the word "Aristolochis."</meta>

...birthwort <note>original: "Aristolochis"</note> when given with pure water, it regulates the menses. It prevents jaundice <note>original: "hictericis"; from the Greek *icterus*, a yellowing of the skin</note> and bloating; and if taken with pure intention, it excludes all chills. It purges the belly if taken and drunk with honey-water <term>mulsa</term> <note>a mixture of honey and water, often fermented like a light mead</note>. If drunk with wine, it counters the most poisonous bites; three obols <note>a small ancient unit of weight, roughly 0.5 to 0.7 grams</note> taken with wine assists. It especially cures all conditions of the intestines according to the strength of the person or the age of the patient, whether given with water or with wine and with oxymel <term>oxymel</term> <note>original: "obsimel"; a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</note>. ## ON RHUBARB
### Rhubarb
It is born in the Bosphorus <note>original: "ios poro"; referring to the region near the Black Sea</note> and thus comes to Greece. Its root is black, similar to the greater centaury but shorter and reddish. It has no odor, is quite soft, and is light in weight. Good rhubarb is not pierced [by insects]. In taste, it is <unclear>macalle ginofio</unclear> <note>likely a corruption of terms describing a spicy or astringent flavor</note>, biting under the tongue and with a moderate color. It is drunk for bloating of the stomach and for colic. It prevents weakness and stomach pain. It is drunk and is beneficial for those with spleen and liver issues. It restores the body after shattering [concussions or fractures] and helps those falling from a height. It heals <unclear>neustreait</unclear> and coughs. It is healthful for conditions of the bladder, the chest, and the hypochondria <note>original: "pocopdrit"; the upper part of the abdomen</note>. It is suitable for jaundice and sciatic conditions. It helps those falling from a height <note>this benefit is repeated from a few lines above</note>; it is used usefully for spitting blood. It benefits the <unclear>armadici</unclear>. It is used usefully for <unclear>gluceniab</unclear>; it provides the greatest effect for the intestines and stomach ailments <note>original: "quiliar"</note>. It tastes good during chills and is a remedy for hiccups <note>original: "siisgultere pridium"; likely *singultui praesidium*</note>. It counters poisonous bites. ...from the same people <note>original: "eadem gente"; referring to the Illyrians and their King Gentius</note> from whom it also received its name. Its leaves and roots have their own distinct odor. It is similar to a plantain <note>original: "plantaginis"</note>, but somewhat reddish at the base, and it has leaves along the middle and upper parts of the stalk. It grows longer than two cubits <note>an ancient unit of measurement, approximately 18 inches or 45 centimeters</note>. It is knotted, and around these knots, its leaves grow. The seeds are found around the leaves and are wide, flat, and grape-like, just like those of the hogweed <note>original: "sfondilio"; the plant *Heracleum sphondylium*</note>. Their root is like birthwort—long, solid, and bitter. It grows in high, shady, and moist places. The potency of the root itself is warm and cleansing <note>original: "saptica"; likely a corruption of "peptic" (digestive) or "styptic" (contracting tissue)</note>.

When this root is taken with pepper, rue, and wine, it resists poisonous bites. When taken by itself, it is useful for pains of the uterus and for [promoting] conception. It is especially beneficial for stomach conditions <note>original: "stomatias"</note> and liver conditions <note>original: "epatias"</note> when drunk with water. Just like a pessary <note>original: "colliuius"; a medicinal plug</note>, the root itself causes an abortion if applied [topically]. It heals wounds when placed upon them. When the juice is dissolved into an ointment, it soothes tumors of the eyes. This power is also mixed into eye-salves <note>original: "collyriis"</note> in place of poppy juice <note>original: "mecomio"</note>. It also removes spots from the body.

Furthermore, if the root is infused in water for five days and afterwards cooked until its strength is released, and if you rub it and then strain the liquid, you should cook that water until it reaches the thickness of honey. Then, store it in a glass vessel and use it.

### IIII. ON BIRTHWORT

Birthwort <note>original: "Aristologia"</note> is so named because it is called "bringer of help in childbirth" <note>original: "foetodo-cas"; a corruption of the Greek *boethos* (helper) and *lochia* (childbirth)</note> by the Greeks, and "ariston" means "best" or "useful" in Greek, because it is considered most fit for the purging of the womb. It took its name from this. There are two kinds of birthwort: the round and the long. The round is called the female. It has leaves similar to ivy, which are fragrant and somewhat round. It produces many shoots from a single root and has elongated flowers.

...white and rounder, it has a yellow flower in the middle, but it is weak. Truly, the long birthwort <term>Aristolochia</term> is the male. It is also called *docialiar* <note>original: "docialiar"; possibly a corruption of a Greek botanical synonym</note>. It has an oblong leaf and thin twigs of two palms’ length <note>about 6 inches or 15 centimeters</note>, but it is moderately longer. It bears a purple flower that is not fragrant and withers; it appears like the flower of a pear tree. The root is also round, like a turnip. Both types have the color of boxwood; the taste is both bitter and full of a strong odor <note>original: "bromo"; from the Greek for a pungent or foul smell</note>.

The third kind of birthwort is called *clematitis* <note>original: "clematar"; *Aristolochia clematitis*</note>, which has thin and long twigs. The leaves are roundish, similar to cyclamen <note>original: "ciclamio"</note> but smaller. It has flowers similar to rue. The roots are oblong and thin. Their bark is very thick and fragrant, and it is mixed by apothecaries <note>original: "pimentariis"; spice-merchants or druggists who prepared medicines</note> for eye preparations and other medicines. Just as it helps for stomach pains and poisoned drinks when taken with wine, it also provides this benefit when applied topically. It expels the afterbirth <note>original: "secundas"</note> and causes abortion. When drunk with pepper and myrrh, it achieves this; and if taken by itself, it has a similar efficacy to the round variety. 

But the birthwort itself is more beneficial; it is particularly healing for hiccups <note>original: "subglutionib;"</note>, chills, and pleurisy <note>an inflammation of the lungs</note> when drunk with water. When applied to the body, it draws out filth from wounds and removes decay. For other uses, it fills up wounds. Mixed with honey and Illyrian iris, it cleanses the gums and teeth from decay; and birthwort <gloss>Aristolochia</gloss> clematitis <margin>virtue</margin> can do all these things by its power. It is warm for all these purposes.

### VI. ON GREAT CENTAURY. Centaury

Great centaury, which they call *mulsanareas* <note>a corruption of a Greek or local synonym</note> or gentian. It has leaves like the royal lily <note>original: "niuar regalis"; likely the white lily</note>, oblong and green like a little hill, and the leaves themselves are round and divided like three fingers. It has twigs similar to hops <note>original: "lupae"; likely *Lupulus*</note>, two or three cubits long. It has many roots and little stems in which it has heads like poppies <note>original: "meconia"</note>. It produces a red-colored seed placed within the flowers themselves. Its root is thick and heavy, and on the outside it has a reddish juice, sap-like, sweet, and oblong. Indeed, the juice itself is dark gold <note>original: "obrusus"</note>. It is prepared for those with fatty humors and for <unclear>fofienis</unclear> <note>possibly a corruption referring to cataracts or skin discolorations</note>. It abounds in the Peloponnese, in Elis, and in Arcadia, Messene, and <unclear>urmispa</unclear> and <unclear>dition</unclear>. The root is effective for bruises, pleurisy <note>inflammation of the lungs</note>, and dyspnea <note>shortness of breath</note>.

### VII. ON LESSER CENTAURY

Lesser Centaury, which the common people now call *limnes* <note>original: "limnes"; likely from the Greek for "marsh-dweller," referring to its habitat</note>, from whose stalk there also grows a "masculine" variety <note>original: "yper mas"; possibly referring to St. John's Wort (Hypericum) which was often confused or grouped with Centaury</note> or it is similar to oregano. Let it then be strained and boiled again until it reaches the thickness of honey. For its juice, one should crush it green... it does better... which juice should be put in an earthenware vessel with water...

## VIII ON THE WHITE CHAMELEON-PLANT
White Chameleon-plant, which many have called *ixion* <note>original: "ixion"; referring to the sticky juice or "bird-lime" often associated with this plant</note> because bird-lime is often found especially at its root, and which women use in place of mastic <note>original: "martice"; likely a corruption of "mastice," a resin used for dental hygiene or as a base for medicine</note>. It has leaves similar to the Golden Thistle <note>original: "scolimo"</note>. They are rough and narrow and dark on the outside, without a central stalk, or similar to thorny bushes, and like a sea-holly or a thistle it has a purple flower like hairs... <note>The Latin "remine-enico" is likely a corruption of "erineo," referring to a woolly appearance</note>. It has a thick and fat root in the earth in mountainous places, with a heavy and aromatic smell, tender and white, and sweet in taste. When one <term>oxybaphon</term> <note>a small Greek measure, roughly 1/8 of a pint or a small vinegar-saucer</note> is drunk, it expels and clears out intestinal worms <note>original: "lumbricos"</note>, especially when given effectively with a dry wine or a decoction of oregano. It heals those with dropsy <note>original: "Hidropicis"; a condition of swelling or edema</note> when taken with wine to thin their humors; the decoction is especially beneficial when drunk for difficulty urinating <note>original: "disuriae"</note>. It counteracts poisons when taken with porridge, but it kills dogs and pigs if it is mixed with honey and cooked in water and oil.

## VIIII ON THE BLACK CHAMELEON-PLANT

Its leaves are also similar to the Golden Thistle, but tender and reddish, having a stalk as thick as a finger and a cubit long and reddish. It has a thorny flower like a hyacinth <note>original: "laquinto"; a corruption of "hyacintho"</note> and varied in color. Its root is thick and black and dense, appearing as if it has been bitten off <note>original: "comestu"; likely referring to the "Devil's-bit" appearance where the root ends abruptly</note>, hooked and reddish-brown in taste...

### X ON THE CODILION

Codilion <note>likely referring to the Black Chameleon-plant or a similar thistle-like herb</note> grows similar to the black chameleon; it has a long and thick root, having a fresh scent like <term>cardamom</term> <note>an aromatic spice known since antiquity</note>. A decoction of it, when drunk, causes blood to flow in equal measures <note>referring to its use as an emmenagogue to regulate menstruation</note>. When taken, it heals those suffering from the spleen.

### XI ON THE DIPSACOS FROM WHICH ONOFERA IS ENCLOSED

Dipsacos <term>Dipsacos</term> <note>The Teasel plant, from the Greek "dipsa" meaning thirst, because the leaves form a basin that holds water</note> is a thorny thing; it has a long stalk full of spines and is curved like a willow branch. It has leaves similar to lettuce, and at each joint, it has a hollow. These leaves are oblong and thorny both inside and outside; they are joined together to hold the rain and dew within the leaves themselves, from which it took the name "cup" <note>original: "cupre", likely from "cupa" or "cyathus"</note>. On these stalks, individual thorny heads rise, similar to the Marian grape but oblong and also thorny. When it dries, it turns a white color, and within the stalk, worms are born. Its root, boiled in wine and crushed like a <term>cerate</term> <note>a medicinal ointment made of wax and oil</note>, is applied to <term>rhagades</term> <note>painful cracks or fissures in the skin</note> and fistulas.

### XII ON THE WHITE ACANTHA

The White Acantha <note>likely the White Thistle or a species of Acanthus</note> grows in the mountains and in damp <note>original: "uisadis", likely a corruption of "uvidis"</note> places. It has leaves like the white chameleon plant, but narrower and whiter, rough and thorny. It has a stalk two cubits long and of a thickness greater than a cubit <note>the scribe likely means the girth of a finger or hand, as a "cubit" thickness would be impossible for this plant</note>; it is white and hollow, and upon the top itself it has thorns like a sea urchin <note>original: "ecinu marino"</note> and is oblong in shape. It has purple flowers in which the seed is like safflower <note>original: "cinico", likely "cnici"</note> but more round. Its root, when drunk, benefits those spitting blood <note>original: "emoptoicis"; suffering from hemoptysis</note>. It brings aid to sciatica <note>original: "scadias"</note> and stomach ailments, provokes urine, and afterward disperses all humors through the skin. A decoction of it calms the pain of teeth; its seed, when drunk, most healthfully cures convulsions in infants. It counteracts venomous bites; if someone carries it on their neck, they do not fear the attack of a serpent.

### XIII ON THE ARABIAN ACANTHA

The Arabian Acantha is similar to the aforementioned <note>original: "ss", shorthand for "supra scriptae"</note>; it grows thorny and white. Its power is <term>styptic</term> <note>an agent that tightens tissue and stops bleeding</note>; it checks the flow of blood, assists those vomiting blood, and counteracts catarrhs <note>original: "reumatismus"; the flow of excess humors or "runny" conditions</note>. Its root can do all the same things as the aforementioned plant.

### XIIII ON THE SCOLYMUS

The Scolymus <note>the Golden Thistle</note> has leaves similar to the white chameleon plant and acanthus, but darker and thicker. It has long stalks around which it has leaves. On these stalks is a thorny head; the wild variety has a black root. Its virtue is: boiled in wine and drunk, it provokes urine and, when applied as a warm compress <note>original: "fomito", likely "fomento"</note>, removes the stench of the armpits <note>original: "alarum"</note> and of the whole body.

### XV ON POTERION

**Poterion** <note>likely *Poterium spinosum*, known as Thorny Burnet</note>, also called *frinion*, *emmera*, or *uacinėton* by many. It is a larger shrub with long, soft, yet strong branches. Its leaves are similar to those of the tragacanth <note>original: "tracante"; referring to the *Astragalus* plant</note> but are smaller and more rounded. The entire shrub is covered in a sort of mossy layer <note>original: "uelut lecha"; possibly a corruption of the Greek 'leichen' or referring to a scale-like covering</note> and is completely thorny. It has very small, greenish flowers. Its seed is sweet and sticky <note>original: "uiscidus"</note>, though of lesser strength. It grows in waysides, damp places, and salty soil. It has roots the size of one or two cubits <note>a cubit is roughly 18 inches</note> which are quite strong. If a root is cut or touched, it stops growing and sends out another root in its place, emitting a tear-colored juice <note>original: "lacrimū... quimo"; a gummy latex</note> similar to the juice of the root itself. When applied, it is used as a medicine for the nerves <note>original: "neruorum causa"</note> and binds together all wounds <note>original: "paracollet"; from the Greek 'parakollao', meaning to glue or heal together</note>. A decoction <note>original: "elixatura"</note> made from it brings aid to all conditions affecting the nerves.

### XVI ON ACANTION

**Acantion** <note>likely *Onopordum acanthium*, the Cotton Thistle</note> has leaves similar to the White Acanthus. Its leaves, when gathered together and applied, heal those suffering from opisthotonos <note>original: "opistotonicis"; a condition of severe muscle spasms where the body bows backward</note>.

### XVII ON ACANTHUS

**Acanthus** <note>likely *Acanthus mollis*, commonly called Bear's Breech</note>, also called *melicas filis* or *pederota*. It grows in gardens <note>original: "paradisīs"</note> and in rocky, damp places. It has leaves that are larger and wider than those of lettuce; they are divided like arugula <note>original: "eu zumi"; likely *eruca*</note>, darker, and thicker. The stalk is two cubits long and has the thickness of a finger. At the head of the stalk itself, it has small leaves, and the head is like a thistle <note>original: "cardos"</note>. Some say the color is like hyacinth <note>original: "iquini no"; likely a corruption of 'hyacinthino'</note>, but their flowers are white. Its seed has a honey-like color. It has many roots that are tough <note>original: "lentinosas"</note>, reddish, and long. When these are applied to burns, they are very effective, and they also heal sores caused by shoes <note>original: "nociuis calceamentoru"</note>. When the herb itself is drunk, it provokes urine, softens the belly, and brings aid to those with consumption <note>original: "asisat"; likely a corruption of 'phthisicis', those suffering from a wasting disease like tuberculosis</note>.

### XVIII ON ONOMIDA
**Onomida** <note>original: "Onomida"; likely Rest-harrow (*Ononis spinosa*)</note>, which some have called *ononida*. It produces branches larger than two cubits <note>a cubit is approximately 18 inches</note> which are sturdy. Upon these branches are smaller heads and tiny leaves, like those of lentils or rue, though some are longer. They grow in rough, rich, and thick soil. People preserve this plant in salt and eat it, as it is very pleasant. The branches are white and have a "warm" quality. Its roots, when drunk with wine, provoke urine <note>a diuretic effect</note> and expel stones from the bladder. It heals foul sores <note>original: "uulperib; sordidis"; likely a corruption of *vulneribus*, meaning wounds or ulcers</note>. When the root is boiled in vinegar and held in the mouth, it stops the pain of teeth.

### XVIIII ON LEUCACANTHA
**Leucacantha** <note>original: "Leucacantu"; literally "White Thistle," possibly the Milk Thistle or Cotton Thistle</note>, also called *polygonoton*, *silon*, or *satiade*. Its root is similar to the [unclear] <note>original: "perite: amerae:"</note>. When chewed thoroughly, it takes away toothache. If boiled in wine and drunk—specifically three <term>cyathi</term> <note>a cyathus was a Roman liquid measure, roughly 0.045 liters or a small cupful</note> on an empty stomach—it heals pain of the colon. It also provides relief for those suffering from pleurisy <note>inflammation of the lung lining</note>, sciatica, and bruises. Its juice is beneficial for all the same conditions mentioned above.

### XX ON TRAGACANTH
**Tragacanth** <note>original: "Tracantu"; refers to species of *Astragalus*, the source of gum tragacanth</note> has a wide and woody root. It has short branches that spread outwards and slope toward the ground. On these branches are many tiny leaves, and around them are small, translucent spines. These spines are white and strong. The root is what we use as tragacanth, which should be selected as follows: it should be white, thin, clear, <unclear>duadus</unclear>, sweet, <unclear>dertis</unclear>, and clean. Its potency is similar to [unclear]...

### XXI ON ERYNGO OR WILD NUT

**Eryngo** <note>original: "Iringiu"</note>, which is also called *irigion* or wild nut. Its prickly leaves are eaten at the beginning of their growth and are preserved in salt. The leaves themselves are smooth and rough; they have an aromatic taste. When the plant has grown, they <gloss>have</gloss> a reddish-brown color <note>original: "obrufo colore"</note> and many stalks. On these stalks are small, round, prickly heads like spears. Around these, they have hard spines, and they are found either white, green, or of a violet color <note>original: "ia quinato"; likely a corruption of *ianthinato*, meaning violet or purple</note>. They have a long and wide root, black on the outside and white on the inside, having the thickness of a thumb; it is long, fragrant, and full of aromatics. It grows in fields and stony places. Its potency is "warm." When drunk, it provokes urine, brings on menstruation, and controls gas <note>original: "inflaziones"</note> of the stomach. It is usefully applied for the liver <note>original: "epatici"</note>. It counters bites and poisonous drinks when drunk with wine; it will work better if you add parsnip <note>original: "pastinace"</note> seed to it. In a poultice <note>original: "catapt"; abbreviation of *cataplasma*</note> and hung around the neck, it cleanses the body.

### XXIV ON WORMWOOD

**Wormwood** <note>original: "Absentio"; *Artemisia absinthium*</note> is known to everyone. The varieties from Pontus and Cappadocia <gloss>appearing</gloss> on Mount Taurus are considered better. Its medicinal quality is binding <gloss>and</gloss> <note>original: "stiptica"</note>, warming, and cleansing for the stomach. It softens the belly and brings down bile <gloss>from the system</gloss>. It is also a diuretic and effective against flatulence; it may soothe pain of the stomach, the belly, the colon, and the twisting pains of colic; it removes a loss of appetite. 

Indeed, a decoction of it cures those with jaundice <term>icterus</term> <note>original: "hictericos"</note>. When infused in water and taken in a measure of three small cups <note>original: "ciatus"; a cyathus was roughly 1.5 ounces</note>, it compels menstruation. It can also provide this same benefit when used as a suppository. When drunk with vinegar, it aids those suffering from the suffocation caused by mushrooms <note>original: "miceae"; referring to mushroom poisoning</note>. For those who drink it, it helps recovery from the effects of hemlock <note>original: "ixina"; likely referring to *ixine* or a similar toxic plant</note>, or the bites of shrews <note>original: "melgalis"</note> or sea-dragons, provided it is drunk with wine. 

With honey and soda added, it serves as a topical ointment <note>original: "diacrisma"</note>. It removes mustard-like spots <note>original: "sinapis"</note> and scales <note>original: "pinocidas"</note>, and it takes away bruises. With the addition of honey, it corrects dimness of the eyes and clears them; if poured into ears that are discharging pus, it is healthful. 

For eye pain, it is boiled with sweet wine and applied, which provides a most powerful effect. It is effectively mixed into poultices <term>cataplasms</term> <note>original: "catteplasmatib;"</note>. Applied to the flanks <term>hypochondria</term> <note>original: "hipocondriis"; the area of the upper abdomen</note> and the stomach, it provides aid to the liver. Mixed into wax-salves <note>original: "cerotis"</note> with soda and lard <note>original: "axungia"</note>, it draws out moisture from the groin and settles the problem of worms. 

Wormwood wine <note>original: "uino absentiati"</note> is also made in Pontus and Thrace; the people in those provinces all use this wine for the sake of their health. If put into a chest with clothing, it keeps away moths. If it is rubbed with oil and applied to the face, it keeps away gnats <note>original: "conopis"</note>. The juice of wormwood is extracted and preserved for many serious causes, which juice is used in potions...

Indeed, the herb is full of tiny seeds, much like the smaller southernwood; it has a bitter and heavy scent and is astringent <note>original: "sapticus"; likely a corruption of *stypticus*</note> with a warming quality. When honey is added, it kills the worms and eases the belly. When boiled and taken with lentils, it can perform all these actions. In Cappadocia, this variety of wormwood is used to fatten cattle.

### ON SANTONICUM. XXIV.

There is a third species of wormwood growing in Galatia which they call **Santonicum** <note>original: "auersandomicum"; referring to *Artemisia maritima* or *Artemisia santonica*</note>, because the place in which it first grew is called Santon. It is similar to wormwood, but its seeds are thicker and slightly bitter. However, it shares the same medicinal virtues as wormwood and the maritime variety.

### XXV. ON SOUTHERNWOOD.

**Southernwood** <note>original: "Abrotonon"; *Artemisia abrotanum*</note>, which many call *Heracleon* or *Chilacon*, is a plant whose shrub is tree-like. It is white, with small and divided leaves similar to maritime wormwood, covering the branches with golden flowers; it grows without fruit <note>meaning it lacks conspicuous seeds or fruit compared to other species</note> and is fragrant with a certain heavy scent and a very bitter taste. Such is the Sicilian variety.

And there is another kind, which they call the male; it is a shrubby plant with many tiny seeds like wormwood. It grows abundantly in Cappadocia, Galatia, Asia, and along the riverbanks in the city of Hierapolis <note>original: "ipra polu"; a corruption of Hierapolis</note>. Its seeds, whether boiled in water or infused raw, are drunk to cure orthopnea <term>difficulty breathing</term>, as well as for internal bruising, pleurisy, sciatica, and difficulty urinating <term>dysuria</term>...

## XXVI ON HYSSOP
**Hyssop** <note>original: "Hysopo"</note> is a herb known to all. But there are two unique species: one is the mountain variety, the other the garden variety. Its virtue is warming when boiled with dried figs, honey, and rue; when drunk, it is effective for many lung conditions <term>pneumonia</term>. it eases catarrh <term>an excessive buildup of mucus in the nose or throat</term> and is useful when taken by those with orthopnea <term>a condition where one can only breathe comfortably while standing or sitting upright</term>. It kills intestinal worms and, with honey, it can perform all the same actions as elecampane <note>original: "helleccruu[m]"; likely a corruption of *helenium*</note>. It purges the humors of the belly and is necessarily mixed into oxymel <term>a traditional medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</term>. It is eaten green with figs. For softening the stomach, cardamom is especially mixed with it. And in [the region of] Illyria, it provides the best results for [improving] the color of the face. It is used with nitre <note>a mineral form of potassium nitrate</note> and tartar <note>a salt found in wine casks</note>, and when applied, it helps the spleen and prevents dropsical humors <term>edema, or swelling caused by excess fluid</term> from returning. When drunk with wine, it disperses all swellings. Boiled and applied as a poultice, it clears away bruises from the body. It is very useful as a mustard gargle, especially when boiled with figs; its water heals toothache. Used as a fumigant, it quiets ringing in the ears.

## XXVII ON STOECHAS
**Stoechas** <note>original: "Sticada"; French Lavender (*Lavandula stoechas*)</note> grows on the islands of Galatia <note>referring to the Mediterranean coast of Gaul/France</note> near Marseilles, which are called the Stoechades islands; from which the plant received its name. It is a herb having tiny leaves and seeds which are similar to thyme <note>original: "foliatimmo"; likely *thymo*</note> but oblong, with a golden taste and a slightly bitter quality. Its decoction eases pains of the chest <note>original: "causa storacis"; likely a corruption of *thoracis*</note> just like the hyssop antidote.

## XXVIII ON OREGANO

They call it Heracleotic oregano <note>original: "Origanum heracleoticu"; a variety named after Heraclea in Pontus, known for its strength</note> or *cronites*. It has leaves similar to hyssop. The stalk of this plant is bent downwards, upon which the seed rises; it is not thick and has a somewhat bitter taste. Its property is warming. A decoction of it given with wine counters poisonous bites. When drunk with something sweet, <gloss>that is, against poisons</gloss> it provides relief for those who have swallowed aconite <note>a highly toxic flowering plant, also known as monkshood</note> <gloss>that is, hemlock</gloss> <note>The glossator clarifies that it acts against *conium*, the Greek term for hemlock</note> or gypsum <note>a mineral powder that is toxic if ingested</note> or *ephemerum* <note>a poisonous plant, likely *Colchicum*</note>. For bruises and all pains, and for dropsy <term>a swelling caused by excess fluid in the body</term> <margin>virtue</margin> it is especially healing when eaten with germander <note>original: "camere"; likely a corruption of *chamaedrys*</note>. An *oxyporum* <term>a fast-acting digestive aid or purgative</term> drunk with honeyed water expels black bile <note>one of the "four humors" of ancient medicine, associated with melancholy and digestive issues</note> through the bowels. It induces menstruation <margin>expels bile</margin>. It cuts short a cough like an electuary <term>a medicinal paste made by mixing herbs with honey or syrup</term>. When smeared on, it heals the itching of the body and removes sores and all spots. The water itself [the decoction], drunk in a bath, heals those with jaundice. Its juice is drunk while fresh to treat swellings of the throat and the uvula. It cures mouth sores when used with iris oil. Its juice, when put into the nostrils, provokes a discharge of blood <note>used as a method to purge the head of "heavy humors"</note>. Infused with milk, it prevents earaches. It provokes nausea; if it is mixed with honey and [lacuna/unclear] and a Syriac remedy <note>original: "rossis riacu"; likely a corruption of *syriacum*, a known multi-ingredient compound</note> cooked in a bronze vessel in the sun during the Dog Days <term>the hottest weeks of summer, usually July and August</term> for forty days and placed underneath [the bedding], it does not allow any animals to suffer from scabies <term>a contagious skin disease caused by parasitic mites</term>.

## XXVIIII ON POT MARJORAM

Pot marjoram <note>original: "Onitis"</note> is the name for another kind of oregano, whose leaves are white and similar to hyssop. Its seed is gathered at the head of the plant. In its medicinal power, it is similar to the former [oregano], but a little weaker.

## XXX ON WILD OREGANO

They call it wild oregano, or *panax* <note>meaning "all-heal"</note>, or *heraclea*, or *cunila*. For this reason it is more pungent. In its color, seed, and leaves, it is similar to the other oregano. [The stalks] are two palms high and thinner, above which the seed rises like dill; it has a white flower and a thin root.

### XXXI ON GOAT-OREGANO

Goat-oregano <note>original: "Traco origano"; the plant *Tragoriganum*</note> is a shrub with leaves similar to wild thyme. There is another kind similar to poisonous nettle <note>original: "urticæ... uenenati"</note> that has broad leaves and is not hairy. There is yet another kind with smaller leaves and a seed, which they call *prasium* <note>original: "prasiam"; likely referring to *Prasium majus* (Great Hedge-nettle) or a leek-colored variety</note>. But the best varieties are the Chian <note>original: "ciaca"</note>, the Alean <note>original: "alex"</note>, the Smyrnian, and the Cretan. The juice of all these is warming and diuretic; it softens the belly. Its decoction, when drunk, relieves colic. For those with spleen issues, it is curative when drunk with vinegar. It aids those who have quinsy <term>a painful abscess or inflammation of the throat</term> when drunk with wine. It induces menstruation and, when mixed with honey as an electuary <term>a medicinal paste or syrup</term>, it is used effectively for pneumonia <note>original: "pemplenmoniam"; a corruption of the Greek *peripneumonia*</note>. It removes the decay of the stomach and cures a loss of appetite. It helps those suffering from nausea. It is usefully applied to <unclear>itp</unclear> seasoned items; mixed with barley meal <term>polenta</term>, it disperses swellings.

### XXXII ON PENNYROYAL

Every drink of pennyroyal <note>original: "Pulejo"</note> is warming <note>original: "termantica"</note>, thinning <note>original: "leptantica"</note>, and beneficial for the liver <note>original: "hepatica"</note>. When drunk, it induces menstruation, expels the afterbirth <note>original: "secunda"</note>, and causes abortion. Mixed with honey and salt <gloss>and shaken</gloss>, it heals and cleanses the lungs. It relieves nausea and irritation of the stomach. When drunk with *posca* <term>a common Roman drink made of vinegar and water</term>, it restores health and expels black bile through the bowels. Drunk with wine, it counters poisonous bites. Applied with vinegar and bread, it frees people from "evil-doings" <note>original: "malefactionis"; likely referring to the effects of poisons or malicious charms</note>. Just as when it is burned [and the ash applied], it strengthens the gums. It is useful for all swellings when used with barley meal <term>polenta</term>, and when applied on its own, it cures gout <term>a painful form of arthritis, traditionally affecting the feet</term>. Mixed with wax-salves <term>cerates</term>, it provides clarity <note>original: "pabulat limpidae"</note>. For those with spleen issues, it is applied with salt. If it draws out good humors... it is rubbed on for itches and removes the swelling of the eyes with a compress.

# XXXIII ON DITTANY

They say that Dittany <note>original: "Dictamnu"; *Origanum dictamnus*, or Dittany of Crete</note> is like a wild pennyroyal or the balm herb. It is pungent and more acrid than pennyroyal; it has larger, thick leaves. The whole shrub is covered in a woolly down <note>original: "ut lhena"; referring to the Greek *chlaina* or Latin *laena*, a thick cloak, describing the plant's fuzzy texture</note>. However, it has neither flower nor seed. Its medicinal power is as great as that of pennyroyal, though a bit more pungent. If it is inserted <term>as a pessary</term> or applied as a fumigation <term>medicinal smoke</term>, it expels dead infants from the womb. Its power is so great that it is most effective for goats struck by arrows <margin>its power</margin> or when eaten by dogs <note>A famous ancient legend claimed that wounded wild goats in Crete would eat dittany to make arrows fall out of their bodies</note>.

# XXXIIII ON <gloss>false</gloss> FALSE DITTANY

False Dittany <note>original: "Seudo dictamno"; likely *Ballota pseudodictamnus*</note> grows in similar places and is similar in appearance, but its medicinal property is less pungent. It possesses the efficacy of true dittany but to a slightly lesser degree. There is, however, another "Dittany of Crete" <note>original: "diptamnu decretu"</note> which has broad leaves like water-mint <note>original: "simbrio"; *sisymbrium*</note>, but it has larger stems upon which there is a flower similar to wild clary <note>original: "hormini agrestis"</note>, though larger, black, and soft. Its leaves have a scent like water-mint, and it is usefully mixed into medicines made as electuaries <term>medicinal pastes mixed with honey or syrup</term>.

# XXXV ON SAGE

*Elelisphakos* <note>original: "Elelisfacu"; the Greek name for Sage, *Salvia officinalis*</note>, or *lolisfakos*, or *sphagnon*, is a shrub with oblong leaves. Its stems are square and whitish. The leaves are similar to those of a quince tree <note>original: "male quidoniae"</note>, but are oblong, smaller, rough, whiter, and fragrant with a reddish tint. They bear seeds on the stem similar to wild clary. It grows in very rugged places. Its property, when drunk, is diuretic <term>promotes urination</term>; it induces menstruation and causes abortion. It mitigates the sting of a sea stingray <note>original: "trigoni marianum"; the venomous *Trygon* or stingray</note>. It makes the hair black and thickens it. It heals veins from flowing blood in wounds and cleanses foul sores.

## XXXVI ON SPEARMINT ##

They say that Spearmint <note>original: "Edyosmu"; from the Greek *Hedyosmos*, meaning "sweet-smelling"</note> is a plant of increasing value. It is known to everyone for its warming, drying, and astringent virtues <note>original: "habentermanica et sapaca et esaptica"; these are corrupted Greek medical terms referring to the herb's specific digestive and heating properties</note>. Because of this, its juice is drunk with vinegar to assist those spitting up blood. It kills intestinal worms, stimulates sexual desire, and suppresses hiccups as well as bile and nausea. 

Two or three spoonfuls taken with sour pomegranate and applied with barley meal <term>polenta</term> disperses abscesses. Applied to the forehead, it eases a headache. It removes tumors and pain when used as a bitter medicine; with salt added, it helps against dog bites. Its juice mixed with honey-water <term>mulsa</term> drives away ear pain. If placed <term>as a pessary</term> before a woman has intercourse, it blocks the genital passage <note>A common ancient belief that mint could act as a contraceptive by cooling or "blocking" the womb</note>. It soothes the roughness of the tongue, curdles milk, and keeps cheese safe from rotting. It is well-mixed into digestive seasonings <note>original: "stomachie condituris"</note>. There is also a wild spearmint which has rougher leaves, is larger in its parts, and is pungent and powerful for the care of humans.

## XL On Wild Thyme

Wild Thyme <note>original: "Herpillo," from the Greek "erpyllos"</note>, which is also called *horanus*, is similar in scent and medicinal power to marjoram. It received this name because the Greeks use the word *herpi* <note>original: "herpi," meaning to creep or crawl</note>. It is so named because once the shrub is planted, it "walks" or spreads extensively by sending out new shoots. The leaves and small branches of wild thyme are like those of oregano, but whiter. There is also a field variety of wild thyme which they call *zigion* <note>original: "zigion," referring to *Thymus zygis*</note>. This variety does not spread across the ground but stands upright; its stalks and twigs are similar to the other, and you will find its leaves are like those of rue, but narrower and longer. It has a flower with a sweet scent, but it is sticky to the taste. It has a strong root and grows in stony places.

It is quite warming and has a sharper medicinal quality. It is effective for regulating menstruation and provokes urine <term>acts as a diuretic</term>. It is drunk for griping pains <note>original: "tortionibus," likely intestinal cramps</note> and for "shaking" pains or concussions. It subdues liver tumors and counteracts poisonous bites; it performs this whether it is drunk or applied topically. Boiled with vinegar and with rose oil added, it subdues headaches. It is especially useful for those suffering from lethargy <note>original: "litargicos," a state of drowsy unconsciousness</note> and frenzy <note>original: "freneticos," delirium</note> when applied to them. It provokes nausea when four [measures] are taken.

## XLI ON MARJORAM

<margin>powers</margin>
Marjoram <note>original: "Samsucus," likely *Origanum majorana*</note> is effective; it is also called *zicenus* and, as previously mentioned, the Egyptians call it *zicenus* and the Sicilians call it *amaracus*. The herb grows tall and is spread out over the ground. It has rough, round leaves similar to *calcamiten* <note>a corruption of "calamintha" or wild mint</note> and is very fragrant. Because of its warming quality, wreaths made from it and its oil are applied to the head when necessary. A decoction <term>the liquid resulting from boiling</term> of it heals those with dropsy <note>original: "ydropicas," a historical term for swelling or edema</note>, provokes urine, and is effective for griping pains. When dried and mixed with honey, it treats bruises.

### XLII On Melilot

Melilot <note>original: "Melilotus," likely *Melilotus officinalis* or Sweet Clover</note> is effective. The varieties from Attica, Cyzicus, and Calydon are best, possessing both good color and fragrance. It grows in Campania and looks like fenugreek. Its medicinal property <term>Virtus</term> is astringent and softening; it disperses all tumors, especially of the eyes when a sweetener <note>likely honey</note> is added. When cooked and applied as a poultice, it restrains swelling of the womb, the anus, and the testicles <note>original: "tesum," a likely corruption of "testium"</note>. When mixed with a medium of fenugreek flour, linseed, or crushed poppy heads <note>original: "codiae"</note> and applied, it brings all these conditions back to health. It mitigates stomach pains when taken with wine. Its juice removes earaches when a sweetener is added. For a headache, it restrains the pain when mixed with rose oil and vinegar and applied as a compress.

### XLIII On Sisymbrium

Sisymbrium <note>original: "Sisymbrio," generally identified as Watermint or Spearmint</note>, which some call "greater wild thyme," is planted in fields; if grown near water, it is similar to *redoformo* <note>perhaps a corruption of a plant name like "rhododaphne" or "erodion"</note> but with broader leaves and a more fragrant scent. Many <margin><note>original: "virt?"</note> medicinal powers</margin> are found in its composition. Its property <term>Virtus</term> is warming; it cures difficulty in urinating <term>strangury</term>. It is especially known for breaking up [kidney] stones; its seed, drunk with wine, provides the greatest relief for griping pains and hiccups. The leaves, applied as a poultice to the forehead, mitigate headache and help those suffering from nausea.

### XLV ON ACINUS

The leaves and tiny seeds of the Acinus herb <note>original: "Acenur," likely *Acinos arvensis* or Wild Basil</note> are used together to be woven into garlands. ### XLVI ON BACCHARIS

Its medicinal property <term>Virtus</term> is astringent and digestive. When applied to the head, it removes pain; it takes away swelling from the eyes and cures the onset of hair loss <note>original: "alopiaas," alopecia</note>. When applied to the breasts, it disperses swelling. It is effective for "Holy Fire" <term>Igne sacro</term>; this herb brings relief to all such conditions.

## XLVIII ON ANOTHER KIND OF RUE

Another kind of rue grows in Macedonia and in Galatia in Asia, which the citizens call **Moly**. It is a shrub growing many roots from a single base, with longer leaves that are uneven <note>original: "anistera"</note> but soft, having a heavy odor and a white flower. It has seed heads larger than our own, divided into three parts. Its seed is dark reddish and triangular with a bitter taste. This seed is gathered at the proper time or in the summer. When honey, wine, capon gall, saffron, and fennel juice are added to it, it clears the dimness of the eyes better than many other rues and relieves pain. Indeed, in Cappadocia they call it **Syr** because it is similar to Moly. It grows in damp places and on hills.

## XLVIIII ON MOLY

Moly has leaves similar to wild rue, but broader and spread over the ground. It has saffron-colored flowers with a milky hue, but the plant is not seen except as if it has a slender rod.

### ON HERACLEAN ALL-HEAL

Heraclean All-heal <term>Panace eracleo</term> <note>Commonly identified as *Opopanax chironium*, a plant famous in antiquity for its "all-healing" properties</note>, from which opopanax resin is gathered, grows abundantly in Boeotia <note>original: "uiotia"</note>, Phocis <note>original: "foadis"</note>, and Arcadia. When gathering it during its bloom for harvest, it has smaller leaves spread upon the ground, green and very rough like a fig leaf, rounded and divided into five parts. It has a long stalk like a giant fennel <term>ferula</term> <note>A tall, flowering herbaceous plant</note> and is full of white pith. On this stalk, the leaves are smaller and curved; upon these, at the top of the stalk, is a head similar to dill <note>original: "aneti"</note>, bearing a honey-colored flower and a fragrant, warm seed. It has a single solid root which sends out many offshoots; it is white with a heavy, thick odor and a bitter taste. It grows in Syria, Libya <note>original: "bis liuie"</note>, and Macedonia. 

Its juice is best collected when the plant begins to wither. It is gathered mostly from its roots in summer, from which a white "tear" <note>original: "lacrimus," referring to the resinous sap</note> emerges; in time, this sap dries and turns a saffron color <note>original: "croceus"</note>. In gathering this juice, many follow the practice of digging small pits in the ground beneath the plant, in which they lay down the leaves of the plant itself; the wounded plant then releases its resinous "tears" onto these leaves. Similarly, they also collect the "tears" from its stalks by making incisions. One should choose roots that are white, dry, thin, and not old, as they are warmer to the taste and pleasant-smelling. The best seed is that which is found in the middle of the head, for the outer seeds are old and useless. 

When choosing opopanax <term>opopanace</term> <note>The gummy resin harvested from the plant, used as a stimulant and antispasmodic</note>, look for that which is saffron-colored on the outside and white within, bitter in taste, fatty, brittle, and porous. It should be easily distinguished from pitch <note>original: "a pice"</note>, possess a heavy smell, and be soft to the touch; be wary, as it is often adulterated.

If it is pure, it dissolves like milk; if not, it becomes like birdlime <note>original: "viscur" / "viscum," a sticky substance used for trapping birds</note>. It has a warming, softening <term>malactica</term> <note>a medicine used to soften skin or tumors</note>, and oily <term>lipantica</term> <note>an emollient or soothing fat-based treatment</note> quality, which is why it treats periodic chills, bruises, side pains, coughs, and griping pains, providing the greatest effect. It helps with difficulty urinating <term>stranguriis</term> and sores of the bladder <gloss>bladder</gloss> <note>the scribe added a small "b" above "uulsice" to correct it to "uulbisice," a corruption of the Latin for bladder, "uesicae"</note> when drunk with mead or wine. It promotes menstruation <term>menstruis</term> and causes abortion. It dissolves hysterical inflations <note>referring to "suffocation of the womb," a historical diagnosis for various female ailments</note> and hard tumors. Added to honey, it is a healthy remedy for sciatica <term>sciaticis</term> when rubbed on; it is also a necessary ingredient in restorative ointments <term>acopis</term> <note>salves used to relieve weariness or muscle pain</note>. Added to a preparation for headache, it mitigates the pain. Applied to carbuncles, it breaks them open. Mixed with grape juice and applied, it heals gout <term>podagrias</term> and takes away the pain when applied again. It is especially effective for teeth when placed into a cavity. It clears away mistiness of the eyes. When mixed with an equal weight of pitch, it cures the bite of a mad dog. It brings wounds to health, and when applied with honey to exposed bones, it restores the flesh. Its seed is added to green wormwood and taken to promote menstruation. Combined with birthwort <term>aristolozia</term> <note>Aristolochia, a plant traditionally used to aid childbirth and treat venomous bites</note>, it counters venomous bites. Drunk with wine, it assists with hysterical suffocations.

# LI ON ASCLEPIAN ALL-HEAL<insert>PANAX</insert>

Asclepian All-heal <term>Panax asclepio</term> <note>Likely *Hypericum coris* or a similar species of St. John's Wort named after the god of healing, Asclepius</note> is an herb with a slender stalk in the middle, about one cubit in length. It is knotty, with leaves similar to St. John's Wort <note>original: "amurca tro," likely a corruption of "androsaimon"</note> but larger and rougher. Upon the stalk itself, it has a small head in which the flowers are very golden and fragrant. Its root is slender, but the flower and its seed, when added to honey, help with wounds and pustules. It especially counters spreading ulcers <term>Phagedaenica</term> <note>original: "Fage denica," referring to "eating" or gangrenous sores</note> when applied as an ointment with wine and oil; so applied, it provides relief.
