They say many things about wild oregano All-heal <note>original: "panace origano agreste"</note>, etc., or with the moon. Book II.

## ON CHIRONIAN ALL-HEAL

Chironian All-heal <note>named after Chiron, the centaur of Greek mythology known for his medicinal skills</note> grows on Mount Pelion; it has bitter leaves and bears a flower that shines like gold. It has a thin root and a taste that is quite sticky <note>original: "uisado," from "viscido"</note>. The root possesses a particular power: when drunk, it counteracts poisonous bites, and when applied to open sores, it performs the same benefit.

## BOOK IV: ON LOVAGE

<margin>Syrian?</margin>
Lovage is relied upon by many in the province of Liguria, from which it took its name; it grows on Mount Viso in the Alps, but some call it All-heal <note>original: "panaceam"</note> because its roots are white and fragrant, similar to All-heal. Its virtues are unified with those of All-heal. It grows in high, rough, and shady places with a long stalk similar to dill and is knotted; on this stalk are leaves similar to melilot <note>a type of sweet clover</note>, though softer and more fragrant. At the very top, the leaves are again very thin and hard. On this stalk is a head where it shows its seed; this seed is blackish and oblong, like the color of hay <note>possibly a corruption of "fennel"</note>, with a sticky and fragrant taste.
<margin>8th [recipe?]</margin>
Its root is white, similar to Heraclean All-heal, and is fragrant in its potency. Both the root and the seed are hot and peppery <note>original: "pepata"</note> and are effective against all pains of the intestines. It dissolves inflations of the stomach <note>referring to gas or bloating</note>; it helps against poisonous things; it provokes urine and compels menstruation when drunk. The root performs this when used as a treatment or placed beneath <note>as a suppository or plaster</note>. Its root and seed are mixed into necessary digestive salts <term>oxyparis</term> <note>a digestive preparation made with vinegar, herbs, and salts</note>; it is effectively added to preparations for digestion. It is stomach-settling <term>eustomachus</term> <note>original: "eustomachur," a medicine that aids digestion and appetite</note>; for this reason, many inhabitants of that province use it in their seasonings and mixes. To its seed, another similar seed is sometimes mixed—one known in Rome that is quite bitter. Many people also add the seeds of hartwort <note>original: "seseli"</note> and fennel to it.
<margin>good for the stomach?</margin>

# LV ON GARDEN PARSNIP

Garden parsnip <note>original: "pastinaca hortina"; in antiquity, this term could refer to both the parsnip and the carrot</note> is eaten by everyone and is healthy for everyone; however, it possesses a slightly less potent medicinal power.

# LVI ON SESELI

<margin>male</margin> One kind of Seseli <note>likely Hartwort or Meadow-saxifrage</note> has long leaves similar to fennel but thicker on the stalks. It is long, with a small head in which the seed is long, angular, thick, and sticky <note>original: "uisado"</note>; it is eaten with pleasure. Its root is long and fragrant in its quality. Both the seed and the root are warming <note>original: "termantiaca," from the Greek 'thermantikos'</note> and diuretic; when drunk, it provokes urine, treats orthopnea <note>original: "botopnoiat," a corruption of 'orthopnoia,' meaning difficulty breathing unless standing or sitting upright</note>, heals obstructions of the uterus, and helps with cramps and epilepsy. It brings on menstruation and causes abortion. It is effective for all internal organs. An old cough is cured when it is drunk with wine; it promotes digestion and is a helper to all. <margin>for the liver</margin> It leads a person back to health when drunk with pepper and wine. It protects the whole man from the cold; it is given to goats and all animals so that they may conceive.

# LVII ON ETHIOPIAN SESELI

<margin>leaves</margin> Ethiopian Seseli has leaves similar to ivy, though shorter, and long like honeysuckle <note>original: "pericleminu," referring to the plant Periclymenum</note>. It is a shrub...

### LVIII ON PELOPONNESIAN SESELI

Peloponnesian Seseli has leaves similar to hemlock <note>original: "conio," referring to *Conium maculatum*</note> but thicker and more pointed. Its stalks are larger and have a myrrh-like scent; the stalk has little pods <note>original: "uterulae," literally "little wombs," likely referring to the seed casings or umbels</note> in which the seed is found. The seed is shining and white as ceruse <note>original: "cerussu," a white lead pigment; used here to describe the color</note> and is fragrant in its quality. All Seseli plants are beneficial, but it is said that this one heals rough areas and provides moisture.

### LVIIII ON GORDILION

Cordilion <note>also known as Tordylium or Hartwort</note> is called "mule's seseli" and "cracuilla." It grows in stony channels <note>original: "canalcia," possibly referring to mountainous or rocky areas</note> and is a spongy shrub. The seeds are round and doubled, like a bean; they are sticky <note>original: "visadu"</note> and fragrant. If drunk, it provokes urine and menstruation. The juice of its stalk and its seed is drunk in the amount of one <term>denarius</term> <note>indicated by the symbol 𐆎</note> and two obols <note>ancient units of weight</note> with a sweet liquid for ten days; it is a remedy for the kidneys. Its root, used like elaterium <note>a potent purgative derived from the juice of the wild cucumber</note>, heals most healthfully and wonderfully.

### LX ON SINON

Sinon <note>Stone-parsley or *Sison amomum*</note> has a very small seed that is quite nourishing; it is similar to parsley but more oblong and black. With its hot taste, it is drunk to heal those suffering from the spleen <note>original: "spleneticis," referring to those with an enlarged spleen or "melancholy" humors</note>; it provokes urine and induces menstruation if used with boiled gourds.

### LXI ON ANISE

Anise <note>original: "Anesos"</note> is hot and dry in its quality. It is both sleep-inducing <note>original: "carotica"</note> and a diuretic <note>promotes urine</note>. It treats those with dropsy <note>original: "ydropicis"</note> and removes heaviness. When drunk, it counteracts poison. It cuts through flatulence, binds the belly <note>stops diarrhea</note>, and induces menstruation. It stimulates milk in women and serves Venus <note>original: "venerem famulat," meaning it acts as an aphrodisiac</note>. When used as a fumigation with nard, it takes away headaches; applied with rose oil, it helps with earaches. It is better when fresh and full of seeds; old anise is pierced by its own strong odor and loses its color. The Egyptian variety is considered second-best.

### LXII ON CARAWAY

Caraway <note>original: "Careu"</note> seed is for everyone...

## LXIII ON DILL

When dill <note>original: "aneto"</note> is dried and boiled and its water is drunk, it provokes milk in nursing women. It is effective against cramps <note>original: "tortionib," literally "twistings" of the gut</note> and flatulence <note>original: "inflationib"</note>. For those who refuse a drink, it still provokes urine. It stops hiccups <note>original: "sugglutarem"</note>. However, it causes blurred vision in the eyes and, if drunk too frequently, affects the genitals. A decoction of it is useful when applied as a warm compress <note>original: "fomento"</note> for the wombs of women. Its seed, when burnt and applied, dissolves condylomas <note>original: "condilomatas," referring to skin growths or warts</note>.

## LXIIII ON OUR CUMIN, GOOD FOR THE STOMACH

Most [cumin] comes from Ethiopia, but the rest grows in Galatia, Spain, Alixa <note>possibly a corruption of a regional name like Achaia or Lycia</note>, and India, and in many other places. It is and was used for cramps and flatulence. Boiled in oil and used as a suppository, it heals. Applied as a poultice <note>original: "catapta," for "cataplasma"</note>, it is used for orthopnea <note>difficulty breathing while lying flat</note>. Given with <term>posca</term> <note>a mixture of vinegar and water</note>, it is essential for venomous bites and provides aid. For swelling of the testicles, it is mixed with bean meal and dried grapes <note>original: "uuae purise"</note>, and applied whole as a remedy. It draws out the menses. Mixed with vinegar, it binds [stops] blood flowing from the nose. It is drunk to restore color to a pale complexion, and also applied as an ointment.

## LXV ON WILD CUMIN

Wild cumin grows abundantly in Chalcedonia and Spain. It has a thin stalk the length of a palm, on which grow very thin and divided leaves, similar to <term>gingidium</term> <note>wild chervil</note>. On this stalk are five or six small, round, and soft heads, in which the seed is found. When you apply it, it is more potent <note>original: "uisadiore," likely from "validiore"</note> than our common variety. For nosebleeds, it is applied locally <note>original: "ectarlo cas," likely "extrinsecus locas"</note>. It is also drunk for cramps and flatulence, and when mixed very healthfully with vinegar, it truly helps those with hiccups. It counteracts poison and, with wine, treats stomach pain. This is what the Egyptians call "Royal Cumin" <note>original: "basilican quiminon"</note>.

It is chewed and, when applied, it clears away bruising <note>original: "liuore"</note>. Added to honey and raisins, it is known to do all the aforementioned <note>original: "ss," an abbreviation for *suprascripta*</note> things. # LXVI ON AMMEOS <note>Known today as Ajwain or Bishop’s Weed</note>

Many also call this Ethiopian cumin <gloss>Ethiopian</gloss> or "basilicon" <note>meaning "royal" or "kingly"</note>, though others say Ethiopian cumin is of a different nature, and that Ammeos is of another kind. Its seed is very small in all respects; it is not like cumin, but has the taste of oregano. One should choose seeds that are fresh and clean. Its power is warming <term>termantic</term> and drying <term>sarantic</term> <note>These are Latinized Greek medical terms for substances that heat and dry the body’s humors</note>. It heals cramps <note>original: "tortionib," literally "twistings" of the gut</note> and, when drunk with wine, it provokes and regulates the menstrual periods. It is mixed into dry medicinal compositions to temper the heat of cauteries. Added to honey, it restores a uniform color to the body <note>likely referring to the removal of skin spots or vitiligo</note>. When used as a fumigant <note>by burning the herbs and inhaling or exposing the body to the smoke</note> with resin and raisins, it cleanses the womb <note>original: "matricem"</note>.

# LXVII Coriander

Its power is cooling. It is crushed and reduced into a poultice <note>original: "catapl." for *cataplasma*</note>; mixed with polenta and wheaten bread and applied, it extinguishes "wild fire" <note>original: "igne agrū," likely *ignis sacer* or erysipelas, an inflammatory skin infection</note> and removes fiery tumors. With honey and raisins added and applied, it cures night-sores <note>original: "epinicadus," a corruption of the Greek *epinyctis*, or inflammatory pustules that appear at night</note>, swelling of the testicles, and carbuncles. Mixed with crushed beans, it is effective against scrofula <note>original: "scrofis," a swelling of the lymph nodes</note> and pustules. Its seed, drunk with something sweet, kills intestinal worms <note>original: "lumbricos"</note>. It causes the genitals of men to grow <note>this may refer to increasing potency or a physical effect</note>; however, if too much of the seed itself is taken, it dulls the human senses or brings death more quickly. Therefore, anyone who uses it should be cautious if using it frequently. Its juice, mixed with vinegar or litharge <note>original: "spume argenti," literally "silver foam," a lead-based mineral</note>, white lead <note>original: "cerussa"</note>, and wine, clears away all boiling and stinging pustules.

# LXVIII ON CELERY
<note>original: "De Apio"; likely referring to Garden Celery, *Apium graveolens*</note>

Garden celery <note>original: "Apio hortenoti," likely a corruption of *hortense*</note> is much desired. It possesses as much effectiveness as coriander. When mixed with bread and applied as a poultice, it disperses swellings <note>original: "tumorof," for *tumores*</note> of the eyes; a mixture with pearl barley <note>original: "polentę"</note> can do the same. It is added to fodder <note>original: "saginatione," though in a human context often implies satiating or nourishing the stomach</note> to assist the stomach. It is usefully applied to swollen breasts. It provokes the flow of urine. A decoction of its roots, when drunk, counters poisons and prevents vomiting. It binds the bowels <note>original: "ventrē fringit," used here to mean it treats diarrhea</note>. Its seed is highly diuretic and counters the bites of venomous creatures. It acts as a remedy for those who have drunk silver dross <note>original: "spuma argenta," referring to litharge or lead oxide, which was toxic</note>; it heals the gut and removes inflation of the stomach. It is a necessary ingredient mixed into soothing antidotes <term>anodyne</term> <note>medicines designed to relieve pain</note>. It provides a beneficial effect for those suffering from rheum <note>original: "dctoriis," likely *distillationibus*, referring to mucus discharge</note> and coughs.

# LXVIIII ON WILD CELERY
<note>original: "De Apio Agreste"</note>

Wild celery, which grows in moist places, is larger than our garden variety <note>The Latin "sed his maiorē. nrō" is abbreviated/garbled but suggests a comparison to the common variety</note>. It is able to produce... [The remaining text for this entry is fragmented and describes its potency].

# LXX ON MOUNTAIN CELERY
<gloss>Mountain Celery <note>original: "Oreo selinon," from the Greek *oros* (mountain) and *selinon* (celery)</note></gloss>

This is mountain celery, having a long stalk and a long root, but with smaller, rounded parts in which the seed is found. The seed is both oblong and green, possessing an odor and power similar to cumin. The power of its root and seed has a diuretic effect; when drunk with wine, it commands the menstrual flow. It is usefully mixed with substances of "hot" medicinal qualities <note>Galenic medicine categorized plants by their "temperament," such as hot, cold, moist, or dry</note>. It is called *Oreo selinon* precisely for this reason: because it is born on the mountain.

<margin>green <note>original: "vire," likely a catchword for the following page</note></margin>

# LXXI ON ROCK PARSLEY
<note>original: "De Petro Selino," the ancestor of modern Parsley</note>

Rock parsley grows in Macedonia in rocky crevices or in caves. Its seed is tiny, similar to ajwain <note>original: "ameō"</note>, fragrant and green with an aromatic scent. Its power is diuretic; it commands the menstrual flow and remedies inflations of the stomach and the colon. It brings relief to "twistings" <note>original: "tortionib," meaning intestinal cramps or colic</note>. It mitigates pain in the side. It assists those suffering from kidney trouble <term>nephretici</term> and relieves pain in the eyes, especially when drunk with wine. It is mixed into diuretic compositions.

# LXXII ON HORSE CELERY
<note>original: "De Ippo Selino"; likely Alexanders, *Smyrnium olusatrum*</note>

They call this "Horse Celery" <note>from the Greek *hippos* (horse) and *selinon*</note>, or *amei londi* <note>possibly a regional or corrupted name</note>, or wild celery, or *smirnion*. The Romans call it... <note>The transcription ends here</note>. It grows from a single root into many stalks, on which there are heads shaped like a cone.

They call Alexanders <note>original: "olusatrum"; likely *Smyrnium olusatrum*, also known as horse-parsley</note> *Autinion* <note>original: "Autinion"; possibly a corruption of *agrioselinon* (wild celery) or *hipposelinon*</note>, but it is larger than the mountain variety and whiter. ### LXXIII ON SMYRNION <gloss> i.e., stone parsley </gloss>

<margin>Characteristics:</margin>
Which they call by another name in the preface. It does not grow much on Mount Amanus <note>A mountain range in modern-day Turkey, known in antiquity for its medicinal plants</note>. This stalk has many branches similar to a turnip; it has broad leaves spread out upon the ground, which are thick and fragrant with a very fine green color. On top of its stalks, it has little heads similar to dill. The seed is roundish, like a small black hillock, with a pungent taste and a smell like myrrh. Its root is pungent, fragrant, and soft, containing a great deal of juice that bites the throat; it has a black skin on the outside and is green or whitish on the inside.

<margin>Virtues:</margin>
It grows in rough and moist places. The property of its root, its seed, and the herb itself is warming. Its leaves are preserved in salt. The root binds the bowels. It counters poisons, and acts as a remedy for coughs and for <term>orthopnea</term> <note>a condition where a person has difficulty breathing unless they are sitting or standing upright</note>. It provokes the flow of urine. Its leaves, when applied to the head, disperse swellings, hard growths, and pustules. Its root leads wounds to form a scar and can perform all the actions mentioned above. Its seed provokes urine and is very effective for kidney and spleen conditions, as well as pains of the bladder. It brings on menstruation...

When drunk, it disperses stomach gas <note>original: "inflationes stomaca"</note>, induces sweating, and is excellent for ruptures. It especially helps those with dropsy <note>original: "ydropiar"; an old term for swelling caused by excess fluid</note> and periodic fevers.

## LXXIIII ON ELAPHOBOSKON <gloss>i.e., wild parsnip</gloss>

The *Elaphoboskon* herb has stalks similar to fennel or rosemary. The stalk is full of nodes; its leaves are two fingers wide and oblong, similar to the terebinth tree, though they are rough and fragile. It puts forth many small branches which have little heads similar to dill. Its root is two fingers long, broad <note>original: "luta," likely a scribe's error for "lata" (broad)</note>, white, and fragrant. It is suitable for eating, and its stalks are eaten preserved in brine <note>original: "amular," likely referring to *halmuria* or pickling juice</note>. This herb is said to be eaten by deer <note>The Greek name *elaphoboskon* literally means "deer-fodder"</note> so they might cast off their horns <note>This reflects an ancient belief that certain herbs helped deer shed their antlers or heal after doing so</note>, and it is for this reason they seek it out to counter poisons in their bodies, whereby the herb resists the venom.

## LXXV ON MARATHRUM <gloss>i.e., fennel</gloss>

Fennel is an herb known to everyone who eats it; it increases the milk of nursing women. It provides the same benefit for the bladder <note>original: "catcept," likely a corruption of "cystim" or "vesicam"</note> when applied or taken with <term>sapa</term> <note>a thick syrup made by boiling down new wine</note>. A decoction <note>original: "elixatura"</note> of it, when drunk, heals those with kidney trouble and bladder pain. It provokes urine and, when taken with wine, counters poisonous bites. It regulates menstruation and takes away hiccups <note>original: "grinautatollit," likely a corruption of "singultum tollit"</note> when drunk with water, and also treats the heat of the stomach. Its root, when cooked with honey, brings dog bites to health. The juice of its leaves and stalks is dried in the sun and mixed into preparations for the eyes. It clears dimness of vision from the eyes. A juice can be expressed from its green seeds and its root, but the most powerful juice is used as a wash for watering eyes.

## LXXVI ON HIPPOMARATHRUM <gloss>i.e., horse-fennel</gloss>

This is wild fennel, but it is larger, both in its seed and its stalk. Its seed is similar to coriander <note>original: "cactis," likely a corruption of "coriandro"</note>, and it has a fragrant root.

## LXXVIII ON CRETAN DAUCUS <gloss>Wild Carrot</gloss>

The plant they call Cretan Daucus has leaves similar to fennel, but they are smaller and tender. It has a stalk two palms <note>A "palm" was a standard measurement based on the width of a hand</note> long, on which the head of the stalk is like coriander with white flowers. In this head is the seed, which is white, rough, and small, with a pungent <note>original: "uisado," likely meaning sharp or acrid</note> taste and a fragrant smell. Its root is one finger thick and two palms long; it grows in rough and sunny places.

But there is another kind of Daucus that is similar to wild celery <note>original: "apum similis agrestis"</note>; it is pungent-smelling and warm in nature, but the Cretan variety is better. And there is a third kind of Daucus having leaves like coriander and a white flower, but in its little head and seed it is like dill. The seed itself is oblong and heavy like cumin, but it is warmer than all the seeds mentioned above. When drunk, it induces menstruation, provokes urine, helps with griping pains in the gut, and is effective for those with a cough. It counters the bites of venomous spiders <note>original: "phalangioner," referring to the *phalangium* spider</note>. Applied as a poultice <note>original: "catapt," likely an abbreviation for *cataplasma*</note>, it soothes pustules and tumors. The Cretan Daucus root has similar powers; especially when drunk with wine, it is a help against poisons.

## LXXVIIII ON PELLITORY <gloss>Piretrum</gloss>

Pellitory is an herb having leaves similar to wild Daucus or fennel. On its stalk, the little head is round, like dill. The thickness of its roots is one finger, with a hot taste. It draws out phlegm if it is boiled with vinegar and used as a gargle. When chewed, it clears phlegm from the head <note>original: "rapae capite," likely a corruption of "proprie capite" or a specific anatomical reference</note>. Rubbed on with oil, it provokes sweat and prevents chills <note>original: "frigura"</note> and shivering <note>original: "pica," which could refer to various tremors or ailments</note>.

## LXXX ON LIBANOTIS <note>likely *Rosmarinus* or an umbellifer such as *Seseli*; the name derives from *libanos*, the Greek word for frankincense</note>

There are two kinds of Libanotis. One kind produces a seed that they call <term>mulcedon</term> <note>meaning "sweetness" or "smoothness"</note> or... <note>original: "causa nemo," likely a scribal error</note> whose seed they call <term>acmū</term>. They have leaves similar to <term>maratrum</term> <gloss>fennel</gloss>, but broader and more rounded, spread upon the ground. In the middle, they have a fragrant stalk <note>original: "uirga"</note> much longer than a cubit <note>roughly 18 inches</note>. On this stalk is a little head in which it produces a white seed similar to <term>spondylium</term> <gloss>hogweed</gloss>; this seed is rounded and angular, and has a pungent <note>original: "uisado," likely acrid or sharp</note> smell. They have the scent of resin, or like burned <term>male frankincense</term> <note>original: "masatū conburae chor," likely a corruption of "masculum conburat"</note>. Its root is white and has the smell of incense.

## LXXXI ON ANOTHER KIND OF LIBANOTIS

The second kind of Libanotis is similar to the one written above. The seed is broad and black, like <term>fundilo</term> <gloss>cow parsnip</gloss>, but the root is not as warm. It is black on the outside and white on the inside.

## LXXXII ON THE THIRD KIND OF LIBANOTIS

The Libanotis which is called <term>acarpos</term> <gloss>fruitless</gloss> is without seed. It is similar in all respects to those written above, but this one has neither a stalk nor a flower... <note>original: "lo arnaceā," meaning unclear, perhaps referring to a woolly texture</note> in rough and rocky places. The leaves of all these kinds, when applied as a <term>cataplasm</term> <gloss>poultice</gloss>, prevent hemorrhoids, take away swelling of the anus, and remove <term>condylomata</term> <gloss>growths or warts</gloss>. It dissolves <term>scrofula</term> <gloss>swelling of the lymph nodes</gloss> and disperses <term>apostemes</term> <gloss>abscesses</gloss>. Similarly, its dry root with honey added cleanses filthy wounds; the whole plant is used as a medicine for all these things. It also counteracts the poisons of bites. That is to say, when prepared with wine, it can induce menstruation and provoke urine. It clears up pustules on the body. The juice of its herb and its roots will not allow "foggy" vision <note>original: "caligine oculi," likely referring to cataracts or blurred sight</note> to remain.

## **LXXXIIII ON HOGWEED**

Hogweed <note>original: "Sfondilion," *Heracleum sphondylium*</note> has leaves similar to a plane tree or all-heal <term>panaca</term>; it has stems two cubits long <note>approximately three feet</note> similar to fennel <term>maratri</term>, upon which are heads similar to <term>seseli</term> <gloss>meadow saxifrage</gloss>. Its seed, when drunk, expels phlegm from the belly. Likewise, it is used for those with liver trouble <term>epaticis</term>, jaundice, and those who suffer from shortness of breath <term>ortopomar</term>. It also benefits epileptics <term>epilenciacis</term>, and it treats uterine suffocations <note>original: "offocationib; steriar," a historical term for various gynecological distresses</note> by its smoke. Boiled in oil and applied as a compress, it is used for the head.

### LXXXV ON THE GREEK FERULA

### LXXXVI ON PEUCEDANUM

Peucedanum <note>Hog's Fennel or Sulphur-wort, *Peucedanum officinale*</note>, which some call *rusia* <note>this may be a corruption of a local name</note>. Its root is black, thick, and has a heavy odor; it contains a great deal of resin <term>lacrimam</term>. It grows in shady and mountainous places. The resin is collected in this way: when the root is fresh, by striking its "neck" <note>the crown of the root</note>, the resin which it emits is collected and dried in the shade, so that it does not perish in the heat of the sun. Because of its odor, it causes dizziness <note>original: *cotossin*, from the Greek *skotosis*</note> and headache for those collecting it, unless rose oil has been applied to the forehead and nostrils. When the root has emitted its resin, it remains in the vessels. Similarly, the juice can be collected from its stalks just like from a mandrake, but the resin of the roots has much more potency than the juice of the stalks. Because the juice also...

Black Cumin <note>original: *Meconio*; likely *Nigella sativa*, often called "poppy-like" due to its seed head</note> is a smaller shrub with tiny and very thin leaves. The shrub itself is about two palms long and bears a small seed. Its leaves are very similar to groundsel <note>original: *ari gerona*; referring to the plant *Erigeron*</note>; at the top, it has a small head resembling a poppy <term>meconio</term>, but it is oblong. In the middle, there is a kind of wall that divides the seed itself. This seed is black, sticky, and fragrant; it is the same seed that people sprinkle on bread with honeyed wine <term>mulsam</term>.

Applied as a poultice <term>cataplasma</term> <note>abbreviated as *catapt* in the manuscript</note>, it mitigates headache. At the onset of a cataract <term>suffusionis</term> <note>literally a "pouring over" the eye; referring to blurred vision or early cataracts</note>, it is ground and put into the nostrils with medicinal additives. Ground with Illyrian iris, it most healthily cures freckles <term>lentiginis</term> and skin eruptions <note>original: *deprics*, likely a corruption of *lepras* or *depascentia* (consuming sores)</note> when applied. It cures old tumors and hard growths with vinegar alone, and treats carbuncles with old urine to bring them back to health.

It is rightly added to vinegar and cooked; when ground and held in the mouth, it does not allow pain in the teeth. Cooked in water and placed as a poultice on the navel <note>original: *uulico*, a corruption of *umbilico*</note>, it drives out worms. Frequently applied so its odor can be inhaled, it checks catarrhs <note>colds or runny noses</note>. Drunk for several days with honeyed wine, it regulates the menses and draws out urine abundantly <note>original: *pro lacce*, likely *prolixe*</note>.
<margin>lep</margin>
Drunk with soda <term>nitro</term> <note>natural sodium carbonate used in medicine</note>, it is a singular defense against shortness of breath <term>dyspnoeas</term>. It counters poisonous bites when drunk with water. Used as a fumigant, it drives away snakes—indeed, it excludes them all.

### LXXXVIII CONCERNING SILPHIUM <note>original: *Silpi*; a famous, now possibly extinct medicinal plant from North Africa</note>

The root is known to everyone; it grows in Syria, Armenia, Media, and Libya. Its stalk is called *aspeton* <note>likely a corruption of the Greek *maspeton*, referring to the leaf or stalk of the silphium plant</note>, which is similar to giant fennel <term>ferula</term>. The leaves are similar to celery <note>original: *apio*</note>, and the broad seed is called *magidaris*.

The virtue of the root is that it is purgative <term>enatica et exeranatica</term> <note>Latinized Greek medical terms for cleansing the bowels</note> for the belly and provokes the breaking of gas in the stomach. It is hard to digest but suitable for the bladder <term>vissicae</term>. Taken mixed with wax-salves <term>cerotis</term> and applied, it disperses rot and scrofula <note>swelling of the lymph nodes</note>; added to oil, it clears bruises on the body.

That which shines with a white color... the sap from Cyrene <note>original: *rinnaci*, likely a corruption of *Cyrenaici*</note>; if anyone tastes it, sweat flows through their whole body, for it has a pleasant odor and a savory taste. When taken, it often makes the complexion clear. In a soft-boiled egg, it benefits those with a cough. It helps pleurisy and dropsy <note>original: *idropias*</note> when combined with dried figs. When drunk with pepper and added wine, it drives out internal chills. With curdled milk, it helps a loose stomach. It treats epileptics when drunk with *posca* <note>original: *puca*, a mixture of vinegar and water</note>. When drunk with myrrh and pepper, it compels the menstrual flow; it softens the belly when drunk with lye-water <note>original: *lixiba*</note>. It helps those falling from a height. It is mixed with *oxyporum* <note>original: *oxigarif*, a digestive condiment made of vinegar and spices</note>. Mixed with bitter almonds and rue <note>original: *eruta*</note, it is eaten as a necessary remedy for all conditions.

## LXXXVIIII ON OPOFILON <note>Likely *opopanax*, a medicinal gum resin</note>.

Opofilon has a very similar efficacy to Silphium, but it repairs roughness of the nostrils and restores the voice; it stops discordant noises in the ears. Many eat it in salads <note>original: *escariola*</note>...

## XC ON GYDARIS <note>Likely *magydaris*, a plant closely related to Silphium</note>.

Gydaris is said to be of two kinds growing in Libya. Its root is similar to Silphium, but it is a little smaller. It softens the... <note>original: *uisada*, likely a corruption of *viscera* (innards) or *vulnera* (wounds)</note> and they do not have the same sap. Its power is that of Silphium.

## XCI ON SAGAPENUM <note>A yellow-brown resin from the *Ferula* plant</note>.

Sagapenum is a "tear" <note>a resinous drop</note> from a giant fennel <note>original: *ferulo*</note> growing in Media <note>ancient Iran</note>; it should be gathered at its source. It is clear and reddish on the outside and white within, with an odor between Silphium and galbanum <note>another aromatic resin</note>. In taste it has power... it is used in compounding medicines for the chest <note>original: *stora cas*, likely *thoracas*</note>.

<margin>For the "frenetic" <note>those suffering from delirium</note> and the "splenetic" <note>those with spleen ailments</note>, it is cooked in oil... it is also said that if a leech <note>original: *sanguis uūga*</note> is swallowed, this drunk with vinegar drives it out.</margin>

XCIIII **Euphorbia**
The Euphorbia is a tree similar to the giant fennel <note>original: *ferule*</note>, whitish in color, found in Mauretania Caesariensis <note>A Roman province in what is now Algeria</note>.
<margin>..it is very hot in nature.</margin>
This tree has a great deal of sap, which is very sticky. Many people collect this sap in the following way for their own provision: first, they wrap the tree in sheepskin <note>original: *pelle berbicina*</note>, and then from a distance they strike the root with spears. When the root has been struck, the sap flows out in a single stream. Once it has congealed, they collect it from the skins held underneath.

However, there are two kinds of this sap: one that falls onto the skins, and another that is found on the trunk <note>original: *cona di*, likely a corruption</note> or on the ground. This first kind is clear and good, much like *sarcocolla* <term>sarcocolla</term> <note>literally "flesh-glue," a Persian tree resin used to heal wounds</note>. Therefore, one should choose the kind that is clear like *sarcocolla*. Adulteration can be detected if it is fresh, because if it is pure, its heat will be felt in the mouth for a long time and it will appear fatty.

### XCIII ON THE DROP OF AMMONIAC <margin>Number 1</margin>

Ammoniac is the teardrop <note>referring to the resinous sap that "bleeds" from the plant</note> of a giant fennel <term>ferula</term> growing in Cyrene <note>original: *quirelsuae*, likely referring to Cyrenaica in modern Libya</note>, which as a shrub with its root is called *agacillis*; it should be chosen for its good color, being clear and without wood, and having clear grains like incense, similar to a bean and dense, not having filth, and having a scent like castor <term>castoreum</term> <note>a pungent secretion from beavers used in ancient medicine</note>; it is bitter in taste.

It is the juice of a tree similar to giant fennel, yellow in color; it is warming <term>termana</term> <note>from the Greek *thermantika*</note> and softening <term>malapatica</term> <note>from the Greek *malaktika*, an emollient</note>, and drawing <term>epispastica</term>. ### XCV ON SARCOCOLLA

**SARCOCOLLA** <note>literally "flesh-glue"</note> is a teardrop-like resin growing in Persia, similar to small pieces of frankincense, reddish in color and bitter in taste; it has a healing <term>paracollitica</term> power <note>the ability to "glue" or close wounds</note> for wounds, and prevents <margin>power</margin> discharges in the eyes; it may be mixed into plasters; for ulcers, use it mixed with cumin.

### XCVI ON GLAUCIA

**GLAUCIA** <note>A medicinal juice, likely derived from the yellow horned poppy, *Glaucium flavum*</note> is the juice of a herb growing in the cities of Syria and Hierapolis: its leaves are similar to the horned poppy <term>meconi ceratiti</term> but are fatty and spread upon the ground. They have a heavy odor and a bitter taste, with much juice similar to saffron; they take the leaves [...] <note>original: *auer mittunt ac acauir*; these may be corrupted local names or technical instructions for harvesting</note> and they are boiled down; they strain what they have cooked, dry out the juice, and make "glaucia," which may be mixed into eye-salves <term>collyria</term>. Its power is partly cooling.

### XCVII ON BULL GLUE

**BULL GLUE** <term>Gluten taurinum</term>, which they call pure glue from the hide. The best is the Rhodian type, which <margin>power</margin> is mostly made from the scrapings of hides. But it should be chosen if it is clear and pale; the black kind is useless. It is smeared when dissolved in vinegar; it cleanses cloth and clears the skin of leprosy; it is applied to burns and prevents them from blistering if it is allowed [to be applied quickly]. It is dissolved in lukewarm water and used for painting various things, in which it makes the colors stick. For wounds, it is dissolved with honey and vinegar.

### CVIII ON MISTLETOE

**MISTLETOE** <term>Viscum</term> <note>often called birdlime when processed</note> is the "tear" or resin of a tree; it is smooth and green on the outside, but when crushed it is rough within. It is gathered from the seeds of the oak <note>original: *drusidem*, from the Greek *drys*</note> and other trees; some seek it from the "Matian" apple tree, pear trees, cypress, and various other trees. Sometimes it is even found on the roots or the shoots of trees. <margin>Power</margin> Its medicinal power is diaphoretic <note>sweat-inducing</note>, softening <term>malactica</term>, drawing <term>epispastica</term>, and digestive. It cleanses pustules from the body and is applied as a necessary treatment for <margin>that is, glandular swellings</margin> parotid swellings <note>swellings of the glands near the ear, such as mumps</note>. Mixed in equal weight with resin and wax, it helps all abscesses. When spread upon a linen cloth as a poultice <note>original: *opadar*, likely *epithema*</note>, <gloss>it heals best</gloss> and when mixed with "male" frankincense <note>original: *masculo*; high-quality frankincense drops</note> and water, it heals bad wounds. It dries out the spleen, especially when mixed and cooked with lime and <margin>jet stone</margin> jet stone <term>lapis gagates</term> and then applied. Mixed with orpiment <note>arsenic trisulfide</note> or sandarac <note>arsenic disulfide</note>, it removes diseased nails, calluses, and scales; when mixed with wine, its power is increased.

### C ON CLEAVERS

**CLEAVERS** <term>Aparine</term>, also called *omphalocarpon* <note>meaning "navel-fruit"</note> or *philanthropon* <note>meaning "man-loving," because the burrs stick to clothing</note>, is an herb that has many small, long, square, and rough stems. It has leaves placed thinly in order, which are white; the seed is round, hard, and pitted in the middle. It clings to the clothing of those passing by; shepherds use it as a strainer for milk <note>original: *laz*, likely *lac*</note> to filter out impurities. The juice of the herb and its stems, as well as its seed, mitigates the bite of venomous spiders <term>phalangiones</term> when drunk with wine; it also acts against poisons. Its leaves are similar to boxwood, which are first produced in the spring.

### ON ALYSSUM
**ALYSSUM** <term>Alliso</term> is a single, pithy <note>original: *fermentosa*, likely referring to the spongy or stalky texture</note> stalk having round leaves, in which it produces a seed in the manner of a viper’s head <note>original: *caput aspidis*</note>. ### ON DISTAFF THISTLE
**DISTAFF THISTLE** <term>Atractialis</term> <note>likely *Atractylis*</note>, which many call "wild cnectos" <note>original: *mector*, likely a corruption of *cnicus*</note>, is a thorny shrub similar to the cnectos but with smaller and more minute leaves upon the stalks themselves. ### CVI. ON LEONTOPETALON

It grows in rocky and rough places; it is a small shrub, less than a palm in length, having tiny leaves like those of the oak <note>original: *drio*</note>. It is bitter, with a small purple flower, but it should be gathered when the seed is ripe. This herb, whether green or dry, when drunk with water, heals convulsions and coughs, and cures the spleen by dissolving its hardness. In the early stages, it treats dropsy <note>original: *idropias*, an old term for edema or swelling</note>; it regulates menstruation and induces <gloss>it expels</gloss> abortion. Drunk with vinegar, it dries the spleen. For poisonous bites, it is effective when drunk with wine. When drunk as pills <note>original: *cataptad*, likely *catapotia*</note>, it can do all things <note>Symbol for a measurement, likely 'semis' or 'scrupulum'</note> in a half-measure. When crushed green and applied to the feet <note>original: *podia*</note>, it is known to do all things in a half-measure. Added to honey, it cleans old wounds; crushed and mixed with oil, it clears the dimness of the eyes. Crushed and rubbed over the whole body, it provides warmth.

### CVIII. ON LEUCA

There are two kinds of **LEUCA** <term>Leuce</term> <note>potentially a species of *Leucas* or a similar Mediterranean herb</note>: *monacna* and *horana*. The *monacna* variety has broader leaves. <gloss>from</gloss> Indeed, it is seen to have the power to cause abortion. When mixed with leaves of henbane <note>original: *iosquiami*</note> for those with jaundice <note>original: *arquatis*</note>, and with vinegar added <note>unclear reading: *incatept*</note>, it removes swelling of the testicles. The seed also, when drunk, counteracts poisons. It extinguishes "wild fire" <note>original: *igne agru*, likely *ignis sacer* or erysipelas, a skin infection</note>; the leaves are used for this, though the purple flower is more useful. It grows mostly in Syria and in Pamphylia, where they use it to make wonderful ointments <note>original: *confectionib: miris*, likely referring to *myris* or fragrant oils</note>. It has small seeds and its power is great for the stomach. Both types, when drunk with wine, prevent the effects of poisonous bites.

# CX ON THE LYCHNIS
The plant **Lychnis** <note>original: *Ligda*, likely *Lychnis coronaria* or Rose Campion</note> is one that many include in garlands <note>original: *corona*</note> because of its flower. It is similar to the white violet <note>original: *leucoio*</note>, but its flower is purple. Its seed, when drunk with wine, soothes the sting of a scorpion.

# CXI ON THE WILD LYCHNIS
In the same manner as mentioned above <note>original: *ss.*, an abbreviation for *supra scripta*</note>, the seed is drunk. This herb, also known as *scorpioides* <note>scorpion-tail plant</note>, softens the belly.

# CXII ON THE LILY
The **Lily** is known to everyone. Many people also use this in garlands, and from it a preparation is made called lily oil, which the Greeks call *susinum* <note>original: *susinū*, from the Greek *sousinon*</note>. Its property is emollient <term>malactica</term> <note>a substance used to soften or soothe tissues</note>. Regarding issues of the womb <note>original: *matricis*</note>, it dissolves hardness when applied. Its cooked leaves, when applied, provide aid against poisonous bites and treat burns when laid upon them. A decoction <note>original: *lixa*</note> of the plant can be made in vinegar; when prepared this way, it helps wounds. The juice, when mixed with vinegar, honey, and wax <note>original: *ineramento*, likely a misspelling of *inceramento* or cerate</note> and cooked, is effective for both old and new wounds.

The root, boiled and placed in rose oil, is a singular protection for burns. It soothes the causes of wounds and regulates menstruation. When added to honey, it leads wounds to form a scar. It "glues" the nature of the nerves <note>here meaning tendons or ligaments</note> and is powerfully applied to dislocations. It cleanses spots on the body and leprosy; it removes dandruff <note>original: *furfores*</note> and sores <note>original: *acoras*</note> of the head. It removes wrinkles from the face. Mixed with the flower of henbane <note>original: *losquiami*, likely *hyoscyamus*</note> and wheat flour, it takes away swelling of the testicles. The seeds and leaves help against poisonous bites. When the leaves and seeds are drunk with wine, it extinguishes "Sacred Fire" <term>Igne sacrum</term> <note>a term for various skin inflammations, often erysipelas</note>. It performs all the actions mentioned above. It grows in Syria and in Pamphylia <note>a region on the southern coast of modern-day Turkey</note>.

# CXIII ON BUBLOTE, that is, HOREHOUND
Many call this *ballote*, and many call it **Black Horehound** <note>original: *marubiu nigrum*</note>. It has black, square, and rough stems. It produces many small shoots from a single root. It has leaves similar to horehound <note>white horehound</note>, but they are roundish, black, and rough.

### CXIIII ON THE HONEY-LEAF

**H**oney-leaf <note>original: *Mellis sofillos*, referring to *Melissa officinalis* or Lemon Balm</note>, which some call *mellitadinam* because bees <note>Latin: *apes*</note> enjoy eating it. Its leaves and stalks are similar to black horehound <term>ballote</term>, but they are larger and more tender, and not as rough to the touch.

They have the scent of a citron <note>original: *cedromeli*</note>. Its leaves, when drunk with wine and vinegar, provide an excellent cure for the power of the scorpion and for poisonous spiders <term>phalangionibus</term>. It brings dog bites to health; a decoction <note>original: *elixatura*</note> of it can do this. When this decoction is used as a warm wash, it regulates menstruation. Held in the mouth, it treats the pain of teeth and helps with dysentery <term>desinteriar</term>.

Because it aids those who are choking, these leaves mixed with soda <note>original: *nitro*</note> can perform all these cures. It is correctly applied for griping pains <note>original: *tortionibus*, usually referring to abdominal colic</note>. It is beneficial as an electuary <term>electarium</term> <note>a medicinal paste made with honey or syrup</note> and a topical remedy. When salt and vinegar are added and it is applied, it disperses scrofula <term>scrofias</term> <note>swelling of the lymph nodes, often in the neck</note>, cleanses wounds, and helps those with arthritis <term>artriticer</term>.

### CXV
### ON HOREHOUND.

**H**orehound <note>original: *Prasiu*, likely *Marrubium vulgare*</note> is a shrub with a single root having many white and rough stalks. The leaves are similar to a large finger, rounded, rough, and wrinkled. It has a bitter taste. The seeds are few and, like the leaves, are somewhat rounded. It grows in pathless and rough places. Its dried leaves and seeds, when boiled and drunk with honey, benefit those suffering from coughs and asthma <term>asmaticis</term>. It clears the chest <note>original: *torace purgat*</note> exceedingly well.

### CXVI ON STACHYS

**S**tachys <note>original: *Staquin*, referring to *Stachys* or Hedge-nettle</note> is a shrub similar to horehound <note>original: *prasio*</note>. It has many oblong leaves that are hard, rough, fragrant, and white. It has many stalks coming from a single root, which are whiter than those of the horehound. It grows in mountainous and rough places. Its property is warming <term>termantica</term> <note>original: *termantica*, from the Greek *thermantikos* (heating)</note> and sticky. A decoction of the leaves regulates menstruation when drunk with wine and expels the afterbirth.

### CXVII ON PYRETHRUM

**P**yrethrum <note>original: *Pyrgias*, possibly referring to a type of *Pyrethrum* or *Potamogeton*</note> has leaves similar to dock <note>original: *lapato*</note>, but they are longer and greener. It has six or seven chosen [leaves], and it appears [to have a] swelling <term>edema</term> inside and out like winter frost <note>original: *pruina hiemis*</note>. It grows tender and long in parks or gardens. Its taste is rough and savory. It has neither a trunk nor a stalk. Its leaves, when drunk with wine, treat poisonous bites; when applied and drunk, they benefit dysentery and those with abdominal pains <term>quiliacos</term> <note>original: *quiliacos*, referring to *coeliacs* or those suffering from chronic digestive issues</note>.

### CXVIII ON SPIDER-WORT

**S**pider-wort <note>original: *Phalangion* or *phalangigian*</note>, which many call "white thistle" <note>original: *leuca cancum*, likely a corruption of *leucacantha*</note>, has two or three stalks, or more. White flowers appear, similar to the lily, but divided many times. It has black seeds, thick like a lentil, and a thin root. When it is fresh and green and pulled up from the earth, it changes into another color.

# CXVIII ON CLOVER

Clover <term>Trifolium</term> <note>original: *Trifolio*; likely *Psoralea bituminosa*, the Pitch Trefoil, rather than common field clover</note> is also called *minos*, *anar*, *asphalation*, *crinition*, or *oxysilon*. It is a small shrub, about one cubit <term>cubitum</term> <note>a unit of measurement roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters</note> in length, having thin branches. It resembles a small tree in its structure, with three leaves on each branch. At first, the foliage looks like Rue, but as it grows, it becomes more like the bitumen-scented plant <term>asphalatos</term> <note>original: *asfalat*; referencing the plant's distinct pitch-like odor</note>. It bears a purple flower and has a rough, oblong seed at the tip. Its root is also oblong. The seed and leaves, when drunk with water, provide relief for those suffering from pleurisy <term>pleureticis</term>, difficulty urinating <term>disuris</term>, epilepsy <term>epilecticis</term>, and the onset of dropsy <term>idropis</term> <note>original: *idropis*, meaning edema or fluid retention</note>. It is also helpful for uterine conditions <term>hystericis causis</term> <note>original: *sterics causis*, a corruption of the Greek *hysterikos*</note> and regulates menstruation. Use four measures of the seed and four of the leaves. The leaves themselves, when taken with honey-vinegar <term>oxymel</term> <note>original: *obsi melli*, a corruption of *oxymelli*</note>, counteract poisonous bites. The whole shrub, when the leaves and root are applied as a warm compress <term>fomentum</term>, works against poisons; this compress is effective for wounds, though it may cause some temporary pain. It treats tertian fevers <term>tritaias</term>, and the "three-leaved" plant or its seeds drunk with wine treat quartan fevers <term>quartanis</term> <note>original: *tritaias* and *quartanis* refer to fevers that recur every three or four days, common in the ancient world</note>. Similarly, the root is beneficial when added in equal parts to various antidotes.

# CXX ON POLY-GERMANDER

Poly-germander <term>Polion</term> <note>likely *Teucrium polium*, known for its medicinal properties and downy, white appearance</note> is a mountain plant. There is another mountain variety which they call *teutrion* <note>original: *teutrion*, a type of Germander</note>, which is the one most commonly used. It is a white shrub with tender leaves, about one palm <term>palmus</term> <note>roughly 3-4 inches or 8-10 centimeters</note> in length. At the top of the stalks, there is a small, full head in which the seeds are found, appearing like white down or long hair. It has a heavy but pleasant scent. The rest of the plant is also shrubby.

### WATER GERMANDER <note>original: *Descordion*; known today as *Teucrium scordium*</note>

Water Germander grows in mountainous and wooded areas. Its leaves are similar to germander <term>camedri</term> <note>original: *camedri*, referring to *Chamaedrys* or Wall Germander</note>, but larger and darker. If eaten, it has the taste and smell of garlic. It has a square stem which bears a reddish flower. It possesses antidotal <note>original: *termantiaca*, likely a corruption of *theriaca*</note> and diuretic properties. When drunk either fresh or dried with wine, it works against bites and every kind of poison, stomach pain, and difficulty urinating <term>disuria</term>. Taken with honey-water <term>idromelle</term>, it heals and cleanses the chest; it is a primary defense for those with a cough. For those with internal bruising <term>conquaxationib;</term> or those who have fallen from a height, it is rightly applied with cardamom <term>cardamio</term>, honey, and dried grapes <note>original: *rasipa na sicca*, likely *passa*, raisins</note> taken as an electuary <term>glectariū</term> <note>a medicinal paste made with honey or syrup</note>. It treats tumors in the upper abdomen <term>ippocondriis</term> <note>original: *ippocondriis*, the area of the torso just below the ribs</note>. Used as a wax-salve <term>cera</term>, it is known to do all the above; mixed with vinegar and used as an ointment, it assists with gout <term>podagrias</term>. Applied as a plaster with water, it benefits gout. It regulates menstruation and is effective for wounds; when added to honey, it cleanses old and filthy wounds and leads them to scarring. Dried and placed on a wound, it makes the flesh recede <note>likely referring to the removal of "proud flesh" or excessive tissue growth</note>. Its juice is drunk and is known to do all the above. The varieties from Pontus, Crete, and <unclear>diuisacum</unclear> are the best of all.

### CXXIII CONCERNING MUGWORT
### <margin>Artemisia</margin>

Mugwort <term>Artemisia</term> <note>Named after the goddess Artemis (Diana), the protector of women, due to its use in childbirth and menstruation</note> is a shrubby herb that grows in coastal areas; it is similar to southernwood but has larger and fleshier leaves. One variety is indeed yellow, and has long stems. Another is tender and has very small white flowers. It has a heavy scent. It grows before the flowering season and, in Mediterranean inland areas, it has minute seeds. One variety has a single stalk full of leaves but possesses very small flowers the color of honey.
<margin>universal virtues</margin>
Many people call this plant Artemisia. They possess the greatest power <term>virtutem</term> in their scent. It is warm and "thinning" <term>leptantica</term> <note>original: *leptantica*, a medical term for substances that thin the bodily humors or fluids</note>. A decoction <term>elixaturas</term> of it soothes women’s complaints: it regulates menstruation, expels the fetus, and brings down infants who have died in the womb. It relaxes the constriction of the matrix <note>the uterus</note> and disperses all tumors. When taken, it breaks stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note> and provokes the flow of urine. If the herb itself is crushed and placed upon the navel <term>bilico</term>, it regulates menstruation. Its juice, mixed with myrrh and applied to the mother, is known to achieve all these things. The dried flowering tops <term>comas</term>, when drunk in four measures, settles stomach complaints <term>stemas causis</term> <note>original: *stemas*, likely a corruption of *stomachus*</note>.

### CXXV CONCERNING BOTRYS
**Botrys** <note>Oak of Jerusalem, *Chenopodium botrys*</note> is a shrubby herb. It is spread entirely over the ground and is honey-colored. The branches themselves are full of seeds. The leaves are similar to chicory and have a very strong scent, so that it is often added to clothes or other items for the sake of the sweetness of its odor. It grows near wine-presses and in pastures. When drunk with wine, it is beneficial for orthopnea <term>orthopnoia</term> <note>a condition where the patient can only breathe comfortably when standing or sitting upright</note>. The Cappadocians call it ambrosia, and some call it mugwort <term>artemisia</term>.

### CXXVI CONCERNING GERANIUM
**Geranium** <note>Cranesbill</note> is a herb; it has leaves similar to anemone, divided and oblong. Its root is round and sweet; when eaten or drunk with wine, it is said to relieve uterine inflations <note>original: *linflationis stericas*, referring to gas or swelling in the womb</note>. It is called *amulus*. There is another kind having thin, dusty stems rising two palms from the earth. The leaves are similar to mallow, upon which are heads like [unclear]. But it is not suitable for [unclear].

### CXXVII CONCERNING GNAPHALION
**Gnaphalion** <note>Cudweed</note> has leaves that women <note>original: *mula*, likely a corruption of *mulieres*</note> use for swelling, because the leaves are white and soft. Indeed, when the leaves are drunk with harsh wine, it treats dysentery.

**Typha** <note>Cattail</note> has leaves similar to the galingale <term>cyperus</term> <note>a type of aromatic sedge</note> and a smooth stalk, upon which is a small head full of thick flowers, like white hair. Women call this *altelin*. This flower, mixed with hog's lard, [is a remedy for] burns <note>original: *conbustio-*</note>

### CXXVIII CONCERNING CIRCEON

**Circeon** <note>possibly *Enchanter's Nightshade* or a similar herb associated with the goddess Circe</note>, which they commonly call [by this name], has leaves similar to *syringium* <note>possibly a reed or a plant with hollow stems</note> and infinite small branches. It grows in rocky and sunny places. When taken, it purges the bowels; the seed, when drunk, promotes the flow of milk in women.

### CXXX CONCERNING ENANTIO

**Enantio** <note>Oenanthe or Dropwort, *Oenanthe pimpinelloides*</note> has leaves similar to parsnip <note>original: *pasanace*, likely *pastinaca*</note> and has white flowers. It has a thick stalk one palm long and a seed similar to orach <note>original: *adrafaxin*, likely *atriplex*</note>. It has a larger root with a large, round head. It grows in rocky places. The root of this plant, along with its leaves and seed, when drunk with wine and honey, expels the afterbirth <term>secundas</term>. When taken with wine alone, it provokes the flow of urine.

### CXXXI CONCERNING CONIZA

**Coniza** <note>Fleabane, *Conyza*</note> has two kinds: the greater and the lesser. The smaller is indeed fragrant, but the larger has leaves with a heavy odor and grows as a larger shrub. Both, however, have leaves similar to the olive, though they are rough and oily. The stalk itself is two cubits <note>about 3 feet</note> long, but the smaller variety is only one foot long. They have a fragile, honey-colored flower with a bitter [scent], and when it has finished flowering, it produces something like hair <note>referring to the downy pappus of the seed head</note>. Its root is useless; the entire shrub with its leaves is used as a fumigant <term>fomigio</term>. When placed beneath [a bed or seat], it keeps venomous creatures <note>original: *uenena*</note> far away. Sprinkled with water, it repels fleas. The leaves themselves, when applied as a poultice <term>incatapl.</term> <note>abbreviation for *in cataplasma*</note>, soothe the bites of venomous animals and heal wounds and pustules. The flower and leaves, when drunk with wine, regulate the menstrual cycle.

## CXXXII CONCERNING THE DAY-LILY

**Day-lily** <note>original: *Emerocalles*, from the Greek *Hemerocallis*</note>, which is also called *cataclepton* <note>original: *ero cataclepton*, likely a corruption of a Greek synonym</note>, has upright leaves similar to a lily. When it first begins to open, it shows a lily-like flower, but after it has bloomed, it turns a fine green color and is fragrant. The root is similar to a bulb but slightly larger; if drunk, it expels foul moisture from the womb and regulates menstruation. The leaves, applied as a **poultice**, disperse swellings resulting from childbirth and also scatter swellings of the eyes. The root and leaves, when applied as a **poultice**, treat burns.

## CXXXIII CONCERNING THE WALLFLOWER

**Wallflower** <note>original: *Leuciun*, likely *Leucoium*</note> is known to everyone, but it has differences in its flowers, as it shows yellow <note>original: *melinu*, meaning quince-yellow</note>, white, and purple flowers. However, the yellow-colored variety is the most necessary for medicinal use. Whether used dry or boiled and applied as a fomentation, it treats swellings of the spleen and regulates menstruation. Mixed into a **wax-salve** <term>ceratum</term> <note>a mixture of wax and oil used as a base for ointments</note>, it restores health to fissures <note>original: *ragadia*, referring to painful cracks in the skin or membranes</note>; when added to honey, it treats pustules <note>the text here is slightly fragmented: *in flatib;* likely refers to inflammations or "windy" swellings</note>.

### CXXXIIII CONCERNING CRATAEGONON

**Crataegonon** <note>likely a species of knotweed, *Polygonum*</note> has leaves similar to **heath** <note>original: *erice*</note>. From a single root, it produces many stalks that are abundant and knotty. It has a seed similar to **millet** <note>original: *cenero*, a corruption of the Greek *cenchros*</note> and grows in shady and thorny places; its potency is very great. It is said that if its seed is drunk by women after their monthly cleansing and before intercourse—taking one pill with water <unclear>diluted</unclear> three times a day for forty days—it causes them to conceive a male child. Likewise, the man ought to drink it for the same number of days before having intercourse with the woman.

### CXXXV CONCERNING THE WILD LEAF

There are two kinds of the **wild leaf** <note>original: *folio agreste*; these are the *Arrenogonon* and *Thelygonon* plants, known today as Dog's Mercury</note>: the male and the female. The female variety grows in rocky places, much like **moss** <note>original: *brio*</note>, but it has greener leaves like those of a young olive tree and a short stalk. It has a thin root, a white flower, and a small white seed like that of a **poppy** <note>original: *meconos*</note>. The male variety, however, is similar in all respects except for the seed; the seed resembles <note>original: *DR. VI*, likely a measurement of six drachms or a visual comparison to a specific coin</note> and it releases full, flowering clusters. It is called **arrenogonon** <note>from the Greek for "male-begetting"</note> because whoever drinks it will father a male, while it is called **thelygonon** <note>from the Greek for "female-begetting"</note> because whoever drinks it will father a female. The most skilled **Crateuas** <note>a famous Greek physician and pharmacologist from the 1st century BCE</note> recorded all these things; thus, this history <note>original: *distoria*, for *historia*</note> has always greatly pleased me.

These leaves are similar to olive leaves, but softer, narrower, and longer. The stalk is two spans long, and upon this stalk...

# CXXXVII CONCERNING THE OTHER ORCHIS

**Orchis** <term>Orchis</term> <note>a genus of orchids; the name comes from the Greek word for "testicle," referring to the shape of the twin tubers</note>, which many call **Serapias** <note>original: *serapiada*; named after the Graeco-Egyptian god Serapis</note>, has leaves similar to **horehound** <note>original: *prassio*; specifically white horehound</note> in size, which are oblong but smoother and of a duller color. Its stalk is two feet long and it produces a purple flower. The roots have the appearance of **beaver glands** <note>original: *castorei*; referring to the twin-tuber shape which resembles the scent glands of a beaver</note>. Its primary virtue is such that when applied as a **poultice** <term>cataplasma</term> <note>a soft, moist mass of herbs applied to the skin to treat aching or inflamed parts</note>, it cleanses all pustules and wounds. It removes **spider-like sores** <note>original: *araneas*; likely referring to thin, spreading skin lesions or perhaps spider bites</note> and treats **fistulas** <note>abnormal tube-like passages in the body</note>. Applied as a poultice, it reduces tumors, but when used dry, it consumes the rot of wounds, as well as "eating" sores and malignant, bloodless growths. It has such great efficacy that it matches the best of treatments.

It has leaves similar to **dock** <note>original: *lepatio*</note> or **lily**, but shorter and more colorful. ### CXXXIX CONCERNING ERYTHRAIC SATYRION

**Erythraic satyrion** <term>Satyrio Eritraico</term> <note>a species of orchid, likely the Butterfly Orchid or Holy Orchid</note> has a seed similar to linseed, but larger, flatter, and smoother. It is said to be very potent, much like **stinkweed** <note>original: *sancus*; possibly referring to a pungent plant used in ancient medicine</note>. However, its root has a tender <gloss>bark-like skin</gloss> <note>the original *cortereo* is glossed with *rtē*, likely clarifying the Latin *cortice*</note>; it is reddish on the outside and white inside. It is used for the throat and the stomach. It grows in mountainous places where there is plenty of sun. It is said that if this herb is <gloss>held</gloss> <note>the original *tentā* is glossed with *te*</note> in the hand, it stimulates **sexual desire** <term>uenerem</term>. When drunk with wine, it likewise stimulates **intercourse** <term>coitum</term>.

### CXL CONCERNING CLARY SAGE

**Clary sage** <term>Orminon</term> <note>identifiable as *Salvia horminum*</note> is an herb similar to **white horehound** <note>original: *prasio*</note> in its flower and stalks. Its stalk is square and half a cubit long, with small branches like the Syrian variety. Its leaves lie upon the root, and the seeds vary: the wild variety has round, reddish seeds, while the other has oblong, black seeds, which are very useful. Indeed, if this is drunk with wine, it arouses **sexual desire** <term>coitum</term>. However, when mixed with honey, it clears the dimness of the eyes caused by **glaucoma** <term>claucomaticā</term> <note>original: *claucomaticā*; in antiquity, this referred to any cloudiness or cataracts of the eye</note>. Mixed with water and applied as a **poultice** <note>original: *catapt*, likely an abbreviation for *cataplasma*</note>, it disperses tumors and draws out things fixed in the body. The herb itself, when applied as a poultice, can treat all kinds of [sores]. The wild variety has a stronger power; for this reason, it is mixed into the preparations of medicinal oils, especially **white oil** <term>leucinu</term> <note>original: *leucinu*; a fragrant oil typically made from lilies</note>, which is called *diron* by the **perfumers** <term>sirmentariis</term> <note>original: *sirmentariis*; likely referring to makers of ointments or unguents</note>.

### CXLI CONCERNING THE HATCHET VETCH

**Hatchet vetch** <term>Pelecinos</term> <note>identifiable as *Biserrula pelecinus*</note> is an herb having leaves like **chickpeas** <note>original: *ciceris*</note> and pods similar to the Greek **carob** <note>original: *silique grece*</note> where the seed is found. These pods have a shape like [notches/altars] on the outside, from which it gets the name *pelecinus* <note>the name is derived from the Greek *pelekys*, meaning "ax" or "hatchet," referring to the shape of the seed pods</note>.

### CXLI CONCERNING ONOMA

**Onoma** <note>likely *Onosma*, a genus in the borage family, or perhaps a type of alkanet</note> is also called **midana**, **flomian**, or **noinidiat**. It has leaves similar to **alkanet** <note>original: *ancusae*</note> but they are longer and softer. They grow to the height of one palm and are spread upon the ground like alkanet, but it has no stalk, nor seed, nor flower. Its root is tender, not very strong, and reddish; it grows in rough places. Its leaves, when drunk with wine, cause an **abortion**. It is said that if a pregnant woman merely passes over the herb itself, it causes this to happen.

### CXLII CONCERNING THE WATER LILY

**The Water Lily** <term>Nimfea</term> <note>identifiable as the White Water Lily, *Nymphaea alba*</note> grows in cultivated and watery places or in ponds. It has leaves similar to a **peony** <note>original: *pauono*, likely a corruption of *paeonia*</note> but smaller and longer. Some of its heads reach above the water; it raises many heads from beneath the water from a single root. It has a white flower similar to a lily, with a saffron-colored seed in the middle. But when it has finished blooming, the seed-head becomes round like a **pomegranate rind** <note>original: *malicoma cana*; typically referring to the tough skin of a fruit</note> or like the heads of a poppy, or black. Within this, the seeds are found deep and thick, and they are mucilaginous in taste. Its stalks are smooth, not thick, and black like **ebony** <note>original: *euomo*; likely *ebeno*</note>. The root is black, rough, and knotty; it is dried in the autumn.

When dried and drunk with wine, it heals **stomach ailments** <term>quiliaca</term> <note>refers to *coeliacus*, relating to the intestines or abdominal cavity</note>. It dries the **spleen** <term>splenẽ</term>. Applied as a **poultice** <term>catapt</term> <note>short for *cataplasma*</note> and placed upon the stomach, it stills pain. Its root, when drunk, mitigates **bladder pain** <note>original: *uissicedolosem*, a corruption of *vesicae dolores*</note>. It cleanses spots on the body and corrects **hair loss** <term>Alopia</term>. When added with gum, it can cause <unclear>ss.</unclear>. Drunk, it is very beneficial <note>original: *p d . e . e .* abbreviation for *prodest*</note> for those seeing many **visions in their sleep** <note>This refers to the ancient belief that the water lily acted as an anti-aphrodisiac, suppressing sexual desire and erotic dreams</note>.

### 143 CONCERNING THE OTHER WATER LILY

There is indeed another **water lily** <term>numfea</term> similar to the one described above, with a white and rough root. It has a flower that is **quince-yellow** <note>original: *mellinum*</note> and bright. ### 145 CONCERNING ANDROSACE

**Androsace** <note>likely *Androsace maxima*, though historically often confused with sea-lavender or similar maritime plants</note> grows abundantly in **Syria** in coastal areas. The herb is slender, having a minute and bitter seed; it is without leaves and has a small pod upon its head in which the seed is contained. Its medicinal power: two **drachms** <note>the symbol ƷII indicates two drachms, a measurement of weight</note> drunk with wine provokes much urine in those suffering from **dropsy** <term>ydropicas</term> <note>edema or swelling caused by fluid retention</note>. A decoction of the herb and its seed, when drunk, can perform all the same functions. Applied to the head, it treats **gout** <term>podagrias</term>.

### 146 CONCERNING SPLEENWORT

They call it **Asplenton**, or **scolopendrion**, or **mionion**, or **splenion**, or **etiga**. It has leaves similar to the **venomous centipede** <note>original: *scolopendre uenenosae*; referring to the leaf's resemblance to the many legs of a centipede</note>. It grows in rocky places and on walls built of stone. Many leaves rise from a single root. They are indeed linear, flowers without a stalk and without seed, divided into leaflets like **polypody** <note>a type of fern</note>. They are reddish and rougher underneath, and greener on top. Its medicinal power: the leaves boiled with vinegar and drunk for thirty days **dries up the spleen**. Its leaves, added to wine and taken, or applied directly to the spleen, works exceptionally well for three days. <meta>catchword: Sanguineas</meta>

## CXLVII CONCERNING SPLEENWORT

**Spleenwort** <term>Emionitis</term> <note>also called *Hemionitis* or Muleswort</note>, or as they call it, **splenion**, has leaves similar to **dragonwort** <note>original: *dracuntea*; likely *Dracunculus vulgaris*</note> but they are oblong. It has many thin roots, but it has no flower, no stem, and no seed. It grows in rocky places and is rough to the taste. Drunk frequently with **vinegar**, it dries out the **spleen**.

## CXLVIII CONCERNING ANTHYLLIS

There are two kinds of **Anthyllis** <term>Antillos</term>. One has leaves like a **lentil** <note>original: *lenaculo*, likely *lenticulo*</note> and hairy stems; it grows two palms high, standing erect with soft leaves. The other kind has leaves and stems similar to **ground-pine** <term>camepitis</term> <note>original: *chamaepitys*; a low-growing plant with a resinous smell</note>, but more hairy than the first, with a smaller purple flower and a heavy odor. Its root is similar to an **iris** <note>original: *cori*, likely *iris*</note>. Drunk, it treats those suffering from **dysentery**. Drunk, it also restrains vomiting; mixed with **rose oil** or milk and applied as a **pessary** <term>pessario</term>, it calms **uterine swellings** <note>original: *tumores istericos*</note>. It is helpful for wounds. That variety which is similar to ground-pine provides the greatest effect for **epileptics** when drunk with **oxymel** <term>oximellin</term> <note>a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</note>.

It assists those with **jaundice** <term>hictericis</term> and is the greatest protection for those with **liver disease** <term>epaticis</term>. A decoction <note>boiled extract</note> of it, applied as a compress, can perform all these things; it settles issues of the **bladder** <note>original: *uissicae*</note>. 

The variety which has **purple** flowers is larger than all others and is naturally called **chamomile** <note>original: *antimon*, likely a corruption of *anthemis*</note>. **White-flower** <term>leucantemon</term> and **gold-flower** <term>crisantemon</term> <note>referring to varieties of daisy or chamomile</note> help those with stones; drunk, they provoke urine. For many types of **decay** <note>original: *incarie*</note> and for **eye fistulas** <term>egilopica</term> <note>ulcers at the corner of the eye</note>—that is, the scales that grow on the eyes—they grind much **elipidan** <note>an unidentified ingredient or preparation</note> mixed with oil and smear it on. They also treat **periodic fevers**. 

From the leaves and its singular flowers, they make and store **lozenges** <term>troascos</term> <note>medicated discs or troches</note>. They also dry and store its root. If it should not have flowers, the leaves and root fulfill the power of its flower; and if the root is lost, two parts of the leaves similarly fulfill the strength and power of its flower. It is suitable to be drunk added to **honey-water** <term>omellia</term>.

->**CL CONCERNING PELLITORY**<-

**Pellitory** <term>Partenion</term> <note>likely *Tanacetum parthenium* or Feverfew</note>, or as some call it, **amaracus** or **white-flower** <term>lecantemon</term>; it has leaves similar to **coriander** and a flower

On the outer edge it is white, but in the middle it is indeed honey-colored. It has a stinking odor <note>original: *bromosu*; referring to a heavy or foul smell</note> and a bitter taste. Its medicinal power is as follows: drunk with **oxymel** <term>oximellin</term> <note>a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</note> and salt—in the same manner as **dodder of thyme** <term>epithimu</term>—it draws out phlegm and bile through the bowels; it treats those with **asthma** <term>asmatias</term> and **melancholy** <note>literally "melancholics," referring to those with an excess of "black bile"</note>. The herb itself, drunk without the flower, provides the greatest health to those with **stones** <note>kidney or bladder stones</note> and **asthma**. A decoction of it, applied as a **warm compress** <term>fomento</term>, dissolves hardnesses and **scirrhous tumors** <term>scirros</term> <note>hard, painless swellings</note>. If applied with its flower, it extinguishes **skin inflammations** <note>original: *igne agrum*, likely referring to *ignis sacer* or Erysipelas</note> and disperses tumors.

### CL I ON OX-EYE

They call it **Ox-eye** <term>Buoptalmon</term> <note>literally "bull's eye"</note> or *bablan*. It is bushy and has soft leaves similar to **fennel**; it has a honey-colored flower like **chamomile** but larger, resembling an eye, from which it also took its name. It grows near cities. The flower, crushed with oil and applied <note>original: *scurtiri ecte toto addito*, likely a corruption of *triti ex oleo*</note>, disperses pustules and hardnesses. Some claim that if applied after bathing, it restores a healthy color to those who have **jaundice** <note>implied by the context of "restoring color" following the previous page's mention of *hictericis*</note>.

### CL II ON PEONY

They call it **Cliadisen**, or **Pentorobos**, or **Cordeur dactylus**, and they call its root **Peony** <term>peonias</term>. Its stalk is **two palms** long and has little branches; the leaves of the **male** <term>masculus</term> plant are almost like those of the [oak] <note>original: *noa regedi*, likely a corruption of *robori*</note>, while the **female** <term>femina</term> plant has divided leaves like **Alexanders** <note>an aromatic herb, *Smyrnium olusatrum*</note>. At the top of the stalk, it puts forth seed-pods <note>original: *cariola*</note> like those of **gourds**; it has follicles like **almonds** in which the seed is contained. When the seed is released, it is numerous and red, similar to a **pomegranate** <term>male granata</term>, but in the middle they are black and purple on top—about five or six of them. The root of the male is the thickness of a finger and two palms long, white, and has a sharp <note>original: *sapaca*, likely *sapida* or *saporis*</note> taste. The female plant indeed has a divided root like **acorns** <note>original: *balanu*; could also refer to date-shaped tubers</note>.

six or eight [seeds], similar to **asphodel** <term>assodillo</term> <note>original: *assodillo*; likely *Asphodelus*</note>, are given; indeed, one should give them in the manner of an **almond** <term>amigdale</term>, and when drunk with wine, it may soothe pain of the belly. ## CLIII ON LITHOSPERMON

They call it **Lithospermon** <note>literally "stone-seed"; likely Gromwell (*Lithospermum officinale*)</note>, or *eganicon*, or *diospyros*, or *heracleon*, named for the strength of its seed. It has leaves similar to the **olive** but wider, longer, and softer. The stalks are thin, leaning toward the ground, and of a uniform thickness, but the wood and the entire stalk itself are divided; on these the leaves are small, and there is a seed that is round, smooth, and white, similar to a **pea**. It grows in rough and sandy places. By the power of its seed, when drunk with white wine, it breaks **stones** and provokes urine.

## CLIIII ON PHALARIS

**Phalaris** <note>likely Canary grass (*Phalaris canariensis*)</note> has many stalks and many roots, which are tender, <unclear>poorly made</unclear>, and knotty, similar to <del>ne</del> <gloss>reeds</gloss> but thinner and sweeter. The seed is similar to white **millet** <term>centrie</term> <note>original: *centrie*, likely a corruption of the Greek *kenchros*</note> and oblong. By its medicinal power, when boiled and mixed with wine or water and drunk, it may soothe pain of the internal organs. The seed drunk in a spoonful <term>cochario</term> with water can do all the [above-mentioned] things.
