## ON MADDER
<note>original: *Erithrodanos*; likely *Rubia tinctorum*, known as Dyer's Madder</note>

**Madder**, or what most call *ereuonon* <note>original: *erionuocat* / *ereuonon*</note>, has a root used for **dyeing** <note>original: *inficiens*</note>. There are indeed two kinds: one is the wild kind, and the other is the sown kind, such as those from **Ravenna** <note>original: *rabenna*; a city in Italy famous for its fertile gardens</note>. It is sown in cultivated places, for they also grow there spontaneously. It has square, long, and rough stems, much like **cleavers** <term>aparine</term> <note>original: *aparinae*; *Galium aparine*, a plant known for its "sticky" hooked hairs</note>, but these are stronger and longer. The leaves are arranged in whorls around the joints, just like the **star-herb** <term>asteride</term> <note>original: *aster ide*; likely referring to a star-shaped leaf arrangement</note>, positioned in a circle. The seed is round; at first it is green, then it becomes reddish, and when it has matured, it turns black. 

The root is long, thin, and red. Its power is **diuretic** <term>diuretica</term> <note>promoting the production of urine</note>, and for this reason, those with **jaundice** <term>hictericis</term> are cured when it is drunk with **honeyed water** <term>mulsa</term>. It also brings relief to those with **paralysis** <note>original: *paralitias*</note>. It provokes thick urine and even blood. Those who drink this herb ought to bathe every day. It acts against **venomous bites**, especially those of **vipers** <note>original: *asceuis*, likely a corruption of *aspis*</note>, when the leaves are drunk for that purpose. The seed, when drunk with **oxymel** <term>oximelli</term> <note>a medicinal drink made of vinegar and honey</note>, dries out the **spleen**. Its root, when applied, brings on **menstruation** and causes **abortion**. It is said that with vinegar, it cleanses **white spots** <note>likely skin conditions like vitiligo or fungal infections</note>.

## CLVI ON LONCHITIS
<note>original: *Loncitir*; likely a species of orchid or a fern like *Polystichum lonchitis*</note>

**Lonchitis** has leaves similar to **leeks** <note>original: *porris*</note>, but wider and reddish. It has thick stalks emerging from the root, with branches that droop down toward the ground. On these branches are flowers similar to **hoods** <note>original: *pelis*, likely from *pelleis*, referring to a helmet or hood shape</note>; their form is vivid and white in the center, like a **beak** or a **tongue**. The seed is similar to a **lentil** <note>original: *lantiari*</note> and is **triangular** <term>trigonu</term>. It is indeed long, which is why it is called **lonchitis** <note>derived from the Greek *lonche*, meaning "lance" or "spear-head"</note>. The root is similar to a **wild carrot** <term>dauco</term>. It is found in rough and dry places. Its root, when drunk with wine, provokes urine. There is a second kind of **rough lonchitis** which has leaves like the **spleenwort** <term>scolopendri</term> <note>original: *scolopendri*; Hart's-tongue fern</note>.

### ON ANOTHER PLANT
<note>The heading "De Alia" simply means "On another," but the text describes the Marshmallow plant.</note>

**Marshmallow** <term>Altheae</term> <note>original: *Alteae*; *Althaea officinalis*</note>, which they also call *hibiscus* <note>original: *uulue uiscum*, a scribal corruption of *hibiscum*</note>, is a species of wild **mallow** <term>malua agrestis</term>. It has round leaves similar to **cyclamen** <note>original: *ciclamini*; a common garden plant with heart-shaped or rounded leaves</note>. It has a flower like a rose <note>original: *rudi*, likely for *rosae*</note> and stands about two **cubits** <term>cubit</term> <note>an ancient measurement of about 18 inches</note> tall. Its root is mucilaginous <term>mucellaginosa</term> <note>thick, sticky, and glue-like</note> and white inside. It is called *Althea* because it has many flowers <note>The author suggests an etymology from the Greek for "many flowers," though the name actually stems from *althaino*, meaning "to heal."</note>. 

Its flower, cooked and crushed and applied, cures wounds and disperses **scrofula** <term>scrofas</term> <note>swollen lymph nodes, usually in the neck</note> and brings relief to the **parotid glands** <term>parotidib;</term> <note>salivary glands located in front of the ears</note>. For, applied to the swelling of the breasts, it disperses them, mitigates pain, and treats **bruises** <term>conquassationib;</term>. It disperses tumors, relaxes the **tension of the nerves**, breaks or disperses **abscesses** <term>apostemata</term>, and makes the scars of wounds heal. 

Indeed, the root boiled and crushed, with added **pig fat** <term>absungia porcina</term> or goose fat and **turpentine resin** <term>resina terebentina</term>, heals swellings of the womb and **suffocation** <term>offocationis</term> <note>referring to "suffocation of the womb," a historical term for various gynecological distresses</note> when applied. A decoction <term>elixatura</term> of the root is also capable of doing all these things. 

A decoction of the root also expels the **afterbirth** <term>secundae</term>. Drunk with wine, it treats **difficulty in urinating** <term>disuriis</term> and helps those with **kidney stones** <term>calculosis</term>. It assists with **sciatica** <term>sciadias</term>, **dysentery** <term>drisinterias</term>, **tremors** <term>tremorias</term>, and those who have fallen from a height. Boiled with vinegar and used as a **gargle** <term>gurgurismo</term>, it helps with toothaches. 

The seed, whether fresh <note>original: *uiride*, green</note> or dry, crushed with vinegar and oil and smeared on, removes skin spots and treats **venomous bites**. A decoction of the seed helps those with dysentery and those spitting up blood, and it is taken for a **loose stomach** <term>soluzione uentris</term> <note>diarrhea</note>. It provides relief against all poisons when drunk with **vinegar-water** <term>pusca</term> <note>original: *posca*; a mixture of vinegar and water used as a common drink and medicine</note>. Its leaves, cooked with oil and applied as a <unclear>poultice</unclear> <term>cataplasma</term>, are effective for venomous bites and **burns** <term>conbustionib;</term>. And the root itself, crushed and mixed in water, curdled...

## CLVIII ON HEMP

**Hemp** <term>cannabum</term> <note>original: *cannabum*; *Cannabis sativa*</note> is known to everyone, and its use is significant, as strong ropes are made from it. It has leaves similar to **honey-clover** <note>original: *melidiodorigiam*, likely a corruption of *melilotos*</note>. It has long, hollow stalks. It can be eaten easily <note>referring to the seeds</note>, but if eaten in excess, it **constricts the genitals** <note>original: *genitalia siringat*; ancient medical texts often claimed hemp seeds could diminish sexual desire or "dry up" reproductive fluids</note>. The juice of the green plant is a safe remedy to mitigate the ringing and pain of the **ears**.

## CLVIIII ON WILD HEMP

Many say that **wild hemp** <term>cannabu agreste</term> <note>original: *cannabu agreste*; likely *Althaea cannabina* or a similar mallow, though sometimes identified with *Leonurus cardiaca*</note> is also called *fausthasar* <note>a synonym of unknown origin, possibly a corruption of a Greek name</note>, but it is darker and smaller, reaching a length of one cubit. Its leaves are similar to the aforementioned kind, but rough and like **honeysuckle** <note>original: *meliuncera*</note>. They have red flowers and a woody stalk. The seed and root are similar to the other kind. Its root, when cooked and applied as a **poultice** <term>cataplasma</term>, checks **tumors** and softens **hardness** <note>original: *duritias*; referring to stiff joints or hardened skin/growths</note>. It is also very effectively added to medicines for the hair.

## CLX ON ANAGYRIS

They call it **Anagyris** <term>anagyron</term> <note>original: *anagyron* or *anagyris*; *Anagyris foetida*, also known as Stinking Bean Trefoil</note> or *acopon*. It is a shrub with leaves and branches similar to the **chaste tree** <note>original: *agno arbor*; *Vitex agnus-castus*</note>. It is a tree full of a heavy, foul odor. It has a flower like <unclear>bricisice</unclear> and bears its seed in small, fleshy, and variegated **pods** <note>original: *folliculis*</note>. It ripens at the same time as the grape. Its leaves, applied as a **poultice** <term>cataplasma</term>, cleanse **pustules** <note>original: *pustulas*; sores or blisters</note> on the body. When one **scruple** <note>original: *gr. i*; a small unit of weight</note> is drunk with **mead** <note>original: *mulsore*; honey-water</note>, it is beneficial for **asthmatics** <term>asmaticis</term>. It also expels the fetus, provokes **abortion**, and brings on **menstruation**.

...relieves <note>original: *mitigat*</note> the bites of venomous spiders <term>spalangiorum</term> <note>original: *spalangiorum*; a term for venomous spiders, likely of the *Loxosceles* or *Latrodectus* genus</note> when drunk with wine. ## CLXI ON SEA PURSLANE

**Sea purslane** <term>cepea</term> <note>original: *cepea*; likely *Sedum cepaea* or *Halimione portulacoides*</note> is similar to **purslane** <term>andragne</term> <note>original: *andragne*; *Portulaca oleracea*</note> but has darker leaves and a tender root. The leaves, when drunk with wine, heal **strangury** <term>stranguriae</term> <note>a condition where urinating is painful or difficult</note> and a rough, irritating cough, especially when taken with something sweet. Its roots, when cooked, and the roots of what is called **asparagus** <note>original: *spag*; likely an abbreviation for *asparagi*</note> <margin>Greek</margin> are also healing.

## CLXII ON ORACHE

**Orache** <term>almea</term> <note>original: *almea*; likely *Atriplex hortensis* or *Halimus*, commonly called saltbush or orache</note> is called *massimon* or *authron* by the Jews <note>original: *a iuda massimon authron*; these are likely transcriptions of Hebrew or Aramaic synonyms</note>. It has leaves similar to **plantain** <term>arnigloso</term> <note>original: *arnigloso*; a corruption of *arnoglossos*, the Greek name for plantain, *Plantago*</note>, but narrower and spread across the ground. In summer, a single stalk rises to the height of one **cubit** <term>cubit</term> <note>approximately 18 inches</note>; it bears small heads and produces a green flower. It has thin roots like **hellebore**, and its strength is fragrant and rich. It grows in watery places. Its root, drunk with wine—if they drink two <note>likely referring to measures or doses</note>—is a remedy for the poison of the **sea hare** <term>lepore marino</term> <note>original: *lepore marino*; *Aplysia punctata*, a sea slug believed to be highly toxic in antiquity</note> and **rhetapium** <note>original: *raetopio*; likely *rhaitapium*, an unidentified toxin or plant mentioned in early herbals</note>. It assists with griping pains <note>original: *tortionib;*</note> and is extremely beneficial for **dysentery**. Drunk alone with **wild carrot** <term>dauco</term> <note>original: *dauco*; *Daucus carota*</note>, it is a singular protection. It suppresses pain in the side and provides a solution for those suffering from **dizziness** <note>original: *scoticas*; likely *scotomaticos*, referring to vertigo or darkened vision</note>. The herb itself, when drunk, binds the belly <note>original: *uentre abstanc*; meaning it stops diarrhea</note>. It regulates the **menstrual flow** and cleanses **pustules** when applied as a **poultice** <term>cataplasm</term> <note>original: *catapt*; short for *cataplasma*, a soft, moist mass of herbs applied to the skin</note>.

## CLXIII ON SAINFOIN

**Sainfoin** <term>onobricis</term> <note>original: *onobricis*; *Onobrychis*, often called "Holy Hay" or Cock’s Head</note> has leaves like those of the **lentil**, but smaller and thick, and they are two **palms** <term>palms</term> <note>a unit of length based on the width of the hand, about 3-4 inches</note> long. They have a red flower <note>original: *florem romanū*; "Roman flower" refers to the deep purple-red color associated with Roman prestige</note>. Its root is smaller and grows in damp places. It has a **dispersing** <term>discussive</term> <note>original: *disp-cular*; likely *discutientis*, a medicine that dissipates swelling</note> virtue; applied as a poultice, it clears away pustules. Drunk with wine, it treats **strangury** excellently. When mixed with oil and rubbed on the body, it provokes **sweating**.

# 164 ON HYPERICUM

**Hypericum** <note>original: *Ypericon*; most likely *Hypericum perforatum*, commonly known as St. John's Wort</note>, also called *androsemon* <note>from the Greek for "man-blood," referring to the red juice of the crushed flowers</note>, *corion*, or *camepituo* <note>original: *camepituo*; a Latinization of the Greek *chamaipitys*, meaning "ground-pine," so named because it smells like resin</note>, is called such because it has the scent of resin. It clearly has leaves similar to those of **rue** <term>rute</term> <note>a bitter, evergreen shrub with distinctively shaped leaves used in ancient medicine</note>. It grows as a shrub <gloss>ss</gloss> <note>likely an abbreviation for "height"</note> about two palms high, bearing a white flower <note>original: *florem album*; while Hypericum usually has yellow flowers, ancient and medieval manuscripts sometimes differ in color descriptions due to variety or scribal error</note>. It has a seed pod that is rough, elongated, and rounded in the manner of a grain of barley. Inside the pod itself are tiny, black seeds that smell of resin. When these are cleaned and drunk, it acts as a **diuretic** <term>diuretica</term> <note>a substance that increases the production of urine</note> and brings on the menstrual flow. When applied as a poultice or drunk, it wards off the chills of **quartan fevers** <note>a form of malaria where the fever returns every four days</note>. If it is drunk with wine for forty days, it is beneficial for **sciatica** <term>sciaticae</term> <note>pain affecting the back, hip, and outer side of the leg, caused by compression of a spinal nerve</note>. Its leaves, when applied as a poultice <note>original: *catcept*; a corruption of the Greek *kataplasma*</note> along with the seeds, are said to be very good for burns.

# 165 ON ASCYRON

**Ascyron** <note>original: *Asquiron*; likely *Hypericum hircinum* or a similar large-flowered variety</note> is also called *androsemon* and belongs to this same species. It is like Hypericum, but the branches are larger and more woody, and the stems have a **purple** <note>original: *fenicia*; referring to Phoenician purple or a deep reddish-brown</note> color. It has honey-colored flowers and seeds similar to Hypericum, but larger. When the plant is crushed, it gives off a scent of resin; indeed, if it is rubbed, it produces a blood-red color. This is why it is called **androsemon** <note>Greek for "man-blood"</note>. Its seed, when drunk with **hydromel** <term>idromelli</term> <note>a medicinal drink made of honey and water</note>, takes away the pains of sciatica. It is drunk in a dose of two **cyathi** <note>original: *coalias*; likely a corruption of *cyathi*, a measurement roughly equal to 1.5 fluid ounces</note>. It satisfies the stomach and clears out an abundance of bile. One must drink from it every day as long as the treatment continues. When applied as a poultice <note>original: *catcept*</note> to burns, it has a cooling effect <note>original: *emrefacit*; likely a scribal error for *refrigerat*, to cool</note>.

# 166 ON ANDROSAEMON

**Androsaemon** <note>commonly called Tutsan, another member of the Hypericum family</note> is also called *dionisi aramula* and *asuim arquiron*. I have spoken of this before, but there is a distinction between androsaemon, ascyron, and hypericum. It is a shrub with tiny seeds and many woody branches; its stems are purple in color...

<summary>This page describes various species of the Hypericum (St. John's Wort) family, detailing their resinous scent, physical appearance, and use in treating sciatica, fevers, and burns.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the description of various types of St. John's Wort (Hypericum), specifically focusing on their physical characteristics such as their wine-colored juice and resinous scent, before moving into related species like Corion and Ground Pine (Chamaepitys). BOOK III.

...it has paired leaves on a square stem. If these are crushed in the hands, they emit a wine-colored juice. It has a stalk with intervals in which there are small yellow <note>original: *melinus*; literally "quince-colored," often used to describe the yellow of St. John's Wort flowers</note> flowers. It has seeds in pods like those of the black poppy <note>original: *meconis nigri*</note>. When its foliage is rubbed and ground with the fingers, it produces the scent of resin. If the seeds of this plant are drunk, they clear bile from the stomach. It helps against **sciatica** <term>sciatia</term> <note>pain radiating along the sciatic nerve, which runs down one or both legs from the lower back</note>. After this purging, one should not take much water. Applied to recent burns, it provides relief, and it stops blood from flowing from a wound.

### 167 ON **CORION**, which some call *Hypericum*

**Corion** <note>likely a variety of Hypericum, such as *Hypericum coris*</note>, which some call *mula* and others *hypericum*, has leaves similar to heather <note>original: *erice*; referring to the genus *Erica*</note>, but they are smaller, thicker, and reddish. It is a shrub about one palm high. It is sticky, good for the stomach <note>original: *eus tomacha*; from the Greek *eustomachos*</note>, and fragrant. The seed of this plant, when drunk, provokes urine and brings on the menstrual flow. It is effectively applied for **strangury** <note>original: *spedangiosis*; a condition characterized by painful, frequent, and drop-by-drop urination</note> and for those suffering from sciatica. It is especially beneficial for **opisthotonos** <term>opisthotonos</term> <note>a severe muscle spasm causing the back to arch and the head to tilt back, often associated with tetanus</note> when drunk with wine. Taken with pepper, it protects the whole body from constant chills. Mixed with oil and used as an ointment, it is also highly effective for opisthotonos.

### 168 ON **GROUND PINE**

**Ground Pine** <note>original: *Camepitiis*; from the Greek *chamaipitys*</note>, which those in Pontus call *quirion* and in Embia <note>possibly a regional name or variant</note> call *sideritis* <note>meaning "ironwort," often used for plants believed to heal wounds made by iron</note>... it is a plant spread out over the ground and tufted. It has leaves smaller than **hyssop** <note>a fragrant herb used for medicinal and ritual purification</note> but they are tender, thicker, rough, and grow densely around the stalk. They have the scent of pitch <note>original: *pice*</note>. It bears small yellow flowers. Its root is like that of the Corion plant. If the root is drunk for seven days, it cures **jaundice** <term>icteriar</term>. If drunk for forty days, it also cures sciatica.

<summary>This page concludes the description of Hypericum species, detailing their ability to stop bleeding and treat burns, while introducing Corion and Ground Pine as remedies for sciatica, jaundice, and severe muscle spasms.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the medicinal applications of Ground Pine (Chamaepitys) and descriptions of its varieties, finishing Book III. It then provides the table of contents for the beginning of Book IV, listing various herbs from Ceterach to Epimedium.</meta>

It brings great aid especially to many liver complaints, and provides diuretic and nephritic <note>relating to the kidneys</note> effects; it relieves griping pains <note>original: *tortionibus*; internal cramping or colic</note>. In Pontus and Achaia, they use this mixture as an antidote. A decoction of it helps the teeth; when applied with barley meal <note>original: *polenta*; here referring to crushed barley groats used as a poultice</note>, it can counteract the power of **aconite** <note>a highly poisonous plant, also known as monkshood</note> and other corruptions. Ground with its roots and given in the form of a pill <note>original: *catapotie*; from the Greek *katapotia*</note>, it softens the belly. Applied warm with resin, it cleanses foul wounds. When added to honey, it settles conditions of the womb, dissolves the hardness of wounds, and acts as a healing glue <note>original: *para colle fin*, likely a corruption of the Greek *paracollema*, a glutinous plaster for wounds</note>. **Ground Pine** <note>original: *bepitis*, a corruption of *chamaepitys*</note> heals and scars <note>original: *cicisat*, likely *cicatrizat*</note> when honey is added.

There is another kind which has branches one cubit long, tender and twisted, but with foliage like a bean <note>original: *babae*, likely *fabae*</note> and a black flower and seed, and they have the scent of resin.

There is a third kind which is called the "male"; it has tender white leaves. They have rough white stalks and a lily-colored flower <note>original: *elinu*, likely *leirinon*</note>. In their seed-pods they also have the scent of resin. It has a power equal to those mentioned above, and it has a purging effect.

<header>BOOK IV</header>

# IN THE FIRST THREE BOOKS WRITTEN
## DEAREST AREIUS

Dearest Areius <note>Areius of Tarsus was the person to whom Dioscorides dedicated his work</note>, we have delivered to you the descriptions of aromatics and the preparations of oils, as well as the wonderful species of trees and their powers; we have also covered the sum of animal products, the efficacy of oils, the effects of herbs and juices, and the properties of roots. In the fourth book, indeed, the remaining herbs and the system for arranging their roots must be set forth.

<margin>BETONY</margin> Cestron <note>original: *Cestron*</note>, which is called the "cold-nourisher" <note>original: *psicrotrofon*, from the Greek *psychrotrophon*</note> because it grows in cold places. The Romans call this herb Betony <note>original: *uittonica*, a variant of *betonica*</note>. It has a thin stalk the length of one <term>cubit</term> <note>a measurement of roughly 18 inches, the length of a forearm</note>, and square, long, thin leaves similar to ivy, though rounded and divided, which are fragrant. It has a larger root, and the lowest leaves and its seed are held like a spike, collected in a cluster like a little husk; these are dried and are necessary for use. It has thin roots like hellebore, which, if taken, provoke nausea and phlegm. If the husks are collected and drunk in large quantities, they are given for "shakings" <note>likely referring to internal trauma or bruising</note> for those who have fallen from a height. It also cures "suffocation of the womb" <note>original: *offocationis stericae*; a historical term for what was later called hysteria, believed to be caused by the womb moving within the body</note> if taken. It most healthfully cures venomous bites and poisoned drinks when drunk with wine, but if someone drinks it beforehand, it may block the power of the poison. It provokes urine and is a maximum protection for epileptics and those with "tremors"—that is, convulsions—when drunk with water. It is effective for the liver and those with spleen issues if provided with <term>oxymel</term> <note>a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</note>. It promotes digestion if a bean-sized grain is taken beforehand, and it is beneficial for indigestion. It treats the mouth and shaken teeth <note>likely meaning loose teeth or gums</note>... [the text continues]

...of the sorb tree <note>original: *sorbi*; likely referring to the fruit of the Service Tree or a related plant</note>. It is usefully given to those spitting blood <note>original: *emoptoicis*, from the Greek for hemoptysis</note>. When two <term>obols</term> <note>a small unit of weight, about 0.7 grams</note> of it are taken with tempered wine and water, it soothes both the kidneys <note>original: *neufreticas*</note> and the bladder pain of those with dropsy <note>original: *ydropicar*; an old term for swelling caused by fluid retention</note>. These are given with honey-water to those with fevers; for those without fever, they are given with wine and honey to make the jaundice <note>original: *ictericis*</note> recede. It assists with menstruation and, when drunk with oil and wine, it softens the belly. ## II ON BRITANNICA

The herb Britannica <note>usually identified as Great Water Dock (*Rumex hydrolapathum*)</note> has leaves similar to wild dock, but they are darker and rough. To the taste, it is <term>styptic</term> <note>astringent; it causes tissues to contract and stops bleeding</note>. It has long stalks and a smaller, thin root. Its leaves should be gathered and placed in the sun, just like <term>orchil</term> <note>original: *fucus*; a sea-dye or lichen</note>. Its power is primarily styptic; it is effective for ulcers of the mouth and throat, and for those who suffer from mouth-rot <note>original: *sapsin*, from the Greek *sepsin*; likely referring to scurvy of the gums or gangrenous stomatitis</note>.

## III ON LOOSESTRIFE

Loosestrife <note>original: *Lisimacion*</note> has tall, long, and bushy stalks. Around their nodes, it has small leaves similar to those of the willow. It is styptic to the taste, with a purple <gloss>or</gloss> golden flower. It grows in damp places. The juice of the herb is styptic and is especially beneficial for those attempting to hold back blood; given as a drink or used as a suppository, it helps with dysentery and stops the flow of the womb in women. If placed under the nostrils, it checks a nosebleed; smeared on a fresh wound, it closes it up. If used as a fumigant <note>original: *fumigatione*; the burning of the plant to produce medicinal smoke</note>, it drives away snakes and kills shrews.

## IIII ON KNOTGRASS

Men call this Knotgrass <note>original: *Poligonon masculus*</note>, or "cancer-tool" <note>original: *carcinetron*</note>, or *tertia dan*, or *lema*, or *mirtolon*, or "many-fruited" <note>original: *policarpon*</note>. It is an herb having many tender, soft, and knotty branches, which are spread over the ground like wild grass. It has leaves...

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions of Book IV, completing the entry for a plant (likely Loosestrife/Lysimachia) before moving to different varieties of Knotgrass and Solomon's Seal. ...similar to rue but oblong and soft. It has seeds and leaves which grow close together, from which it is also called *myrtalis* <note>original: *mirtalis*; meaning myrtle-like, a common name for Loosestrife due to its leaves</note>. It has a white or bluish flower. Its power is <term>styptic</term> <note>astringent; it causes tissues to contract and stops bleeding</note> and cooling, hence its juice is drunk by those spitting blood <note>original: *emoptoicis*; suffering from hemoptysis</note>; it restrains the belly, checks <term>rheumatism</term> <note>original: *reumatismum*; here meaning a "runny" flow of bodily fluids or discharge</note>, and helps with <term>strangury</term> <note>original: *stranguiriosis*; a condition causing painful, drop-by-drop urination</note>. 

It provokes urine. Drunk with wine, it treats the bites of venomous creatures. Taken for periodic fevers one hour before the onset of a chill, it is extremely beneficial. Used as a suppository, it binds the flux of women <note>excessive menstrual or uterine bleeding</note>. It relieves ear pain, and if cooked with much [taenis] <note>possibly a corruption referring to a type of bandage or a specific plant part like "stems"</note> in wine and honey, it cures wounds of a private nature. An application of the leaves as a <term>poultice</term> <note>original: *cataeptmi*, a corruption of the Greek *cataplasma*</note> removes stomach effusions, assists with fresh bleeding, and cures <term>herpes</term> <note>original: *herpetas*; used here to mean spreading skin rashes or sores</note>. It extinguishes <term>St. Anthony's Fire</term> <note>original: *ignem sacrum*; a historical term for inflammatory skin conditions like erysipelas</note>, and when applied, it disperses tumors and hard swellings; it is especially beneficial for fresh wounds.

### ON FEMALE KNOTGRASS
<note>original: *Poligonon femina*; likely referring to common knotgrass, *Polygonum aviculare*</note>

Female knotgrass is a shrub. It consists of a single rod that is soft, fleshy, and thick, appearing somewhat fatty and fragrant. In its nodes, leaves can be seen similar to those of a pine. Its root is useless. It grows in damp places. Its power is entirely <term>styptic</term> and it can perform all the same functions as the plants described above, though it possesses less potency.

### ON SOLOMON'S SEAL
<note>original: *Poligonation*; literally "many-kneed," identifying the plant's jointed rhizome</note>

Solomon's Seal grows in mountainous places. It is a shrub with many leaves similar to laurel but wider. In taste, it is similar to a <term>quince</term> <note>original: *malo quidonice*</note> or a pomegranate. It is slightly <term>styptic</term>. Numerous white flowers grow from the base of the individual leaves. Its root is white and soft, knotty, rough, and long, having a heavy odor and the thickness of a finger. Applied as a <term>poultice</term>, it heals wounds and clears bruises <note>original: *liuoris*; livid marks or discolorations</note> from the face.

## VII ON CLEMATIS

They call it **clematis**, or **daphonidis**, or **polygoninidis**, or **misionides**. It grows upon the ground, having long shoots like linen cords. They have the thickness of [unclear] <note>The scribe omitted the object of comparison for thickness</note>. The leaves are long, similar in shape and color to those of the laurel, but the leaves are shorter. The leaves, taken <note>original: *charta bibita*; literally "soaked paper," likely a scribal error for *carpta* (plucked) or referring to the dried leaf</note> with wine, bind a loose belly and assist with **dysentery** <term>dysentery</term> <note>an inflammatory infection of the intestines resulting in severe diarrhea with blood</note>. Added to **pessaries** <note>medicated vaginal suppositories</note> with milk, rose oil, and cypress oil, it mitigates dysenteric pains. When chewed, it takes away the pain of the teeth. It is effective against venomous bites; it is even said to soothe the bite of an **asp** <note>a venomous snake, often the Egyptian cobra</note> when drunk with vinegar. It grows in common places.

## VIII ON POLEMONION

**Polemonion** or **phileterion**; the Cappadocians <note>people from Cappadocia, in modern-day Turkey</note> call this herb **elimonica**. It is thin, with square stems and leaves a little larger than **rue** <note>a bitter herb used in ancient medicine</note>, being oblong and similar to **polygonia** <note>knotgrass</note> or **calaminar** <note>likely calamint</note>. Above these are little husks containing the seed, which is black. The root is long, one **cubit** <note>an ancient unit of length, about 18 inches</note> in size, but whitish, similar to **struthium** <note>soapwort, used for cleaning wool</note>. It grows in mountainous and rough places. Its root drunk with wine is effective against venomous bites. Drunk with water, it provides the greatest effect for dysentery, **dysuria** <note>painful or difficult urination</note>, and **sciatica** <note>original: *adiadias*, a corruption of the Greek *ischiadas*; nerve pain in the hip and thigh</note>. For those with spleen ailments, it is a singular defense if drunk with vinegar. The root, when tied on as an amulet, has power against the sting of a scorpion; chewed, it checks the pain of the teeth.

## VIIII ON COMFREY

**Sinfitiū** <note>Symphytum, or Comfrey</note> grows in rough places. It has shoots similar to **oregano** but thin, and heads like **ammis** <note>original: *ammos*; Bishop’s weed</note>, but they are woody, fragrant, and sweet to the taste. It provokes **phlegm**. Its root is long and reddish-black, having the thickness of a finger. Boiled in **mead** <note>original: *mulsa*; water sweetened with honey</note>, it purges the lungs. For those spitting blood and for **nephritics** <note>original: *neufrotias*; those suffering from kidney disease</note>, it is prepared with water or cooked with wine.

[Drunk], it stops the flow of women's discharge. It helps against **dysentery** <term>dysentery</term> <note>an inflammatory infection of the intestines resulting in severe diarrhea with blood</note> when given with **oxymel** <term>oxymel</term> <note>a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar; original: *obrimelli*</note>. ### X ON COMFREY

They call it **Symphytum** <note>original: *Symphonia*</note> or others call it **pecten** <note>original: *psittenu*</note>. Its stalk is rough and long, two **cubits** <term>cubit</term> <note>an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches</note> in height, and angular, being hollow inside. It has leaves that are rough, narrow, and oblong like **bugloss** <term>bugloss</term> <note>literally "ox-tongue," a plant with rough, tongue-shaped leaves; original: *buburra*</note>. Indeed, the stalk itself has angles where the leaves are attached. It has quince-colored <note>yellowish</note> flowers and bears seeds upon the stalk itself like **mullein** <note>original: *flommus*</note>. It is like a shrub and has a dust-like roughness; when this is applied to the skin, it causes **pruritus** <term>pruritus</term> <note>severe itching; original: *plurigine*</note>. Its root is black on the outside, appearing white and mucilaginous when broken. Its use is necessary for bruised things, and when drunk it heals **haemoptysis** <term>haemoptysis</term> <note>the coughing or spitting up of blood; original: *emoptoias*</note>. It restores one from internal bruising and scatters the swelling of **ranulae** <term>ranula</term> <note>a cyst or swelling under the tongue; original: *rani*</note>. When the leaves are ground <note>original: *irigerunt*, likely *triverint*</note> or applied as poultices, it can perform all the actions mentioned above. It provides **parakollesis** <note>gluing</note> to wounds and, if pieces of meat are placed in a cooking pot, it makes them glue themselves back together.

### XI ON HOLOSTEON

The herb **Holosteon** <note>original: *Olositon*</note> is small, three or four fingers high. It has leaves and a stalk similar to **buck's horn plantain** <note>original: *coronopi*</note>, or it is similar to **couch grass** <note>original: *agrosan*</note> in its properties. Its root is very thin, like a white thread, with a wine-like odor <margin>*</margin> and four fingers long. It grows in cultivated places. This herb can also [congeal meat] just as described above. When drunk with wine, it [stops] **rheum** <term>rheum</term> <note>a watery discharge from the eyes, nose, or mouth</note>.

### XII ON SAGE

**Sage** <note>original: *Sabis*, likely *Salvia*; the chapter heading *STIPE* may be a corruption of *Stoechas* or a scribal error</note> has leaves and seeds [which are useful]. From it, a decoction <note>original: *elixatura*</note> is taken, and when applied [locally], it helps with **dysentery**. It also mitigates ear pain.

### ON CLYMENON
<note>Likely *Lathyrus clymenum*, or Spanish Vetchling; the text notes its similarity to beans.</note>

**Clymenon** <note>original: *Climinon*</note> has square stalks similar to the **green bean** <note>original: *fabe uiridi*</note>. It has leaves similar to the small leaves of **arnoglossa** <term>arnoglossa</term> <note>literally "lamb's tongue," known today as plantain</note>. Upon the stalk itself, two leaves cling together, similar to **ivy** <note>original: *siri*, likely a corruption of *cissos*</note>, and it is better than **polypody** <term>polypody</term> <note>a type of fern; original: *polopedio*</note>. Its juice, given with its root, benefits those suffering from **hemoptysis** <term>hemoptysis</term> <note>the coughing up of blood; original: *emoptoicis*</note>. It is also effective for any individual case; the remaining [juice] binds the flow of women <note>menstrual discharge</note>. Its properties are **styptic** <note>original: *sapaca*, likely *styptica*; meaning it shrinks or constricts tissue</note> and cooling. It resists flowing blood, and when its leaves are applied to wounds, <margin>+</margin> it causes **parakollesis** <term>parakollesis</term> <note>the medicinal "gluing together" or sealing of a wound</note>.

### XIIII ON PERICYMENON
<note>Commonly identified as Honeysuckle or Woodbine.</note>

Some call **Periclymenon** "splenion" <note>the spleen-plant</note>. It is a simple shrub, arched in form, having white leaves similar to ivy. Around these leaves are thin twigs in which the seed is found. The seed is similar to ivy and clings to the leaves; it is hard, but is softened <note>original: *leuatur*</note> when taken with wine. Its root grows thick in cultivated places <note>original: *loar culrar dinorar*, likely *locis cultis*</note> and they cling to nearby things. Its seed, collected and dried in the shade and drunk with wine for eleven days, withers the spleen <note>reduces swelling</note> and restores bodies after labor. It heals those with **orthopnea** <term>orthopnea</term> <note>shortness of breath when lying down; original: *hortopnoicis*</note> and those with **hiccups** <note>original: *subglutiaenab;*</note>. It provokes bloody urine on the sixth day and aids those who have been in labor for a long time. It has similar virtues when the leaves are drunk for thirty-seven days. The seed nourishes a person when mixed with oil and it excludes periodic cold stings <note>chills from a recurring fever</note>.

### XV ON TRIBULUS
<note>Usually *Tribulus terrestris*, or Puncture Vine, known for its sharp-spined fruits.</note>

There are two kinds of **Tribulus**. One has leaves similar to **purslane** <note>original: *andrazecumiditne*, likely *andrachne*</note> but they are tender and hard. It has long stalks, tenderly extended and hard, on which thorns grow. It grows in river places and deserts. Another kind, indeed, which is said to grow in damp rivers, has its foliage extended over the water, with its leaves floating on top.

...the ones grown in water have broader and oblong leaves, spear-shaped <note>original: *hastate*</note>, being thicker at the base. They reach a point at the tip, but are thin at the root. They possess thin thorns upon them, like an ear of grain. The seeds of both types <note>land and water varieties of Tribulus/Caltrop</note> have medicinal properties. They are cooling and **styptic** <term>styptic</term> <note>a substance that shrinks or constricts body tissue to stop bleeding or secretions</note>; when applied to any tumor, they disperse it. ### XVI ON LIMONIUM
<note>Likely *Statice limonium* or Sea Lavender.</note>

**Limonium** <note>original: *Olimonio*</note> has leaves similar to **beets**, but they are tender and oblong. It has many long, tender, and upright stalks. It has a **golden** <note>original: *obrussa*, possibly referring to the color or a sharp, refined quality</note> and **styptic** taste. The seed is like a lily. Its seed is drunk with wine for **dysentery** <note>original: *disintericis*</note>, and it helps those with **celiac disease** <note>original: *quiliacor*, a corruption of the Greek *koiliakos*, referring to stomach or intestinal distress</note>. It binds the flow of women <note>excessive menstrual discharge</note>. It grows in cultivated places.

### XVII ON HARE’S-FOOT
<note>Commonly identified as *Trifolium arvense*, Hare's-foot clover.</note>

**Hare's-foot** <note>original: *Lagopa*</note>, when drunk with wine, binds the bowels. For those with a fever, it is given with water; for those without a fever, it is given with wine. When ground and applied, it disperses tumors of the **groin** <note>original: *inguinum*</note>. It grows in cultivated places and where olives are abundant.

### XVIII ON MEDION
<note>Often identified as a species of *Campanula* (Bellflower) or *Convolvulus*.</note>

**Medion** grows in rough and shady places. Its leaves are similar to **chicory** <note>original: *seridi* (seris)</note>. It has long stalks, three cubits <note>approximately 4.5 feet</note> in height. It has larger, purple, and oblong flowers. The scent of the seed is similar to **safflower** <note>original: *cnicii*</note>. The roots are long and...

## XVIII ON EPIMEDIUM
<note>Likely *Epimedium alpinum*, known today as Barrenwort or Bishop's Hat.</note>

**Epimedium** has a stalk no larger than **ivy**, with leaves numbering ten or twelve. It has neither flower nor seed. Its root is tender, black, and has a heavy odor with a bland <note>original: *fatuo*, meaning insipid or tasteless</note> taste. It grows in damp places. Its leaves, crushed with oil and applied as a poultice, do not allow the breasts to grow <note>an ancient cosmetic treatment to keep breasts small or firm</note>. The leaves and root, if drunk with wine for five or eight days after a woman's period <note>original: *post purgatione*</note>, stop the ability to conceive.

## XX ON XIPHION
<note>Commonly known as Corn-flag or *Gladiolus italicus*.</note>

They call it **Xiphion**, **Sparganion**, or **Machaerida** <note>original: *machaerida* from the Greek for "sword"</note> because of the shape of the leaves; they are similar to the **Iris** but smaller, narrower, and sharp like a sword <note>original: *machera*</note>. It has rough stalks, one positioned over the other like a small bulb. One part is thin and the upper part is thicker. It grows in cultivated places. Its root, applied as a plaster <note>original: *cataplasma*</note> with wine and frankincense, draws out bones stuck in the body. When applied with barley-meal <note>original: *pulenta*</note>, it soothes and removes many pustules and bodily humors; for this reason, it is mixed into various medicines. Used as a suppository, it induces menstruation. The upper part of the root drunk with wine stimulates the belly. Taken in a bath, it treats intestinal issues <note>original: *intero cellis* (enterocele)</note> in children.

## XXI ON SPARGANION
<note>Commonly known as Bur-reed (*Sparganium*).</note>

**Sparganion** has leaves similar to **Xiphion**, but they are narrower and reclining. Upon the stalks, they have a small head in which the seed is found. Its root and seed are given to treat poisonous bites.

## XXII ON XERIS
<note>Likely *Iris foetidissima*, the Stinking Iris.</note>

They call it **Xeris**, **Ectris**, **Xyris**, or **Wild Iris**, but the Romans call it **Gladiolus** <note>literally "little sword"</note>. Its leaves are like the **Iris**...

It heals fractures, draws out broken bones, and removes everything stuck in the body. ## XXIIII ON ANCHUSA
<note>Likely *Anchusa officinalis* or *Alkanna tinctoria*, known as Alkanet or Bugloss. It was famous in antiquity for the red dye extracted from its roots.</note>

**Anchusa**. <unclear>Others</unclear> have said it has leaves similar to **lettuce**, but sharp, rough, larger, and many spread out across the ground. The spike is somewhat thorny. Its root is the thickness of a finger and stains the fingers with a blood-red color; this power is present even before the flower is born. Its root, made into a grease <note>original: *saprica*, likely referring to an ointment base</note> with wax and oil added, heals burns and excellently cures wounds of the kidneys. It also soothes "Sacred Fire" <term>Sacred Fire</term> <note>original: *Ignem antrum* (ignis sacer), a term for inflammatory skin conditions like erysipelas</note> when applied with barley meal. It cleanses spots on the body and leprosy when applied with vinegar. Used as a suppository, it induces menstruation and causes abortion. Its decoction is correctly applied for women in labor <note>original: *fariar*, likely *parientibus*</note>. It helps those suffering from kidney or spleen ailments; it is given with mead <note>original: *mulsa*, a mixture of honey and water</note> to those with a fever, and with wine to those without a fever. Its leaves, when fresh, bind the belly if drunk with wine.

### ON THE OTHER ANCHUSA
<note>Anchusa is likely *Anchusa officinalis* or *Alkanna tinctoria*, commonly known as Alkanet or Bugloss.</note>

There is another Anchusa which many call *alcibiadion* <note>original: *alabiadion*</note> or *onochiles* <note>original: *oncalo*</note>; the difference in this plant can be very easily understood because it has smaller and rougher leaves than the former kind. Its upper branches are similar but thin, upon which it bears a purple flower or one like groundsel <note>original: *senecinum*, referring to the plant *Senecio*</note>. It has reddish and elongated roots. It grows in sandy places. The power of its root and leaves is effective against venomous bites, provided it is eaten and drunk; if tied around the neck, it does not allow the power of the poison to take effect. If someone chews its leaves and spits upon a serpent, it will kill it. There is another kind similar to Anchusa but having smaller seeds; they have this seed of a similar color, and likewise, when chewed and spat, it brings death to a serpent more quickly. Its root, given with vinegar and hyssop <note>original: *isopu*</note> and drunk from a bean-pod <note>original: *ex ifabu*, likely *ex faba*</note>, destroys wide intestinal worms <term>intestinal worms</term> <note>original: *lumbricis latis*, likely referring to tapeworms</note>.

### XXV ON LYCOPSIS
<note>Lycopsis, often called "Bugloss," is a rough-leaved plant in the borage family.</note>

Lycopsis, which many have also called Anchusa, has leaves similar to lettuce but elongated, rough, and thick. From the root, it sends up a stalk <note>original: *hasta*, literally "spear"</note> that is long, rough, and straight, having many branches a cubit <term>cubit</term> <note>an ancient unit of length, roughly 18 inches</note> in length. At the top, it has a tiny purple flower and an obscure taste <note>original: *obrusu sapacu*, likely a corruption of *obscuro sapore*</note>. It grows in fields. Its root, applied fresh <note>original: *incarupt*, likely *incorrupta*</note> with pearl barley <term>pearl barley</term> <note>original: *pulenta*</note>, heals erysipelas <term>erysipelas</term> <note>original: *igne agrum*, likely a corruption of *ignem sacrum* or "holy fire," a skin infection</note>. Crushed and rubbed on with oil, it induces sweating.

### XXVI ON ALCHION, THAT IS, ECHIUM
<note>Alchion is identified here as *Echium* or Viper's Bugloss, named for its seeds' resemblance to a snake's head.</note>

Alchion, or *dorida*, which many also call *alcibiadion*, has elongated, rough, tender, and fleshy leaves similar to Anchusa, but they are very small. They are rough between one another, but the leaves are tiny and smaller. Above the hairiness <note>original: *hirtu*</note> they have purple flowers around the leaves, in which is the seed, shaped like the head of a serpent. The root is as thin as a finger and black in color. Drunk with wine, it counteracts venomous bites and keeps all bodies very safe against poisons. Its seed does the same, and it relieves the pain of sciatica <term>sciatica</term> <note>pain affecting the back, hip, and outer side of the leg</note>.

### ON OCIMOIDES
<note>Ocimoides is likely *Silene dioica*, commonly known as Red Campion or Catchfly. The name suggests it resembles basil (Ocimum).</note>

### ON AGROSTIS
<note>Agrostis usually refers to "Couch Grass" or "Dog Grass" (*Elymus repens*), valued since antiquity for its medicinal roots.</note>

Agrostis has knotted stalks spread upon the ground, upon which the leaves are sharp, elongated, and hard, like those of a reed <note>original: *tanda*, likely a corruption of *typha*</note>. It has a smaller root, and animals feed upon it. Its root, when crushed and applied to wounds, acts as a binding agent <term>binding agent</term> <note>original: *paracollosin*, from the Greek for "gluing together" or healing a wound</note>. A decoction of it, when drunk, treats griping pains in the bowels and difficulty in urinating <term>difficulty in urinating</term> <note>original: *disuriae*</note>; it heals internal wounds excellently and breaks up kidney stones <term>kidney stones</term> <note>original: *calculos*</note>. # XXX ON IRONWORT (SIDERITIS)
<note>Sideritis, also known as Ironwort or Mountain Tea, was named from the Greek word for iron (*sideros*). It was traditionally used to heal wounds caused by iron weapons.</note>

This type of Ironwort, which is called by the same name, has leaves similar to horehound <note>original: *prassio*; specifically *Marrubium vulgare*</note>, but they are more elongated. It has rough, four-sided stems about two palms long <note>A "palm" is an ancient measurement of about 3 inches; thus, the stems are roughly 6 inches long.</note> or more. It is sweet to the taste. On these stalks are round heads like those of mullein <note>original: *ueruas*, likely referring to *Verbascum*</note>, and within these heads, a black seed is found <gloss>is found</gloss>. It grows under rocks. Its leaves, when crushed and applied to fresh wounds, heal them <term>paracolesin</term> <note>original: *paracolesin*, a Latinization of the Greek word for "gluing together," referring to the closing of a wound.</note> wonderfully.

# XXXI ON ANOTHER TYPE OF IRONWORT

This other Ironwort has stems two cubits long <note>A "cubit" is approximately 18 inches, making these stems about 3 feet long.</note> and tender. It has leaves similar to water germander <note>original: *scordi*; *Teucrium scordium*</note>, but they are very deeply divided around the edges. Towards the top, they are thin and elongated. At the peak of the stem, there is a round and rough head containing a seed similar to that of a grape vine, being round and hard. Its wound-healing <term>traumatica</term> <note>From the Greek *traumatikos*, meaning "pertaining to wounds."</note> properties are similar to the ones mentioned above.

# XXXII ON THE THIRD TYPE OF IRONWORT

There is also a third kind of Ironwort which Crateuas <note>Crateuas was a famous ancient Greek pharmacologist and physician to King Mithridates VI; he is renowned for his illustrated herbals.</note> and others have described. It grows on walls and in crevices. It has very small and tender leaves, many growing from a single root, similar to coriander <note>original: *coriandro*</note>. Its stems are two palms long, soft, and quite white. It has [yellowish] flowers and is mucilaginous to the taste. When crushed and applied to fresh wounds, it provides healing <term>paracolesint</term>.

# XXXIII ON ANOTHER TYPE

Another type, which is called *quemula* <note>The name *quemula* is obscure but likely refers to a regional variant of Ironwort or a related *Stachys* species.</note>, has stems longer than two palms but twisted like a snake <note>original: *ut coluber*</note>. On these are tender leaves, divided around the edges like coriander. It is bitter and mucilaginous, with a [strong] odor. It has round heads on top and flowers of a golden color.

### XXXIIII ON THE BRAMBLE (BATOS)
<note>original: *Batos*, referring to the blackberry or bramble bush (*Rubus fruticosus*). Ancient doctors used almost every part of this plant—leaves, shoots, and berries.</note>

The Bramble's virtues are known to all. It has astringent and preservative qualities. A decoction of it dyes the hair <note>Blackberry juice or leaf decoctions were used in antiquity as a dark hair dye.</note>, binds the belly, and stops the flow [of blood] in women. It counteracts venomous bites. It protects the gums from rot and calms swelling of the mouth, especially if the leaves themselves are chewed with vinegar, which cleanses them thoroughly. It clears scabs on the head <term>acoras</term> <note>original: *acoras*, referring to *achores*, a type of scalp eruption or crusting similar to cradle cap or severe dandruff.</note>, relieves swelling of the eyes, and dissolves anal growths <term>condilomatis</term> <note>original: *condilomatis*, from the Greek for "knuckle," used here for warts or tumors.</note>. When applied, it assists with hemorrhoids and acts as a mouth medicine <term>stomatica</term>. It helps those suffering from heart-pain <note>original: *cardiacis*, which in ancient medicine often referred to a "weakness of the heart" or severe stomach distress/heartburn.</note>. The juice of this herb, dried in the sun, can perform all these cures. The juice of its seed, when ripened, is applied effectively for all conditions of the mouth. It binds the belly when eaten unripe. Its flower, drunk with wine, is beneficial for anyone with dysentery.

### XXXV ON THE WILD BRAMBLE

It is effectively used with water as a mouth medicine.

### XXXVII ON FLUELLEN
<note>original: *Elatine*, likely referring to Sharp-leaved Fluellen (*Kickxia elatine*). The name is derived from the Greek word for "fir," perhaps due to the shape of its leaves.</note>

Fluellen has leaves that are smaller than those of Pellitory <note>original: *elixine*, referring to Pellitory-of-the-wall (*Parietaria officinalis*).</note>; they are round and rough. It has thin stalks, two spans long; there are five or six stalks from a single root, and they are full of leaves with a styptic <note>original: *saptico*, a corruption of *styptico*, meaning an astringent or "puckering" taste.</note> taste. It grows in cultivated places and in the fields by its own power. Its leaves, when used in a poultice <term>cataplasma</term>, soothe the discharge of the eyes and prevent swelling. A decoction of the plant, when drunk, wonderfully cures dysentery.

### XXXVIII ON AGRIMONY
<note>original: *Eupaturio*. This is likely *Agrimonia eupatoria*, named after Mithridates Eupator, King of Pontus, who was a famed herbalist.</note>

Agrimony is a twiggy shrub; it has straight and woody stalks that are thin, black, and rough, reaching a length of one cubit <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of measurement based on the length of the forearm, approximately 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note> or more. It has leaves arranged in a circle, divided like Cinquefoil or Hemp, whose leaves are notched at the tip like a saw. The seed is found in the middle of the rough stalk, on a sharp incline. When its dry leaves are ground with added old hog lard <term>axungia porcine</term> and applied, it leads hard wounds to a scar. Furthermore, its seed and leaves drunk with wine act as a medicine against dysentery and poisonous bites. Many have said this plant is Mugwort <note>original: *artemonion*, referring to *Artemisia*.</note>, but it is something else.

It has a green flower <note>While the text says "green," most varieties of Cinquefoil have bright yellow flowers; this may refer to the sepals or a specific variety.</note> and grows in damp places and along paths. ## XI ON DARNEL
<note>original: *Fenica* or *Fenix*. This refers to a species of grass, likely *Lolium* (Darnel) or *Hordeum murinum* (Wall Barley), rather than the mythical bird.</note>

Darnel—or as some call it, *anquino*—has leaves similar to barley, but they are smaller and narrower. Its spike is similar to darnel <note>original: *leraroa*, likely a corruption of *lolio*.</note>; it has stalks six inches long, bearing seven or eight spikes. It grows in cultivated places and near plantations. It has a known power: drunk with harsh wine, it binds a loose belly, stops blood flowing from the womb, and greatly restrains urine. It is said to stop all bleeding if it is enclosed in a small bag <note>original: *daculo*, likely *sacculo*.</note> and hung from the neck.

# XLII ON IDEX
Idex has leaves similar to butcher’s broom <note>original: *oximirsine* (Ruscus aculeatus), a low evergreen shrub with prickly leaves.</note> when it is seen with its flowers. Its root is very styptic <term>a substance that shrinks tissues and stops bleeding</term> and is a necessary styptic medicine in all places. When drunk, it restrains flux of the belly <note>original: *reumatismū uentris*, referring to diarrhea or watery discharge.</note> and dysentery, checks the flow of the womb, and stops all loss of blood.

# XLIII ON ROSE-ROOT
Rose-root <note>original: *Rodia radix*; likely *Rhodiola rosea*, known for its rose-scented roots.</note> is a root growing in Macedonia. It is similar to costus <term>an aromatic root used in ancient perfumes and medicine</term> but is a little lighter and not as uniform. When rubbed, it gives off the scent of roses for a long time. Mixed with oil <note>original: *leo nardino*, possibly referring to spikenard oil or a specific scented oil blend.</note>, it is the greatest remedy for headache <note>original: *cefalargiae*, from the Greek *cephalalgia*.</note>; when applied to the forehead and smeared on the forehead and temples, it is the greatest protection.

# XLIIII ON HORSETAIL
Horsetail <note>original: *Hypporis* or *Ipparis*, referring to the *Equisetum* genus.</note> is what they also call *anaut* or *estendran*. It grows in damp places and on monuments; it has stalks that are red, rough, and knotted. These stalks gather whatever moisture they can find, and on them the leaves are quite sharp, similar to a rush, and grow thick and upward-climbing. Just as they hang from a wall, they are full of abundant "hair" and are so black as to look like a tail; it is woody and hard in its nature and is styptic. Wherefore its juice stops blood flowing from the nostrils; taken as a drink, it medicates dysentery and provokes urine. Its leaves, placed upon fresh wounds, perform a "gluing" <note>original: *paracolesin*, from the Greek *parakollesis*, meaning to glue or solder together; here, it refers to the closing of a wound.</note>. The root of this herb heals those with asthma and orthopnea <term>a condition where one can only breathe comfortably when standing or sitting upright</term>, and it should be applied to crushing injuries <note>original: *conqua sationib;*.</note>. Indeed, it is said that for a disaster of the bladder and the intestines <note>original: *uissicae et intestinarū*.</note>, its leaves drunk with water provide relief for internal colic.

# XLV ON THE OTHER HORSETAIL
There is another horsetail having smaller, whiter, and soft foliage. When ground with vinegar and applied to fresh wounds, [it heals].

<meta>This page continues the botanical and medicinal survey from the previous page, moving from styptic roots like Horsetail to the dye-producing Kermes "berry" and various plants known as Tragion and Tragos, focusing on their ability to heal wounds, expel foreign objects, and treat digestive issues.</meta>

### XLV ON THE DYER’S BERRY AND HOW IT IS USED
### FOR DYEING

The dyer’s berry <note>original: *Coccu*, referring to the Kermes insect (*Kermes ilicis*), which lives on Mediterranean oaks and was historically mistaken for a berry or "grain" used for red dye</note> grows on a twiggy shrub. On these branches, round grains like lentils are gathered and prepared. The best kind is the Gallic and the Armenian; the second best is the Asian and the Galatian <note>original: *diacu*, likely a corruption of *Galaticum*</note>; the Spanish kind is the newest of all and is of poor quality. It is a styptic <note>original: *saptica*, a substance that shrinks tissues</note>; when ground with vinegar and applied to wounds, it provides a binding effect <note>original: *paracollesin*, from the Greek for "gluing together," referring to the closing of wounds</note> and is a great protection for the nerves in the armpits <note>original: *in asis*, likely *axillis*</note>. It grows in Crete <note>original: *alitas*, a common medieval corruption of *Creta*</note>, in the place called Idrisi; it is small like a grain <note>original: *ebelia*</note>, which women gather and use, calling it "the berry."

### XLVI ON TRAGION

Tragion <note>likely *Hypericum hircinum* or Stinking Tutsan</note> grows in sunny places in Crete; it has spear-like leaves and seeds similar to hemp <note>original: *cano*, likely *cannabi*</note>, but all parts are smaller. It produces seeds and sap-drops <note>original: *lacrimus*, literally "tears"</note>. When ground and applied with vinegar, it draws out objects fixed in the body <note>such as thorns or arrowheads</note>, and when drunk, it heals difficulty in urinating <term>stranguria</term>. It breaks stones in the bladder and regulates the menses. If taken, it is said that a goat <note>original: *capria*</note> struck by an arrow will eat this herb and thus expel the arrow sticking in its body.

### XLVII ON THE OTHER TRAGION

The other Tragion <note>possibly *Asplenium scolopendrium* or a similar fern</note> has leaves similar to the spleenwort. Its root is white and thin, similar to the wild radish, which when eaten raw or cooked is a healthy remedy for dysentery. At the time when it has leaves, if it is rubbed in the hands, it has a goat-like smell <note>original: *tragiodore*, from the Greek *tragos* for goat; this explains its name</note>. Its leaves and seeds are also used.

### XLVIII ON TRAGOS

Tragos <note>possibly *Ephedra distachya* or a species of sea-grape</note>, also called *scarpion* or *tragunon*, grows in coastal places. It is a shrub that stands about one palm’s length or more above the ground, without leaves. It has stalks, and at the top of the stalk it has very small red berries <note>original: *acinas*</note>, sharp like wheat, with a starchy <note>original: *amulu*</note> taste. Its seeds have a styptic quality; when drunk with wine, they [stop] the flux of the belly <note>diarrhea</note>.

## ON THE RUSH
There are two kinds of Rush <note>original: *Squinus*, from the Greek *schoinos*, likely referring to various types of rushes or Camel Grass (*Cymbopogon schoenanthus*)</note>. One they call the Sharp-Rush <note>original: *oxianor*, a corruption of the Greek *oxyschoenos*</note> because it has a pointed head; the other is the Entire-Rush <note>original: *sem ba bas*, likely a corruption of *holoschoenos*</note>, which is black, round or thick, and hollowed. There is truly a third kind of rush that is a little thicker; where it begins, it has a similar distinction. The seed of both, when roasted and drunk with wine, binds the flux of the belly and the womb. It provokes the flow of urine and stirs up a headache, but the leaves grow at the root. Applied as a poultice <note>original: *catapt*, an abbreviation for *cataplasma*</note>, it mitigates the bite of a venomous spider <note>original: *falenzionis*, referring to the *phalangium* spider</note>. It is believed that the rush or the *simacus* <note>possibly a corruption of a plant name like *smyrnium*</note> has a seed with caustic properties <note>original: *scaroticum*, from "escharotic," meaning it can burn or scar tissue</note>, but it must be given moderately, lest it cause lethargy.

## ON LICHEN, THAT IS, BRYON
Lichen <note>original: *Licena*</note>, which grows upon maritime rocks, is *brion* <note>a Greek term for moss or seaweed</note>. Applied as a poultice, it restrains the flow of blood, reduces swelling, and provides relief for those suffering from jaundice <note>original: *hiterias*</note>. With honey added, it soothes roughness of the mouth and tongue and restrains "rheumatism" <note>original: *reumatismum*, here meaning a "running" or discharge of bodily fluids</note>.

<margin>LI.</margin>
## ON WHITLOW-GRASS
Whitlow-grass <note>original: *Paronitia*, from the Greek *paronychia*, named for its use in treating infections around the fingernails</note> grows among stones; it is a shrub similar to the *peplos* <note>a type of spurge</note> in length, but slightly smaller, though with larger leaves. Applied as a poultice, it cleanses whitlows <note>original: *pharitias*, infections of the nail bed</note> and shingles <note>original: *herpetae*, or "creeping" skin rashes</note>.

<margin>LII.</margin>
## ON GOLD-SOLDER PLANT
The Gold-Solder plant <note>original: *Criso colla*, likely referring here to *Chrysocome* (Goldylocks) rather than the mineral of the same name</note>, which is called *uirgice*, is two spans <note>original: *palmo ru*, a "palm" or hand-breadth</note> in height, on which there is a small head similar to a poppy <note>original: *rropo*, likely *rhoeadi*</note>. Its root is rough and thin, similar to black hellebore; it has a taste that is somewhat sweet and astringent. It grows in shady and rocky places. It is also called *ermaniaca* and *suprita*. Its root is a remedy <note>original: *iptece*</note> for those with liver complaints and pleurisy <note>original: *peripleomoniar*, infections or inflammations of the lungs</note>. It is taken when boiled in many purgative medicines; it is most effective for the stomach <note>original: *stericus*</note>... <unclear>plin</unclear>

# ON CHRYSOGONON
Many call this plant *Chrysogonon* <note>original: *Crisogonon*, likely refers to a plant like the "Golden-Knee" or a species of Leontice</note>, and they also name it Amaranth <note>original: *amarantum*, meaning "unfading"</note> because, when woven into crowns, it adds honor to the name of the stems. It has straight, white leaves arranged in a circle, like the foliage of Southernwood <note>original: *aproutenum*, a corruption of *abrotanum*</note>. At the very top, it has a head <note>original: *canziero*, likely a corruption of *cancamum* or referring to the flower-head</note> that looks as if it were full of gold; in this rounded head is the seed. Its root is thin. It grows in rough, rocky places. The foliage, when drunk with wine, is a helpful remedy for dysuria <note>difficulty or pain during urination</note> and for venomous bites. It also treats bruising and regulates the menstrual flow; it dissolves clotted blood in the belly and relieves diarrhea. Drunk with wine or in honey-water <note>original: *omelix*, a corruption of *hydromeli*</note>, it restrains purging <note>original: *catarton*, referring to catharsis or excessive bowel movements</note>. <insert>L II.</insert> Prepared with white wine, it frequently protects clothing from moths <note>original: *adinea*, a corruption of *tinea*</note>.

# ON AGERATUM
Ageratum <note>original: *Ageraton*, meaning "non-aging" or "everlasting"</note> is a shrubby plant <note>original: *sarmossa*, likely from *sarmentosa*, meaning having many runners or twigs</note> about two palms long, similar to Oregano <note>original: *oricani*</note>. It has a head on top in which there is a golden flower, but it is slightly smaller in color; its name was given to it because of this color <note>likely referring to the flowers not fading quickly</note>. Its virtue: used as a fumigant <note>inhaling the smoke or steam</note>, it provokes the flow of urine. Its decoction <note>original: *elixatura*</note>, applied as a warm soak or fomentation, settles uterine conditions <note>original: *srericas*, a corruption of *hystericas*</note>. <insert>I V de pe</insert>

# RISTERIO
Peristerion <note>original: *Peristerio*, commonly known as Vervain or Pigeon-grass</note> grows in damp places. It received the name *Idoonoma* <note>possibly a corruption of a Greek synonym</note> because doves <note>original: *columbi*</note> use it freely, as doves are called *peristera* in the Greek language. It is a plant two palms high or more, having divided white leaves and a single stem. Its leaves, when applied with rose oil or with hog’s grease <note>original: *ab srugia poruna*, a corruption of *axungia porcina*</note>, mitigate the pain of jaundice <note>unclear: <unclear>hicter</unclear>, likely *ictericos*</note>. When applied as a poultice <note>original: *carupt*, an abbreviation for *cataplasma*</note> with vinegar, it extinguishes "wildfire" <note>original: *igne agrū*, referring to *ignis sacer* or erysipelas, a skin infection</note>, stops the rot of wounds, and provides a scar <note>aids in healing and closing</note> for old sores.

## LVII ON STRAGULOS
<note>original: *Desiragulo* / *Stragulos*, likely referring to the plant *Tragos* or *Tragion*, often identified as a species of Ephedra or Goat-shrub</note>

Stragulos is a small shrub spread over the ground, with leaves and twigs similar to a Maple <note>original: *aceris*</note>, whose flowers are a smaller purple. It has a small and round root like a radish. It has strong and larger branches with black bark, as hard as horn, clinging to one another. Its quality is savory <note>original: *sapuita*, likely *sapida*</note>. It grows in windy and shady places, especially in hayfields. Drunk with wine, it provokes urine. The powder of its root, sprinkled on old wounds, provides a very great effect; when taken internally, it is known to stop flowing blood. They are difficult to store <note>or perhaps "to pound"</note> because of their hardness.

## 59 ON POPPY
<note>original: *Meconio* / *Mecon*. This section describes the Corn Poppy or Field Poppy, *Papaver rhoeas*.</note>

The poppy is called *rhuas* <note>from the Greek *rhoeas*, meaning "shedding," because the petals fall off quickly</note> because its flower falls very quickly. It grows locally in the springtime. It has leaves similar to very pungent coriander, but they are divided, oblong, and rough. It has a stem like a rush, which is straight, rough, and one cubit <note>an ancient unit of length, about 18 inches or 45 centimeters</note> long. Its flower is either reddish-purple <note>the text says *femina*, perhaps a corruption or referring to a "feminine" type</note> or white, like a wild anemone. It has a small, oblong head <note>the seed capsule</note>, and its seed is smaller than that of the anemone and reddish. The root is oblong, somewhat white, relatively thin, and bitter. Give five or six of its capsules in a drink to anyone you wish to make sleep. A measure of its seeds <note>original: *oxisabū*, likely referring to an *oxybaphon*, a small bowl used as a measurement</note> is mixed with sweets. The leaves and their heads, when mixed into a poultice, disperse swellings. Indeed, its decoction <note>the liquid resulting from boiling the plant</note>, when applied to the head as a wash, provides sleep.

## 60 ON THE OTHER POPPY
<note>This likely refers to the Opium Poppy, *Papaver somniferum*, and its varieties.</note>

There are two kinds of poppy: one from the garden and the other wild. The seed of the first poppy is mixed into bread and honey; it is used in place of sesame. It is also called *phylaktis* <note>original: *filactis*, from the Greek for "guardian" or "protector"</note> because it has an oblong head and a white seed. The wild poppy has a short head and black seed; it is also called *kopis* <note>original: *copit*</note>. It is also described as "flowing" because it loses its juice when it has matured. A third kind of wild poppy is smaller, greener, and <margin>or</margin> oblong. It has a head; the medicinal nature of all these poppies is "cold" <note>in ancient medicine, plants were classified by "temperaments": hot, cold, moist, or dry. Cold plants were used to reduce inflammation or induce sleep</note>. Its leaves and capsules, boiled in water and used as a wash for the face, provide sleep for everyone. Similarly, its decoction, when drunk in the amount of one small measure <note>original: *oxisabum*</note>, softens the bowels.

### BOOK 4

...from a good odor, it scatters like milk. Adulterated [poppy juice], however, when mixed with yellow-horned poppy <note>original: *glaucio*</note> or gum, is recognized when you wipe it with a finger; it will lose its odor and, when it becomes fatty, it hides many various heads <note>The Latin here is somewhat corrupt; it likely refers to the residue or the appearance of the adulterated mass</note>. They place the juice [in a vessel] as long as it appears red and is found to be of a soft color; it is necessary to mix it well. If a wise use rejects this fraud, it mitigates ear pains and clears the dimness of the eyes. 

<margin>Virtue</margin> Its potency <note>original: *uirtus*</note> is saffron-colored. Its power is so great that if an eye-salve <term>collyrium: a medicinal lotion or salve for the eyes</term> without adulteration is applied to the eyes as it is mixed, it can cause blindness. We have said its potency lies in its odor, in which the saffron-colored juice has the greatest virtue. Many have not admitted this method of treatment, but it has pleased us greatly, as we have proven it through complete use. Many take the small heads of the poppy and the leaves while they are [fresh], press and liquefy them, and by grinding them, they make lozenges <term>trochiscos: small medicinal discs or tablets</term>. This is called meconium <note>original: *meconium*, which in this context refers to the juice extracted from the whole plant parts, considered less potent than the pure 'tears'</note>, which has secondary efficacy after its "tears" <note>the pure sap that exudes from the poppy head</note>. These tears are collected thus: 

When the sun begins to grow warm and the dew has moved off, the heads must be lightly cut from the top, so that the incision does not penetrate the interior, but the juice is to be caught only by touching the skin <note>the outer rind of the poppy capsule</note> itself. Thus you wipe it with a finger and put it in a small bowl <term>cocula: a small vessel or spoon</term> or another similar vessel, or draw it with a finger into a cup so that the thin edge of the vessel wipes the finger well. When you have collected it, you return at intervals to collect more, as more is found to have gathered after you have returned. Grind it in a mortar, make lozenges, and use them. But diligence must be paid so that when you cut, the juice does not fall away, until you have collected it all.

<meta>This page continues the botanical descriptions from the previous section, moving from the processing of poppy juice to the specific physical characteristics and medical applications of the Horned Poppy, Meconaphrodis, Hypekoum, and Henbane.</meta>

The Horned Poppy <note>original: *meana* refers to *Glaucium flavum*</note> has white and thick leaves, similar to mullein <note>original: *flomo*</note>, which are divided in the middle like the wild poppy. From its flowering stem <note>original: *hasta*</note>, it bears a seed that is very small and curved like a horn or like fenugreek; it is from this horn-like shape that it received its name. Its root is long and black, growing in coastal areas and rough terrain. 

<margin>Virtue</margin> Its root, when boiled in water until the liquid is reduced by half, can be drunk to treat those with liver conditions <note>original: *epaticis*</note>. It also aids those who produce thick and rough urine. One oxybaphon <term>oxybaphon: a Greek measure of volume, roughly 68ml or a small cupful</term> of its seeds, when drunk with honey-water, purges the belly. Its leaves and flowers arrest the spread of ulcers <note>literally "feeding wounds"</note>. When mixed with oil and applied as an ointment, it clears away dimness from the eyes. Indeed, many have falsely said that the medicinal substance *glaucium* is made from this plant simply because of the similarity of the leaves.

### LXII ON MECONAPHRODIS

Some call it *Meconaphrodis* <note>likely a species of poppy, perhaps the "frothy poppy"</note> or *anteredis*. It has leaves two palms long, which are small and similar to the fennel plant. It has white seeds, and the entire herb itself is white. However, the root is thin. Its seed is collected when the plant is found to be at its greatest dryness and is then stored. One oxybaphon <note>original: *oxi fabu*</note> taken with honey-water induces vomiting and thoroughly cleanses the stomach; this purgation is a treatment for those suffering from epilepsy.

### LXIII ON HYPEKOUM

Hypekoum <note>original: *hipecon*</note> grows in wheat fields and in cultivated places. It has leaves similar to rue and a smaller stem. Its medicinal power is the same as that of meconium <note>juice extracted from the poppy plant</note>.

### LXIIII ON HENBANE

Some call Henbane <note>original: *Iosquiamo*</note> *amanti*. It is a small shrub with a thick stem and wide, oblong, divided leaves that are black and rough. Along its stems are seed heads similar to those of the poppy, filled with seeds; however, there are three types of Henbane. One has purple flowers and leaves similar to the smilax <note>original: *similace*</note>, with black seeds and small leaves that are hard and thorny. Another, however, has honey-yellow <note>original: *millinus*</note> flowers, leaves, and seed pods...
