...soft seeds. Others call it *obrufo*, *sicuterim*, *simon*, or *amboueroistimania* <note>these names are likely corrupted transcriptions of synonyms for poppy in other ancient languages like Gaulish or Egyptian</note>. It excels other varieties, including the carrot-like and the smaller *asalos*. 

The third type, however, which is used most frequently, has thick and soft leaves full of juice <note>original: *gito*, likely a corruption of *suco*</note>. It bears white flowers and produces white seed. It grows in maritime regions and throughout Europe. The white seed is the most effective; if it cannot be found, the reddish seed is the second best choice. The black seed is used for specific health needs. 

The juice is extracted from both the seed and the leaves; the stem is also crushed and pressed, and the resulting juice should be dried in the sun. This juice is effective and is typically used after it has aged for a year. Its juice is also mixed with wheat flour and formed into lozenges <note>original: *trociscos*</note> for storage. This juice, like that of the seed, is useful in preparations for eye-salves <term>collyrium: a topical medicinal lotion or salve for the eyes</term> to check viscous and hot rheum <note>original: *reuma*; a discharge of fluids</term>. It soothes ear pain and assists in curing the causes of jaundice <note>original: *hictoricus*</note> when it is not allowed to spread from the pale skin. When applied as a poultice <note>original: *cataplis*</note>, the seed is known to be capable of many things: it especially cures coughs and catarrh, and not only checks the rheum of the eyes but also stops pain. 

One obol <term>obolus: an ancient Greek unit of weight, roughly 0.7 grams</term> of this taken with poppy seed and other mixtures and drunk will restrain the flux of the belly and stop the flow of blood. Its seed alone is a help for gout <note>original: *podagris*</note> when mixed with wine and used as a poultice. When drunk, it relieves swelling of the testicles and breasts, and it is a necessary ingredient in many other poultices. Its leaves, when applied as a poultice, similarly take away pain. When drunk with wine three or four times, it prevents epial fevers <term>epialos: a type of fever characterized by simultaneous shivering and heat</term>. If the plant is cooked like a potherb and eaten, it induces a state of madness <note>original: *amania facit*</note>; the juice similarly causes madness if infused into wounds. Its root, boiled in vinegar and held in the mouth, soothes the pain of the teeth.

**LXVIII.**

### ON SLEEP-INDUCING NIGHTSHADE.

**Sleep-inducing Nightshade** <note>original: *Strignu ipnoa*; likely *Withania somnifera*, also known as Ashwagandha or Winter Cherry</note>, which is also called *halicaccabus* or *callion* <note>original: *halicaccabo*, *callion*</note>, is a shrub. It has thick, numerous, and twiggy branches that are not easily broken. Its leaves are quite thick, similar to those of a quince tree. The flower is reddish and quite large, and the seed is contained within small pods and is saffron-colored. Its root is covered in a thick bark and grows on the shore in rough, maritime places. It is said that when drunk with wine, it induces sleep. Its power is potent, or if you prefer, it acts as a sedative <term>sopio: an ancient term for a drug that causes deep sleep or a stupor</term>, though slightly less so than opium. Its seed strongly provokes the flow of urine and is given to those with dropsy <term>idropicis: people suffering from edema or an accumulation of fluid in the body's tissues</term> in a dose of twelve seed-heads. If more is given, it provokes mania <note>original: *maniam*; in this context, it refers to hallucinations or agitated delirium</note>, which can be remedied by drinking an abundance of honey-water <term>mulsa: a mixture of honey and water, often used as an antidote or restorative</term>. It is mixed into essential medicines or pain-relieving lozenges <term>trocis anodinis: small, medicinal discs or lozenges intended to alleviate pain</term>, specifically using its bark. Its juice, boiled in wine and used as a gargle, soothes the pain of teeth. When the juice is added to honey and applied to the eyes, it clears away dimness of vision and cleanses them.

### LXVIIII. ON MANIC NIGHTSHADE

Some have called this **Manic Nightshade** <note>original: *Strigno manicon*; likely *Datura stramonium* (Thorn Apple) or *Atropa belladonna* (Deadly Nightshade)</note> or *perisson* <note>meaning "excessive" or "redundant"</note>. Some call it *Lucem* <note>original: *Lucem*; literally "Light"</note>. Its leaves are similar to basil <note>original: *ozimo*</note> or rocket <note>original: *eruce*; also known as arugula</note>, but they are larger and prickly. Some have called it "wheel-foot" <note>original: *α' pede rotā*; likely a corruption of a Greek name referring to the shape of the leaves or plant</note>. It has ten or twelve long stalks; the heads are like rough olives, similar to those of a plane tree but larger and wider. It has a black flower, from which comes a seed similar to a cluster of grapes. It has ten or twelve round, black berries, soft like wool. Its root is white, thick, deep, and a cubit <term>cubit: an ancient unit of length, approximately 18 inches or 45 centimeters</term> long. It grows in mountainous and windy places and where plane trees are abundant. When eleven [grains/weight units] of its root are drunk with wine, it causes unpleasant dreams and—

### 70. ON DORIGNION.

**Dorignion** <note>original: *Dorignion*; likely *Anagyris foetida* or a related toxic shrub</note>, which others have called *halicaccabus* or *calliada*, is a shrub. It is similar to a smaller olive tree, possessing stalks less than a cubit <term>cubit: an ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</term> in length. The leaves are the color of olive leaves, oblong, narrow, and rough to the touch. It has a white flower among the head-leaves; these have a thick color like the wood of a maple, in which the seed is contained. The seed is round, appearing in groups of five or six, like a lentil plant or variegated. The root is the thickness of a finger and one cubit long. It grows in rocky, maritime places. This plant is said to be carotic <term>caroticum: a substance that induces a heavy, death-like stupor or deep sleep</term>. If a larger amount is taken, it brings death. It is said that women give its seed for fatal purposes <note>original: *ad mortem*; likely referring to its use as a poison</note>.

### 71. ON MANDRAKE

**Mandrake** <note>original: *Mandragora*; one of the most famous plants in ancient medicine and folklore, known for its humanoid roots and powerful sedative properties</note>, also called *anamon*, *bolboquilon*, or *arecon*. Women give the root of this plant for love <note>original: *ad amorem*; used as an aphrodisiac or in love potions</note>. There are two kinds: one is the female, and the other is a kind named *thridacias* <note>original: *tridacias*; likely referring to the "lettuce-like" appearance of the leaves</note>.

The leaves are narrow and smaller [than the male variety], then turn reddish or black, and are spread out over the ground. In the middle, "apples" <note>original: *mala*; the round, fleshy fruit of the mandrake</note> grow, similar to green grapes, containing seeds like those of parsley. It has two or three large roots joined together, black on the outside and white on the inside, with a thick bark; they do not have a central stalk.

The male variety, however, which people call *morion* <note>original: *morion*; often identified as *Mandragora officinalis*</note>, has white leaves that are larger, broad, and smooth like those of a grapevine. Its fruit is twice as large, saffron-colored, and has a sweet but heavy scent. Shepherds eat these fruits, and it brings on sleep <note>original: *somnium capit*</note>.

### DE CONIO
### ON HEMLOCK

Hemlock <term>conion: from the Greek *koneion*, poison hemlock (*Conium maculatum*)</term>; this herb has knotty stems like fennel <term>maratro: Greek *marathron*, fennel</term>; it has leaves similar to the giant fennel, narrow and with a heavy, oppressive odor. At the top are round heads where there are white flowers, in which is the seed; it is similar to dill, but whiter. The root is not deep. If taken in excess, it brings death through extreme <insert>cold</insert>; whoever drinks it and is afflicted by it is cured by warm, undiluted wine. 

The heads and the seed itself are juiced before they dry; the juice is squeezed out by crushing the plant. This juice is then dried in the sun. Its use is indeed great, as it is mixed into pain-relieving eye salves <term>colliris: medicinal eye cakes or ointments</term>. Similarly, it is applied to creeping skin rashes and "sacred fire" <term>ignē sacrum: a skin infection, likely erysipelas or shingles</term>. The herb and its foliage, when applied, stop the flow of seed <note>historically used to suppress libido or nocturnal emissions</note>; similarly, it is beneficial when applied to the breasts of young girls <note>to prevent them from growing too large or to soothe pain</note>. It powerfully constricts... <unclear>as</unclear>. The strongest varieties are said to be the Cretan, the Megarian, and the Attic. 76.

## LXXVI ON ASTROQUINON

They call it *Astroquinon*, or *quinarchon*, or *pardaliances* <note>original: *pardaliances*; from the Greek for "leopard-strangler," a common name for types of Aconite</note>, or *quinomeron*, or *quinocranbin*. ## LXXVII ON OLEANDER

They call it *Nerion*, or *rhododendros*, or *rhododaphne* <note>original: *rododafni*; literally "rose-laurel"</note>. It is a shrub known to everyone; it has leaves similar to the almond tree, but larger and thicker. It has a flower very similar to a rose. It has seeds in an open pod like a horn... <unclear>sielena de maior</unclear>... it has a similar root; the root is elongated and narrow, and is said to have a salty taste. It grows in watery and coastal places. Its power is such that if it is eaten by animals, it brings death; but for humans, it is a remedy. Taken with wine, it saves those facing death from venoms; it is especially effective when drunk with rue. Small livestock, however, die if they even come near its scent.

## LXXVIII ON MUSHROOMS

There are two types of mushrooms <term>micetum: a general term for fungi</term>. One is fit for use, and one is lethal <note>original: *homicidalis*; literally "homicidal" or "murderous," used here to mean "deadly to humans"</note> and should not be eaten. These grow from either rusted iron or old linens, or are generated by the venom of a serpent near its den, or are created by the roots of a poisonous tree. Those described above, which are found in this way, have a layer of slime over them; if these are collected and set aside for even a single hour, they become infested with worms. The other kind is fit for eating, but even if many of these are consumed, they are harmful because they cause indigestion and bring on suffocation. Against this, however, those who have tasted such things should drink nitre <term>nitro: naturally occurring sodium carbonate or saltpeter, often used as an emetic</term>, or salt and vinegar, or oil, or a decoction of savory <note>original: *timbrae*; likely *Satureja*, a pungent herb used in ancient medicine</note>, or chicken dung drunk with vinegar or honey; just as when taking cornel <note>likely referring to the fruit of the Cornelian cherry, *Cornus mas*</note>, it fattens and nourishes with unhealthy moisture.

### LXXX ON COLCHICUM

They call it Colchicum <term>Colchicum: also known as Autumn Crocus or Meadow Saffron; it contains the toxic alkaloid colchicine</term>, or wild bulb, or *ephemeron* <note>original: *ephemero*; from the Greek for "short-lived"</note>. It grows at the end of autumn; it has a white flower similar to the crocus flower, and afterwards it bears leaves similar to a bulb but thicker. It has a stalk two palms long and a reddish root—reddish and somewhat blackish on the outside—which, when peeled, is found to be white, soft, sweet, and full of juice. The bulb itself has a notch in the middle from which the flower emerges. It grows in many places in Messenia <note>a region in the Peloponnese, Greece</note> and Colchis <note>OCR: *incolaria*; likely a corruption of *in Colcho*, the region on the Black Sea where the plant was famously associated with the sorceress Medea</note>. If consumed, it causes suffocation, much like [poisonous] mushrooms; for this reason it is mentioned in this record so that it is not eaten instead of a common bulb, because its potency is that of a poison, even though its taste is sweet. But for those who have eaten it, one must provide aid in the same way as for those who have eaten [poisonous] mushrooms; but there is a unique protection...

### LXXXI ON EPHEMERON

Ephemeron <term>Ephemeron: literally "short-lived"; likely a species of wild Iris or Lily (*Iris foetidissima*)</term>, which some call wild lily <note>original: *mula hirina agreste*; likely a corruption of *moly irina*</note>, has leaves and stalks similar to a lily, but they are tender. They have a white flower, smaller [than a lily], and a soft seed. The root is thick, the length of a finger, and of great potency. It has an astringent <note>original: *sapaca*; likely a scribe's corruption of *styptica* (astringent)</note> taste and a pleasant scent. It grows in shady places and in the woods. Its root, boiled and held in the mouth, soothes the pain of teeth. Truly, its leaves boiled in wine and applied as a poultice <term>catcepta: a corruption of *cataplasma*, a soft, moist mass of herbs applied to the body</term> disperse tumors and hard swellings.

### LXXXII ON ALSINE

They call it Alsine <term>Alsine: likely *Stellaria media*, or Common Chickweed</term>, or *parthenion*, or *perdicion*, or *siderenam*, or *eradia*, or wild *quis sani*, or *liniana*, or *poliomon*. It grows on roofs or walls, having minute stalks and leaves similar to the olive. It has small, rough seeds <note>original: *linos aut precal spera*; likely describing the seed husks or burrs</note> around the stalk itself which cling to things. Its virtue is this: its seed is astringent and cooling. Applied as a poultice, it extinguishes Sacred Fire <term>Ignem agrum: a corruption of *ignis sacer*, likely referring to Erysipelas, a skin infection</term>, disperses growths <term>condilomata: small skin tumors or warts</term>, and heals burns. It checks every swelling and clears up pustules. Its juice, mixed with white lead <term>cerussa: a white pigment made from lead, commonly used in ancient ointments despite its toxicity</term>, extinguishes Sacred Fire and clears "herpetic" sores <term>herpiticos: spreading skin eruptions or rashes</term> when used as an ointment; it also treats gout <term>podagrias: inflammation of the joints, typically the big toe</term>. Combined with unheated wax-salve <term>ceroto apirino: a 'cold' cerate or ointment made without heating the wax</term> or with goat fat <term>absungia: a corruption of *axungia*, meaning animal grease</term>, its juice—taken by those who are thirsty—helps those with a cough and asthma. It disperses swelling of the throat when used as a gargle or poured over the area. When injected with rose oil, it soothes the pain of the ears.

### LXXXIII ON ALSINAN . LXXXIIII ON COALIDANA

Coalidana <term>Coalidana: a corruption of *Cotyledon*, or Navelwort (*Umbilicus rupestris*)</term>, or *squitadion*, has leaves like a small saucer <term>acetabulum: a vinegar cup, used here to describe the cup-shaped or "peltate" leaves</term>, round and deep. It has short stalks in which the seed is placed. The root is round like an olive.

## <gloss>A</gloss> LXXXV ON ALICORNIDONA <gloss>NAVELWORT</gloss>

Another Navelwort <term>Cotilidona: likely *Umbilicus rupestris*, also known as Pennywort or Navelwort</term> has thick, broad, and dense leaves like "little tongue" leaves. Those around the root are marked as if painted with an eye in the middle, just like the Greater Houseleek. It has an astringent <note>original: *sapica*; a corruption of *styptica*</note> taste. It has a slender stalk upon which is the flower, and the seed is similar to St. John's Wort <term>ipperico: *Hypericum*</term>. It has a larger root, the potency of which is similar to Houseleek.

## LXXXVI ON FACON

Water Lentil <term>Facon: from the Greek *phakos*, meaning lentil; referring here to Duckweed (*Lemna minor*)</term>, which is found upon the water, is round like a lentil and floats on the surface. Its color is green and its nature is cooling. Therefore, it disperses all tumors, extinguishes Sacred Fire <term>igne agrum: a common corruption for *ignis sacer*, likely Erysipelas, a painful skin infection</term>, and is necessary for gout <term>podagrias: gout or foot-pain</term> when applied alone with pearl barley. For infants, it provides a cure for intestinal hernias <term>enterocelliar: a protrusion of the intestine into the scrotum or groin</term>.

## LXXXVII ON THE GREATER AISDO

It is called Greater Aisdo <term>Aisdo: a corruption of the Greek *aizoon*, meaning "ever-living"; the Houseleek (*Sempervivum*)</term> because it has green leaves at all times. They also call it *bulaeman* <note>original: *bouphthalmon* or "ox-eye"</note>, *zortalmon* <note>original: *zoophthalmon* or "living-eye"</note>, *stergetro* <note>original: *stergethron*</note>, or ambrosia. The stalks of the larger variety are a cubit high and as thick as a thumb, green and fleshy, divided like horns. The pith is white. The leaves are very fleshy, similar to a thumb or a tongue; all the leaves spread themselves out over the ground. The upper ones are striated and thick, and they are marked as if painted with an eye. It grows in mountainous places and remains in the cracks of pottery or roof tiles. Its nature is cooling and astringent. Therefore, it is applied as a necessary remedy for shingles <term>herpias: likely *herpes zoster* or similar spreading skin rashes</term> and Sacred Fire.

### LXXXVIII ON THE LESSER HOUSELEEK

The Lesser Houseleek <term>Aizoon: likely *Sedum album* or a similar stonecrop</term> grows on walls and in rocky places, and upon hills among monuments. It has many leaves from a single root; they are fatty and sharp at the tip. From the middle rises a stalk two palms long. On the head of this stalk, it shows a delicate flower. Its medicinal potency is the same as that described above.

### LXXXVIIII ON THE THIRD HOUSELEEK

The third Houseleek is that which many call Wild Purslane <note>original: *andragne agreste*</note> or *celefion*; the Romans call it *alcebran*. It has broad leaves similar to purslane, but they are rough. It grows in rocky places. Its quality is warming <note>original: *termantica*; from the Greek *thermantikos*</note>, sticky, and effective for healing wounds. Applied with whey and flour, it disperses swellings; it is also applied with southernwood <note>original: *abrunzia*; likely a corruption of *abrotanum*</note>.

It cures dull <note>original: *surda*; literally "deaf" wounds, referring to those that are slow to heal or non-responsive</note> wounds and aids in cases of dislocations. ### ON THE DEAD-NETTLE

Dead-nettle <term>Galliopsis: likely *Galeopsis* or *Lamium*, plants that look like stinging nettles but do not sting</term>, or as they call it, *galeobdolon*, is a shrub smaller than a rod. Its leaves are similar to those of a stinging nettle, but thinner. When crushed between the fingers, it has a heavy, foul odor. It bears tiny purple flowers. It grows around gardens and walls. Above all other things, its primary power <note>original: *regulas uirtutis*</note> lies in its leaves and stalks, which dissolve hard swellings and disperse cancers of the breasts, scrofula <term>scrofas: a form of tuberculosis affecting the lymph nodes of the neck</term>, and parotid tumors <term>parotides: swellings of the glands near the ears</term>. It treats putrid sores when applied as a poultice <term>cataplasmata</term> with <note>original: *ss birindie*; likely a corruption of *brine* or a specific local ingredient</note> which should be mixed with vinegar. A decoction of it used as a fomentation <term>fomento: a warm, moist medicinal compress</term> cleanses spreading wounds and clears away putrefaction. With the addition of salt, it disperses tumors and cancers. 92

### XCIII CONCERNING GROUNDSEL

Groundsel <note>original: *Erigeron*; from the Greek for "early old man," referring to the white, downy seed heads that look like an old man's hair</note> has a stem a cubit long and reddish. It has tender leaves, smaller than those of rocket <note>original: *euzema*, likely *eruca* or arugula</note>. It has a yellow flower <note>original: *mileno*, likely meaning honey-colored or yellowish</note> that opens quickly and appears white like hair, with a small round head—which is how it got its name. It flowers in the spring. Its root is useless. It grows upon walls and around buildings. Its property is cooling. Its flower and leaves, applied as a poultice <term>cataplasma: a soft, moist mass of herbs spread on a cloth and applied to the body to heal or reduce inflammation</term> with sweet wine, soothe swellings of the testicles and the anus. If mixed with frankincense <note>original: *manna*, often referring to "manna thuris," the small crumbs or dust of frankincense resin</note>, it heals all wounds and sinews. The seed heads themselves, where the "hairs" turn white, can perform all the same healing functions as the leaves. However, if the green heads are drunk, they cause choking.

### XCIIII CONCERNING TELGEIRON

Telgeiron <note>The identity of this plant is uncertain; it may be a species of Stonecrop or Orpine, often related to Telephium in ancient texts</note> has leaves similar to coriander and is fleshy. The stalk is the thickness of a finger. Its leaves, crushed and applied, cleanse old wounds. It grows in fields.

### XCV CONCERNING SEA MOSS

Sea Moss <note>original: *Brion maritimo*; likely referring to certain types of seaweed or algae found on rocks</note> grows upon rocks and remains in the sea. It has smaller stems and is used for swellings and cases of gout <term>podagras: a form of inflammatory arthritis, often affecting the feet, characterized by severe pain and swelling</term>, for which cold applications are necessary.

## XCVII CONCERNING PONDWEED

Pondweed <note>original: *Potamogiton*; from the Greek *potamos* (river) and *geiton* (neighbor)</note> has leaves similar to a bean. It is seen floating in the middle of the water. Its property is cooling and styptic. It especially heals fresh <note>original: *pancentia*, likely *recentia*</note> wounds and prevents old ones [from spreading]. It is called "pondweed" because it grows in water and in marshy fields <note>original: *campi saquosir*, likely a corruption of *stagnosis*, meaning swampy or waterlogged</note>.

## XCVIII CONCERNING WATER SOLDIER

Water Soldier <note>original: *Stratiotes*; from the Greek for "soldier," likely due to its sword-shaped leaves</note>, which grows in the water, is so named because it floats upon the water without a root. It has leaves similar to the larger houseleek <note>original: *ais de maiore*, referring to *Aizoon*</note>. Its property is styptic and cooling. When taken, it restrains the flow of blood from the kidneys. It keeps wounds free from swelling; when vinegar is added, it subdues "holy fire" <term>ignis sacer: a historical term for various skin infections, such as erysipelas or shingles, characterized by a painful, red rash</term> and swellings.

## XCVIII. CONCERNING THE OTHER STRATIOTES (YARROW)

The "thousand-leaved" Stratiotes <note>original: *Stratiotes alio fillus*, from the Greek *chiliophyllos* meaning "thousand-leaved"; commonly known today as Yarrow</note> is a shrub. It is smaller [than the water variety], longer than two palms. It has leaves similar to a dove's feather, on which many minute and hairy leaves grow, similar to wild cumin. At the top, it has thick and dense little heads, in which there are small stalks like dill. Its flower is very small and white. It grows in deserted and rugged places, especially along roadsides. This herb strongly binds the flow of blood. It treats both old and recent wounds and fills <note>original: *replet*; meaning it promotes the growth of healthy tissue to close a wound</note> fistulas.

### HERE CONCERNING MULLEIN

There are two kinds of Mullein <note>original: *Flommo*, the Latinized form of the Greek *Phlomos*, known today as *Verbascum*</note>: the male and the female, and the white and the black. The female variety has leaves similar to a small cabbage <note>original: *colliculo*, likely *cauliculo*</note> but rougher and more vibrant. It has a long stalk, a cubit in length <note>approximately 18 inches</note>, which is white and rough, with green and white flowers. The seed is black. It has a hard root the thickness of a thumb and grows in the fields.

The other kind, which is called the male, has white, oblong, and narrow leaves and a tender stalk. The black variety is broad in all its parts and is called "black." The wild mullein has long, woody branches; its leaves are similar to sage <note>original: *elelis faciis*, likely a corruption of the Greek *elelisphakos*</note>. Around these branches, it has flowers that are golden or honey-colored like those of horehound <note>original: *prasii*</note>, but its leaves near the ground are rough and rounded.

There is another kind of mullein which is called *lignitis* <note>from the Greek for "woody"</note> or *emallit*; it has three or four leaves and is used very often for lamp wicks <note>Mullein leaves were historically dried and used as wicks for oil lamps</note>.

If the roots of both types are boiled, a drink of the liquid with wine binds a flux of the belly <note>treats diarrhea</note>. Indeed, a decoction of it, when drunk, removes the pain of bruising and side pain <note>pleurisy</note>, and it mitigates a cough. Applied as a gargle, it checks the pain of teeth. The mullein that has golden flowers dyes the hair. Its leaves, boiled in water and applied as a poultice, are useful for [painful joints] <note>original: *dunti asolusi*, likely a corruption of *dentibus* or *articulis*</note>.

With honey and wine added, it brings healing to eye swellings and malignant wounds. Mixed with vinegar <note>original: *Adiouero*, likely *aceto*</note>, it is a singular protection for fresh wounds. It soothes the sting of a scorpion. The leaves of the wild mullein help with burns. The leaves of the one called "female," when used with vinegar, do not allow rot <note>infection or gangrene</note> to take hold.

From a single root, it divides into many long and thick roots which are woolly to the taste; when these have been dried, they turn black and hard, much like horns. It grows frequently in Messenia. The root itself, when boiled and drunk, heals and treats pleurisy <note>an inflammation of the lungs</note>. It stops those who are spitting up blood and, with the addition of honey, it soothes the roughness of the throat <note>original: *arteriarum*, referring here to the windpipe and throat</note> if taken as an electuary <note>a medicinal paste or syrup</note>. 102.

### CONCERNING ARCTION.
Arction <note>likely Woolly Burdock, *Arctium tomentosum*</note>, also called *asturon* or *staphyle*, has leaves similar to mullein but they are rounded and rougher. The root is soft, white, and sweet. The stalk is long and soft. The seed is similar to the smaller bean <note>original: *cuanno*, a corruption of the Greek *kyamos*</note>. The root and its seed, when boiled in wine and used as a gargle, ease the pain of teeth. When applied as a warm compress, it helps with burns and chilblains <note>painful inflammation of small blood vessels in the skin in response to cold</note>. Boiled in wine and consumed, they heal and treat dysentery. 103.

### CONCERNING ARCTION <insert>Another kind</insert>.
They also call this *prosopis* or *prosopium*. It has leaves similar to the garden gourd <note>the calabash</note> but they are harder, larger, darker, and rougher. The stalk is larger, as are the leaves. The root is larger and white. If drunk with the kernel of a... <note>original: *semoprotas*, an unclear term possibly referring to a specific dose or a corruption of the Greek *hemitritaios*, a type of fever</note> it is a singular protection. It also eases pain in the joints, and the leaves themselves treat old wounds. 104.

### CONCERNING PETASITIS
Petasitis <note>Butterbur, named for the Greek *petasos*, a wide-brimmed sun hat, due to its large leaves</note> has a stalk longer than a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> and the thickness of a finger, upon which it has very large and broad leaves. It works for phagedenic <note>spreading or "devouring" ulcers</note>, malignant, and old wounds when applied as a poultice. 105.

Epaptis <note>also known as *epipactis* or *elleborine*</note> is a herb having one or two pods.

### 106. CONCERNING FUMITORY
Fumitory <note>Latin: *Capnos*</note> grows among the barley; it is a fruitful herb similar to coriander, but soft, white, and tender. It has many flowers, which are numerous and purple. Its juice is sticky. It clears the darkness of the eyes <note>dimness of vision</note> and provokes tears, which is how it received its name <note>The Greek *kapnos* means smoke; the plant was said to make eyes water like smoke</note>. When mixed with what they call gum and applied to the hairs of the eyelids, it does not allow them to grow back. The herb itself, when eaten, provokes much bile <note>original: *colera*</note> through the urine.

### 107. CONCERNING WILD LOTUS
The Lotus that grows in orchards, which the common people <note>original: *ula*, likely *vulgus*</note> call trefoil <note>original: *trifolium*</note>. Its juice mixed with honey heals wounds of the eyes and clears away darkness.

### 108. CONCERNING WILD 
### LOTUS
Wild lotus grows mostly in Libya. It has a stalk <note>original: *hasta*, literally "spear"</note> two cubits long and a little more. It has many small branches and leaves similar to trefoil which grows among fodder. It has seeds smaller than fenugreek and a poisonous taste. Its power is styptic <note>original: *emtermastica*, likely a corruption of *epismastica* or *stiptica*, meaning it shrinks or constricts tissue</note> and it cleanses dark bruises; it also cleanses spots and blemishes when honey is added. When drunk, or dissolved with mallow seed and sweet wine, it mitigates the pains of the bladder.

### 109. CONCERNING CYTISUS
Cytisus <note>Latin: *Quinissos*, a corruption of the Greek *kytisos*</note> is a white shrub having branches longer than a cubit. On these are leaves similar to fenugreek or the trefoil lotus, but smaller, and good in the middle. When rubbed between the fingers, they smell like a small jar <note>original: *urcellum*, perhaps referring to the scent of a specific oil jar or resin</note>, similar to green maple in its quality. The leaves themselves are astringent for inflammations <note>original: *inforeaca*, likely *erysipelas* or skin heat</note> at the beginning of abscesses <note>original: *apostomatu*</note> when ground with bread.

### 110. CONCERNING THE EGYPTIAN LOTUS

The Lotus that grows in Egypt is found in the fields when the Nile floods. It has a stalk <note>original: *hastico*</note> similar to cumin <note>this may refer to the Egyptian Bean or Colocasia</note> with a white flower, and is smaller, like barley. They say it spreads itself at the rising of the sun and hides itself in the water at the setting of the sun. It has a small head similar to a poppy <note>Latin: *meconio*</note> but larger, in which is a seed like a chickpea <note>original: *cenero*, likely *cicere*</note>. When the seed is dried, the Egyptians mix it with salt and bread. Its root is like a quince <note>Latin: *mele quidoniae*</note>. It is eaten both raw and cooked; when cooked, it is like the yolk of an egg.

### 111. CONCERNING MILFOIL

Milfoil <note>Latin: *Mirio fillo*, from the Greek for "thousand-leaf"</note> has a soft stalk. It has many leaves, smaller than a line, similar to tamarisk <note>original: *mararum*, likely *myricae*</note>, from which it received its name. It grows near the margins of ditches and in watery places. Applied to wounds, it keeps them from swelling, especially when used with vinegar, whether green <note>fresh</note> or dried.

### 112. CONCERNING MYRRHIS

Myrrhis, also called *mirra*, has leaves and stalks similar to hemlock <note>original: *conisẽ*, likely *conio*</note>. The root is oblong, soft, and fragrant. Drunk with wine, it helps against the bites of venomous spiders <note>original: *palonzione*, a corruption of *phalangiorum*</note> and regulates menstruation. It aids fertility <note>or helps expel the afterbirth</note>. Cooked in water and given, it corrects dropsy <note>original: *ascit*, likely *ascitem*</note>. Many have proven that if anyone drinks it three times a day, they are protected from every disease.

### 113. CONCERNING MYAGRUM

Myagrum <note>Latin: *Miacron*</note>, also called *mellan*, is a plant full of seeds, two cubits <note>about 36 inches</note> long. It has leaves similar to rocket <note>Latin: *eruca*</note>...

When this herb is green, it is roasted, pounded, and bound in strips; it is also used as a wick for a mule <note>original: *procandela mulae*; this may refer to a veterinary suppository or a literal torch-like application</note>. Its juice soothes all roughness of the body.

### 113. CONCERNING ONAGRA

Onagra, also called *onotrant* or *onotrum* <note>names derived from the Greek for "wild-ass catcher"</note>, is a shrubby plant. It has large leaves similar to those of an almond tree, and even larger flowers, as clear as a lily. Its root is small and white, and when dried, it has the fragrance of wine. It grows in mountainous places. Its power is so great that water in which it has been infused will make all wild beasts tame if they drink it. Applied as a poultice <note>Latin: *catieplasmi*</note>, it treats venomous bites.

### 115. CONCERNING CIRSION

Cirsion <note>Latin: *Crision*; likely a species of thistle</note> is a soft, long rod, two cubits in length, triangular in shape, and thorny. Around it are leaves similar to bugloss <note>Oxtongue</note>, but rougher, smaller, somewhat white, and thorny. The rod has a round, rough head, upon which is a reddish-purple flower-top. In these flowers, things like gray hairs <note>referring to the downy seeds of a thistle</note> appear. Many claim that if anyone pricks <note>original: *stitizauerit*</note> this herb in the place where it grows, it will take away all the pain from whatever part of the body it is bound to.

### 116. CONCERNING STARWORT

Starwort <note>Latin: *Aster actico*</note>, also called *bubonion* <note>named for its use in treating "buboes" or swellings in the groin</note>, is a woody rod which has a flower with a thousand petals, similar to chamomile <note>Latin: *antemis*</note>. When the flower head is split, the leaves appear like spears, but the leaves at the root are oblong and rough. Applied to the stomach, it aids digestion <note>original: *estirationem*</note>, and it subdues tumors of the testicles <note>Latin: *loculorum*</note> and the groin when applied as a bound bundle.

## 117. CONCERNING CACHRYS

Cachrys <note>Latin: *Cocton* or *Cacton*; likely *Cachrys libanotis*</note> is called "the seeker of fate" <note>Latin: *fatipetul*</note> by the seers. It has leaves above it like those of a tendril or a gourd, or like a vine above its small head. Its seeds are similar to <term>black cumin</term> <note>Latin: *melanaon*, a corruption of *melanthion*</note>. In taste, the leaves are similar to dill. The seed is drunk with <term>mead</term> <note>Latin: *mulsa*; honeyed water</note>; for the sake of the chest, it settles and mitigates a cough, and it treats those <term>spitting blood</term> <note>original: *emoptoicos*</note>.

## 118. CONCERNING THE VIOLET

The Violet <note>Latin: *Ion*</note> has leaves smaller and darker than ivy, and they have a "heart" shape. It has a stalk in the middle upon which are little heads, and it grows with a fragrant and purple flower in shady and rough places. Its power lies in the dried leaves alone, or mixed as a powder in a <term>poultice</term> <note>Latin: *cataplasma*</note>; it may soothe a <term>discharge</term> <note>original: *fuzactione*, likely *fluxione*</note> and swelling of the eyes. It also restores a prolapsed anus, and it treats <term>epileptics</term> among infants.

## 119. CONCERNING CANCOLION

Cancolion, or <term>Lion's Leaf</term> <note>Latin: *leontice*</note>, has larger leaves and a white stalk. It has a flower similar to moss <note>Latin: *brio*</note> or an olive. It grows in mountainous places. Its root, when infused like <term>tragacanth</term> <note>a medicinal gum</note> and taken by mouth as an <term>electuary</term> <note>a medicinal paste made with honey</note>, checks a cough and mitigates the roughness of the <term>windpipe</term> <note>original: *arariarum*, likely *arteriarum*</note>. The seed that grows after the flower, when ground and mixed with wax and smeared on, prevents chills. It also treats wrinkles and <term>inflammation of the throat and uvula</term> <note>original: *uula brencha*</note>.

## 120. CONCERNING EARTH-NUT

Earth-nut <note>Latin: *Bunion*</note>, which they also call *accon*, has a stalk that is square and long.

## 121. CONCERNING FALSE EARTH-NUT

False Earth-nut <note>original: *Pseudo bunion*</note> is a shrub. It grows to the height of two <term>palms</term> <note>a measurement of roughly 3 to 4 inches</note> in chalky soil. It has leaves similar to the Earth-nut plant. It has three or four stalks <note>original: *hastae*, literally "spears"</note>. When drunk with water, it helps with <term>griping pains</term> <note>original: *tortionibus*</note>, the spitting of blood, and pains in the side. For <term>scrofula</term> <note>swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck</note>, it is applied warm like a <term>poultice</term> <note>a soft, moist mass of herbs applied to the skin</note> with a little salt and wine added. 122.

## 122. GROUND IVY

Ground Ivy <note>original: *Camecissos*</note> has leaves similar to heather <note>original: *ericae*</note>, but they are oblong and tender. It has many twigs of two palms in length, with five or six leaves on a single twig. It flowers with white <note>original: *canos*</note> and smaller blossoms. It is very bitter in taste and has thin, weak roots. It grows in wooded places. The leaves themselves, taken in the weight of a <term>triobol</term> <note>an ancient Greek weight, approximately 1.5 grams</note> with water for two or three drinks over eleven days, provide relief for the side. It also cures <term>sciatica</term> <note>pain affecting the back, hip, and outer side of the leg</note> when drunk for six or seven days.

## 123. CONCERNING BUGLOSS

Bugloss <note>original: *Buglossos*; literally "ox-tongue"</note> has leaves similar to mullein <note>original: *flommo*</note> spread out upon the ground, but they are rougher, darker, and smaller. If these are mixed with wine, they bring <term>merriment</term> <note>original: *letitiam*</note> to the guests at a banquet. It is similar to <term>coltsfoot</term> <note>original: *cameleucen*</note>, but it provides more singular help for those with <term>sciatica</term> when drunk in water. 124.

## 125. ON HORSE-TONGUE

**Horse-tongue** <note>original: *Ippoglosson*, from the Greek *hippoglosson*</note> is a shrub similar to wild myrtle. It has tiny leaves and a prickly tuft shaped like a tongue. Small branches are displayed around the leaves. When bound with many threads <note>original: *colo*, perhaps referring to a headband or fillet</note>, it removes a headache. It is also mixed into necessary <term>emollients</term> <note>original: *malacmatibus*, softening ointments used to reduce swelling</note>. 125.

## 126. ON SNAPDRAGON

**Snapdragon** <note>original: *Antiripon*, likely *Antirrhinum*</note> or *anaron*, which many have called "wild lychnis" <note>original: *lignida agreste*</note>. It is a herb with leaves similar to pimpernel <note>original: *apagallidi*, likely *anagallidis*</note> and stalks bearing tiny flowers of saffron-yellow or purple. For this reason, it is called "wild lychnis." Its seed is said to be quite similar to that of St. John's Wort <note>original: *coridi*, referring to the plant *Coris*</note>. <gloss>that is, by its description</gloss> When taken internally, it counteracts poisons, especially when mixed with oil and used as an ointment. 126.

## 127. ON CUPID’S DART

**Cupid's Dart** <note>original: *Catainance*, from the Greek *katananke*, meaning "compulsion"</note> has tiny leaves similar to coriander or <term>buckshorn plantain</term> <note>original: *coronopici*</note>. It has thin roots like a rush, with six or seven heads in which the seed is found. Like the herb <gloss>so</gloss>, when you dry it, the stems bend toward <insert>the</insert> earth; it is similar to claws. When taken <gloss>it is</gloss>... there is another kind of *Catanance* like "maluma diatia" <note>An unidentified plant name, likely a corruption of a Greek term</note> which has a similar but smaller root. It has long leaves like those of the olive tree, but softer. The seed is tiny and pitted like that of a maple, and reddish. Both varieties are used to create love-charms, which the women in Thessaly <note>A region in Greece famous in antiquity for witchcraft and herbalism</note> use most of all. 127.

### 131. ON TRICHOMANES

Many call **Trichomanes** <note>original: *Tricomades*, likely referring to *Asplenium trichomanes* or Maidenhair Spleenwort</note> a variety of Maidenhair. It grows in similar places and has similar leaves, though they are quite small and grow in clusters <note>original: *colonia*</note>. They are full on both sides, just like coriander, being small and resembling little teeth. Its tender tips turn black, and this plant is known to perform all the same medicinal functions as the aforementioned Maidenhair.

### 132. ON SANCTION

**Sanction**, also called *sarganion* or *philanthropon* <note>original: *quira doletrõ*, a corruption of the Greek *philanthropon*, meaning "friend of man"—so named because the plant's burrs cling to clothing</note>, which is commonly known as **Aparine** <term>Cleavers</term>, grows in shady places and near standing water. It has stalks like a spear that are angular and thick, upon which are smaller spear-like branches and many leaves similar to those of *androsace* <note>a coastal plant often mentioned in classical herbals</note>. At the top, it is spread out, having the scent of watercress <note>original: *cardami*</note>. Its seed is round like an olive or a berry, and the plant is so rough that one might fear to brush against it. Its seed, if collected before it is dry and stored in a thin vessel to be rubbed on the head, makes the hair red, especially when mixed with water and lye <note>original: *lino*, likely a transcription error for *lixivio*</note> with one bunch of grapes added. It is stored and used later. When applied as a plaster <note>original: *catteptr*, likely for *cataplasma*</note>, it disperses tumors.

### 133. ON AEGILOPS

**Aegilops** <note>Greek for "goat's eye," likely referring to wild oats or a grass used for eye ailments</note> is a herb. It has leaves similar to wheat, but they are soft. At the top is a small head in which two or three blunt seeds grow; this is also where the flower is. When dried and mixed with white wool <note>original: *capillo albo*, literally "white hair," but often referring to unwashed wool or the plant's own downy fibers</note> and resin, it treats all tumors...

## On Glis

**Glis** <note>likely *Glaux maritima*, or Sea Milkwort</note>, also called *quias*, has leaves similar to lentils <note>original: *lenacula*, likely *lenticula*</note>. Its flowers are white like a rose, while its upper parts are green. Its stalks are five or six in number, measuring three and two palms <term>a palm is about 3 inches</term> long, and it spreads along the ground. It has a golden or purple flower. Rosemary <note>original: *los marinus marcens*, likely *ros marinus*</note> cooked with barley meal, salt, and oil, when taken like a juice, promotes milk production in women. **135**

## On Poligaion

**Poligaion** <note>original: *Polygala*, or Milkwort</note> has a stalk two palms long and leaves similar to lentils, with a sharp taste like a turnip <note>original: *rapaco*</note>. When drunk, this also causes women to produce milk.

## 136. On Osiris

**Osiris** <note>likely *Osyris alba*, or Poets' Cassia</note> has thin, dark, flexible branches <note>original: *fermentosa*, likely meaning supple or "yeasty" in texture</note> that are not very fragile. Around these, it has leaves like flax, which are black at first and become red when they have ripened. This herb, boiled in water and drunk, helps those suffering from jaundice <term>ictericos</term>. **137**

## On Herchinos

**Herchinos** <note>possibly *Erinos* or *Echinos*</note> grows in rivers and in steep places <note>original: *arcaputea*, likely a corruption of a term for rocky or clayey ground</note>. It has oblong leaves similar to basil <note>original: *oamo*, likely *ocimo*</note>, which are divided at the top. It has five or six stalks, two palms long. They have a white flower and a black seed that is small and hard. The juice of its leaves is very full; its seed, mixed with this, is used as an ointment to check the dimness of the eyes <note>original: *caliginis oculorum*</note> and running sores. Its juice, poured into the ears, mitigates earache, especially when mixed with pomegranate juice <note>original: *frontis ro*, likely *rhoa*</note> and sulfur. **138**

## 139. On Smila Celeni

**Smila celeni** <note>original: *Smila celeni*, likely referring to *Smilax* or Black Bryony</note> has leaves similar to ivy <note>original: *edere*</note> but they are soft and tender; the shoots themselves are thinner and do not have thorns. It has many white flowers that grow close together, <unclear>sreb;</unclear> entwining themselves. The seeds are similar to lupins but smaller, and it has white flowers on individual branches which are round and hard. In the summer these flowers fall, and in autumn the fruit is produced. Its seed, when drunk with wine in the amount of one **triobol** <term>an ancient Greek unit of weight, about 1.5 grams</term>, induces bad dreams <note>original: *ambrosomnia*, possibly a corruption of *insomnia* or *insomnia mala*</note> or visions <note>original: *fantasma*</note>.

## 140. On Wild Myrtle

**Wild Myrtle** <note>original: *Mirta agrestis*, likely Butcher's Broom (*Ruscus aculeatus*)</note>, or *ot*, is similar to flax, also called *mirta canta*, *caciana*, *anion*, *licena*, or *cane mirtuon*. The Boeotians <note>an ancient Greek people</note> called it **zoraam**. Its leaves are similar to myrtle; at the ends, it has seeds that are round, wide, sharp, and red when they have ripened. Inside, the seeds have something like small bones. It has many branches growing from a single, very thick root. It has a taste like a turnip <note>original: *sapaco*, likely *rapaco*</note> in its potency. Its leaves and seeds, when drunk, provoke urine. It regulates menstruation and breaks stones in the bladder. It also treats jaundice <term>hicticos</term> and fevers...

## 141. ON ALEXANDRIA LAUREL
**Dafnis**—which some call Alexandria laurel, or Idaean, or Danaean, or *antipoglosson* <note>original: "under-tongue," referring to the small leaf-like structures</note>, or *zalion*, or <gloss>fasteni</gloss>—has leaves similar to *oximina* <note>Butcher's Broom</note> but larger. It bears blood-red seeds in the middle of the leaves. Like the maple, it has twigs two palms <term>about 6–8 inches</term> long or longer. The root is similar to that of the larger myrtle, fragrant and soft. It grows in mountainous places. By its medicinal power, two [measures] of its root drunk with sweet wine assists women in labor. It also treats strangury <term>painful or difficult urination</term> and removes blood through the urine.

## 142. ON SPURGE LAUREL
**Dafnoidis**, also called *petalios* or *camedafne* <note>ground laurel</note>, has twigs a cubit <term>about 18 inches</term> in length. It has many twigs and is not fragile; in the upper half, the bark of the twigs is mucilaginous. It has leaves similar to the laurel, but softer, tougher, and less brittle. They are hot to the taste and sharp <note>original: *guilcipra*, likely a corruption of *gustu acria*</note>, causing a burning sensation. It has white flowers and black seeds. When the fruit ripens, the root also increases in strength. It grows in mountainous places. Its leaves, whether dried or green, when drunk, purge phlegm from the belly and induce vomiting. It regulates menstruation. When chewed, it serves as an *apofleumatismus* <term>a remedy to draw out phlegm from the head</term>. It also provokes sneezing. Ten grains of the seed, when drunk, soften the belly <note>act as a laxative</note>.

<margin>ON GROUND LAUREL</margin>
**Ground Laurel** <note>original: *Camedafne*</note>, which some call *mula* and others Alexandria laurel, has branches two cubits <term>about 3 feet</term> long, which are thin, upright, and smooth. Its leaves are similar to the laurel but thinner and greener. It bears a reddish seed in the middle of the leaves. Its leaves, when applied as a poultice <note>original: *catapta*</note>, remove headaches. It settles sharp pains of the stomach and, when drunk with wine, treats griping pains <note>original: *tortionib.*, referring to intestinal cramps</note>. Its juice, drunk with wine, regulates menstruation and provokes urine; it performs all these same functions when used as a pessary <term>a medicinal substance inserted vaginally</term>.

### 143. ON HELLEBORE

**White Hellebore** <note>original: *Elleboro albo*; likely *Veratrum album*, a highly toxic plant</note> has leaves similar to ribwort plantain <note>original: *arnoglossae*</note> or wild beet, but they are shorter, darker, and slightly blunt at the tips. It has stems two palms <term>about 6–8 inches</term> long, which are hairy and entirely prone to wilting in the sun when they begin to dry. Many hair-like roots proceed from a single main root, much like the plant of Apuleius <note>a reference to the *Herbarium* of Pseudo-Apuleius</note>. It grows in mountainous places. The root ought to be dug up at harvest time. The most useful variety is that which is white, thin, brittle, solid, sharp to the taste, and hooked. When you break it, it releases a sort of dust like smoke. It should be given by order of a physician in a warm liquid; it does not greatly provoke saliva, but if a person takes too much, it causes suffocation. The best varieties are those grown in Galatia <note>modern-day Turkey</note>, Italy, and Cappadocia; these are whiter. It purges phlegm and every humor by inducing vomiting. It is famously mixed into eye-salves <note>original: *colliriis*</note> to clear away dimness of the eyes. Used as a suppository, it causes abortion and kills the infant in the womb. It provokes sneezing <gloss>sneezes</gloss>. It is mixed with *polemo* <note>likely pearl-barley or polenta</note> and honey; Homer <note>Homer's works often mention powerful drugs, though the specific reference here is unclear</note> denies... it is boiled with meat.

## ON THE LARGE SESAME-LIKE PLANT

Some of the ancients called this hellebore because it is mixed with white hellebore for purging, and it is similar to it. Its leaves are also similar to *eterontes* <note>possibly a corruption of *erigeron* or groundsel</note>; it has small white flowers and a thin root. The seed is similar to sesame but with a bitter taste. It purges bile and phlegm through vomiting. Therefore, if one fills three fingers <term>a three-finger pinch</term> and takes it with white hellebore—specifically, one and a half obols <term>an ancient Greek unit of weight</term>—with honeyed water, it can perform all the aforementioned functions. 146

## ON THE WILD CUCUMBER

The seed of the wild cucumber <note>original: *Cocumeris agrestis*; likely *Ecballium elaterium*, known for its explosive seed pods</note> is similar to these, but a little larger; it has leaves like the long cucumber and its stalks are similar to them. Its root is thick and white. It grows in fields and in deserted and sandy places.

### 147 ON ELATERIUM

Elaterium <note>original: *elateria*; a powerful purgative</note> is the juice of the wild cucumber. It is not made from the leaves or the root; rather, the ripe fruits must be chosen so that they can release their moisture when pricked. The gathered cucumbers should be left for one night. After this, they are passed through a sieve into a vessel <insert>and as written above, you place it and prick each with a needle and do not press them before you draw it out <unclear>axi</unclear> <unclear>xi</unclear></insert>. If you wish to make a second-grade elaterium, it is strained again with mixed water and the juice is dried in the sun. Soon, that secondary moisture itself must be dried, so that the necessary part remains; it is then put into a mortar to be dried, from which troches <gloss>lozenges or medicinal tablets</gloss> are made, and they acquire a strength similar to that mentioned above. Some, however, prefer to strain the liquid itself three times and leave it in the sun, collecting the first sediment. <margin>some things were passed over and should be omitted</margin>

Instead of fresh water, they add sea water to the honey-water <note>original: *mulsi*; a mixture of water and honey</note>, and when it has dried out, the honey-water is added again and it is washed; then they dry it again and in this way they make lozenges <term>original: *trociscos*; small, round medicinal tablets</term>. This is the useful kind; however, that which is not smooth, but is rough and of an unserviceable color—appearing as if decayed <note>original: *canteroso*; likely a corruption of *carioso*, meaning decayed or rotten</note> and heavy—is useless. This Elaterium is useful for purging the belly. If the primary juice is well-prepared, it can last for ten years. If by chance you wish the vomiting to occur more easily, you may add some hellebore <note>original: *uirino*; likely a scribal error for *ueratro* (white hellebore), a common emetic</note> and set it in place. Once the bowels <note>original: *ancillis*; likely a scribal error for *anellis*, referring to the rectal/anal area or the lower intestines</note> have been purged of their contents, the patients should be allowed to sleep. But if, after the vomiting is provoked, they vomit too much, they must be sprinkled with cold water; you shall give them barley-meal <term>original: *palenta*</term>, vinegar-water <term>original: *pusca*; also known as posca</term>, Matian apples <term>original: *mala matiana*; a famous variety of firm, tart apples from Rome</term>, and all things that have the power to bind the bowels. 

Taken as a suppository, it brings on the menses and causes abortion. Mixed with milk and applied to the nostrils, it is a singular protection for those with jaundice <term>original: *ictericis*</term>. It mitigates long-standing headache. Rubbed on those suffering from delirium <term>original: *freneticis*; refers to "phrenitis," an acute fever with delirium</term>, it provides the greatest effect, especially when oil or honey is added.

### CXLVIII CONCERNING STAVESACRE

Stavesacre <term>original: *Stafisagria*; a species of Larkspur used in ancient medicine to treat parasites</term> has leaves like the wild vine, and the divided herb has long, black [stems]. It has seeds similar to [lentils] and a flower. These seeds are contained in pods that are somewhat hard <note>original: *surdiorib*; likely meaning thick-shelled or muffled</note> and three-angled. The plant is black, though it produces a fruit of a white color, and its taste is pungent and burning <note>original: *uisado et calido*</note>. 

Fifteen of its grains taken with honey-water expel thick phlegm <note>original: *fleuma pingui*</note> through vomiting. However, those who take it should drink honey-water continuously and walk about, because otherwise it may cause choking. When ground and applied, it is said to destroy lice <note>original: *peduclor*; a corruption of the Latin for lice, *pediculorum*</note>, and if taken, it removes scabs and itches. If boiled and held in the mouth, it is known to perform all the aforementioned tasks; it checks the discharge of the gums and disperses swellings of the throat. It is also mixed into warm salves <term>original: *malacumatibus*; softening ointments or poultices</term>.

### CXLVIIII CONCERNING THAPSIA

Thapsia <term>original: *Tapsia*; likely *Thapsia garganica*, known as the "deadly carrot"</term> is so named because it was first found on the island of Thapsos. It is a shrub similar to giant fennel <note>original: *ferule*</note>. Its leaves are like fennel <note>original: *maratro*</note> and it has thin stalks upon which are small heads, just as in dill, with a honey-colored flower. The seed is broad and similar to giant fennel, but smaller. Its root is white and large with a thick rind and a pungent, scentless quality. 

To extract the juice, the earth is dug away to expose the root; you then hollow it out in one place and pierce it with an iron tool so that when the moisture is released, the "tear" <note>original: *lacrimum*; the medicinal resin or sap</note> collects in that hollowed-out spot. You must then collect this the following day.

It cures old pains in the side or inflammations <note>original: *fleumonit*, likely a corruption of *phlegmone*</note>; it brings the greatest relief to those suffering from arthritis and gout <note>original: *podagrias*</note> when applied as a compress with old oil <note>original: *ueteri nudi*; likely a corruption of *ueteri oleo* (old oil) or *ueteri uino* (old wine)</note>, and it achieves this when the poultice is applied.

### 151. ON SPANISH BROOM

Spanish Broom <note>original: *Spartu* (Spartium junceum)</note> is a shrub known to all. Its seed is produced in pods like a bean. The seed is tiny, like a lentil. It has a yellow flower <note>original: *millino*, referring to the color of millet or quince</note> like a white violet <note>original: *leucum*</note>. An obol <term>original: *obolum*; a small unit of weight</term> of its seed and flower, when drunk with honey-water <note>original: *mulsa*</note>, purges humors by vomiting. It purges the belly with some straining, much like hellebore <note>a potent and dangerous purgative often used in antiquity</note>, but without the harmful effects. Taken similarly, the branches <gloss>rods</gloss> are infused in water, beaten, and dried to be stored and used as a remedy. One cyathus <term>original: *quiatis*; a small liquid measure, about 45ml</term> is drunk thinly. Also, they truly soak the broom itself in seawater and place it beneath <gloss>as a suppository</gloss> to provoke the flow of blood <note>referring to the menstrual cycle</note>.

### 153. ON THE EMETIC BULB

The emetic bulb <note>original: *Bulbum erepsicum*, a corruption of *Bulbus emeticus*</note>, which they call *nautalem*, has hard leaves similar to our common bulb. It is a shrubby plant; the bulb is black and has a pungent bite <note>original: *quico morsum*</note>. A decoction made from it induces nausea.

### 155. ON HIPPOPHAES

Hippophaes <note>original: *Ippofaes* or *ippe fees*; likely Sea Buckthorn (*Hippophae rhamnoides*), known for its medicinal berries</note>, which produces clear substances in the East, grows in maritime and sandy places. It is a spreading shrub with thin twigs and leaves like those of an olive tree, but narrower, softer, and sharp like the hawthorn <term>original: *oxiacantha*; a thorny plant often identified as the barberry or hawthorn</term>. They are whiter and angular, and the twigs bear what look like small grape-clusters <note>original: *uina*; likely a corruption of the Latin *uuae*, meaning grapes or berries</note> cast upon them; the flowers are similar to ivy. They have seeds like hanging berries <note>original: *acina*</note>, but they are soft, whitish, and possess sufficient color. Its root is thick, soft, and full of juice with a bitter taste. The juice is extracted from it just like that of the *thapsia* <note>original: *tiepfia*; a medicinal plant used as a powerful purgative</note>.

Its collected juice is stored. Especially when combined with the powder <note>original: *pollinē*</note> of the herb, it is dried in the shade and stored. When the juice itself is taken, it purges bile <note>original: *colora*; referring to yellow bile, one of the four humors</note> and phlegm <note>original: *fleuma*</note>; by loosening the bowels, it carries away many humors <note>referring to the bodily fluids that medieval medicine sought to balance</note>. It is most effective when mixed with the powder of the herb. The shrub itself, along with its leaves and roots, is dried with honey and taken with honey-water <term>original: *mulsio*; a beverage made of honey and water</term>... <note>the text here contains some corrupted phrasing: *coalicā una diuerdi raplinas*</note>.

## 157. ON CIAS

CIAS <note>likely the Castor oil plant, *Ricinus communis*, often called *Kiki* in Greek</note>, which many have said is either wild sesame, *seliapmon*, or *crotonia*. It is a shrub similar to elderberry <note>original: *Sembabcx*, likely a corruption of *sambucus*</note>. It has a white flower like that of the fig tree but smaller; it has leaves similar to the plane tree but larger, thinner, and darker. It is similar to *thapsia*, cypress, and the laurel reed. The seed is bitter in composition, but for purging it is truly effective. The *crotonia* [castor bean] is valued, from which an oil is expressed called *cicinum* <note>original: *cianu*</note>, which is useful for medicines and plasters. <gloss>from where</gloss> if thirty grains are cleaned and taken, it moves the bowels and provokes vomiting, though the taste is not good. This purgative harms the stomach. Dried, ground, and applied, it clears away spots. The leaves, ground with pearl barley <term>original: *palenta*; a flour made from toasted barley</term>, clear away tumors of the eyes, soothe all hardnesses and tumors of the breasts, and extinguish "sacred fire" <note>original: *igne agrum*, referring to *ignis sacer*, a painful, red skin infection like erysipelas</note> when applied alone or mixed with vinegar.

### CLVIII ON SESAMOIDES

Sesamoides <note>likely *Reseda luteola* or *Daphne gnidium*</note> has white stalks <gloss>hastas</gloss> two palms long, and has leaves similar to buck's-horn plantain <term>coronopodo; *Plantago coronopus*, a medicinal herb</term> but rougher and smaller. On these stalks are tiny heads; it has purple flowers in which there is a seed like white sesame. Below is a thin, reddish root which, when taken, clears bile <gloss>colera</gloss> and phlegm from the belly. Its seed, drunk in one acetabulum <term>oxifabo; a small Roman unit of volume, about 68ml</term> with honey-water <term>mulsa; a mixture of honey and water or wine</term> and used in a poultice, dries the spleen; it similarly dissolves pustules and softens hard growths. It grows in rough places.

### CLX ON TITHYMALUS

There are seven types of Tithymalus <note>Spurge; plants of the genus *Euphorbia* known for their milky sap</note>. One of these is the male, called *characias* <note>original: *caratias*</note>. It is also called *amygdalites* <note>original: *Amizdalites*</note>, or *cometes* <note>original: *comites*</note>, or *comaraphe* <note>original: *comorap*</note>. Another, the female, is called *myrsinites* <note>original: *mirsinitir*</note> or *charitides* <note>original: *caritides*</note>; in Parnassus they call it *fove*... <note>The text here is corrupted: *fouere mulaton malida* likely refers to regional folk names</note>. There is another named *helioscopius* <note>original: *elioscopus*</note>, and *cyparissias* <note>original: *quiparissas*</note>, and *dendroides* <note>original: *dendroides*</note>, and *platyphyllos* <note>original: *platifillos*</note>. The one called *characias* <note>original: *coratias*</note> has long stalks one cubit high, which are reddish and produce a green sap <gloss>lacrimo; literally "tears"</gloss>.

...white and thick. They are found full of "tears" <term>lacrimum; the milky latex or sap</term> in certain places. It is a large shrub. ### **CHAPTER 162: ON THE CAPER-SPURGE**

The **caper-spurge** <term>Lateris; referring to *Euphorbia lathyris*</term>: some also consider this to be a variety of spurge <note>original: *lacteridam*</note>. It has a stalk a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note> long, and it is the thickness of a finger. It has a small round head. The leaves on the stalk are oblong like those of an **almond** <note>original: *amizdale*</note>, but they are longer, harder, and more densely packed. At the top of the stalk, it has seeds that are oblong, like those of **birthwort** <term>aristologa</term> or **ivy** <term>edera</term>. At the tip of its branch, it is round like a **caper** <term>cappari</term>, with heads that are distinct from one another. The seeds are black on the outside and white on the inside, and the taste is sweet. Its root is thin and annual. Indeed, the entire shrub is full of "tears" and sap. Like the **ground-pine** <note>original: *camellot*, likely referring to the *chamaeleon* plant or *chamaepitys*</note> in its power, if seven or eight grains are taken as eaten **pills** <term>catapodia</term> and followed with warm water, it purges phlegm and bile. The sap, prepared like that of the *chamaeleon*, can do all the things mentioned above. Its leaves, taken with chicken or in a broth, loosen the belly.

# CHAPTER 164: ON THE SEA-SPURGE

**Peplos**—also called wild **purslane** <note>original: *andrachne agrestis*</note>, or called **peplion** by Hippocrates—certainly grows in maritime places. It is a shrub full of white sap, having leaves similar to wild purslane and rounded, which are curved downwards. Its seed is round, growing under the leaves themselves just like the standard **peplus** <note>Petty-spurge</note>. The root is thin and weak. When the shrub is collected, it is stored just like the *peplus*; its medicinal power is similar to that of the *peplus*.

# CHAPTER 165: ON THE GROUND-FIG

**Chamaesyce** <note>literally "ground-fig"; original: *Camsice*</note>, or as they have called it until now, **Sycen**. It has long "fingers" <note>referring to the stems or branches</note> spread out upon the ground, full of milky sap. The leaves are small <note>original: *tenacula*</note> and similar to those of the **peplus**, but smaller and thinner. It has round seeds under the leaves, just like the **peplus**. It has no flower. The root is thin and weak. Its medicinal power is like that of a star <note>original: *aster illius*</note>; taken with wine or applied as a **pessary** <note>a medical plug</note>, it soothes pains of the womb. Applied as a poultice, it disperses tumors, removes **calluses** <note>original: *clauos*</note> from the body, and clears away **warts** <note>original: *mirmicias*</note>. When cooked and eaten, they loosen the bowels <note>original: *ventrem solvent*</note>; the sap itself can do this as well. It drives away **scorpions** <gloss>scorpions' stings</gloss>, clears away cataracts and dimness from the eyes, and cures scars in the eyes when honey is added. It grows in rough and rocky places.

### **168. ON ACANTHUS, THAT IS SAEBU** <note>original: *Acandidis se id saebu*; *Acandis* is a scribal corruption of *Acanthos*. "Saebu" is likely a local or vernacular name for the plant.</note>

There are two kinds of **Acanthus**. One is woody, having stalks that are <gloss>REEDY</gloss>, round, and upright. It has 3 or 5 leaves on the stalks, which are fringed <note>original: *fimbriatuas*; referring to the jagged, ornate edges of the Acanthus leaf famously used as a motif in Corinthian columns</note>, with an excellent <note>original: *regali*; literally "royal," perhaps implying a noble or strong scent</note> heavy scent, and are oblong. On these stalks are the flowers, which are themselves whitish. The seed is similar to a beet <note>original: *benzo*; likely a corruption of *beta*</note>, somewhat blackish and purple, arranged in the manner of a grape cluster and containing much juice. The second kind is called **Chamaelea** <note>literally "ground olive"; likely *Daphne oleoides*</note>, and is also called **Amul** and **Iosacti**. This one is shorter and more herbaceous, having stalks that are square and knotted. It has leaves at each knot similar to an almond, but veined and oblong, with a heavy odor. On these stalks are little heads similar to a squill <note>original: *scia*; likely *scilla*, the sea onion</note> in seed and flower.

<margin>117</margin>Its root is the thickness of a finger but long. Its power is cooling, <term>emetic</term> <note>original: *amexotic*; from the Greek *emetikos*, causing vomiting</note>, and <term>styptic</term> <note>original: *stapica*; a substance that stops bleeding</note>. Taken [as a drink], it draws out watery fluid from the belly <note>original: *orem aquosum*; likely *humorem aquosum*, referring to the treatment of dropsy or edema</note>. For a bad stomach: the leaves themselves, boiled and taken, soften the belly, especially drawing out bile. If they are boiled and eaten while they are still warm <note>original: *aestu se tenere*; "holding their heat"</note>, they can achieve all the aforementioned effects. The root itself boiled in wine is the greatest remedy for those with dropsy <note>original: *hydropicis*</note>. Applied to viper bites and also drunk, it soon dissolves the "hardness of the opening" <note>original: *duritias mox oris*; likely referring to the cervix of the womb</note>, and it will settle all the mentioned conditions of the womb.

<margin>ms</margin>Its seed with wine is known to achieve all the same effects. When smeared on with oil, it turns the hair black. Its leaves disperse tumors in the case of edema <note>original: *idia*; likely *oidemata*</note> when mixed with barley meal <note>original: *pallente*; likely *polenta*</note> and applied. Applied to burns, it provides a cure; it also heals dog bites. For wounds, it acts as a <term>paracolisin</term> <note>a Greek-derived term likely referring to a plaster or a treatment to prevent the "closing" or infection of a wound; original: *paracoli sin*</note> and leads the cavities of wounds to health. It is provided to those suffering from gout <note>original: *podagricis*</note> when applied with winter-fungus <note>original: *abfungia bruma*; "bruma" refers to the winter solstice, though the specific substance is unclear</note>.

### **170. ON POLYCNEMON** <note>original: *Policomo*; likely *Polycnemon*, a low-growing herb often compared to savory or rocket</note>

**Polycnemon** has leaves similar to rocket <note>original: *euzomo*; the Greek *euzomon*, or Arugula</note>, with a sticky taste. It has thick and square stalks, with a flower similar to a fingernail <note>original: *onice*; likely *onyx*, referring to the shape or the translucent, layered color of the petals</note>.

## ON APIUM
<note>While "Apium" usually means celery, the description here—particularly the mention of "asphodel" and its emetic use—indicates the author is likely describing the **Asphodel** (*Asphodelus*) or a related wild variety.</note>

They call it **Apium**, or *scada*, or *cameua lanu*, or wild radish, or *andiastam*. It has two types: those that are reedy and old, and those that are tender and reddish. It has leaves similar to rue, but they are long and green. The seed is found with a root similar to an **asphodel**, but it is round like a pear, full of juice, black on the outside and white on the inside. Two of its roots, when scraped and taken, cause vomiting and expel <term>choler</term> <note>Yellow bile, one of the four bodily humors associated with heat and aggression</note> and phlegm. The **iosana** root does the same. Indeed, all of these, when crushed and taken, are known to perform all these actions. Its juice is collected in this way: if you wash the roots and place them in water, you can then collect what floats on the surface with a feather. Dry it and store it. From this, you give three <term>half-measures</term> <note>original: *emiboxia*; likely a scribal corruption of a Greek measurement like *hemidrachma* (half-drachm) or *hemioxion*</note>; when taken, it purges the upper body through vomiting. **182**

## CLXXIII ON EPITHYMUM
<note>Epithymum is the Dodder of Thyme (*Cuscuta epithymum*), a parasitic plant that grows in thread-like strands over other herbs.</note>

It especially treats those suffering from **melancholy** <note>associated with an excess of "black bile"</note> by purging black bile. One <term>oxybaphon</term> <note>original: *oxifabus*; a Greek measure of capacity, roughly 68 milliliters or 1/8 of a pint</note> taken dissolves gas; all these things can be achieved with four [measures]. It grows abundantly in **Pamphylia** and **Cappadocia** <note>Ancient regions in what is now southern and central Turkey</note>.

## 175 ON EMPETRUM
<note>likely *Frankenia pulverulenta* (Sea-heath) or a similar salt-tolerant plant; the name literally means "on a rock"</note>

**Empetrum**, also called *saco* <note>possibly a corruption of *saxo*, "rock"</note>, grows in mountainous and maritime places. Its taste is salty and its root is bitter. When given in **mead** <note>original: *mulsa*; a mixture of honey and water</note> or in broth, it expels **bile**, **phlegm**, and watery fluids <note>original: *humores*; referring to the bodily fluids that were believed to cause illness when out of balance</note>.

## 176 ON CLEMATIS
<note>Likely *Clematis vitalba* (Old Man's Beard) or *Clematis cirrhosa*</note>

**Clematis** has reddish <note>original: *obrufa*</note> stalks and a foul odor; its leaves are sticky and have a salty taste. Its medicinal power is such that it binds itself to wounds from the surrounding areas <note>likely referring to its climbing nature or its use in poultices</note>, much like the **smilax** plant. Its seed, when drunk with mead or with tempered water, expels phlegm and bile. The leaves themselves, when applied, drive away **leprosy** <note>original: *lepras*; in this period, this often referred to any scaly or chronic skin disease rather than modern Hansen's disease</note>. The stalk itself is prepared and eaten with the leaves.

## 177 ON THE WILD VINE
<note>original: *Ampelos agria*; likely referring to Black Bryony (*Tamus communis*) or a similar wild climber</note>

The **wild vine** has long stalks similar to our cultivated grapevines. It is woody and rough, with leaves similar to [garden ivy] <note>original: *istorig-no hortino*; likely a corruption of *hederae hortensi*</note>, but broader and smaller. It has hair-like flowers and a seed cluster arranged like grapes; when the seeds ripen, they become reddish and round. Its root, boiled in water and drunk mixed with "maritime wine" <note>wine treated with sea water, used as a purgative</note> in the amount of two <term>cyathi</term> <note>original: *quiati*; a small cup measure, approximately 45 milliliters</note>, purges those with **dropsy** <note>original: *hydropicis*; an old term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid</note> and removes all spots from the body. Its **tendrils** <note>original: *caprioli*; the young, curling shoots of the vine</note> may also be preserved in salt.

## 178 ON THE WHITE VINE
<note>original: *Ampelos leuce* or *Bryonia alba*; known for its toxic but powerfully purgative root</note>

The **white vine**, also called **bryony**, or *osustasilon*, or *candron*, or *maletron*, or *filocron* <note>these are various Greek and regional synonyms for White Bryony</note>.

<summary>This page describes the physical characteristics and medicinal applications of Empetrum, Clematis, and the Wild Vine, primarily focusing on their ability to purge the body of excess phlegm, bile, and fluid.</summary>
