--- Page 302 ---
<meta>This page continues the botanical and medicinal survey from the previous page, moving from the description of Clematis into a detailed entry on the Wild Vine or White Bryony (Vitis alba). It focuses on the plant's dual nature as both a powerful healer for skin and internal ailments and a potentially dangerous substance that can cause mania or abortion.</meta>

...or the arts of the desert <insert>☩</insert> as a sign of the wild. This **wild vine** <note>original: *vitis alba*; White Bryony (*Bryonia alba*)</note> has leaves and **tendrils** <note>original: *caprioli*</note> similar to our cultivated vine, but they are rougher and smaller; the tendrils themselves entwine themselves in neighboring spots. Its seed is similar to a grape. If the tendrils are boiled and eaten at the beginning of their growth, they ease **bloody urine**. 

Its medicinal power is found in its leaves, its shoots, and its sticky root. Therefore, when applied fresh as a medicine to wounds, it leads **cancers** and **phagedenic ulcers** <note>original: *fageden. ca*; spreading, "eating" sores that consume the flesh</note> back to health. It removes wounds in three [days?] when salt is added and an untouched poultice is prepared. 

Truly, its root restores a good color to the body. It smooths **wrinkles** on the face, clears **freckles** <note>original: *lentigines*</note>, and returns the proper color to dark scars. It heals bruises and **whitlows** <note>original: *panariae*; painful infections around the fingernails or toes</note> when used with wine; and applied as an untouched poultice, it disperses hard swellings. 

It is mixed with necessary medicines for **epileptics**; one pound <note>original: *l. i.*; likely a specific measurement or ratio in a larger preparation</note> is drunk, [and] it waits for the **South Wind** <note>original: *Notori praestolatur*; this may refer to the patient waiting for specific weather conditions or a humoral change associated with the south wind</note>. Taken in a similar way, it is a singular protection for **apoplexy** <note>strokes or sudden loss of consciousness</note> and stomach ailments, especially when five pounds <note>original: *l. u.*</note> are taken for individual causes, such as **poisonous bites**. 

It counters [accidents], but it also induces **abortion**. Indeed, if too much is taken, it causes **mania**. It expels the afterbirth and provokes urine. With honey added as an **electuary** <note>a medicinal paste or syrup made by mixing herbs with honey or sugar</note>, it helps those with shortness of breath and feelings of suffocation. It suppresses a cough and pain in the side. For those who have fallen from a height and for those with **bruising** <note>original: *quassationibus*; can also refer to internal shaking or concussions</note>, it is a supreme remedy. An **obol** <note>a small Greek unit of weight, roughly 0.5 to 0.7 grams</note> drunk with vinegar dries up the **spleen** if drunk for thirty days...

<summary>This page describes the White Bryony (Vitis alba), detailing its effectiveness in treating skin conditions like wrinkles and scars, and its internal use for serious conditions like epilepsy and trauma from falls.</summary>

...with dried figs. Made into a **poultice**, it can do all the same things <note>original: *ss.*; abbreviation for *supra scripta*, meaning "written above"</note>. It is boiled in water and, when applied as a warm compress, it cleanses the **womb** <note>original: *isteriam* / *hysteriam*</note>.

It also expels a fetus that has not yet formed. In the springtime, the herb itself is juiced. When this juice is drunk in large quantities, it is known to perform all the actions mentioned above and it clears away **phlegm** <note>one of the four "humors" or bodily fluids in ancient medicine, associated with coldness and moisture</note>.

Truly, its seed is ground and, when rubbed on the skin, it cleanses **scabies** and **leprosy** and encourages the flow of milk in women. Its juice, boiled with the juice of **barley water** <note>original: *tisfane* / *ptisanae*</note>, provides the same benefit for women.

### 178. CONCERNING <term>AMPELOS MELENA</term> <note>Black Bryony (*Dioscorea communis*), though "Ampelos melena" literally translates from Greek as "black vine"</note>

**Black Bryony**, which most call the **black vine** or the **Aronia vine**, has leaves similar to ivy, or very similar to it; its stalk is also similar, but larger. It bears a seed similar to a grape, which is green at the beginning and turns black when it reaches maturity. When these seeds are rubbed, they yield a color like boxwood <note>original: *bexeum* / *buxeum*; a pale yellow color</note>.

The **tendrils** <note>original: *caprioli*</note> and shoots are eaten just as [other greens] are consumed, but they do not have the same nutritional quality; rather, they possess medicinal power. It commands the **menstrual flow**.

It dries the **spleen** and treats **epilepsy**, **spasms**, and stomach ailments. The medicinal power of its root is similar to the things mentioned above. It is especially helpful for the wounds of animals when the seed-pods and heads are applied.

### 180. ON <term>DIPTERIS</term> <note>Likely a species of fern, possibly the Male Fern (*Dryopteris*); the name suggests "two-winged."</note>
**Dipteris**, which many call *ablecton* or *poliziron*, is a herb without a flower, without a stalk <note>original: *hasta*; literally "spear," referring to the central stem</note>, and without seed <note>original: *feminae*; likely a corruption of *semine* (seed), as ferns were traditionally thought to lack seeds</note>. Its leaves are divided into a single tendril; it is astringent to the taste <note>original: *sapaca.ē.*, likely a corruption of *stiptica est*</note>. It grows in rocky and rough places. Its root, taken as a drink of four [drachms] with honey-water, expels broad **intestinal worms** <note>tapeworms</note>. It works better if drunk with **scammony** <note>a harsh purgative resin from *Convolvulus scammonia*</note> and **black hellebore**. This is most effective when two obols <note>a small unit of weight</note> are drunk. However, those who are about to take it ought to eat quite a large amount beforehand.

### 181. ON <term>FILICTERON</term> <note>Likely a variant of *Phyllitis*, such as Hart’s Tongue Fern</note>
They call it **Filicteron**, *nitifon*, or *opion*. It has leaves similar to a fern. This plant has many tendrils, and its roots are long, yellow, reddish, and somewhat black. When honey is added and it is taken with wine, it expels worms. In a dose of four round [pills/measures], it expels **roundworms**. Once taken, it may induce labor in women or cause an **abortion**. The dried roots themselves, when applied as a **poultice** <note>original: *decataplectris*; a corruption of the Greek-derived *cataplasmatis*</note>, cure malignant and weeping wounds. Indeed, its soft leaves, when eaten like vegetables, soften the bowels.

### 182. ON <term>POLYPODY</term> <note>*Polypodium vulgare*, a fern known for the many "feet" or nodes on its rhizome</note>
<margin>+</margin> **Polypody** grows on damp walls. It reaches a length of two palms <note>approximately 6 to 8 inches</note>. It is similar to the rough fern.

...and divided like the breath of a serpent <note>original: *serpentis spiritum*; this may refer to the swaying or creeping appearance of the fern's fronds</note>. Its roots, however, are rough and entangled like the tentacles of an **octopus** <note>original: *polippus*</note>; they are as thick as a finger. When scraped on the inside, the root appears green and somewhat white; it is firm and sweet to the taste. It possesses a **purgative** <note>original: *catartica*; a substance used to cleanse the bowels</note> quality. ### 183. ON <term>DRYOPTERIS</term> <note>Likely the Oak Fern (*Gymnocarpium dryopteris*), often found growing near ferns or on mossy oaks</note>

**Dryopteris** grows in cold places. Its root is rough and firm, and its parts cling together; it is sweet to the taste. When applied as a **poultice** using its root, it can heal all wounds if applied and changed daily. **184**

### 184. ON <term>CNICUS</term> <note>Safflower (*Carthamus tinctorius*), known for its yellow-orange dye and medicinal seeds</note>

**Cnicus** has oblong leaves that are divided, rough, and thorny. It has stalks two **cubits** <note>a unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18 inches or 45 cm</note> high, which are also thorny, and upon which are round heads with a saffron-colored flower. They have a white seed that is blunt, oblong, and angular. They eat its flower boiled in a decoction of **honey-water**. They extract the juice of its seed with honey-water; when given with honey-water, it purges the belly. It is **bad for the stomach** <note>original: *cacostomaco*; from the Greek *kakostomachos*, meaning difficult for the stomach to digest</note>; it is prepared by boiling it and adding sweet honey-water.

...purging the belly from the seeds themselves. Mixed with **almonds** <note>original: *amigdalis*</note>, **nitre** <note>original: *nitro*; a naturally occurring mineral salt (potassium nitrate) used as a cleansing agent</note>, **anise** <note>original: *aneso*</note>, and **cooked honey** <note>original: *melle cocto*</note>. If two or three pieces the size of nuts are taken before dinner, it softens the belly and regulates digestion. Its preparation is as follows: take three measures <note>original: *quiato III*; a *cyathus* was a standard Roman liquid measure, roughly 0.045 liters</note> of **white safflower** <note>original: *cnico albo*</note>, roasted and cleaned; one pound <note>original: *Li*; an abbreviation for *libra*</note> of anise; one pound of nitre; as much honey as is sufficient; and thirty **Carian figs** <note>original: *carnis caricum*; dried figs from Caria in Asia Minor, prized for their sweetness</note>. This preparation, when taken, is known to accomplish all the aforementioned effects. The juice of its seed also curdles milk.

### 185. ON <term>LINOZOSTIS</term> <note>Commonly known as Mercury herb (*Mercurialis annua*). The name *linozostis* comes from the Greek for "linen-girdle"</note>

**Linozostis** is also called *pasteneon* or the **mercurial herb** <note>original: *herba mercurialis*</note>. It has leaves similar to **basil** <note>original: *ozime*</note>; it clings to things just as **bindweed** <note>original: *helsine*</note> does. It has shorter branches. The female plant has many seeds, which are like berries. The male plant, however, has small heads around the leaves, like **groundsel** <note>original: *eritimi*</note>, and its seed is round. This whole bush, when boiled and eaten, softens the belly. Its decoction <note>the liquid resulting from boiling the plant</note>, when taken, clears out **bile** and watery humors. It is said that if the leaves of the female plant are crushed and smeared on the genitals <note>original: *ueretre*</note>, or likewise drunk, it causes the conception of females. If the same practice is performed using the leaves of the male plant, it causes the conception of males.

<header>BOOK III.</header>

<unclear>Scor</unclear>piuron they call it because its flowers are similar in shape to a **scorpion** <note>original: *scorpii*; the plant described here is likely *Heliotropium europaeum*, known for its curled flower spikes</note>; however, it took the name **heliotropion** <note>original: *elio tropion*; from the Greek for "sun-turner"</note> because it follows the course of the sun. It has leaves similar to **basil** <note>original: *ocimi*</note>, but rougher and darker; it has stalks growing from a single root, or as many as six branches. The flowers on the feathered branches are white and slightly purple and curved, just like a scorpion's tail. Its root is thin and of no use. It grows in rough places. If a **handful** <note>original: *manipulo uno*</note> is boiled and drunk, it expels **phlegm** and **bile** <note>original: *fleuma ex colera*</note>. When drunk with wine, it counters the **stings of scorpions** <note>original: *hicabus scorpionum*; likely a scribal variant of *ictibus scorpionum*</note>. Applied as a **poultice** <note>original: *cataplasma*</note>, it is very effective; also, a single root of it hung around the neck protects against the venom of scorpions. Four grains of its seed drunk with wine before the **onset of a fever** <note>original: *accessione*; referring to the periodic return of symptoms in diseases like malaria</note> is a most powerful remedy. Three grains are effectively administered in the weight of three **denarii** <note>original: *denariis*; a Roman silver coin, used here as a unit of weight</note>. Its leaves, when used in a poultice, disperse **tumors**, clear away **warts** <note>original: *mirmicias*; small, hard warts</note> on the body, and remove **corns** <note>original: *clauos*</note>. Furthermore, its dried leaves are very effective for **gout** <note>original: *podagrias*</note>. When ground and applied as a **pessary** <note>original: *matricae subposita*; literally "placed under the womb"</note>, it induces **menstruation** and causes **abortion**.

<header>BOOK IV.</header>

The smaller kind <note>original: *Minor*; referring to the *Heliotropium minus* or Lesser Heliotrope</note> grows in cultivated places and meadows and similar locations. It has seeds that are round and hanging. Its herb, when boiled with the seed, crushed with **nitre** <term>likely natron, a naturally occurring mineral salt used as a cleansing agent</term>, hyssop, and cardamom, and then drunk, draws out and excludes round **worms** <note>original: *lumbrias*; referring to intestinal parasites</note>. Applied as a poultice with salt, it removes **corns** <note>original: *clauos*; hard, thickened skin on the feet</note>; it is most effective if the herb has been boiled before being applied.

### 189. ON SCORPION-PLANT

**Scorpion-plant** <note>original: *Scorpiodes*; likely *Scorpiurus sulcatus*, known for its curled seed pods</note> is a herb that has leaves and seeds similar to the tail of scorpions. When applied as a **poultice** <note>original: *cataplasma*; a soft, moist mass of herbs applied to the body</note>, it soothes the stings of scorpions.

### 190. ON WILD CARDAMOM
### ALSO CALLED IBERIA

**Wild Cardamom** <note>original: *Cardamo agreste*; likely a species of *Lepidium* or pepperwort</note> grows everywhere in very many watery places. It is a shrubby plant reaching the length of a **cubit** <term>an ancient unit of length, approximately 18 inches or the length of a forearm</term>. It has full leaves similar to **wild asparagus** <note>original: *aspami*, likely a corruption of *asparagi*</note> but larger. Sprouting in the springtime, it has a "worn" appearance and bears flowers on all its branches that are much smaller but whiter than the foliage. The seed is tiny, and the root is oblong, thin, and <unclear>luisada</unclear>; they possess the scent of cardamom. When prepared as a medicine, it is satisfying; it soothes **temporal headaches** <note>pain localized in the temples</note> and provides a beneficial effect for long-standing issues of the **windpipe** <note>original: *arteriaar*; likely referring to the bronchial tubes or trachea</note>.

### THE INDEX ENDS. <note>original: *elenchos*; the Greek term for a table of contents or list</note>
### THE LETTER BEGINS AUSPICIOUSLY.

In the fourth book, most dear Areius <note>the physician to whom Dioscorides dedicated his work</note>, we have written with a wise mind and through investigated reason concerning the preparations of aromatics and oils and myrrh; the nature of trees and their seeds; plant "tears" <note>resins or saps</note> and animal products; the properties of honey and milk; the efficacy of grains; and the power of vegetables, herbs, roots, juices, and seeds. In this fifth book, however, we make mention of wine, metals, and the various ordered species of stones.

### THE LETTER ENDS.
### THE FIFTH BOOK BEGINS.

->ON THE COMMON GRAPEVINE.<-

The leaves and tendrils <note>original: *caprioli*; the curling vine-shoots</note> of the **common grapevine**, when prepared as a poultice <note>original: *catapl.* / *cataplasma*</note>, ease and mitigate headaches. The leaves applied alone act with a cooling and astringent <note>original: *stiptica*; a "puckering" effect that stops bleeding</note> power. Its juice is drunk for dysentery <note>intestinal inflammation</note> and for those spitting blood <note>original: *imoptuicis*, from the Greek *haemoptysis*</note>.

<summary>This page concludes the list of medicinal earths and stones, provides Dioscorides' introductory summary of the previous books, and begins the clinical description of the grapevine's medicinal uses.</summary>
<keywords>Samian earth, Chian earth, Areius, grapevine, astringent, dysentery, pharmacology, minerals</keywords>

--- Page 314 ---
<meta>This page continues the medical instructions regarding the grapevine (Vitis) and its various parts, following the introductory sections of Book V that were outlined in the previous page's table of contents. The text moves from the medicinal uses of vine sap to the classification of wild varieties.</meta>

...for foul odors of the stomach caused by indigestion <note>original: *exfagacionib*; likely referring to gaseous eructations or bloating</note>. The same is true for ivy. It helps pregnant women when the **tendrils** <term>capreoli: the curling, climbing stems of the vine</term> are taken in a drink. These can also be made into a decoction <note>original: *elixum*; a liquid produced by boiling medicinal plants</note>. 

The **tear** <note>original: *lacrimam*; the sap that exudes from the plant</note> of the vine has a similar medicinal power. When it is drunk, it breaks up stones <note>referring to kidney or bladder stones</note>. Applied as an ointment, it cleanses the body of freckles <note>original: *fernas*; likely a corruption of *phirnas* or *lentigines*</note> and scaly skin <note>original: *lepras*</note>. If the area is first rubbed with **natron** <term>nitro: a naturally occurring sodium carbonate used as a cleansing agent</term> or oil and then anointed continually, it removes hair. The "tears" of green wood that has been burnt can also do this; this ointment can also remove skin eruptions <note>original: *min mita*; likely a corruption of *mentagra*, a skin infection often affecting the face</note>. 

The "tears" are collected in this way: place green vine-shoots in the hearth <note>original: *foco*</note> so that their ends are not entirely consumed by fire. When they begin to glow in the middle, whatever sap it "vomits" out should be collected in a clean vessel. 

Furthermore, the dry ash of the vine-shoots <note>original: *sarmentorū*</note> and dried grape skins <note>original: *vinaceae*</note>, when collected and applied as a poultice <note>original: *cataplasma*</note> with vinegar, restores health to **growths** <term>condylomata: wart-like growths or swellings</term> and tumors of the anus. It also heals dislocations and poisonous bites. **Rue** <note>a bitter herb used widely in ancient medicine</note> added to rose oil, water, and vinegar reduces the swelling of a tumor of the spleen.

## **ON THE WILD VINE**
There are two kinds of wild vine. One kind has berries that are unripe; from these, when they begin to flower, **oenanthe** <note>the fragrant flower of the wild vine, often used in perfumes and medicines</note> is prepared. The other kind has small berries that are somewhat riper and black in their properties. It is astringent <note>original: *suptica*; styptic</note> and is similar in its power, leaves, and tendrils to the common vine.

### III **ON OUR GREEN GRAPE**

<meta>This page continues the medical discourse on the products of the grapevine, specifically focusing on the medicinal properties of various types of grapes—fresh, preserved, and dried (raisins)—following the previous discussion on vine sap and ashes.</meta>

BOOK V.

Every ripe grape, when eaten, causes a loosening of the bowels <note>original: *uentris soluzionem*; a laxative effect</note> and bloating. If they are hung up <note>to dry slightly</note>, however, this effect is diminished. Small grapes possess a beneficial quality and are **good for the stomach** <term>eustomacha: from the Greek *eustomachos*, meaning aiding digestion or soothing the stomach</term>; they take away a loathing for food and are well received by both the sick and the healthy.

### IIII CONCERNING GRAPES PRESERVED IN VINE LEAVES AND JARS

They are good for the stomach and bind the bowels. They are also suitable for wounds to the head and bring relief when taken by those **spitting blood** <term>emoptoicis: from the Greek *haimoptuikos*, referring to coughing up blood from the lungs or airway</term>.

### V CONCERNING GRAPES PRESERVED IN RAISIN WINE

Grapes preserved in **raisin wine** <term>passo: a sweet wine made from grapes that have been partially dried</term> are **bad for the stomach** <term>cacostomacae: from the Greek *kakostomachos*, meaning causing digestive upset</term>. However, grapes are also prepared using a third part of rain water <note>original: *aqua caelesti*</note>. They should be placed in the water dry, especially the largest ones that still have a branch. Giving this preparation to those suffering from chronic fevers and thirst provides a beneficial effect. <insert>It works wonderfully and helps with dysentery.</insert>

Their **grape skins** <term>vinantia: the skins or husks of the grapes after pressing</term>, when crushed with salt and applied, dissolve tumors and hardness of the breasts. A decoction of these, when drunk, cures dysentery and loosening of the bowels. When used as a suppository or applied as a compress <note>original: *fomento*</note>, it checks the flow of the **womb** <note>original: *matricis*; likely referring to excessive menstrual bleeding or discharge</note>. It is also a most powerful remedy for burns. Their **seeds** <note>original: *nuclei*</note> have an **astringent** <term>staptica: a corruption of *styptica*, a substance that shrinks tissues and stops bleeding</term>, cooling, and stomach-soothing quality. Their flour, applied as a poultice before being cooked, treats and strengthens a relaxed stomach.

### VI CONCERNING THE RAISIN

Raisins <note>original: *uuae passae*</note> have a very great astringent quality. When the flesh of white raisins is eaten, it soothes the roughness of the **windpipe** <note>original: *arteriarum*; in ancient medicine, this often referred to the trachea or bronchial tubes</note> for those with a cough, and it assists those with **kidney ailments** <term>neufroticis: from the Greek *nephritikos*, relating to the kidneys</term>, especially if the seeds are removed.

<meta>This page continues the medical discourse on grape products. The previous page ended mid-sentence discussing a decoction for "loosening of the [bowels]." This page completes the discussion on preparations involving dried grapes (raisins) and moves into the medicinal use of the flowers of the wild vine.</meta>

...when eaten, they should be mixed with wheat flour <note>original: *pollinae cereri*; literally "flour of Ceres," the goddess of grain</note> and fried eggs; they are also well received and effective when eaten dried in the sun with pepper. When used in a **plaster** <term>cataplasmis: a soft, moist mass of herbs or flour applied to the body to heal</term> combined with roasted **bean** <term>fabae: specifically the broad bean or fava bean, often used as a base for medicinal pastes</term> flour, it disperses tumors. With wine added, it improves dark spots on the skin. It removes **calluses** <note>original: *clauos*; also refers to corns or warts</note> from the body. It dries out moist wounds and brings wounds arising from swellings <note>original: *nodis nata*</note> back to health.

When the seeds are removed, it brings aid to **cankers** <note>original: *cancris*; in this period, the term referred to any spreading, ulcerous sore</note>. Crushed and applied, it treats **gout** <term>podagrias: a painful form of arthritis, traditionally associated with the feet</term>. It is especially effective when applied with **opopanax** <note>original: *apopanace*; a medicinal resin from the juice of the Hercules-all-heal plant</note>. If applied, it also removes loose or displaced nails.

### VII CONCERNING ENANTHE

**Enanthe** <term>Enantio: the flower of the wild vine (*Vitis vinifera sylvestris*)</term> flowers should be collected from the wild vine when it first begins to bloom. They are best preserved in a flat vessel and coated [in salt]. They possess infinite virtue and are very savory. Therefore, if the preparation is drunk, it is **good for the stomach** <term>eustonica: from the Greek *eustonachos*, meaning strengthening or comforting to the stomach</term>. It acts as a **diuretic** <term>diuretica: a substance that promotes the production of urine</term> and binds the bowels. It also helps those **spitting up blood** <note>original: *sanguinem reiaenab*; likely a corruption of *reiectantibus*, those coughing or spitting blood</note>.

It is used both as a drink and as a topical application. It brings relief to the stomach, corrects the humors, and speeds up digestion. Mixed with oil and vinegar and applied as a medicinal compress, it removes headaches. Whether dry or fresh, it is used in a plaster to keep recent wounds from swelling and removes excessive **eye discharge** <note>original: *ezilopar*; likely a corruption of the Greek *epiphoras*, referring to watery or running eyes</note>. It is effective for wounds of the mouth and gums, and it brings wounds of the genitals back to health. With honey, rose oil, saffron, and myrrh added, it should be used in necessary **pessaries** <term>pessariis: medicinal plugs or suppositories designed for vaginal use</term>; used as a pessary, it stops the flow of the womb. It halts the discharge of fluid from the eyes and, when applied in plasters, treats looseness of the stomach.

### VIII CONCERNING OMPHACIUM

**Omphacium** <term>Omfatium: the juice of unripe grapes, used since antiquity as a sharp, astringent medicine or condiment known today as verjuice</term> is the juice of unripe white grapes. These grapes must be collected before the **Dog Days** <term>caniculariaas: the hottest days of summer, associated with the rising of the star Sirius, the Dog Star</term>. They should be dried and stored; they dry best in **copper** <note>original: *eramine*; likely referring to bronze or copper vessels</note> vessels. But if they have been kept dry with care, [the juice may be extracted]. That which rises to the top should be collected. Take care that it does not remain outside under the dew at night, for the night is harmful to this juice. One should choose the juice that is reddish <gloss>and brittle</gloss> and sharp, so that it bites the tongue. For **apples** <note>original: *mela*; from the Greek 'melon,' often used for various tree fruits</note>, they likewise collect the squeezed juice of the fruit, dry it, and store it.

When taken, it helps the throat and the gums. It either dries out **fluxes** <note>original: *reuma*</note> when applied with honey, or, when mixed with **raisin wine** <term>passo: a sweet wine made from grapes dried in the sun</term>, it soothes earaches. More of it should be poured into **fistulas** <term>fistulis: narrow, tube-like sores or abnormal passages in the flesh</term>, and it heals **spreading wounds** <note>original: *uulneribus pascentibus*; literally "grazing wounds," referring to ulcers or gangrenous sores</note> when applied. It may be usefully applied as an ointment for **dysentery** <note>original: *disinterias*</note> and **uterine flux** <note>original: *fluxum matricis*</note>. It clears **dimness** <note>original: *calligines*</note> of the eyes, removes itching from the eyelids, and aids those **spitting blood** <term>empictis: likely a corruption of the Greek 'hemoptoicus,' referring to coughing up blood</term>. It also aids a ruptured vein. It is clear that this medicine should be used; it is no less effective [than others].

### VIII CONCERNING OLD WINES

Old wines, by virtue of their age, are said to be more <gloss>sharp</gloss>. They are harmful to the nerves and the senses. However, because of their sweetness, they are good when drunk in moderation; for this reason, they should not be given to the sick. Fresh **must** <note>original: *multu*; likely 'mustum,' freshly pressed grape juice that has not yet fermented</note>, on the other hand, causes the belly to bloat.

Many people also cook the must and make it sweet; if it is cooked until it turns black and thick, it is good for medicinal use. It is necessarily given to those who require the properties of **honey**. ### X ABOUT RESINATED WINE

Resinated wines <note>original: *vina psitina*; likely referring to *pityites*, wine flavored with pine resin similar to modern Greek retsina</note>, which have pine resin added to them, are hot and digestible; they induce vomiting and are bad for the eyes.

### XI ABOUT ASPARAGUS WINE

Asparagus wine, which is known to have sweetness mixed into it, weighs down the head and heats both the head and the whole body similarly. Intoxicating a person quickly, it causes bloating and is bad for the stomach <note>original: *cacostomachum*; a Greek medical term for something that causes indigestion or nausea</note>.

### XII ABOUT ITALIAN WINE

Regarding Italian wine, Falernian <note>one of the most famous and prestigious wines of the Roman world, grown in Campania</note> is said to be more useful when it is very old. It is digestible, stimulates the pulse, and constricts the belly. It is good for the stomach but is contrary to the bladder; it causes dimness of the eyes <gloss>just as</gloss> many other wines do, and when drunk in large quantities, it can harm the whole body.

### XIII ABOUT ALBAN WINE

Alban wine <note>produced in the Alban Hills south of Rome</note> is stronger than Falernian, with a sweetish taste; <gloss>bloating</gloss> the belly and stomach, it softens the belly. It is useless for digestion and contrary to all the nerves, especially the <gloss>head</gloss>; however, when it has aged, it becomes very harsh <note>original: *austerum*; dry, sharp, or astringent</note>.

### XIV ABOUT CHIAN WINE

Chian wine <note>original: *quibio*; likely a corruption of *Chio*, wine from the Greek island of Chios</note> is stronger than Alban wine; it dries the body and provides a good complexion, but it is contrary to digestion and weighs down the head by causing bloating.

### XV ABOUT SURRENTINE WINE

Surrentine wine <note>from the Sorrento peninsula</note> is very harsh; it <gloss>constricts</gloss> the flux of the stomach and intestines. It binds the belly and does not affect the head much because it is quite light when it has aged.

### BOOK V

Thick [wines] are mixed from all varieties; they bring relief to weary men, provide strength, and produce a healthy complexion. If drunk in excess, however, they counter all poisonous <term>venenosis|poisonous substances or venom</term> things and venomous bites. They turn the stomach <note>likely referring to inducing vomiting to expel toxins</note>, treat flatulence, assist the swellings of the hypochondriacs <term>ypocondriaci|those suffering from ailments in the upper abdomen, below the ribs</term>, restrain rheumatism <term>reumatismum|the flow of harmful bodily humors, often associated with inflammation or discharge</term>, and check excessive sweating of the belly. 

The white of an old wine is especially fragrant. Indeed, the power of old and sweet wine settles the ailments of the liver <note>original: *fice*, likely *ficati* (liver)</note> and kidneys. It is applied as a necessary dressing for wounds and tumors when the juices are exhausted; it most healthfully cures venomous bites, phagedenic <term>fagadenica|spreading or "devouring" ulcers</term> wounds, and rheumatic ones when aided by a warm compress. <unclear>And also</unclear> they are useful even for healthy drinkers, especially those without sea water <note>Ancient winemakers often added sea water to preserve wine or improve flavor</note>. 

But the wines for the aforementioned causes are better, such as Falernian <note>the most famous and prestigious wine of ancient Rome</note> and Surrentine, from which also come the Paesenian <note>original: *presenianos*, likely a corruption of a regional variety</note> and all Campanian wines, as well as the Praetutian from the Adriatic, Sicilian wine, and Mamertine. All of these are better than Egyptian wine. <unclear>Among the Greek</unclear> wines, the best are all the aforementioned: Chian <term>chios|wine from the Greek island of Chios</term>, Lesbian <term>lesbiu|wine from the island of Lesbos</term>, and Sicyonian <note>original: *sigillu*, likely *Sicyonium* from the Peloponnese</note>. 

If a dark and thick wine is produced from these, it is bad for the stomach <term>caco stomachu|from the Greek *kakostomachos*, meaning upsetting to the digestion</term>, inflates the belly, and adds flesh to the body. But white wines, wherever they are found, are diuretic <term>diuritica|promoting the passage of urine</term> and especially stimulate the digestion <term>eustomaca|good for the stomach</term>. White wine and vinegar <note>original: *acetere*, likely *acetum*</note> are harmful to the nerves. 

A wine of middle age and color is most necessary for use, especially from seven up to ten years old. The time must be chosen when it should be drunk in greatest quantity, and the age of the patient must be considered to determine to whom they ought to give a sufficient amount of wine.

## ON OMPHACINE WINE

Omphacine wine <note>original: *vinum omfacino*; wine made from unripe grapes</note> is prepared for its sweetness; they collect the grapes at mid-maturity, which grapes they then allow to ripen on their own after the vintage season. They tread and press them, collect the wine itself, and store it in new vessels—that is, earthenware—and they hang them up and place them in the sun for several days; this is where its strength lies. This wine is flavorful and good for the stomach <term>eustomaca|Greek-derived term for substances beneficial to digestion or the stomach</term>; it aids indigestion, binds a loose stomach <note>referring to its astringent properties used to treat diarrhea</note>, removes the cravings of pregnant women, treats griping pains <term>torsionibus|internal twisting or cramping pains in the intestines</term>, and counters all diseases of the belly. These wines improve with age. **XXV**

## ON THE SECOND TYPE OF OMPHACINE WINE

The second kind of omphacine wine, which the common people call a "potion," is prepared as follows: they take fifty-seven ounces of wine, thirty pitchers <term>urcios|large jars or pitchers used as a liquid measure</term> of water, and ninety pitchers of grape skins <term>uinaciae|the pomace or remains of grapes after the first pressing</term>. It is trodden and pressed just like wine, put into vessels, and boiled until only a third of the volume remains. It is especially important to add one pint <term>sextarios|a Roman measure roughly equivalent to half a liter or a pint</term> of salt for every pitcher of water. You pour it back into vessels during the winter, and it should be used after a year because it turns sour <note>original: *acescet*</note> quite quickly. It is truly useful for the sick to whom it is not advisable to give standard wine, and anyone who cannot tolerate wine after an illness may rightly take this instead. **X**

# XXVI ON ADYNAMON WINE

Regarding **adynamon** wine <note>original: *uino adinamo*; from the Greek for "powerless" or "weak," referring to its low alcohol content</note>, it possesses a similar potency <gloss>ss</gloss> <note>original: *semis*; likely a scribal mark for "half" or a specific measure</note>. It is prepared and easily received: take 10 urns <term>urnas|a Roman liquid measure approximately equal to 3.5 gallons</term> of must <note>original: *musti*; freshly pressed grape juice that has not yet fermented</note>, to which you also mix 10 urns of water; likewise, simmer over a slow fire until the water itself is consumed. Then, pour it back into pitched vessels <note>vessels lined with resin or pitch for sealing</note>. Many, however, prepare it this way: one part seawater and one part rainwater, with individual parts of honey and must. All these things, mixed into one, they pour back into vessels and leave them in the sun for ten days; after this, they use it. After a year, it possesses similar medicinal virtue.

## XXVIIII ON HONEY-WINE

<margin>+</margin> **Honey-wine** <note>original: *uinomelli*; a mixture of wine and honey</note> is useful when it is prepared from a dry, aged wine and good honey, because it produces less bloating <note>original: *inflationem*</note> and is more quickly digested. If it is aged, it adds flesh to the body. It is better received [on an empty stomach]; it softens the belly <note>acts as a laxative</note> and provokes urine. If taken on a full stomach, it causes harm. When first consumed, it may cause bloating, but salt helps to <unclear>remove</unclear> this. It is prepared with [eight] <note>the Latin *residuas* here is likely a corruption of a numerical value like *VIII*</note> parts of wine and one part of honey. Indeed, many boil it with the honey so that it matures more quickly before they store it. Others, however, out of greed, take two hundred **sextaria** <term>sextarius|a Roman unit of volume, approximately 1 pint or 0.5 liters</term> of must <note>freshly pressed grape juice</note> from the vat to one **sextarius** of honey; they boil it this way and store it in vessels <gloss>ss</gloss> <note>possibly an abbreviation for *semis*, meaning half-sized containers</note>, and these varieties are exceedingly sweet.

## XXX ON MELIGRATON

<margin>+</margin> **Meligraton** <note>a Greek-derived term for a mixture of honey, water, and wine</note> possesses a medicinal virtue similar to **hydromel** <note>original: *idromelli*; honey-water or mead</note>. Meligraton is used in its uncooked state; with much water, it heals a weak pulse, parched bodies, and those suffering from thirst. This preparation of meligraton, which they especially call "honey-water-must," is best given in its "middle time"—that is, when it is neither too fresh nor too old. When consumed, it is similar to **second wine** <term>uino deuterio|a "small wine" or "kin" wine made by soaking grape skins in water after the first pressing</term>; it restores strength but [is better for] the weariness caused by daily fevers <note>original: *emeramorum*, likely a corruption of the Greek *ephemeron*</note> than the second wine is. Aged meligraton is useless. <gloss>ss</gloss> It is most effective for those with stomach pain and "rheuma" <note>original: *rema*; a watery discharge or catarrh</note>; it causes [relief] and takes away **nausea** <term>fastidium|a medical term for loss of appetite or a loathing of food</term>. It is prepared by mixing [eight] parts [of water] with one part of honey.

...and those which have been exposed to the sun for a longer time, composed of two parts of rainwater <note>original: *caelestes*</note>; many, however, boil spring water mixed with honey and store it.

## XXXI ON HONEY-WATER

**Honey-water** <note>original: *apomeli*; literally "away from honey," referring to the liquid derived from honeycombs</note> is what many make by mixing honeycomb <note>reading the Latin *fabo* as *favo*</note> with water, washing it, and storing it. It should become honey-like when steeped, not watery and poor. They set this aside after cooking, as it is useful for all sick people because it contains a mixture of medicinal properties.

## XXXII ON WATER

Water is known to everyone to be harmful to the internal organs <note>referring to stagnant or poor-quality water</note> if not chosen carefully. The best water to be taken is sweet, without a foul smell, and without any earthy scent in the mixture. It should not cause bloating in the **hypochondrium** <term>hypochondrium|the upper part of the abdomen, just below the ribs</term>, nor should it disturb the urine; all these qualities must be observed in water.

## XXXIII ON SEA WATER

<gloss>that is, warm</gloss>
Sea water has a viscous and cleansing quality; it is bad for the stomach and disturbs the belly, but it brings down phlegm. When heated and applied as a **fomentation** <term>fomentation|a warm, moist medicinal compress</term>, it brings abscesses to a head <note>original: *dealbo*</note> and ripens them. It disperses all hardness and provides **diaphoresis** <term>diaphoresis|the process of inducing sweating for medicinal purposes</term>. It treats conditions of the nerves. It helps with swellings <note>original: *promontibus*; likely a corruption of *prominentibus*</note> that are not wounded when used in **poultices** <term>poultice|a soft, moist mass of material, typically of flour or herbs, applied to the body to relieve soreness and inflammation</term>; for this, it must be mixed with flour. Although it is poor as a food, it is added to noble medicines as a **diaphoretic** <term>diaphoretic|a substance that induces sweating</term> and is especially <unclear>digested</unclear> <gloss>applied</gloss>. Taken warm, it aids the bowels of stronger people. It heals "wild" scabies <note>severe skin irritations</note> and itching when applied as a warm compress; it cleanses the neck and removes swelling.

## XXXIIII ON SEA-HONEY

**Sea-honey** <note>original: *thalassomeli*</note>, when taken, acts as a purgative. It is prepared in this way: take equal measures of sea water and rainwater <note>reading *carle is* as *caelestis*</note> and mix in one part of honey. This is strained and placed in the sun during the **dog days** <note>the hottest period of summer, usually late July to August</note>. Alternatively, they boil down two <gloss>parts</gloss> of sea water and mix it with one part honey and let it settle in vessels. If the preparation is made in the spring, it should be stored...

## XXXV ON VINEGAR

<margin>Good for the stomach.</margin>
**Vinegar** <note>original: *acetum*</note> has astringent properties and is good for the stomach, removing all nausea. It stops the flow of blood when drunk or applied topically. It checks a "rheum" <note>a discharge of fluids</note> of the belly; for this, it should be taken cooked in a stew. When applied to all fresh wounds with a sponge or with greasy wool <note>original: *lanis suidis*; unwashed wool containing natural lanolin</note>, it treats the wounds. It does not allow the wound to become infected with **erysipelas** <term>erysipelas|a bacterial skin infection characterized by large, red, inflamed patches</term>... <unclear>and</unclear> <unclear>likewise</unclear>.

### XXXVII CONCERNING SALTY VINEGAR
**Salty vinegar** <term>oxysalme|a medicinal mixture of vinegar and salt or brine</term> applied as a warm compress heals the rot of wounds and leads dog bites to health. It counters venomous bites and stops the flow of blood, especially when small stones <note>original: *cauculi*, likely referring to bladder stones or sharp grit</note> begin to cut [internally]. Indeed, when poured in warm at the same hour, it restores a **protruding anus** <note>likely referring to a prolapse</note> when used as a compress. It cures foul wounds of the intestines by way of a **clyster** <term>clyster|an enema used for medicinal or cleansing purposes</term>, especially if someone has been suffering from **dysentery** <term>dysentericus|an inflammatory disorder of the lower intestinal tract</term> from the first milk <note>this may refer to the onset of the disease in infants or the first stages of the illness</note>. If a leech has been swallowed, it is expelled with a gargle. Rubbing [the head] removes phlegm and sores of the head.

### XXXVIII CONCERNING THYME-SALT-VINEGAR
**Thyme-salt-vinegar** <term>thymoxysalme|a digestive preparation made from thyme, vinegar, and salt</term>, which the ancients used for a sluggish stomach. Mixed moderately with warm water, it quiets a chronic cough; and similarly, it suppresses joint pains and bloating of the stomach. When taken, it discharges thick and **black humors** <note>referring to black bile, one of the four fluids believed in ancient medicine to regulate health</note>. It is prepared thus: crushed thyme and one *oxybaphon* <note>original: *oxi fabos*, a Greek unit of measurement roughly equal to 1.5 ounces</note> of salt, boiled rue and **pennyroyal** <term>pulei|a medicinal herb in the mint family</term>, six parts each, and half a small measure <note>original: *coūla*, likely *congiola*, a liquid measure</note> of vinegar. Mix all these together, strain through a linen cloth, and store it; and if it is to be administered, grind [the ingredients again].

# BOOK V.

**Squill vinegar** <term>acetum squilliticum|a medicinal vinegar made from the sea onion, used since antiquity for various ailments</term> is prepared in this way: you clean the **squill** <term>squilla|the sea onion (Drimia maritima), a bulbous plant used in medicine</term>
and cut it into very small pieces and thread them on a linen cord so that they do not 
touch each other; dry them in the shade for 40 days. From there, take 
one **mina** <term>mna|an ancient unit of weight, roughly 1 pound</term> and put it into twelve **sextarii** <term>sextaria|a liquid measure roughly equivalent to a pint</term> of vinegar, and place it 
in the sun for 40 or 60 days; once infused, you shall cover 
the vessel itself <note>original: *uenenum ipsum*; while "uenenum" often means poison, in late Latin medical texts it can refer to the "potency" of a drug or may be a scribal error for *vas* (vessel)</note>. After this, strain it and 
pour out the squills themselves and store the vinegar. 
Many people, however, put these squills into five sextarii of vinegar 
without drying them, using an equal weight, and 
leave it for 6 months. This preparation is stronger and 
more powerful than the one written above. Indeed, for cutting **phlegm** <term>fleuma|one of the four humors, associated with coldness and moisture</term>, 
it strengthens **gums** <term>ginauas|gingivas</term> full of blood when held in the 
mouth, and it steadies **shaky teeth**, 
removes the **stench of the mouth**, and indeed strengthens the throat and 
gullet; it makes the **voice** clear and bright, it 
strengthens the stomach, removes **loss of appetite** <term>fastidia</term>, and treats **epilepsy** <term>epilentias</term> and 
**melancholy**; it is effective for 
overcoming **suffocation**, dissolves **tumors**, 
thoroughly dries out **sciatica** <term>ischiadias|nerve pain originating in the hip or back</term>, and brings 
cheerfulness to men. It is given effectively to restore **good color**, 
it wipes away the **fog of the eyes**, and when poured 
into **deaf ears**, it restores hearing; it settles all 
disorders of the **intestines** <term>interaneorum</term> unless the 
causes are wounded <note>meaning unless there are internal ulcers or lesions</note>. 
Every day you shall give one **spoonful** <term>cochariu|cochlearium, a small medicinal measure</term> to a fasting person; 
however, when one is on a journey, you shall give more as time goes on.

### XLIII ON THE PREPARATION OF WINES

Wines made from all fruits are powerful and necessary for medical use, and we have written this for their utility—how they are prepared and how they may be usefully consumed. Regarding **quince wine** <term>quidonia|the fruit of the Cydonia oblonga, known for its astringent properties</term>, which many call **cydomiten** <note>original: *quidomiten*</note>,

Stir it and store it. This preserves its potency and acts as **concentrated must** <term>sapata|likely a variation of 'sapa,' which is must boiled down to a syrup</term>; it is good for the stomach, binds the belly, and helps those with **dysentery** <term>disinterias|inflammatory disorder of the lower intestinal tract</term>. It is **good for the stomach** <note>original: *eustomacum*</note> and **liver** <note>original: *sapacum*</note>, and it binds the bowels.

### 50 ON MYRTLE WINE

**M**yrtle wine is prepared in this way: take ripe **black myrtle berries** <note>original: *mirta nigra*</note>, crush them, and press out the juice. Boil this juice down to one-third. Others, however, dry the myrtle berries in the sun and crush them. To six pounds of these, they mix in three **spoonfuls** <term>cochilura|a 'cochlear', a Roman unit of measure roughly equal to a modern tablespoon</term> and three [parts] of **dry wine** <note>original: *uino austero*; a 'harsh' or non-sweet wine</note>. They let these infuse for eight days, and afterwards, they press them and store the liquid. Its potency is **good for the liver** <note>original: *sapica*, a corruption of the Greek *hepatica*</note> and **good for the stomach** <note>original: *tomica*, a corruption of *eustomaca*</note>. It restrains flux of the belly and stomach, heals **internal ulcers** <note>original: *uulnera interapeorum*, likely *uulnera interaneorum*</note>, and it **dyes the hair** <note>original: *capitellos inficit*; literally 'stains the heads'</note>.

### 51 ON MASTIC WINE

**M**astic wine <note>original: *Uino samino*, likely referring to *Schinos*, the mastic tree</note> is prepared in a similar way to what was **written above** <note>original: *ss*, abbreviation for *supra scripta*</note>; it is made similarly with **terebinth** <term>terebentini|the resin from the terebinth tree, a relative of the pistachio</term>. Its potency is good for the liver and the stomach; it prevents all flux of the stomach and intestines. As a **fomentation** <term>fomento|a warm, medicated soak or compress</term>, it soothes **hemorrhoids** <note>original: *mozroidas*</note>. It protects all wounds from flux, and as a fomentation, it helps with **uterine conditions** <note>original: *sterica*, likely *hysterica*</note> and **hip pain** <note>original: *anicon*, likely *ischiadicum*</note>.

### 55 ON RESINATED WINE

<margin>X</margin>
**R**esinated wine <note>original: *vino resinatu*; similar to modern Retsina</note> is abundant in **Gaul** <note>original: *galicia*, likely referring to the Roman province of Gallia</note>, but because of the excessive cold, they add **pine resin** <note>original: *resina peuana*, likely pitch or resin from the spruce tree, *picea*</note> to this wine, and thus it is preserved. The resin itself is crushed and added, and when it has settled <note>original: *digesserit*</note>, the resin liquefies and the resin itself stays on top. Indeed, many add the resin at a certain time because the wine is made pleasant by aging. It stirs up <note>original: *commovet*</note> head pain; it acts as a **stomachic** <note>original: *scitofin*, a phonetic corruption of *stomachicum*</note>, aids digestion, and **promotes urination**. For those with a **cough** <note>original: *tussi enab*, likely *tussientibus*</note> and for **rheumatisms** <term>reumatismis|an old medical term for watery discharges or inflammatory pains</term>, <margin>+</margin> it should be drunk strongly. It helps those with **colic** <note>original: *liaci*, for *iliaci*</note> and **dysentery**, and is a singular remedy for those with **dropsy** <term>hydropicis|a condition of swelling or edema caused by excess fluid</term>. It binds the flow of blood and helps with intestinal wounds. This is more flavorful than dark wine, [or if made] from white wine.

## ON CEDAR WINE

**C**edar wine is prepared similarly to resinated, juniper, bay, pine, and cypress wines. Each of them is used in the same way, but these wines must be prepared when the seeds are mature; as soon as the plant begins to have seeds and leaves, they are given to be dried either in the sun or in a bath, from which one <term>modius|a Roman unit of dry measure, roughly 2 gallons or 8.7 liters</term> is to be put into one amphora of wine so that it may be made; let it sit there for two months, and after this, strain it and store it; however, you must fill the vessels themselves to the top so that the wine does not turn sour. This preparation is healthy for well people. Its power is **warming** <note>original: *termantica*, from the Greek *thermantikos*</note> and **diuretic**; among all the preparations mentioned above, these are flavorful, though the cypress wine <note>original: *lucinnum*, likely a corruption of *elatinum*</note> is more warming. It is also made from cedar berries like this: you put half an <term>emina|a Roman liquid measure, approximately half a pint or 0.27 liters</term> of berries into one amphora of must and leave it for forty days; afterwards, strain it and pour it back into a vessel. It is made similarly with wine and berries of juniper.

## ON CEDAR-RESIN WINE

**C**edar-resin wine <note>original: *cedriten*, referring to *cedrites*, a wine infused with cedar resin or pitch</note> is prepared like this: take cedar resin and wash it with fresh water and strain it; put a half-measure <note>original: *ss*, the standard abbreviation for *semis*, meaning one-half</note> of cedar resin into vessels and let it settle, and add it to vessels of must until the vessel is filled. Its power is **warming** and it **purifies** <note>original: *lepanacatur*, likely a corruption of *leptunyntica*, a medicine intended to "thin" or refine the bodily humors</note>; it takes away pain at the same time. It is given to those who do not have a fever for **pain in the side** <note>historically referring to pleurisy or localized respiratory pain</note> and it takes away a **cough**, and is used to treat **griping pains** <note>original: *tortionibus*, referring to intestinal cramping or colic</note> and **ulcers of the intestines**; similarly, it heals wounds of the belly. It provides relief for **internal abscesses** <note>original: *empuae*, from the Greek *empyoi*, referring to those suffering from internal pus or suppuration</note> and **dropsy** <note>original: *idropis*, an old medical term for edema or swelling caused by fluid accumulation</note>; it clears out **hysterical suffocations** <note>original: *offocationes stericas*, a historical medical condition where respiratory distress or fainting was attributed to the movement of the womb</note> and aids with griping pains.

### 65. ON LAVENDER VINEGAR

<margin>60</margin>

### LXVI. ON THE WINE
### OF GOAT ORIGANUM

Goat origanum wine <note>original: *Vinotragoriganiten*; likely made from *Tragoriganum*, or Winter Savory</note> is prepared thus: put four <term>sextarii|a Roman dry and liquid measure, roughly equivalent to a pint or 0.5 liters</term> of goat origanum into must <note>original: *mustu*; freshly pressed grape juice that has not yet fermented into wine</note>. Tie it in a small linen cloth and let it sit for three months; afterwards, strain it and store it. It is effectively given for griping pains <note>original: *tortionis*; internal twisting or cramping of the bowels</note>, and it is useful for bruising <note>original: *conquassationis*; literally a "shaking up" or internal trauma</note> and pain in the side. It also treats bloating.

### LXVII. ON PERIWINKLE WINE

Periwinkle wine <note>original: *Vinobono*; while literally "good wine," the text suggests *Vinca pervica* (Periwinkle) based on the corrupted "uini septe" which follows</note> is prepared in the same way as above. Put seven [parts] of crushed periwinkle <note>original: *uini septe*, likely a corruption of *vica pervica*</note> in a linen cloth and steep it in four <term>cotylae|a Greek and Roman measure of volume, approximately half a pint or 0.25 liters</term> of must using the method described above. It is used for stomach ailments and is effective against the exhaustion of iron-working <note>original: *labori ferri*; physical strain from smithing or heavy labor</note> and the soreness from horse riding.

### LXVIII. ON DITTANY WINE

<margin>+</margin> Dittany wine <note>original: *Vinodictamni*; made from *Dictamnus*, specifically Dittany of Crete</note> is prepared thus: put four [parts] of dittany into eight or four [parts] of must and follow the method of preparation described above. It calms <unclear>aferoris</unclear> <note>possibly a corruption of *aphoris*, referring to external pains, or a variant of *aphrodisiac*</unclear> and regulates the stomach and the menstrual flow; it also helps to expel a [dead] fetus.

### LXVIIII. ON THE PREPARATION OF WINE FOR CATARRH

Let a wine be prepared for catarrh <term>catarrh|excessive buildup of mucus in the nose or throat</term>, for a cough, and for bloating, as it also soothes stomach pain. [Take] <gloss>myrrh and white pepper</gloss> and <gloss>orris <note>original: *yreos*; the root of the Iris plant</note>, lily, and <unclear>aspetu</unclear></gloss>. Crush all these things, tie them in a linen cloth, and put them in six sextarii of wine. After one day, strain it and pour it back into a vessel. Use it after going for a walk, because when it is given with wine after exercise, it will provide a tempered [effect].

### LXXVI. ON AROMATIC WINE

Grind these together, place them in a small linen cloth, tie it, and place it into one <term>amphora|a large ceramic storage jar, approximately 6-7 gallons</term> of must <note>original: *musa*, a misspelling of *musta*; unfermented grape juice</note>. Cook it over a slow fire. It is effective for all ailments of the chest, the side, and the lungs <note>original: *pleumonis*</note>, and it serves as a remedy for blood issues. It regulates menstruation and preserves the warmth of the whole body against the cold. It dissolves all phlegm <note>original: *pituitas*; one of the four bodily humors, often associated with dampness and sluggishness</note>, restores a healthy color to the face, induces sleep, and provides relief for coughs and tremors.

### LXXVII. ON NECTARIAN WINE

Nectarian wine is prepared from elecampane <note>original: *elenio*; a bitter herb of the sunflower family used for respiratory and digestive health</note>, which many call *mendicen*, though they call the nectarian plant *elenion*. Take one pound of dried elecampane, tie it in a linen cloth, and place it into six <term>sextarios|a Roman measure roughly equivalent to a pint</term> of must. After three months, strain it and store it. It soothes stomach pain, promotes urination, and heals ailments of the chest.

### ON SYRIAN NARD WINE

Syrian nard wine is prepared this way: take half an <term>emina|roughly half a pint</term> each of strained nard and malabathrum <term>malebatru|the leaf of the Cinnamomum tamala tree, used similarly to cinnamon or bay leaves</term>. Put these into two <term>urba|likely a corruption of *urnas* (urns)</term> of must. After several months, strain it and store it. # XCIII ON HELLEBORE WINE

For Hellebore wine <note>original: *Vino elleuoritu*; wine infused with the hellebore plant, used in antiquity as a powerful, though dangerous, purgative</note>: in one vessel of must <note>original: *mustu*; freshly pressed grape juice that has not yet fermented into wine</note>, add sea water and mix in 21 pounds of black hellebore <note>original: *elleboro nigro*; the root of *Helleborus niger*, known for its toxic and laxative effects</note>. Tie a small amount of bdellium <note>original: *Bdellu*; a perfumed resin similar to myrrh</note> in a linen cloth and put it into an amphora of must. After ten days, strain it and store it; give four [measures] of the wine with water after a bath.

Another is prepared like this: 70 [units] of hellebore, 62 [units] of camel's hay <note>original: *isquini*, for *schoenus*; an aromatic medicinal grass</note>, [and] 63 [units] of... <note>original: *ista qui ossi manu*; the Latin is corrupted here, possibly referring to *stachys* or another herb</note>. All these are crushed and ground, tied in a linen cloth, and stored; put them into 18 measures of concentrated wine and let it sit for 40 days. Afterward, one should add three measures <note>original: *emina*; a Roman unit of volume equal to about half a pint</note> of sea water to 12 [measures] of the hellebore wine. Use what is prepared in this way.

Another is prepared like this: 12 [units] of hellebore, 63 [units] of aconite <note>original: *asonitiu* for *aconitum*; a highly poisonous plant also known as wolfsbane or monkshood</note>, and 15 measures of must. Infuse for 15 days, then strain and use. This indeed acts as an abortifacient <note>original: *abortiu*; a substance used to induce a miscarriage</note>. This preparation should be used after six months [of aging].

Another they prepare with black grapes <note>original: *acunas nigras*; likely *acinas*, referring to grape berries</note>: add 70 [units] of gypsum <note>original: *gipsu*; a mineral used in ancient winemaking to clarify the liquid and stop fermentation</note> and let it sit for two days. Then add four pounds of hellebore, 80 [units] of camel's hay, 80 of sweet flag <note>original: *calamu*; *Acorus calamus*, a wetland plant with a spicy scent</note>, half of a two-pound weight of juniper <note>original: *arceuador* for *arceuthos*</note>, and one pound of myrrh and saffron. Put these in a linen cloth and suspend it in the must for 30 days. Afterward, strain and store it. If you give two or three measures, it purges [the body]; it is used after childbirth or to cause an abortion, and it treats uterine conditions <note>original: *stericas causas* for *hystericas causas*; referring to health issues related to the womb</note>.

# XCIIII ON SCAMMONY WINE

You prepare scammony wine <note>original: *Vino scammonito*; wine infused with the root of *Convolvulus scammonia*, a plant known since antiquity for its extremely potent purgative properties</note> in this way: Take 65 [units] of scammony roots and put them into one amphora <note>a large ceramic jar used as a standard Roman liquid measure, roughly 26 liters</note> of must <note>freshly pressed grape juice</note>, tied in a small linen cloth. After 30 days, strain and store it. It clears out phlegm and bile; similarly, it works effectively from below <note>original: *desusu*, likely for *deorsum*; meaning it can be used as an enema or simply that it acts as a laxative rather than an emetic</note>.

# XCV HERE BEGINS THE SECTION ON MINERALS
## ON CADMIA

**G**ood cadmia <note>original: *Cadmia*; a term used in antiquity for zinc-rich ores like calamine or the zinc oxide deposits found on the walls of smelting furnaces</note> is that which is easily crumbled and grape-like <note>original: *uotriter*, likely for *botryitis*; referring to a clustered, grape-like physical structure</note>, and which is dense and moderately heavy. However, it is better if it is lighter and has an upper part shaped like a cluster of grapes <note>original: *botru* (botrys)</note>. When broken open, the inside should be rosy, while the outside keeps its own color. On one side, it has the color of an ornamental stone. Such is the cadmia that is dug from a mine.

There is also another cadmia which is called *placitis* <note>original: *placote*; "plate-like" cadmia that forms in flat layers</note>, which has markings like a belt, which many call *zonites*. Another is called *onychitis* <note>original: *ostritiar*; likely a corruption of *onychitis*, meaning "shell-like" or "fingernail-like"</note>, which is thin and black, the color of earth. Before processing, these are all black. There is also a little bit of white. The grape-like variety <note>original: *botritur*</note> is useful for the preparation of eye-salves <note>term: <term>collyrium</term> (a topical medicine for the eyes, often pressed into a cake or dissolved in liquid)</note>, and this variety is also called *onychitis* <note>original: *loniater*</note>.

The rest are useful for medicines and for drying wounds; they are said to produce a scar <note>meaning they promote the final stage of healing</note>. The best quality comes from Macedonia, Cyprus, and Spain. In strength and virtue among all types of cadmia, they are caustic and cleansing <note>original: *saptica et pleotica*; likely corrupted forms of *septic* (here meaning corrosive) and *pleotic* (filling/healing)</note>; they cleanse deep and foul wounds and clear away growths of flesh <note>original: *crementa carnis*; referring to "proud flesh" or granulating tissue that hinders healing</note> in wounds.

...it heals by consuming <gloss>eating away</gloss> <note>original: *comederdo* for *comedendo*; refers to the mineral's caustic ability to remove proud flesh</note> [excess growths] and induces the formation of scars. Cadmia <note>zinc oxide or zinc-rich ore</note> is also produced from the burning of ore, for it is the smoke itself that adheres to the walls; this collected smoke is called cadmia. Many people place iron rods <note>original: *hastas*</note> and bars <note>original: *lorzas*, possibly *loras* or iron plates</note> in the furnaces so that the smoke may cling to them, and in this way, it is correctly gathered.

Others produce it from the material called pyrites <note>original: *pituriter*; iron or copper sulfides</note>, in which there are flakes <note>original: *lepidis* (lepis)</note> that are burned. In this material, much is found in various places: *chalcitis* <note>original: *dallica* and *calater*, likely corruptions of *chalcitis*, a copper-bearing mineral</note>, *misy* <note>original: *missum*; a yellowish sulfate mineral</note>, *sori* <note>a mineral related to copper sulfate</note>, *melanteria* <note>original: *malonteria*; a green vitriol or mineral-based ink</note>, *cyanus* <note>original: *quianu*; a blue mineral, possibly azurite</note>, *chrysocolla* <note>literally "gold-glue," used for malachite or mineral solders</note>, *chalcanthum* <note>copperas or blue vitriol</note>, and *diphryges* <note>original: *difrigur*; the residue or slag found in copper smelting</note>. Many scale-like minerals are found and called cadmia, but these are false.

This stone is tested to see if it is smooth; cadmia that is chewed does not have any roughness <note>original: *haspridine* for *asperitatem*</note>. When cadmia is ground and placed in the sun, it does not change color. If it is put into the hearth, it makes a [cracking] sound, which real cadmia does not do. 

Cadmia is burned by placing it among live coals; this causes the cadmia to take on a reddish-purple color <note>original: *pongi lize*, likely a corruption of *puniceus* or "pomegranate-colored"</note>. After this, you moisten it with Aminean wine <note>a high-quality white wine from Italy, highly prized by ancient physicians for its purity</note>. After you have moistened it, place it again in a new pot <note>original: *caccabo nouo*</note> and cook it until it takes on a purple color. Then, having been ground with wine, it is burned in the pot until it becomes a powder. 

They also prepare *prospodium* <note>original: *prospodiu*; a fine metallic soot or zinc oxide found in the upper parts of smelting furnaces</note> by washing it <note>original: *elicuas*; referring to elutriation, the process of separating particles by weight using water</note> in a mortar with constant water until you find the water remains clear and limpid; then you dry it.

## ON POMPHOLYX

Pompholyx <note>original: *Ponfolix*; a high-grade zinc oxide produced by sublimation in a furnace</note> is superior in its medicinal power to spodos <note>original: *aspondio*; a heavier, less refined zinc oxide or furnace ash</note>. While related <gloss>they are of one kind</gloss>, there are two types. One type is heavy and black, full of hair-like fibers on the outside, and it is found attached to walls; this kind they call spodos <note>original: *spondium*</note>. The other type, pompholyx, is somewhat white, fatty, and light, so that it does not vanish at the touch like a breeze. Truly, if the white pompholyx is to be produced, which is the dry form found when metals <note>original: *esusa*, likely a corruption of *aes*, copper or bronze</note> are burned in the mines, the workshop laborers grind cadmia <note>zinc ore</note> and put it into the furnaces as they are prepared, just as blacksmiths hammer out their work. From the fire that rises, the pompholyx is collected.

The method for collecting pompholyx and burning the metal <note>original: *esusu*</note> is this: let there be a place like a white-washed chamber, in which there is a small window; let there also be a small entrance, secured and sloped. In this place, a furnace like that of blacksmiths is set up. The bellows are placed outside of the room. When the metal is put in the furnace, all the fire and ash settle in that clean place. Through the small window, they sprinkle the ground cadmia as I mentioned above, and they seal it; they do this as long as the metal is being burned. When it has cooled, they sprinkle the entrance of that place and enter naked and clean <note>workers entered naked to prevent the valuable, light powder from clinging to their clothes and to ensure purity</note>; and thus they collect the pompholyx from the walls. But the dust which, by its weight...

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for the production of medicinal zinc oxides. It was unable to stick together in the same way and is found on the floor <note>original: *pauimento*; the floor of the collection chamber described on the previous page</note>. This material is spodos <note>original: *spodum*; a less-refined furnace ash or zinc oxide</note>; therefore, it is necessary to clean it. Indeed, many call this spodos *confia* <note>original: *confia*; possibly a local or technical corruption of a Greek term for furnace ash</note>. Truly, the Cyprian pompholyx <note>original: *cipria ponfolix*; zinc oxide from Cyprus, highly prized in antiquity</note> which is prepared with vinegar is valuable. Pompholyx should be chosen that has the color of copper <note>original: *eraminis*; referring to a bronze or metallic sheen</note>; near the soot, it should be placed as if over charcoal fires, where the color tends toward that of copper-ore <note>original: *calctor*; likely *chalctis*, a copper-bearing mineral</note>. 

But if it does not have these signs, it is worthless. It is often adulterated <term>adulterated|the practice of mixing pure medicinal substances with cheaper, look-alike fillers</term> with bull-glue <note>original: *tauro colla*; an adhesive made from boiling bovine hides</note> and sea-lungs <note>original: *pulmonis agminos*; likely a corruption of *pulmonis marinos*, referring to jellyfish used as a deceptive filler due to their texture</note>, as well as burnt marble and the burnt wood of the wild fig tree <note>original: *capro fici*; *caprificus*</note>. It is adulterated with many other things as well. However, if you apply yourself diligently to this discipline <unclear>ss:</unclear>, you will easily discover this. 

Pompholyx is washed in this manner: wrap it in a linen cloth and shake it for a very long time in water, until whatever is pure <gloss>the clean substance</gloss> settles in the water. You will find all the impurities remaining in the linen cloth. Let it settle, pour off the liquid from the top, and add water again. Do this repeatedly until the water is found to be clean. Then, dry it and set it aside. 

Others wash it in this way: they put the pompholyx <note>original: *ponfolinga*</note> into water and stir it with their hands. Then, they pour it through a stretched linen cloth into another vessel. They dry it and set it aside; however, the first washing and the use of the wash-water <unclear>ss.</unclear> is better. For those who wish to mix medicinal pastes <note>original: *scialla*; likely a corruption of *psillothra* or a similar topical application</note>, they grind the substance with wine and [?] <note>original: *ionmarmamo*; obscure, possibly a mineral or botanical additive</note> and dry it. They are washed again with the addition of boiled wine syrup <note>original: *sapapaca*; from *sapa*, a concentrated grape juice or wine reduction</note>; such is the full power of pompholyx.

## CONCERNING ANTISPODIA

It is necessary to explain what may be substituted for *spodium*—called *antispodia*—which possesses similar properties. You take unripe myrrh <note>original: *mirra in matura*</note> with its flowers and unripe grapes, and put them in an unfired clay pot <note>original: *caccabo crudo*</note> and cover it with a perforated lid. Place the vessel in a furnace and leave it as long as it takes for the pot itself to be thoroughly fired. Then pour it into an unfired pot again and cook it in the same way, and do so a third time; the ash itself shines according to this method. 

A better *spodium* is made from olive leaves, or if it is made from the wild olive tree <note>original: *oleastro*</note> together with its blossom. Myrtle <note>original: *mula*; likely a corruption of *myrtus*</note> and quinces <note>original: *guidonia*; *cydonia*</note> are likewise placed in a vessel <note>original: *in asa*; likely *in vasa*</note>; the seed itself is thrown in and they are prepared similarly. Many scammony plants <note>original: *scammonia*; a potent medicinal root</note> dried in the sun are prepared this way. Truly, box-leaved myrtle... and ebony... and sea-wormwood <note>original: *nasta*; possibly *nascaphthum*</note> or "false" plants, or wild fig <note>original: *caprisia*; *caprificus*</note> leaves dried in the sun are prepared similarly. Otherwise, bull-glue <note>original: *tauro colla*</note> or dried "moon-plants" <note>original: *lunar*; possibly *lunaria*</note> [are used].

# XCVIII CONCERNING BURNT COPPER
<note>Latin: *Aes ustum*. A medicinal copper oxide prepared by roasting copper with sulfur and salt.</note>

Burnt copper is good if it is red; when you rub it, it produces the color of cinnabar. However, black copper is useless and is over-burned. It is prepared from sharp scraps of the earth <note>original: *acutis terre*; likely referring to copper ore fragments or metal shards</note> because they are not placed in the pot <term>caccabo|a deep cooking pot or crucible</term> raw; rather, one sprinkles them with native sulfur and salt in equal measure. Once the pot is covered, it is well-secured and placed in the furnace for as long as it takes for the pot itself to be fired. In another method, they add sulfur on top; in yet another, they add neither sulfur nor salt, and thus they cook it for very many days. Others, however, smear these same sharp scraps with a mixture of <unclear>sapsura</unclear>, sulfur, and vinegar, and so they cook it according to the method. Others cook it in a bronze vessel with vinegar added, not just once or twice, but they cook it a third time. However, that which is burned in Moesia <note>A Roman province in the Balkans, famous for its mineral wealth and mines</note> is stronger. Its power is astringent <note>original: *sapaca*, corruption of *styptica*</note>, drying <note>original: *exerana*, corruption of *xerantica*</note>, cleansing <note>original: *exalupanaca*, corruption of *eckathartica*</note>, and caustic <note>original: *caustastica*, corruption of *caustica*</note>. It draws out and cleanses wounds, causes scars to heal, and clears films from the eyes. It does not allow "proud flesh" <note>original: *superfluę carnis*; overgrown granulation tissue in a healing wound</note> to grow in wounds. It stops spreading wounds <note>original: *pascentia uulnera*; potentially gangrenous or ulcerative sores</note>, either on its own or with honey so that it may be made into an electuary <term>electarium|a medicinal paste or syrup</term>. It is washed just like *cadmia* <note>zinc oxide or furnace calamine</note> until it throws off clean water. Regarding the plates of copper: when they have been softened, let him put them aside for longer, or he may use similar ones as before. **XCVIIII**

<margin>⁒</margin> and it is drunk in great quantities to stop vomiting.

# CONCERNING FLOWER OF BURNT COPPER
<note>original: *Flos esusti*; also known as *flos aeris*. This is the fine metallic dust or oxide that collects on the surface or sides of smelting vessels when copper is purified.</note>

Many ancient authors have said that this "flower" is of primary importance. Its quality is truly good when it is fragile upon grinding, reddish in hue, and possesses a fine color. It should be heavy, moderately clear, and free from metal filings <note>original: *limaturam staminis*; likely referring to adulteration with lead or tin shavings to increase weight</note>, as it is most often adulterated with such filings. This can be detected by biting it with the teeth. It is collected in the mines when burnt copper is being purified; the "flower" itself clings to the sides of the vessels. Its power is astringent <term>saptica|a corruption of the Latin *styptica*, referring to the ability to contract tissues and stop bleeding</term>. It does not allow the overgrowth of "proud flesh" <note>original: *super crescere carnis*; excessive granulation tissue that prevents a wound from healing properly</note> in wounds. It clears dimness from the eyes. Taken as an astringent in a dose of four obols <note>A small Greek unit of weight; roughly 3 grams</note>, it purges phlegm <note>original: *fleuma*; one of the four humors of ancient medicine, associated with coldness and moisture</note>. Given through the nostrils, it removes excess growing flesh. It cures anal growths <term>condilomata|wart-like skin lesions or hemorrhoidal swellings</term> by dissolving them. Smeared on with wine, it cleanses pustules. It restores hearing to the deaf when blown into the ear through a tube. It checks the flow of "rheum" <note>Inflammatory discharge</note> in the throat and the uvula; it achieves this when honey is added.

# CONCERNING SCALES
<note>original: *Lepida*; refers to *lepida aeris*, the metallic flakes that fly off copper when it is hammered.</note>

Good scale is that which is sharp and of the first rank; it is called "shield-like" <note>original: *clparia*, likely a corruption of *clypealis* or *clipearia*</note>. Previously, there is also the "puga" <note>possibly a corruption of *pupa* or *phrygia*</note>, which is made from soft copper <term>aeramine|copper or bronze alloy</term>; these are of middling strength. One should choose those that are solid and reddish, which, if you pour vinegar over them, turn to verdigris <note>The green pigment/crust formed by the reaction of copper with acid</note>. Its power is astringent. It prevents wounds from spreading and leads to the formation of a scar. When drunk with honeyed water, it removes excess moisture from the belly. Many people also burn these scales and administer them via pills <term>catapodia|small medicinal boluses or pills meant to be swallowed</term>. It is also mixed into preparations of eye-salves <term>collyriorum|medicinal washes or ointments for the eyes</term> which stop the flow of inflammatory discharge.
