...It dries these <note>referring back to the pustules and growths mentioned on the previous page</note> beforehand. It also relieves the tension of the eyelids. 

It is washed, however, in this way: take half a mina <note>A unit of weight roughly equal to 1 pound or 430 grams</note> of **dry scales** <note>original: *lepidas siccas*; these are the flakes that fall off hot copper when it is hammered</note> and grind them in a mortar with water. ### CI. CONCERNING THE DROSS OF HARD IRON

The dross <note>original: *scobe*; filings or scale produced during the forging of iron</note> of hard iron has a similar effect to tutty <term>tute|zinc oxide collected from the flues of smelting furnaces</term>. It is washed very thoroughly and stored in the same way as the copper described above, but this substance does not purge the bowels.

### CII. CONCERNING CAMPANIAN VERDIGRIS

**Campanian verdigris** <note>original: *erugine campane*; a green pigment and medicinal crust formed by the weathering of copper or bronze. Campania was a region in Italy famous for its bronze work.</note> is prepared in this way: put wine—or <gloss>vinegar</gloss>—into a bronze vessel and cover it with another bronze vessel (it is better if the vessel is deep and concave, but if not, a flat one will do). It must be sealed so that no vent <note>original: *spiramen*; a breathing hole or air gap</note> admits air from any spot. After ten days, open it and scrape the vessel itself, collecting the verdigris that has formed within the vessel.

For if you wish to make **copper layers**, place them over jars where you have put **vinegar**, so that the vinegar does not touch the metal. Seal it in a similar way. Afterward, you open it and collect what has formed. Do this as many times as you wish. You can also place the copper over **grape pomace** <note>original: *uinacia*; the pulpy remains of grapes after pressing for wine</note> mixed with vinegar; put the copper underneath and after ten days, take it out and collect the residue. Do the same with the **scum of copper** <note>original: *scumatura eraminis*; the dross or impurities skimmed from molten metal</note> and the copper scales put into vinegar: shake it or let it settle for a day, and then take it out and collect it. It is said that **verdigris** <term>erugine|The green patina or crust formed on copper or bronze by the action of acetic acid, used historically as both a pigment and a medicinal ointment</term> is born in mines and in the finest metals. One type is that which is found upon copper; this is the kind said to be found in the fissures of caves. That which is found upon the copper is small in quantity but of good quality. That which distills <note>likely referring to a liquid byproduct or a refined form</note> is indeed white, but the colored variety is the one that is good. It can also be tested by the teeth <note>original: *denab; probatur*; likely 'dentibus,' meaning the texture or grit is tested by biting</note> to see if it contains a fraudulent mixture. And if it is placed over a fire to be tested: if it contains vitriol, it will turn a reddish color and burn entirely when it touches the flame.

## CIII ON IRON RUST

Iron rust or its filings <gloss>filings</gloss> has a grasping <note>original: *rapica*; likely meaning astringent or styptic, a quality that constricts tissues</note> power. It stops the flow of a woman <note>referring to excessive menstrual bleeding or hemorrhaging</note>. It is drunk <gloss>so that</gloss> a woman might conceive <note>original: *non fina*; the meaning is obscure, but in this context, it likely refers to aiding a woman who is not currently fertile</note>. Taken ground and smeared on, it cures "sacred fire" <note>original: *ignem agrum*; likely erysipelas, a painful skin infection characterized by redness</note> and pustules. It dissolves whitlows <term>panaritia|painful infections at the base of the fingernail or toenail</term> and skin growths <note>original: *torrigia*; likely corns or calluses</note> when smeared on; it treats condylomata <note>warts or growths, often in the genital or anal area</note>.
<margin>condylomata</margin>
It corrects hair loss <term>alopecias|patchy loss of hair from the scalp or body</term>. Iron heated red-hot and extinguished in wine or water is drunk by those for whom it treats dysentery. It heals those with spleen complaints, those with excess bile, and stomach ailments. It restores a loose stomach.

## CV ON IRON DROSS

Iron slag <term>merda ferri|literally "iron dung," referring to the dross or scoria left over from smelting iron</term> is just as powerful as its rust, but it is slightly less effective when given with oxymel <term>oximellen|a medicinal drink made of vinegar and honey</term>. It is beneficial to those who have drunk aconite <gloss>.. poisons</gloss> <note>aconite, also known as monkshood, is a highly toxic plant; iron slag was used as an ancient remedy for its ingestion</note>.

## CVI ON THE WASHING OF LEAD

For the washing of lead, take a lead mortar and pestle, add water, and grind it until the water itself turns black; afterward [strain it] in a linen cloth and pour it back; that is, with water added. <gloss>Likewise</gloss> it cures also skin eruptions <note>original: *spidme*; likely a corruption of *epinyctis*, a type of pustule that appears at night, or *spodium*, a medicinal powder</note> when smeared on.

### ON LEAD DROSS

Lead dross <term>scoria|the slag or stony waste matter separated from metals during smelting</term> is useful when it appears split like white lead, and is thick and not fragile, having no appearance similar to lead; it has a color like *maziane* <note>original: *maziane*; likely referring to a deep brownish-red or pomegranate-like color</note> and is somewhat glassy. ## CX ON MOLYBDENUM

Molybdenum <term>molipdena|lead ore or a lead-like stone, used here for its medicinal properties</term> is more useful when it has the color of silver dross <term>spume argenti|literally "silver foam," also known as litharge, an oxide of lead</term> and is shiny and reddish when rubbed. In cooking with oil, it makes a scarlet color. It is born from silver and gold mines and is dug up; it is better when it has a "woody" quality. Its power is similar to silver dross or the dross and burnt remains of lead. It is indeed mixed into fatty plasters and those that heal the flesh <note>original: *sarcotian*; from the Greek *sarkotikos*, meaning promoting the growth of flesh</note> and those that lead to a scar. It is not mixed into medications intended for purging.

### 114 ABOUT WHITE LEAD, THAT IS CERUSE <note>original: *DE PSIMITHIU ID EST CERUSSA*; psimithiu is the Latinization of the Greek *psimythion*</note>

**Ceruse** <term>ceruse|white lead, a pigment and medicinal substance produced by exposing lead to vinegar vapors</term> is made thus: put green vinegar <note>original: *aceto uiride*; likely a strong or unrefined vinegar</note> into an earthenware vessel and cover it with lead. See to it <note>original: *monit*; likely *monetur* or *monere*</note> that no air <note>original: *spiramen*</note> escapes until the lead itself dissolves into the foam of the cooking. 

And in turn, pour off the vinegar that floats on top, and again pour off the vinegar from whatever has settled. Dry it in the sun, and afterward grind and sift it. Do this three or four times, especially so that the substance passes through the sieve.

## CXV ON ARMENIAN STONE <margin>+</margin>

The best **Armenian stone** <term>Armenio|likely azurite, a blue copper carbonate mineral often used as a pigment and medicine</term> is light and of good color, without stony fragments, fragile, and not heavy, much like **chrysocolla** <term>chriso colla|literally "gold-glue"; malachite or a copper-based solder</term>. In its medicinal property, it is like chrysocolla; it makes hair grow on the eyelids.

## CXVI ON CYANUS <margin>+</margin>

**Cyanus** <term>Quianus|from the Greek *kyanos*, a deep blue mineral or pigment, often associated with azurite or lapis lazuli</term> is found in Cyprus in metal workshops and in caves by the shore. The most useful kind is chosen for its clear and emerald-green color. It is roasted like **chalcitis** <term>chalcitem|a copper ore, likely copper pyrites</term> and washed like **cadmia** <term>cadmiae|zinc oxide or metallic soot found in furnace linings</term>. Its properties are astringent <term>catastaltica|from the Greek *katastaltikos*, meaning suppressing or cooling</term>, escharotic <term>scarotica|scab-forming</term>, and corrosive <note>original: *saptica*</note>.

### CXVIII ON OCHRE

<margin>+</margin> **Ochre** <term>Ochra|an earth pigment consisting of silica and clay, colored by iron oxide</term> should be chosen that has a honey-like color and is free from stony fragments. Such is the Attic variety. It is burned and washed just like **cadmia** <term>cadmias|likely calamine or zinc ore used in medicinal preparations</term>. Its power <note>original: *uirtutē*</note> is caustic <note>original: *sapuca*; a corruption of *septica*, meaning it breaks down tissue</note>, and it treats tumors and pustules. It fills deep wounds and smooths down overgrown flesh <note>excess granulation tissue, often called "proud flesh"</note>; it restrains them greatly when added, and it dissolves hard swellings.

### CXVIIII ON CINNABAR

<margin>X</margin> Many think that **cinnabar** <term>Cinnabari|mercury sulfide, the primary ore of mercury and a bright red pigment</term> is the same as **minium** <note>original: *minium*; red lead, which was often confused with or used to adulterate cinnabar</note>, but they are mistaken. This is because minium is created from the "foam" of the stone that is mixed with silver-bearing sand. If minium is kept for a long time, it changes its color. However, the odor of cinnabar in the mine suffocates humans. Therefore, those who work in the mine <gloss>are called</gloss> [miners] cover their faces <note>original: *infantiae ponunt liberofocalor*; this appears to be a corruption of the historical practice described by Pliny where miners used bladders (*vesicis*) as masks to avoid inhaling toxic dust</note>. This cinnabar is born in Libya, which is why it is not sold in great quantities. Its color is blood-red, which many have thought to be the actual blood of dragons <note>A common medieval and ancient myth suggested cinnabar was the congealed blood of dragons killed in combat with elephants</note>. In its power, it is similar to the stone **hematite** <note>original: *maaten*; likely *haematiten*</note>. It is effective for making eye-salves <term>collyriorum|medicinal lotions or ointments for the eyes</term>, but even more so for its caustic properties. It restrains the flow of blood. It helps with burns and pustules when added to wax-salves <term>ceroat|cerates; medicinal ointments made with a wax base</term>.

## CXXI ON RED OCHRE

**Sinopian earth** <term>Miltu sinopi|a high-quality red earth pigment or ochre named after the city of Sinope</term> should be of good quality: thick, heavy, <margin>+</margin> consistent in color, free of stones, and moist when ground down. It is collected in **Cappadocia** <note>a region in modern-day Turkey</note> where it flows into caves, and it is brought to be sold in the city of **Sinope**, from which it takes its name. Its power is caustic <note>original: *sapuca*, a corruption of *septica*</note>, drying <note>original: *exerapitca*, a corruption of *exsiccatica*</note>, and effective for plasters <note>original: *exemplastica*, from *emplastica*</note>; for this reason it is mixed into preparations to be used effectively on fresh wounds. It is mixed into lozenges <note>original: *troasas*, likely *trochiscos*</note> to dry the bowels if taken with an egg; it is also used by craftsmen for marking <note>original: *sub positu riosu*, likely referring to a ruddle or marking line</note>. It is also produced in Egypt and in **Chalcedon** <note>an ancient maritime town in Asia Minor</note>; those varieties are <unclear>more dual</unclear> <note>possibly *duriores*, "harder"</note> and empty, and the color changes when the earth is burned.

<margin>+</margin>The **Lemnian Seal** <note>original: *Lemnias fragis*, a corruption of *Lemnia sphragis*</note> is a crumbly earth taken from a muddy pit. When mixed with goat’s blood, many pieces are gathered to make tablets <term>troascos|small medicinal lozenges or troches</term>, and they stamp them with the seal of a goat, which is why it is called a "seal" <note>original: *sphrada*, a corruption of the Greek *sphragis*</note>. Its power is potent against poisons when drunk with wine; the body will vomit up any poisons it has received. It works against all poisonous maritime attacks <note>stings or bites from sea creatures</note>; [it is used when] <note>original: *anadoxar*, likely a corruption of *antidotos*</note> mixed. This is strongly carried by those who deal in charms <note>original: *incantato*</note>.

### CHAPTER 124: ON VITRIOL

<margin>+</margin>**Vitriol** <term>Calcantu|from *chalcanthum*, blue vitriol or copper sulfate</term> is of one general kind because it is "coagulated water." However, there are three species: one is indeed called *allura* <note>possibly a corruption of a term for native or mined vitriol</note> found in certain channels and pits, which is why it is called "manufactured" <note>original: *factone*</note>, as water drips from the metal workshops and is collected there. The second species is called *apscon* <note>likely *stalacton*, meaning "dripped"</note>. It is found in caves, collected, and poured into vessels where it coagulates; many call this *picton* <note>possibly a regional name or corruption</note>.

<margin>Indeed</margin>There is <gloss>indeed</gloss> a species of earth which is called *epston* <note>likely *heptaston*</note> found in Spain <note>original: *spe niar fia* for *Spania*</note>. It is prepared in this way: the material which is without color and without power is mixed with water and boiled; they pour it into basins <term>pisanis|referring to *piscina*, or settling vats</term> and after some days it coagulates. Thus it separates into larger parts; in some places it hangs like a cluster of grapes <term>botru|from the Greek *botrys*</term>. If these are held to be good, they have a **blue** <note>original: *neo*, likely a corruption of *cyaneo*</note> color, being heavy, thick, and clean. It is clear, just as they have called it *stacton* <note>original: *stacton*, meaning "dripping"</note> or *concoton*. When cooked, it is useful for dyeing and for blackening things, as its power has shown in use; it also has a corrosive <term>saptica|from the Greek *septikos*, meaning "putrefying" or caustic</term> quality...

### CXXXII ON SULFUR

**Sulfur** <note>original: *Sulpur*</note> should be chosen that has a vivid, fiery color and is clear and free of stones. When placed in the fire, it produces a green color and appears quite oily. It is produced in Melos, Claros, and Lipara <note>Melos and Lipara are volcanic islands famous in the ancient world for high-quality sulfur</note>. Its properties are heating <term>termantica|from the Greek *thermantikos*, meaning substances that produce heat in the body</term> and sweat-inducing <term>dia foretica|diaphoretic, used to describe medicine that induces perspiration</term>. It stops a cough and helps those with internal abscesses <term>empyeas|referring to empyema, a collection of pus in a body cavity, usually the lungs</term> and those who are asthmatic <note>original: *asmatias*</note>. Taken in an egg, it acts as a remedy. Through its smoke <note>fumigation</note>, it induces abortion. It cleanses leprosy <note>original: *lepras*</note> and skin eruptions. Mixed with resin, it soothes the stings of scorpions and sea-dragons <note>original: *deaconu marimorum*, likely *draconum marinorum*, venomous fish known as weevers</note>. It prevents itching of the body. Mixed with nitre <term>nitro|natron or natural soda, not modern saltpeter</term>, it can treat lichen-like skin diseases. One spoonful <note>original: *cochario uno*</note> taken in an egg is beneficial for catarrh <note>original: *cataron*, an excessive buildup of mucus</note>; sprinkled on the body, it removes excessive sweat.
<margin>+</margin> Mixed with nitre and water, it is effective against gout <note>original: *podagras*</note>. Used as a fumigant, it restores hearing and cures those in a lethargic state. When ground with wine and myrrh and smeared on, it treats bruising of the ears.

### CXXXIIII ON SALTS

Salts indeed are useful when they are clear and free of stone, possessing a single color. **Ammoniac** salts <note>original: *Admoniaca*, named for the temple of Zeus-Ammon in Libya where these salts were collected</note> should be chosen that have straight veins and are fragile. **Marine** salts <note>original: *marianum*</note> should be chosen similarly: white, of one color, such as those found in Akte <note>a coastal region of Greece</note>, in the city of Salamis in Cyprus, and in Megara. Second to these are Sicilian and Libyan salts. There are fossil salts <note>original: *fora ores*, likely referring to *fossiles*, or salts dug from the earth</note> which occur naturally, such as the red ones. The properties <gloss>est|is</gloss> for all <gloss>omnibus|of them</gloss>: astringent <gloss>sapaca</gloss>, styptic <gloss>isticicaca</gloss>, purgative <gloss>catartica</gloss>, digestive <gloss>dialectica</gloss>, and corrosive <term>scarotica|escharotic, a substance used to burn or cauterize skin</term>. 

It removes putrefaction and treats the itch <note>original: *scauis*, likely *scabies*</note>. It is mixed for the benefit of the eyes to treat roughness and cleanses growths in the eyes; it does not allow flesh to overgrow in wounds when used as a fomentation. Rubbed on with oil, it removes the discoloration of the spleen <note>original: *lanteris*, likely a corruption of *splenis*</note>, dropsical <term>ydropicos|edema, or the accumulation of fluid in the body's tissues</term> tumors, and pains; divine heat will dissolve them. Mixed with vinegar and oil and applied, they should be left on; this heals the throat.

Stings <note>original: *cerusa punctu*, likely a scribal error for a specific insect or wasp sting</note> are treated with pitch, or cedar oil, or honey applied; centipede <note>original: *scolopendri*</note> stings applied with honey and vinegar cure swellings of the head and wounds. Raisins <note>original: *ubae passae*</note> and wormwood mixed together dissolve swellings of the testicles; mixed with leaven and oregano, they cure styes <term>ordiola|a small, painful infection of the eyelash follicle</term>. Ground up, bound in linen, smeared with vinegar, and applied, they counter poisonous bites. They remove bruises <note>original: *liuores*</note> of the body. Applied with honey or drunk with oxymel <term>oximelli|a traditional remedy made from honey and vinegar</term>, it heals; and it counters [the effects] for those who have drunk poppy juice <term>meconio|an extract of the poppy, used here to mean opium juice</term>. For dislocations, they should be applied as necessary with flour and honey. Ground with oil and applied, they do not allow pustules or blisters to form from burns. They quickly relieve gout <term>podagrias|inflammatory arthritis, typically affecting the joints of the feet</term>. Mixed with vinegar, they check pain in the ears. Mixed with vinegar and applied, they extinguish the "sacred fire" <term>igne sacrum|a term used in antiquity for skin inflammations such as erysipelas or shingles</term> and cleanse spreading skin sores <term>herpetas|from the Greek word for "creeping," referring to spreading skin lesions</term>. Truly, they are to be burnt in this way: you put them in a new earthenware vessel <note>original: *testo*</note> and place it on live coals, and it must be covered, lest they be scattered by jumping <note>referring to the crackling or "popping" of salt crystals when heated</note>. ## CXXXV ON ALOSANTHOS

Alosanthos <note>literally "flower of salt"</note> or the foam of salt is found on maritime rocks. In its medicinal power, it is similar to that [salt].

## CXXXVI ON BRINE

Salt water <note>original: *Almen*, from the Greek *halmē*</note> has a power similar to salt; it has a cleansing <note>original: *ismitica*, a corruption of *smectica*, meaning detergent or cleansing</note> property <gloss>and is a panacea</gloss> <note>original: *depanacae*, likely referring to a "cure-all" or the herb all-heal</note>. It cures dysentery and foul ulcers with an enema <term>clisteris|a liquid preparation injected into the rectum for medicinal or cleansing purposes</term>; it is very effective as a fomentation <note>original: *fomento*</note> if seawater is used.

## CXXXVII ON ALOSANTHOS

Alosanthos is found upon the rocks of the Nile river and in its pools. The variety to be chosen should be saffron in color <note>original: *colore croceo*</note>, with a heavy odor, of a uniform hue, fatty, and with a biting taste. ~~But that which is red in color...~~ <insert>but that which is gathered in a red color</insert> is very effective. That which is placed in oil dissolves immediately, but in water it does not dissolve easily. It is very effective for wounds; indeed, it cleanses gold, removes dimness <note>original: *caliginis*</note> from the eyes, and clears away glaucoma <term>claucomata|a condition causing increased pressure in the eyeball and vision loss</term> and scars. It may be mixed into plasters and preparations of oils, such as rose oil, to induce sweating. It purges the belly. Mixed with wine and water, or boiled with sumac <note>original: *sumachū*</note>, it is a necessary ingredient for restorative ointments <term>acopis|soothing medical salves used to relieve weariness or pain</term>. It thins the hair. Its power is primarily caustic <term>ectirotica|substances that have a corrosive or "eating" effect on the skin, similar to salt</term>, like that of salt.

## CXXXVIII ON NITRE

Nitre <note>original: *Nitro*, referring to natron, a natural soda ash used for cleaning and medicine</note> should be chosen that is light, reddish or white in color, and has holes like a sponge; such varieties indeed come from Egypt <note>original: *ex iem uenio*, likely a corruption of *ex Aegypto veniunt*</note>.

## CXXXVIII ON THE FOAM OF NATRON

The foam of natron <note>original: *Spuma nitri*, referring to *aphronitrum*, a light, porous form of natron or sodium carbonate</note> is to be chosen if it is light, with an odor like cassia <note>original: *cassagilis*, likely a corruption of *cinnamomi* or *cassiae*</note>, reddish, and foamy. Such is that which comes here from Philadelphia <note>referring to the city of Philadelphia in Egypt, a known source of natron</note>; the Egyptian variety is second best. It is also found in Magnesia in Caria <note>a region in modern-day Turkey</note> as a green variety. It is similar to salt [in its properties], and when burned it is more powerful. 

When drunk with cumin and mead <term>mulsa|a mixture of water and honey</term>, it helps with stomach cramps <note>original: *tortionibus*, literally "twistings"</note>. It removes swellings <note>original: *influtiones*</note> when taken with rue or vinegar before an attack [of fever], and when rubbed on, it prevents periodic chills. It is necessarily mixed into diaphoretic <term>diaforeticis|medicines that induce sweating</term> remedies for obscure ailments <note>original: *edumbrias*, an obscure term, possibly a corruption of a Greek word for a specific disease or skin condition</note>. Mixed with water or wine, it is applied and removes ringing in the ears <note>original: *sonur aurium*</note> and pus. 

In treating filth, <unclear>iuum</unclear> [it is used] when purged with vinegar; mixed with pig's fat <note>original: *sungia porcina*, likely *axungia*</note>, it cures dog bites. Mixed with turpentine resin, it cures sties <term>ordiola|a small, painful boil on the edge of the eyelid</term>. Mixed with walnuts <note>original: *caria*, referring to *caryis*</note>, it helps those with dropsy <term>ydropicis|a condition of excess watery fluid in the body's tissues</term>. When applied mixed with honey as an ointment, it clears away dimness <note>original: *caligines*</note> from the eyes. 

When drunk with oxycrate <term>puca|likely a corruption of *posca*, a common Roman drink of vinegar and water</term>, it counteracts the toxic power of mushrooms <note>original: *micetarum*, from the Greek *myketes*</note>. Stings from buprestis beetles <note>a type of beetle toxic to livestock</note> are cured [when it is applied] with water or bull’s gall. With the addition of silphium <term>silphi|a medicinal plant, now extinct, that was highly prized in the ancient world</term>, it helps with cramps. For those suffering from opisthotonos <term>opisthotonoiis|a state of severe muscle spasm where the body bows backward</term>, it is added to a wax salve <term>cerotus|a medicinal ointment made primarily of wax</term> and, when rubbed on, it achieves its effect. Similarly, it is useful for dislocations. Mixed with bread, it prevents paralysis of the tongue. It should be burned on coals; it stays active <note>original: *uiuit*, literally "lives"</note> like salt as long as it glows in the fire.

### LIII ON ASBESTOS, THAT IS, LIME

Lime <note>original: *Calcae*, a variant of *calx*</note> is prepared thus: collect the shells of sea mollusks, 
place them on live coals or in a furnace, and leave them for the whole night. 
On the next day, take them out; if they have turned white, they are ready. If not, 
return them to the fire again.

# ON GYPSUM

<margin>+</margin> Gypsum has a binding <term>stiptica|styptic or astringent</term> and plaster-like power, which is to say it is glue-like <term>paracolletica|from the Greek for 'gluing together'</term>. It holds back the flow of blood and perspiration. If drunk, it suffocates a person. 142.

# ON ASHES FROM VINE-CUTTINGS

Ashes from vine-cuttings have a caustic power. They are mixed with oil and grease and applied to bruises of the side and collections of the nerves <note>referring to swellings or knots in the tendons and ligaments</note>, and it dissolves arthritic conditions. Mixed with vinegar and nitre <term>nitro|a term for native soda or sodium carbonate</term> and applied, it counters dog bites and poisons. It is mixed with corrosive <term>scaroticas</term> powers. <margin>+</margin> This ash applied alone treats falling hair. <margin>+</margin> Drunk with salt and vinegar, it tempers the force of sharp mushrooms <note>original: *mice acrum*, likely referring to the toxicity of pungent or poisonous fungi</note>. 143.

# ON SEA-FOAM

The third is found like eye-parchings <note>original: *torrizia oculorum*, possibly referring to the dry crusts or scales found on the eyes</note> and is light like a sponge.

### 114. ON ADARCE

<margin>+</margin> Adarce is produced in Galatia <note>a region in central Asia Minor, modern Turkey</note>; like a sponge, it grows upon the earth in salty places, and it attaches itself to reeds and hay. It has the color and appearance of a salty stone, similar to the "flower of salt" <note>original: *asiam flori*, likely referring to 'halos anthos'</note> and to sea-foam <note>original: *alononom*, a corruption of 'alcyoneum'</note>. Indeed, it is soft and hollow on the inside; it grows in stagnant waters. When used as an ointment for lepers, it drives out spots, and when applied, it removes skin eruptions. Its power is drying and <term>metafisicmatica|a 'metasincritic' power, meaning it alters the body's constitution or opens the pores to draw out unhealthy humors</term>.

## 146 CONCERNING SPONGES

**T**here are two kinds of sponges: male and female. The male is said to be the one that has tiny holes and is dense and white; the female, however, is round and has larger cavities. There is also a third type called <term>atragus|from the Greek 'achragas', a hard, stony type of sponge</term>; this one is hard and contains stones within itself and has many cavities. These are burned just like <term>alcyoneum|sea-foam or sponge-like marine substances</term>. A new and <term>fat sponge|meaning a fresh sponge still containing its natural sea-juices</term> provides <term>paracollesin|from the Greek 'parakollesis', the act of gluing or binding together</term> for wounds. They open closed wounds just like inserted lint dressings. An old sponge is useless for wounds because it causes <term>rheum|the discharge of fluids or inflammation</term>; however, when applied dry to old sores, it keeps away filth. They are burned and mixed into medicinal preparations, such as those for the eyes. When burned, they possess <term>styptic|astringent or blood-clotting</term> and <term>ismictica|from the Greek 'smektikos', meaning cleansing or detergent</term> properties when washed and mixed. For use in <term>collyria|medicinal eye salves</term>, they are first burned in liquid pitch, and they check the flow of blood. Smaller and soft sponges should be washed in seawater and set out at sunset so that the side that was cut is placed facing downward.

# 148 CONCERNING THE PHRYGIAN STONE

<margin>+</margin> **T**he Phrygian stone is used by dyers <note>original: *infectores*</note> in Phrygia, which is where it gets its name. It is produced in Cappadocia; it has a strong green color, is moderately heavy, and features varied white veins. It is burned in the same manner as <term>cadmia|a mineral byproduct of smelting, often zinc-based</term>. To process it, place the stone into fragrant wine upon live coals and blow upon it until it turns a reddish color; then drench it a second and third time with wine, returning it to the coals each time. This process should be repeated three times. Care must be taken so that the stone does not break or swell. Its power, whether raw or cooked, is <term>septic|corrosive</term>, <term>anacatartic|a substance that purges the body upward, such as an emetic</term>, and <term>escharotic|a substance that causes tissue to slough off, forming a scab</term>. When mixed with <term>cerate|a medicinal ointment made of wax and oil</term>, it heals burns. It is washed in the same manner as cadmia. 150 <note>original: *CL*, likely the beginning of a new section number</note>

# CONCERNING THE PYRITES STONE

The Pyrites stone <note>original: *Lapide piriten*; literally "fire-stone," so named because it strikes sparks</note>, from which copper is produced, should be selected. It possesses the true color of copper and produces sparks or fire <note>original: *fricia siue focum*</note> when struck. It is processed by being burned in this manner: let it be anointed with honey and placed upon live coals. It should be blown upon with bellows until it turns a reddish color. Others cook it on the coals like a millstone <note>original: *mular*</note>, and having anointed it a second time with honey, they return it to the fire until the scales change color—though one can be deceived by the appearance during the cooking. Afterward, they remove it and wash it just as they do <term>cadmia|a mineral byproduct of smelting, often zinc-based</term>, and then they store it.

The medicinal power of this stone, whether cooked or raw, is <term>thermantica|warming</term> and <term>smectica|cleansing</term>. It clears the dimness of the eyes, and it provides <term>diaphoresis|the dispersion of fluids or softening of tissues</term> to treat hard swellings and aids in digestion. When resin is added, it levels out the flesh <note>meaning it reduces "proud flesh" or overgrown tissue in a wound</note>. When burned by itself, it is used for "wolves" <note>original: *lupis*; a term for corrosive skin ulcers</note> and constricts discharges.

# 150 CONCERNING THE ASIAN STONE

The Asian stone <note>original: *Lapide asio*; likely a light, porous limestone or salt-crusted stone from the region of Assos</note> should be selected. It has the color of pumice; it is light, hollow, and breaks easily, containing fragile veins. It is found with the "flower of Melos" <note>original: *melinar flore*; likely referring to the white earth of the island of Melos</note> upon it. Indeed, the "flower" of this stone is said to be the substance that forms upon the stone itself.

This substance is like a thin flower with a whitish color, appearing like pumice or slightly honey-colored. When applied to the tongue, it has a biting sensation. Both the stone and the flower have <term>septic|corrosive or erosive</term> and <term>diaphoretic|dispersive</term> powers. It is applied when mixed with resin and pitch, but the flower itself has greater power; for this reason, it is applied dry to old wounds to draw out moisture and induce scarring.

Both this and <term>cadmia|a mineral byproduct of smelting zinc or copper ores</term> <note>original: *carmian*</note> are washed...

<margin>+</margin> -># CONCERNING THE HEMATITE STONE<-

The hematite stone <note>original: *Lapide ematites*; literally "blood-stone" due to its reddish hue</note> is strong. It is brittle and hard, with a consistent reddish color, and it does not have impurities or varied veins. It possesses properties that are <term>stiptica|astringent</term>, <term>lepuntica|thinning or smoothing</term>, <term>termantica|warming</term>, and <term>ismictica|cleansing or detergent</term>.

It clears scars and dimness from the eyes. It removes <term>trachoma|a contagious bacterial infection that causes roughness and scarring on the inner eyelids</term> when honey is added. Mixed with breast milk and applied as an ointment, it cures eye pain and ruptures; it also stops bleeding in the eyes. When drunk with wine, it treats <term>dysuria|difficulty or pain during urination</term> and binds the flow of women <note>meaning it stops excessive menstrual bleeding</note>. It aids those spitting up blood, especially when taken with <term>pomegranates|original: *mala granata*</term>. Eye salves for the skin are made from it, which are <unclear>necessary</unclear> for eye pains. They are burned just like the Phrygian stone, and the addition of wine provides the signs that it has been properly cooked.

->CIIII CONCERNING THE SCHIST STONE<-

The stone <term>schistos|a stone that easily splits into layers</term> <note>original: *iscistus*</note> is produced in the Iberian vein <note>original: *isperi uena*; referring to Spain/Hesperia</note>. The best kind is chosen for its saffron-yellow color and its brittleness. When burnt, it separates along straight veins, by which the burning is guided. In appearance, it is similar to <term>sal ammoniac|a rare natural mineral composed of ammonium chloride</term>; in its properties, it is similar to hematite, though it possesses its own hardness. 

For if it is softened with milk <note>original: *laca*; likely a corruption of *lacte*</note> and mixed, it can be applied as a <term>pessary|a small medicinal substance inserted into the vagina</term> to treat conditions of the womb <note>original: *matricis*</note>. It also heals strikes to the eyes, as well as <unclear>eye-sores</unclear> <note>original: *solomata*; possibly *psorophthalmia*, an itchy inflammation of the eyelids</note> and roughness of the eyelids. When used as a treatment, it is applied as a reliable <term>collyrium|an eye salve or wash</term>.

# 154 CONCERNING THE JET STONE
<note>original: *gagaten*</note>

The jet stone should be selected as follows: it is such that when set on fire, it has the odor of <term>asphalt|a naturally occurring petroleum or bitumen</term> <note>original: *asfalta*</note>. It is black in all its parts, hard, broad, and very heavy. Its power is <term>malactic|softening or emollient</term> <note>original: *maleptica*</note> and <term>diaphoretic|inducing perspiration</term>. Through its smoke, it identifies those with <term>epilepsy|the "falling sickness," often tested in antiquity by the inhalation of pungent fumes</term> <note>original: *epilenticos*</note>. It settles "hysterical" conditions <note>original: *causas istericas*; referring to the ancient belief that the womb could be calmed by specific odors</note> through fumigation. It drives out poisons and relieves <term>gout|a painful form of arthritis</term> <note>original: *empt podagrias*; "empt" is likely an abbreviation for *emendat* (improves) or *emplastrum* (poultice)</note>. It is mixed into very strong lye <note>original: *lixa*</note>. It is found in a certain river that flows into the sea; where the stone itself is found, the place is called Gages, and it took its name from there.

# 155 CONCERNING THE THRACIAN STONE
<note>original: *tratiol*</note>

The <term>Thracian stone|likely a type of coal or bitumen</term> <note>original: *traccaarnas*</note> is found in <unclear>Scythia</unclear> <note>original: *isquintia*</note> in a river named Pontus. Its power is similar to that of jet. Many have seen it be set on fire by water and extinguished by oil, just like <unclear>asphalt</unclear> <note>original: *saltus*; likely a corruption of *asphaltus*</note>.

# 156 CONCERNING THE MAGNESIAN STONE
<note>original: *magniten*</note>

The magnesian stone should be selected which attracts <note>original: *rapit*; referring to its magnetic properties</note> more quickly, and which has a thick color and is very heavy. It has the power, when taken in food as a single lump <note>original: *bolo uno*</note>, to clear out thick <term>humors|the bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to govern health</term> when drunk with <term>honey-water|a mixture of honey and water</term> <note>original: *mulsa*</note>. Many people burn this stone in place of a <term>magnet|lodestone</term>.

### 160 CONCERNING THE MORACTUS STONE
The Moractus stone—which many have called *galaxias* <note>original: *zalaxian*</note> or "white-writer" <note>original: *leuco grauidu*, likely a corruption of *leucographis*</note>—is found in Egypt. Linen-weavers <note>original: *linteones*</note> use it to whiten linens <note>original: *linteamina*</note> because it softens them. When ground, it resolves <term>hemoptysis|the coughing up of blood</term> <note>original: *emoptoias*</note> and stomach ailments <note>original: *quiliacos*</note>. Applied as a plaster, it treats visceral pain. Taken with water, it checks the flow of women <note>referring to excessive menstruation</note>. Used as a suppository <unclear>abran</unclear>, it is also mixed into the preparations of eye-salves. It fills deep wounds, stops rheum in the eyes, and when mixed with wax-salves <note>original: *cerotis*</note>, it fills up wounds.

### 161 CONCERNING THE ALABASTER STONE
<margin>Alabaster stone</margin>
The Alabaster stone, which is also called <term>onyx|referring to 'onyx-alabaster,' a banded variety of carbonate</term>, is burnt with pitch and resin added. It disperses all hard swellings. Mixed with wax-salves and applied, it mitigates stomach pain and checks rheum in the gums.

### 162 CONCERNING THE LIVING STONE
<margin>Living stone</margin>
The Living stone <note>original: *Lapis uiuos*</note> is found in Ethiopia. It has a green color and is somewhat sharp <note>original: *sub acer pido*</note>. When ground, it yields a milk-like substance. It is biting to the taste. Used as an ointment, it clears darkness <note>original: *caligines*</note> from the eyes.

### 163 CONCERNING THE JEWISH STONE
<margin>Jewish stone</margin>
The Jewish stone <note>original: *Lapis iudaico*</note> is found in Ethiopia, having the shape of an <term>acorn|the text uses the Greek-derived 'balanus' for an acorn or date-shaped object</term> <note>original: *scema balani*</note>.

### 165 CONCERNING THE SAPPHIRE STONE

### 166 CONCERNING THE MEMPHITE STONE
The Memphite stone is found in Egypt; it is shaped like a <term>tessera|a small square tablet or die</term> and is greasy, with varied colors. They say that when it is ground and smeared over a place intended for burning or cutting <note>referring to cauterization or surgical incisions</note>, it allows the procedure to be performed without pain <note>Ancient authors believed this stone acted as a local anesthetic</note>.

### 167 CONCERNING THE SELENITE STONE
The Selenite stone is what many call <term>aphroselinon|moon-foam</term> <note>original: *afros elinuis*</note>, because it is said to be found at night by the light of the moon. It is produced in Arabia and is clear, white, and smooth. Its scrapings are given to <term>epileptics|those suffering from the "falling sickness"</term> <note>original: *epilentiis*</note> to drink. It is also hung around their necks as a <term>phylactery|a protective amulet or charm</term> <note>original: *filacteria*</note>. Women likewise hang it upon themselves so that they might conceive. It is also said that when hung from trees, it causes them to bear fruit.

### 168 CONCERNING THE JASPER STONE
<note>original: *Lapis Iaspis*</note>
There are many kinds of jasper stone. One kind has the color of an emerald <note>original: *smaragdi*</note>; another kind is similar to crystal. A white kind, which is born in the Spains <note>The Roman provinces of the Iberian Peninsula</note>, is like the air; it has white veins like smoke. There is also a bright kind which many call <term>astrion|star-stone</term>. Another kind, truly observed in the zodiac <note>likely referring to astrological associations</note>, is a bluish color <note>original: *subvenetu*</note>. They say that all of these, when hung from the neck, act as amulets <note>original: *phylacteria*</note>. Tied to a woman's thigh, it facilitates a swift birth.

### 169 CONCERNING THE OPHITE STONE
<note>original: *Lapis Ofites*; a mottled green stone named for its resemblance to snakeskin</note>
There are two kinds of Ophite stone. One kind is heavy, with an ashen color and spots. The other kind has markings like letters and a pitch-black color. This latter kind treats eye-troubles <note>original: *lucerzas*, likely referring to inflammation or cataracts</note> and <term>cephalurgias|severe headaches</term>.

### 170 CONCERNING THE STONES FOUND IN SPONGES
<note>These are small calcareous concretions sometimes found inside sea sponges</note>
They are found [in sponges]; ground up and drunk with wine, they break up stones in the bladder <note>original: *calculis uissia*</note>.

### 171 CONCERNING STONE GLUE
<note>original: *Lithocolla*</note>
It is a mixture <note>original: *confectio*</note> made from ground marble and bull’s glue <note>A common ancient adhesive made from hides</note>. This preparation can make the eyelashes stand upright <note>This was likely used to treat trichiasis, where eyelashes grow inward and irritate the eye</note>.

### 172 CONCERNING THE OSTRACITE STONE
<note>original: *Lapis Ostracites*; a stone resembling a pot-sherd or a shell</note>
The Ostracite stone is similar to a thick piece of earthenware and has a good clay color. Many people carefully rub it and use it in place of pumice. Drunk with wine, its juice binds <note>stops</note> menstruation. If a woman drinks it for four days after childbirth, it prevents [further] conception. Ground with honey and applied, it reduces swelling of the breasts <note>original: *didarum*</note> and stops spreading sores.

### 174 CONCERNING SEA SAND
<note>original: *De Lacena Maris*, a corruption of *Arena Maris*</note>
Sea sand, which is found on the shore, when heated by the sun, dries out "moist flesh" <note>likely referring to edemas or fluid retention</note>. A person buried [in the sand] except for their head will find it dries them out. When cooked in small bags, it restrains swellings of the internal organs; it is also applied for <term>podagra|gout</term> and used alongside salt.

### IN THE OIL-VAT 175 CONCERNING THE CRUST OF METALS
<note>The original headings *DE CONCY* and *DE CORTICULA OLEORU* appear to be overlapping titles or a scribe's correction</note>

**Copper scale** <note>original: *Squama eris*; the flakes that fly off copper when it is hammered</note> is the name given to that which is produced when the iron [hammer] strikes. When ground up and smeared on, it cures <term>alopecia|patchy hair loss</term>. ### 176 CONCERNING THE GEODE STONE
The geode stone <note>original: *Lapide geode*; a hollow stone often containing crystals or earth</note> possesses astringent and cleansing powers. Smeared on with water, it clears the dimness of the eyes. When ground and applied, it heals swollen breasts and hard tumors.

### 177 CONCERNING COMMON EARTH
Common earth, if sought from moderate or middle-depth sources, possesses a cooling and <term>emollient|original: *parimplectica*, likely a corruption of *emplastica*</term> power. There is both cultivated and wild earth; it is white and ash-colored. The ash-colored kind is useful and soft. It is washed in the same manner as **white lead** <note>original: *cerussa*; a common white pigment in antiquity</note>. If you wish to burn it, let it be washed and then formed into the shape of a small shingle or "head," and placed in a pot that has no holes. Place this in a circle of burning coals and let it cook until it releases a very fine powder and acquires a white color, which gives it its potency.

### 178 CONCERNING SAMIAN EARTH
<note>original: *Gessamia*, a corruption of *Terra Samia*. This was a famous medicinal white clay from the island of Samos.</note>

Samian earth should be selected when it is very white and light. It sticks to the tongue <note>The OCR reads *unguibus* (nails), but in classical pharmacology, Samian earth was famous for sticking to the tongue (*linguae*)</note> and is soft and fragile against the skin. There are two kinds: one is the "star" variety <note>original: *aster*, referring to *Aster Samios*</note>, which is a dense slab like a small star-shaped chip. Both have the same medicinal power when burned and washed. When ground and applied, it helps the flow of blood and the "flux of women" <note>likely referring to excessive menstruation or uterine bleeding</note>. When ground with water and smeared on, it relieves swellings of the <term>breasts|original: *didarum*</term> and the testicles. Mixed with rose oil, it prevents excessive sweating. Taken with wine, it acts as an antidote against all poisons.

The **Samian stone** <note>original: *lapor*, likely a corruption of *lapis*</note> is also found in Samos, which goldsmiths use for polishing gold. It should be chosen for its smoothness. It has a cooling and astringent quality; when taken internally, it heals the stomach and restrains discharge <note>original: *reuma*, or rheum</note> from the eyes. Infused with milk, it helps wounds. Taken by women, it is said to help them conceive children or is worn as <term>amulets|original: *filacteris*</term>.

### 179 CONCERNING ERETRIAN EARTH
<note>original: *Terracia*, likely *Terra Eretria* from the city of Eretria</note>

Eretrian earth should be selected when it is white and soft, similar to Samian earth, though its "veins" are softer. It possesses a power similar to Samian earth. It cleanses the face and the entire body; many people use it in the baths in place of <term>soda|original: *nitro*, referring to natron, a natural mineral used as a soap substitute</term>.

### 180 CONCERNING SELINUSIAN EARTH
<note>original: *Terra Selinosia*, from Selinus in Sicily</note>

Selinusian earth should be selected when it is white, shining, and fragile.

### 181 CONCERNING CIMOLIAN EARTH
<note>original: *Terra Cimolia*. This was a famous medicinal clay from the island of Cimolus in the Cyclades, often used by ancient fullers for cleaning clothes and by physicians for cooling treatments.</note>

### 182 CONCERNING PNYGITIAN EARTH

### 183 CONCERNING THE POTSHERD

...it purges effectively. It is useful in such a way, and for painters in diversifying colors. Every earth <unclear>ss</unclear> <note>original: *ss*. Likely a scribal abbreviation for *secundum* (according to) or *semis* (half).</note> according to the writing should be chosen as follows: without stones, fresh, soft, and fragile; when it receives moisture, it dissolves more quickly.

### 186 CONCERNING THE EARTH IN WHICH VINES <unclear>ARE PLANTED</unclear>
<note>original: *Terra Ampelitis*. This is "vine earth," a bituminous or carbon-rich earth found in Syria, used both in agriculture and medicine.</note>

Which the <term>pharmacists|original: *farmaci*. From the Greek *pharmakoi*, referring to those who prepare drugs or medicines.</term> say is such as that which is born in Seleucia, Syria. The black kind should be chosen, similar to coals, oblong and shiny, and not dissolving too quickly. Its power is cooling and <term>absorbent|original: *diaquatica*. Likely meaning it draws out moisture or watery humors.</term>. It is mixed into preparations for <term>eye-salves|original: *serocollyrius*. A dry collyrium or medicinal powder for the eyes.</term>; it is used for dyeing the hair, and when applied, it kills the worms that are born in the <term>eyes|original: *uisib;* (visibus). This could also be a corruption of *vitis* (vines), as this earth was famously used to kill insects on grapevines.</term>.

### 187 CONCERNING THE EARTH FROM THE FURNACE WHICH IS FOR PAINTERS

This is collected from the furnaces of <note>original: *amorum*. Likely a corruption of *vasorum* (vessels/jars) or *amphorae*.</note>, because its power is effective for <term>drying|original: *sapia*. Possibly related to *septic* or *styptic* properties.</term>; it heals burns and is added to rose oil.

### 188 CONCERNING BLACK PIGMENT
<note>original: *Adramentio* or *Atramentum*. While this usually means ink, in a medical context, it refers to various black substances including soot, charred resins, or copperas (iron sulfate).</note>

<term>Myrrh-honeyed ink|original: *Myrnomelatum*. A compound of myrrh, honey, and black pigment.</term> is prepared thus: let it be mixed from collected smoke, in one pound with three parts of ink. It is also made from the smoke of resin and from the ink of glassmakers. Take one <term>mina|a Greek unit of weight, roughly 430 grams or 15 ounces.</term> of this ink, one and a half pounds of honey, some <term>bull's glue|original: *tauri colla*. An adhesive made by boiling cattle hides, used here to bind the ingredients.</term>, a pound of <term>vitriol|original: *calcantu* (chalcanthum). Blue vitriol or copper sulfate, used for its astringent properties.</term>, three pounds of myrrh, and one <term>obol|a small unit of weight.</term> of <note>original: *unotrio*. Likely a corruption of *veratrio* (hellebore) or *nitrio* (soda/nitre).</note>. This is mixed and used for preparations for <gloss>abscesses and boils</gloss>. Applied with water, it heals; the ointment itself should be left on until it falls off dry. Amen.

Dearly beloved <note>original: *Karissime*. A standard liturgical opening for a reading from the Epistles.</note>, the grace of God <note>original: *di* (Dei)</note> our Savior has appeared to all people, instructing us: That, denying impiety and worldly desires, we should live soberly, justly, and piously in this age, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ <note>original: *ihu xpi* (Ihesu Christi)</note>, who gave himself for us that he might redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself an acceptable people, a follower of good works. Speak these things and exhort in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Dearly beloved, the kindness and humanity of our Savior God appeared, not from the works of justice which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, through the washing of regeneration <note>This refers to the rite of Baptism.</note> and the renewal of the Holy Spirit <note>original: *sps sci* (Spiritus Sancti)</note>, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Christ Jesus our Savior. So that, having been justified by his grace, we might be heirs according to the hope of eternal life, in Christ Jesus our Lord.
